# FreePascalOS architecture

## Layers

The kernel follows the layering of Windows NT, using plain descriptive names
instead of NT's terminology.

```
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
|  User mode: sh, coreutils -> libcoreutils, libsystem       |
|  graphical programs -> libcontrols -> libwindowing ->      |
|    libfont -> libdrawing -> libsystem                      |
|  image files: libimage -> libdrawing (see "Images")        |
|  compression: libcompression -> libsystem                  |
+=================== system calls (syscall) ================+
|  Processes (processes, threads, address spaces, handles,   |
|             image loader, system calls)                    |
|  I/O       (block devices, file systems, pipes, console)   |
|  Objects   (object manager, reference counting, names)     |
|  Memory    (page frames, page tables, heap, stacks)        |   "executive"
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
|  Kernel core                                               |
|  priority levels, spin locks, interrupt dispatch,          |
|  scheduler, clock, events, panic                           |
|  core/<arch>: descriptor tables, stubs, context switch     |
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
|  HAL (hal/<arch>): interrupt controller, timers, serial    |
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
|  Hardware                                                  |
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
```

Unit names carry their layer as a prefix: `Hal.*`, `Kernel.*`, `Memory.*`,
`Objects.*`, `Processes.*`, `Io.*`, `Network.*`, `Drivers.*`, `Runtime.*`
and `Debug.*`. Architecture specific
units have `Arch` in their name (`Kernel.Arch.*`, `Memory.Arch.*`) or live in
`hal/<arch>`.

## Architecture independence

Every architecture provides units with the **same names and interfaces** in
its own directory (`kernel/core/amd64`, `kernel/memory/amd64`, `hal/amd64`,
`shared/amd64`, `boot/uefi/amd64`, and so on). The Makefile puts only the
selected architecture's directories on the unit search path, so the rest of
the kernel never contains `{$ifdef CPU...}` blocks.

The AArch64 port (`ARCH=arm64`, see "The AArch64 port" below) supplies,
among others:

| Unit                          | x86-64 implementation           | AArch64 implementation             |
|-------------------------------|---------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `Kernel.Arch.Cpu`             | cli/sti, CR registers, MSRs     | DAIF, system registers (`.s`)      |
| `Kernel.Arch.PriorityLevel`   | CR8 task priority register      | GIC priority mask register         |
| `Kernel.Arch.ContextSwitch`   | saves RBX, RBP, R12-R15, RFLAGS | saves X19-X30, DAIF                |
| `Kernel.Arch.TrapFrame` etc.  | IDT, interrupt stubs, TSS       | exception vector table (VBAR_EL1)  |
| `Memory.Arch.PageTables`      | 4-level x86-64 paging           | 4-level AArch64 translation        |
| `Hal.Platform`                | local APIC, PIT                 | GICv2, generic timer, PSCI         |
| `Hal.InterruptController`     | I/O APICs, MSI to a local APIC  | GIC SPIs, MSI through GICv2m       |
| `Hal.SerialPort`              | 16550 UART                      | PL011 / mini UART from ACPI SPCR   |
| `Hal.DmaCoherency`            | nothing (DMA snoops the caches) | DC CVAC / CIVAC / IVAC by address  |
| `Processes.Arch.UserContext`  | x86 exception context           | AArch64 exception context          |

Code that cannot be Pascal is in GNU assembler files next to the units
(`kernel/core/<arch>/*.s`, `boot/uefi/<arch>/*.s`); the Makefile
assembles every one of them.

## Toolchain approach

Free Pascal has no target for "UEFI application" or "freestanding kernel" in
release 3.2.2, so two ordinary targets are borrowed:

- The **loader** is compiled for `win64`. That target produces PE32+ images
  and uses the Microsoft x64 calling convention, which is exactly what UEFI
  requires. `objcopy --subsystem efi-app` then marks the image as an EFI
  application.
- The **kernel** is compiled for `linux` (System V calling convention, ELF
  objects) and linked by GNU `ld` with `kernel/link/amd64.ld`.

Both are built against `rtl/freestanding/system.pas`, a minimal System unit
with only what the compiler insists on. Nothing in the kernel uses the stock
runtime library. User programs are compiled for FreePascalOS itself
(`-Tfreepascalos`, a target the project adds to the compiler: see "Native
Free Pascal") and get the full Free Pascal runtime library, ported to this
kernel (see "The runtime library"). The compiler that does all this is
built from the Free Pascal 3.2.2 sources with the project's patches
(`build/toolchain/ppcx64`, `ppcrossa64` for AArch64; `make toolchain`).
Unit initialization sections are never used; every subsystem has an explicit
`Initialize...` routine called in a defined order from `Kernel.Startup`.

The kernel does not save floating point or SIMD registers, so `make` fails if
the compiler ever emits SSE instructions in kernel code (`check-kernel`;
on AArch64, any V/Q/D/S register outside the routines that save and
restore a thread's registers).

For AArch64 the same two targets are borrowed from the AArch64 cross
compiler, which `scripts/build-cross-compiler.sh` builds from the Free
Pascal 3.2.2 compiler sources into `build/toolchain/ppcrossa64` (`make
toolchain ARCH=arm64`; it takes seconds and installs nothing). Release
3.2.2 has no win64 target for AArch64 and no internal AArch64 assembler,
so GNU binutils for AArch64 (`aarch64-linux-gnu-as`, `-ld`, `-objcopy`)
do the assembling and linking:

- The **loader** is compiled for `linux` (AAPCS64 is also the UEFI calling
  convention on AArch64), linked by `ld -pie` into a position independent
  ELF (`boot/uefi/arm64/loader.ld`) and converted by `objcopy -O
  pei-aarch64-little --subsystem efi-app` into `BOOTAA64.EFI`. The
  conversion makes no PE base relocations, so the image relocates itself
  first thing (`LoaderEntry.s` applies the ELF's `R_AARCH64_RELATIVE`
  relocations found through `_DYNAMIC`) and carries one empty `.reloc`
  block so the firmware loads it anywhere.
- The **kernel** is compiled for `linux` and linked by `ld` with
  `kernel/link/arm64.ld`, as on x86-64.

AArch64 division does not trap, so the compiler checks divisors itself
and calls `fpc_divbyzero`, which the freestanding System unit provides
(the kernel panics); it also calls `Move` for large copies, which the
System unit provides too.

## Native Free Pascal

The system compiles Pascal programs for itself: `/bin/fpc` (the driver)
and `/bin/ppcx64` (`/bin/ppca64` on AArch64) are Free Pascal 3.2.2 built
as FreePascalOS programs, with the runtime library and the system's own
libraries as their units. `fpc hello.pas` in a shell makes a program that
runs; a program of several units, a `library`, and the system's own tools
(`userland/bin/wc.pas`, `sha256sum.pas` against libcoreutils and
libcryptography) build the same way, and the compiler compiles itself
(about 5.5 s under KVM; the result compiles itself again to the same
size).

### A target of its own

Release 3.2.2 has no FreePascalOS, so the userland used to borrow the
`linux` target with `UNIX` and `LINUX` undefined. That works for cross
compiling, but not for a compiler that runs here: the compiler's idea of
its own system (`source_info`, its default target, where it looks for
`fpc.cfg` and the units), the target's name in unit folders
(`x86_64-linux`), and every build tool keyed on the target's name -
fpmake's and fpcmake's OS lists, Lazarus's `$(TargetOS)`, its package
conditions and widget set defaults - would all say Linux, and Linux code
paths (`BaseUnix`, `/proc`, glibc) would be taken. So the compiler gets
real targets, `x86_64-freepascalos` and `aarch64-freepascalos`
(`system_x86_64_freepascalos` = 104, `system_aarch64_freepascalos` =
105 in the ppu's target field), as a patch set against the 3.2.2 sources
in `toolchain/fpc`:

- `compiler/systems/i_fpos.pas` (the target records) and `t_fpos.pas`
  (imports, exports and both linkers), new files laid over the sources;
- `patches/0001-freepascalos-target.patch`: the targets in `systems.inc`
  and the system sets of `systems.pas` (each wherever Linux on the same
  processor is: weak linking, exports from programs, the x87 extended
  size, AArch64's caller-copied value parameters, the "no executable
  stack" note), the linkers `ld_freepascalos` and
  `ld_int_freepascalos`, and the assemblers that may write for it;
- `0002-elf-position-independent-executables.patch`: the internal ELF
  linker writes position independent executables (below);
- `0003-freepascalos-host.patch`: the compiler and the driver running
  here (`fpc.cfg` in `../etc` beside the executable, `~/.fpc.cfg`, the
  units in `/usr/lib/fpc/<version>`, programs found through `PATH`, an
  internally linked program made executable with the umask applied, as
  GNU ld does);
- `0004-ppudump-target-names.patch`: ppudump names the new targets;
- `0005-units-in-shared-libraries.patch`: a unit that lives in a shared
  library (see below) brings its library into the link.

`toolchain/fpc/prepare-source.sh` copies the compiler sources from
`FPC_SOURCE` (the fpc-src package, or the official
`fpc-3.2.2.source.tar.gz` unpacked), lays the new files over them and
applies the patches; `scripts/build-cross-compiler.sh` builds the host's
compiler from the result (`build/toolchain/ppcx64`, which also compiles
the loader for win64 and the kernel for linux, and `ppcrossa64`). The
whole userland is compiled for the new target. The target defines
`FREEPASCALOS` and neither `UNIX` nor `LINUX`, makes position
independent code by default (`tf_pic_default`), starts programs in
`si_prc` and libraries in `si_dll` (`systems_internal_sysinit`, so the
compiler adds them itself), defines `FPC_HAS_INDIRECT_ENTRY_INFORMATION`
on both processors, and takes extra unit folders from `FPOSUNITS`.
Code generation is Linux's: the runtime library's objects compiled for
`linux` and for `freepascalos` are byte for byte the same on x86-64; on
AArch64 only `fpintres` differs, which now finds the resources through
the entry information as on x86-64.

### Linking

x86-64 programs need no other tool: the compiler's internal assembler
writes the objects and its internal ELF linker links them. Release 3.2.2
could link only fixed address executables and shared libraries, so patch
0002 adds position independent executables (`TElfExeOutput.
PositionIndependentExecutable`, set by `t_fpos` for programs): ET_DYN,
linked at address zero, every absolute address and every GOT entry of a
symbol of its own getting a RELATIVE relocation (as in a shared
library), functions of libraries called through the PLT without a
canonical address in the program and no copy relocations (the code is
position independent, so neither is needed), no interpreter, and an
entry point. Segments are aligned to 4 KiB (`-z max-page-size=4096`).
The loader's other needs hold already: a System V hash table, `DT_NEEDED`
for each library, DT_INIT `FPC_SHARED_LIB_START` and DT_FINI
`FPC_LIB_EXIT` for libraries, and only the relocation types it applies.

The other linker is GNU ld (`-Xe`; and on AArch64, which has neither an
internal assembler nor an internal ELF linker in 3.2.2, the compiler
runs `as` and `ld`): programs `-pie --no-dynamic-linker -e _start`,
libraries `-shared -Bsymbolic -soname lib<name>.so` with the init and
fini functions, both `--hash-style=sysv -z max-page-size=4096 -z
noexecstack` - the same switches the userland's own build uses - with
the objects and `-l<library>` in an implicit linker script (`link.res`),
and a version script keeping everything but the `exports` local in a
library that names them. On the host both are checked on every build
of the test (`native-fpc-test` links with the internal linker; GNU ld
was checked by hand on both processors).

In the guest, `as` and `ld` are the `binutils` port (`ports/devel/
binutils`, on the system disk through `ports/image.list`): binutils 2.47
built by the C toolchain with host = target = the system's own triplet,
from the same release and the same patch as the cross binutils (the
port's patch is a symbolic link to `toolchain/patches/binutils`),
linked against mlibc's `libc.so`, without plugins, NLS, gprof(ng) or
the debugger. It installs `as`, `ld`, `ar`, `ranlib`, `nm`, `objcopy`,
`objdump`, `readelf`, `size`, `strings` and `strip` in `/usr/local/bin`,
which `fpc.cfg` names with `-FD` (and which is on every `PATH`). On
AArch64 native Free Pascal assembles and links with them; on x86-64 the
internal assembler and linker stay the default and these serve C work.
A checkout without the C toolchain makes a system disk without them,
and the coretest line that compiles in the guest is then skipped on
AArch64 (it checks for `/usr/local/bin/as`).

### Units in libraries

The runtime library and the Sys.* units are in `libsystem.so`, not
copied into each program, and the other libraries likewise. A program
the native compiler links must therefore link against the library rather
than the units' objects. Free Pascal has the mechanism (ppumove, from
the days of Linux shared RTLs): a unit's ppu marked "in library" and
"shared linked" names its library, and a program compiled with `-XD`
(link shared) links `-l<library>` instead of the unit's object. 3.2.2
skipped such units altogether (it took them for units of dynamic
packages), which patch 0005 undoes for units without a package. The
build runs ppumove (`-b`: the library itself is already made) over
copies of the userland's ppus, library by library; `si_prc` and
`si_dll` stay ordinary units with their objects, since they are linked
into every program and library.

### On the system disk

`toolchain/fpc/fpc.mk` (included by `userland.mk`) stages, in
`build/<arch>/user/fpc-root`, and `make-system-disk.sh` copies:

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `/bin/fpc` | the driver: runs `ppcx64` / `ppca64` from beside itself or `PATH` |
| `/bin/ppcx64`, `/bin/ppca64` | the compiler (stripped; about 4.4 MB) |
| `/etc/fpc.cfg` | `-Fu/usr/lib/fpc/$fpcversion/units/$fpctarget/*`, `-XD`, `-Fl/lib`, `-OoNOSTACKFRAME` (frames for back traces), `-CE` on AArch64, `-l -viwn` |
| `/usr/lib/fpc/3.2.2/units/<cpu>-freepascalos/rtl` | the runtime library's units (libsystem) and `si_prc`, `si_dll` with their objects |
| `.../system`, `cryptography`, `coreutils` | the units of those libraries (`NATIVE_FPC_LIBRARIES`, `all` for every library's) |
| `.../fcl-process` | TProcess and the pipe streams, ordinary units |

About 11 MB in all (the system disk grows to fit);
`NATIVE_FPC=no` leaves it out. The compiler and the driver are linked
by GNU ld from the host's cross compilation like the other programs.
Programs a user compiles are linked by the internal linker on x86-64.

`fcl-process` for FreePascalOS (`toolchain/fpc/packages/fcl-process`)
starts programs with `Sys.Processes.StartProgram`, giving them the pipes
of `poUsePipes` (or `/dev/null` for `poNoConsole`) as standard handles,
an environment and a working folder; it waits on the process handle
(`WaitForProgramWithTimeout`, so `Running` and `WaitOnExit(Timeout)`
work), stops, continues and ends programs through the job control and
end request calls, and a pipe reports something to read when
`CallWaitForHandles` says so (`NumBytesAvailable` then says 4096: a read
returns what is there). `RunCommand('fpc', ['-iV'], S)` works, as the
Lazarus IDE will need.

On AArch64 `ppca64` runs here and writes the assembly and the link
script, then needs GNU `as` and `ld` in `PATH` (the binutils port for
`*-freepascalos`); without them `fpc -s` stops after writing
`ppas.sh`.

### Ports

The ports framework (`ports/`, `scripts/ports.py`, `pkg`) has not
landed yet, so the port is a self-contained piece for it to wrap:
inputs `FPC_SOURCE` and the userland's build, `toolchain/fpc/` holding
the patches and new files, `prepare-source.sh`, `fpc.mk` and the
configuration, output the staged tree `build/<arch>/user/fpc-root`
(laid out as installed).

### Tests

A coretest line compiles a program and a unit of its own with `/bin/fpc`
in the guest and runs the program (it prints the expected line and a
note on standard error when the system disk has no compiler). On the
host, `make native-fpc-test` (part of `make test`) checks that the
staged compiler and driver are programs the loader takes (64-bit ELF
for the processor, ET_DYN with an entry, no interpreter, needing
`libsystem.so`, DT_HASH, no text relocations, only RELATIVE, 64,
GLOB_DAT, JUMP_SLOT and COPY relocations), that `fpc.cfg` links shared
and finds the units, that System, SysUtils and Sys.Files are
FreePascalOS units marked as living in their library while `si_prc` is
not, and links a sample program with the internal linker and checks it
the same way.

### Towards Lazarus

The IDE and the LCL come later; what they need:

- **A widget set over libwindowing and libcontrols** (`lcl/interfaces/
  freepascalos`, `LCLPlatform` `lpFreePascalOS`): a `TWidgetSet`
  descendant and the `TWS*` classes mapping forms to libwindowing's
  windows and the standard controls to libcontrols' (buttons, edits,
  memos, lists, trees, menus, dialogs, scroll bars), the LCL's `TCanvas`
  and GDI calls (`LCLIntf`: device contexts, pens, brushes, fonts,
  regions, bitmaps) onto libdrawing's surfaces and libfont, the message
  loop onto the display server's events, the clipboard, timers, the
  cursor, and DPI from the display's scale. Lazarus itself has to learn
  the OS name in its target lists (`IDEProcs`, codetools'
  `DefineTemplates`, `lazbuild`), as fpmake's `TOS` and fpcmake's list
  have to.
- **Packages the IDE needs**, compiled as fcl-process is: rtl-objpas,
  fcl-base, fcl-process (done), fcl-xml (configuration files), fcl-json,
  fcl-image and fcl-res (icons, resources), fcl-registry (XML
  registry), fcl-extra, paszlib, fcl-db and fcl-web for packages built
  on them, simpleipc (one instance), and Lazarus's own LazUtils,
  CodeTools, SynEdit, IDEIntf and BuildIntf over them; units like
  `dynlibs` and `fileutil` take their Unix paths unless taught this
  system.
- **Debugging**: the IDE's debugger needs either GDB (a port) or FpDebug
  taught the system's process control: stopping another process,
  reading and writing its memory and registers, breakpoints and single
  steps, from kernel calls a debugger may use.
- **Memory and disk**: the IDE is an executable of tens of MB and its
  units take hundreds; it is better a package (or another volume) than
  part of every system disk, and the RAM disk the Pi boots from.

## Boot sequence

1. **Firmware** loads `\EFI\BOOT\BOOTX64.EFI` (the loader;
   `BOOTAA64.EFI` on AArch64, see "The AArch64 port").
2. **Loader** (`boot/uefi/OsLoader.pas`):
   - records the GOP framebuffer and the ACPI RSDP,
   - reads `\FreePascalOS\options.txt` and `\FreePascalOS\kernel.elf`
     (or fetches them, and the system image, from a server: see
     "Network boot") and copies the kernel's segments into one
     physically contiguous block,
   - allocates the boot information record and a 64 KiB boot stack,
   - builds page tables: the physical memory window (never executable),
     an identity mapping of the same range, and the kernel image (4 KiB
     pages, per-segment permissions: see "Kernel memory protection"),
   - captures the memory map into the boot information record and exits
     boot services,
   - loads CR3, switches to the boot stack and jumps to the kernel.
3. **Kernel phase 0** (`KernelEntryPoint`, interrupts disabled): debug
   output, processor tables, memory management, object and process managers,
   HAL, scheduler. The boot code becomes the idle thread.
4. **Kernel phase 1** (a system thread): starts the drivers and the
   system threads, runs the self tests (and the debug shell with
   `kshell`), then starts the first user program and waits for it.
5. **The first program** is the service manager (`/bin/servicemanager`),
   unless `init=` names another (the tests' `init=/bin/coretest`; a
   system volume without the manager gets `/bin/sh`). It starts the
   services of the boot mode: in graphical mode (the default) the
   display server, then the session (the login window, then the user's
   desktop) and a login on the serial console; in text mode
   (`mode=text`) a login on the console. See "Startup, services and
   sessions".

The loader tags its own allocations with OS-reserved UEFI memory types
(`0x80000001`-`0x80000004`), so the memory map tells the kernel exactly which
pages hold the kernel image, boot data, page tables and the RAM disk.

The boot data pages hold the boot information record (with the memory
map), the boot stack and, after a native boot, a copy of the device tree.
Once phase 1 has run the self tests, everything start-up needed from the
record has been copied or used (options, memory map, firmware tables,
framebuffer, RAM disk; the AArch64 clock copies the firmware's time at
its first reading), so `Memory.BootDataReclaim` gives the boot data pages
back to the page allocator - all but the boot stack, which is the boot
processor's idle thread's for good, and the device tree, which the
drivers keep using (`[memory] Boot data given back: 16 KiB (kept: boot
stack 64 KiB)`). The boot information must not be used after that.

### Network boot

The loader can take everything but itself from a server, so a rebuild
on the development machine takes effect at the next reset of the board
(the Raspberry Pi 4 workflow, see "Trying it on a Raspberry Pi 4"; the
Pi 5 boots natively over TFTP from its EEPROM bootloader instead, see
"Trying it on a Raspberry Pi 5"). It boots from the network
(`Loader.NetworkBoot`)

- when the firmware loaded it by HTTP boot (its device path ends in the
  URI it came from),
- when the firmware loaded it by PXE (the PXE client holds the DHCP
  answer: the server's address and the boot file's name),
- when `options.txt` on its boot volume says `netboot=URL`, with URL
  `http://host[:port]/path/` or `tftp://a.b.c.d/path/` - the usual setup:
  the loader on the SD card, nothing to change on the network's DHCP
  server.

The base URL is the directory holding `EFI/` and `FreePascalOS/` (for a
boot file `.../EFI/BOOT/BOOTAA64.EFI` the part before `EFI/`). From it
the loader reads `FreePascalOS/options.txt` (if the server has one it
replaces the boot volume's options), `FreePascalOS/kernel.elf` and
`FreePascalOS/system.img`, and puts `netboot=<base URL>` first on the
kernel command line. If the network or the kernel cannot be had it falls
back to the boot volume; without a system image the kernel uses its
disks as usual.

Everything goes through the firmware's network stack, so it works before
any driver of ours does (the Pi's GENET driver is untested):

- **The interface** (`Loader.NetworkInterface`): the handle with
  EFI_IP4_CONFIG2_PROTOCOL the loader came from, else the first. The
  firmware binds its network stack only to devices it boots from, so the
  loader connects the drivers to the network cards, or to every device,
  when there is none. Without an address the loader sets the interface's
  policy to DHCP (the firmware keeps that setting) and waits up to 30
  seconds. edk2's network drivers since 2024 also need EFI_RNG_PROTOCOL
  (the Pi has its RNG; QEMU's virt machine needs `-device
  virtio-rng-pci`).
- **HTTP** (`Loader.HttpTransfer`, EFI_HTTP_PROTOCOL): a fresh child of
  the interface's HTTP service binding for each file, GET, the headers
  first (no body) so the size is known from Content-Length, then the body
  straight into its memory, polling the client until each piece is done
  (20 seconds without progress is an error). A host name works where the
  firmware's DNS does; an address is safer.
- **TFTP** (`Loader.TftpTransfer`, the PXE client's Mtftp): the size with
  the `tsize` option, then the file in 1468-byte blocks. The PXE client
  is started with the interface's address (`SetStationIp`) rather than
  its own DHCP, which ignores offers that name no boot file - what a
  home router sends. Without a gateway the server must be on the same
  network; the port is always 69.

The system image is read into pages of the loader's memory type
`0x80000004`, reported as `MemoryRegionRamDisk`, and handed over in
`TBootInformation.RamDiskPhysicalBase`/`RamDiskSizeInBytes` (since boot
information version 5; both zero otherwise, so x86-64 and disk boots are
unchanged). The kernel never gives those pages away (they count as
driver memory) and `Drivers.RamDisk` offers them as the block device
`ramdisk0`: writable, its changes lost at reset. Its partition is scanned
like any disk's, and the system volume is an FPOSROOT volume on the RAM
disk in preference to one on a disk (`Processes.Paths`), unless `root=`
names another. The image is the whole 64 MiB system disk; the Pi in ACPI
mode has 3 GiB, of which the firmware gives the image any free range.

**A compressed RAM disk.** The image is served compressed: a Raspberry
Pi 5's EEPROM bootloader fetches it over TFTP at about 230 KB/s and gives
up on a file after 60 s (`TFTP_FILE_TIMEOUT`), which cut the plain
64 MiB image off at 14 MB. Of its 64 MiB only 24 MiB are not zero (ext4
leaves its free blocks zero, mke2fs writes a fresh sparse file), and
those are the files themselves. `make served-system-image` writes
`build/<arch>/system-disk.img.xz` (`xz -6 -T0 --check=crc32`: 4.9 MB,
about 21 s at that speed; `xz -9` saves 70 KB more, gzip -9 makes
7.6 MB, about 33 s). `SYSTEM_IMAGE_COMPRESSION=gzip` serves
`system-disk.img.gz`, `none` the plain image; the network boot targets,
the Pi 5 boot files and the native and network boot tests take it.
Neither loader looks inside: the UEFI loader fetches the file into its
RAM disk pages and the Pi's firmware passes the initramfs on untouched,
so the kernel gets the compressed bytes.

`Drivers.RamDiskDecompression`, called by `Drivers.RamDisk` in phase 1
(MMU and caches on; the native stub runs with the data cache off, which
would make it many times slower), tells the format by its magic
(`Compression.MemoryImages`: xz `FD 37 7A 58 5A 00`, gzip `1F 8B`; zstd
`28 B5 2F FD` is recognized and refused), takes the decompressed size
from the format (the xz index, read from the footer back; gzip's ISIZE
trailer, or `ramdisksize=MIB` for an image over 4 GiB), allocates that
many physically contiguous pages, decompresses into them and frees the
pages of the boot memory map's `MemoryRegionRamDisk` region. It logs
`[ramdisk] xz image: compressed 4.7 MiB -> 64.0 MiB in N ms, checksum
verified; 4776 KiB of the compressed copy freed` (1.5 s in QEMU's
emulated Cortex-A76); a damaged image is reported and no RAM disk is offered (the
disks' system volume is used instead). The same path serves the UEFI
network boot (x86-64 and AArch64) and the device tree initrd.

The decoders are the freestanding part of libcompression
(`userland/lib/compression`, on the kernel's unit path; no heap, no
strings, the caller's 40 KiB workspace): `Compression.XzDecoder` (stream
header and footer, index, block headers, each block's CRC-32 or CRC-64;
LZMA2 as the only filter, no BCJ, no SHA-256), `Compression.Lzma2Decoder`
(chunks: stored, LZMA with state, property and dictionary resets),
`Compression.LzmaDecoder` and `Compression.RangeDecoder` (the LZMA
decoder over a flat output that is its own dictionary, every distance
and length checked), `Compression.GzipDecoder` and
`Compression.BufferInflate` (deflate into a flat buffer, sharing the
streaming decoder's Huffman tables, `Compression.HuffmanDecoding`), and
`Compression.CyclicRedundancy` (CRC-32, also behind
`Compression.Checksums`, and CRC-64). On the host they decode the 64 MiB
xz image in about 0.4 s (`-Cr`), xz's own tool in 0.17 s.
`make decompression-test` (in `make test`) checks them over fixtures
Python's lzma and gzip write at build time
(`tools/DecompressionTest/make-fixtures.py`): random, disk-like, text,
tiny and empty data, several blocks with and without sizes in their
headers, stream padding, truncated streams, damaged checks and data,
junk after a gzip member, a BCJ filter, an SHA-256 check and a zstd
frame.

`scripts/netboot-serve.py` (`make pi-netboot-serve`) serves a build:
`EFI/` and `FreePascalOS/` from the ESP directory (names matched without
regard to case, as on FAT), `FreePascalOS/system.img` from the
compressed system disk image and `FreePascalOS/options.txt` from `NETBOOT_OPTIONS=file`
(else the ESP's, if any). It reads each file at each request, so it
never needs restarting; HTTP/1.0 with Content-Length on port 8000 (no
root), and with `TFTP=1` a built-in TFTP server (`blksize`, `tsize`,
block numbers wrapping past 65535) on port 69, which needs root. It
prints the machine's addresses and the `netboot=` line to use.
`make arm64-netboot-test` (`scripts/test-arm64-netboot.sh`, not in
`make test`) boots QEMU's virt machine at EL2 with a boot volume holding
only the loader and `options.txt`, once over HTTP from netboot-serve.py
and once over TFTP from QEMU's own server, and checks that the kernel,
the served options and the system image came over the network, that the
system volume is `/ramdisk0p1` and that user mode ran. The firmware's
own PXE or HTTP boot of the loader is not tested: QEMU's edk2 offers no
network boot option on the virt machine.

## Virtual address space (x86-64)

```
0000_0000_0000_0000 - 0000_7FFF_FFFF_FFFF   user space (one per process)
FFFF_8000_0000_0000 - FFFF_BFFF_FFFF_FFFF   physical memory window
FFFF_C000_0000_0000 - FFFF_C0FF_FFFF_FFFF   kernel dynamic region (heap, stacks)
FFFF_FFFF_8000_0000 - FFFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF   kernel image
```

The physical memory window maps all RAM (and at least the first 4 GiB, for
devices) at a fixed offset with 2 MiB pages. Page tables, page frames and
device registers are reached through it with `PhysicalToVirtual`.

## Kernel memory protection

**W^X.** No kernel page is both writable and executable, on both
architectures, from the first instruction of the kernel on:

- The linker scripts (`kernel/link/*.ld`) start `.text`, `.rodata` and
  `.data`/`.bss` on pages of their own, each in its own program header,
  and name the boundaries (`KernelTextStart`, `KernelReadOnlyDataStart`,
  ...). The loaders map the code read-only and executable, the read-only
  data read-only and no-execute, the data writable and no-execute. On
  x86-64 the loader turns EFER.NXE on first (`Loader.Arch.NoExecute`,
  when CPUID says the processor has the bit; without NXE the bit is
  reserved and faults); on AArch64 the code is UXN and everything else
  PXN and UXN (`Boot.TranslationTableBuilder`, shared with the native
  boot stub).
- The physical memory window is never executable: on x86-64 through the
  no-execute bit of its top level entries (the identity mapping the
  hand-off runs on shares the window's lower tables but not those
  entries, so it stays executable until the kernel removes it), on
  AArch64 in every block and page.
- The window's view of the kernel's code and read-only data is read-only
  too (those 2 MiB pages are split into 4 KiB pages; on AArch64 the
  window is mapped over again for them), so the code cannot be changed
  through its other address either.
- Everything the kernel maps later - the heap, stacks, device registers,
  DMA buffers - is no-execute unless asked for (`MappingExecutable`,
  which only user mappings use).
- User pages are never executable by the kernel: on AArch64 every user
  mapping is PXN, on x86-64 SMEP enforces it.

**The processor's protections** (`Kernel.Arch.ProcessorProtection`,
turned on in phase 0 before the other processors start, which copy the
boot processor's settings; logged as `[cpu]`):

| | x86-64 | AArch64 |
|---|---|---|
| The kernel never runs user code | SMEP (CPUID 7 EBX bit 7) | PXN on every user page |
| The kernel reaches user memory only through the copy routines | SMAP (CPUID 7 EBX bit 20; STAC/CLAC around the copy) | PAN (ARMv8.1, ID_AA64MMFR1_EL1.PAN; PSTATE.PAN cleared around the copy) |
| Programs cannot read the descriptor tables' addresses | UMIP (CPUID 7 ECX bit 2: SGDT, SIDT, SLDT, SMSW and STR fault in user mode) | - |

On AArch64, SCTLR_EL1.SPAN is cleared so every exception taken to EL1
sets PAN again whatever the interrupted code had, and the exception
return restores it; a copy that faults (memory another thread freed)
leaves through `ArchUserCopyFault` with PAN set again in the saved state.
MSR PAN does not exist on ARMv8.0, so the copy routines test
`ArchPanEnabled` first. The Cortex-A72 (QEMU's default here, the
Raspberry Pi 4) has no PAN; the Pi 5's Cortex-A76 and QEMU's "max"
processor have it (`CPU=max scripts/run-qemu-arm64.sh`; the AArch64 boot
test boots it once). Every system call reaches user memory through
`Processes.UserAccess` (`CopyFromUser`, `CopyToUser`,
`CopyStringFromUser`, the transfer buffers) or through the physical
memory window (`ReadFromAddressSpace`, the image loader), never through
a user pointer: the x86-64 test runs coretest under SMAP (QEMU's "max"),
and coretest passes under PAN with `CPU=max
scripts/test-qemu-arm64-user.sh` (the native boot test's Cortex-A76 has
PAN too).

**Tests.** `Kernel.ProtectionSelfTest` runs at every start: it walks the
kernel's page tables (`Memory.Arch.MappingAudit`, honouring the rights
every level takes away) and finds no page both writable and executable;
checks each page of the kernel's code (read-only, executable), read-only
data (read-only, not executable) and data (not executable), and the
window's view of each; builds a small user address space
(`Kernel.TestUserSpace`) whose pages must not be executable by the
kernel; copies to and from it with SMAP or PAN on (and from a missing
page, which must fail and leave the protection on). Deliberate
violations, one per boot, are chosen with `selftest=KIND`
(`Kernel.ProtectionFaultTest`) and must stop the system with the right
report; `scripts/test-protection-faults.sh amd64|arm64 ESP` boots each:

| Kind | Does | Report |
|---|---|---|
| `nx` | runs a return instruction placed in the kernel's `.bss` | `Instruction fetch from ... (protection violation` |
| `textwrite` | writes into the kernel's code | `Write to ... (protection violation` |
| `userexec` | calls code on a user page | `Instruction fetch from ... (protection violation` |
| `useraccess` | reads a user page without a copy routine | `Read from ... (protection violation` |
| `pagepoison` | writes into a freed, held back physical page (with `heapchecks`) | `physical page written after it was freed` |
| `copyfault` | marks a user copy under way and reads an unmapped low address outside the copy routines | `Read from ... (page not present` (not taken for a failed copy) |

Where the processor lacks a protection, the test stops with an assertion
that says so instead.

## Interrupt priority levels

| Level | Name                  | Meaning                                      |
|-------|-----------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| 0     | `PassiveLevel`        | normal thread execution; may block           |
| 2     | `DispatchLevel`       | scheduler; no thread switches; may not block |
| 3-12  | `DeviceLevel*`        | device interrupts                            |
| 13    | `ClockLevel`          | clock (one-shot, per processor)              |
| 14    | `InterProcessorLevel` | inter-processor interrupts                   |
| 15    | `HighLevel`           | everything masked (panic, debug output)      |

On x86-64 the level is the value of CR8, and each interrupt's vector is
chosen so its APIC priority class (vector div 16) equals its level (see
`Hal.InterruptVectors`). Interrupt handlers run with interrupts enabled at
their own level, so higher-priority interrupts nest naturally.

Rules that follow from this:

- Mutexes, shared locks and semaphore waits may only be used at
  `PassiveLevel`; they put the thread to sleep instead of spinning.
- Spin locks are acquired at `DispatchLevel` or above. A lock that an
  interrupt handler takes must be acquired at that handler's level.
- Raising to a lower level, or acquiring a dispatch-level lock while at a
  higher level, is a fatal error (`RaisePriorityLevel` checks).
- Code holding the debug output lock (`DebugBeginMessage`) runs at
  `HighLevel` and must not take other locks.

## Scheduling

- 32 priorities. Every processor has a run queue per priority
  (`Kernel.ReadyQueues`); the idle thread (priority 0) runs only when
  nothing else is ready and is never queued.
- A thread that becomes ready goes to the processor it last ran on if that
  one is idle (its data may still be cached there), else to an idle
  processor, else to the one running the least important thread if that
  is less important, else back to its last processor; that processor is
  sent its dispatch interrupt if the thread should run there now. A
  processor choosing its next thread takes from another processor's
  queues a more important thread than its own best, or, with its own
  queues empty, any thread - so no processor idles or runs something
  less important while a thread it may run waits elsewhere.
- **Affinity.** A thread's `AffinityMask` (bit N: processor N) limits
  where it is queued and run; `SetThreadAffinity` moves a thread that is
  queued or running where it may no longer be. A process has a mask in
  its credentials, inherited by the processes it starts and applied to
  all its threads (`CallGetAffinity`, `CallSetAffinity`; `taskset`, and
  `nproc` counts only the processors it may use).
- Time slices of `QuantumTicks` clock ticks (100 Hz) rotate threads of
  equal priority. Timeouts and sleeps end when due, to well under a
  millisecond (see The clock and timers).
- The clock interrupt never switches threads itself. It requests the dispatch
  software interrupt (a self-IPI on the dispatch vector), which the APIC
  delivers as soon as the processor drops below `DispatchLevel`. The same
  mechanism handles a thread becoming ready at a higher priority.
- **Locks.** Two kinds, both spin locks at DispatchLevel, always taken
  in this order:
  1. the *dispatcher lock*: every wait queue (events, mutexes, shared
     locks, semaphores), the per-processor sleep queues of timed waits,
     alerts, the list of exited threads, and a thread's change into or
     out of the waiting state;
  2. each processor's *scheduling lock* (`Kernel.ReadyQueues`): its run
     queues, the thread it runs and at what priority, its time slice and
     its processor time. A processor holding its own takes another's
     only if it is free at that moment (`TryLockProcessor`), so no two
     processors ever wait for each other.

  Time slices, preemption by a more important thread and yields take
  only the processor's own lock; waits and wake-ups take the dispatcher
  lock and then the lock of the processor the woken thread goes to.
  The processor's lock is held across a context switch, and so is the
  dispatcher lock when the old thread blocks or exits; the thread that
  runs next releases them (`FinishThreadSwitch`). So a thread never runs
  elsewhere before its registers are saved: it sits in a queue that is
  locked, or is blocked and cannot be woken while the dispatcher lock
  is held, or - preempted while it should go to another processor (its
  affinity changed, or one it may run on is idle) - is in no queue
  until the next thread places it once the switch is over.
- **Work stealing.** Taking a thread from another processor's queues
  (more important than its own best, or any when its own are empty) is
  done only if that queue's lock is free; when it was taken and might
  have held something, the processor remembers it, and its idle loop
  pulls the thread over (waiting for that lock, holding no other)
  instead of halting.
- Exited threads are put on a list and cleaned up by the idle thread
  (stack freed, object dereferenced).
- Processor time is taken at every switch (`Kernel.ProcessorTime`): each
  processor remembers since when its running thread runs, and the switch
  charges the time since then (in clock nanoseconds) to the thread it
  leaves and to the processor's busy time, or its idle time when it
  leaves its idle thread. So a thread's time is exact to the clock, not
  counted in ticks; reading it adds the run going on now. Where the
  clock tick finds the thread (user mode or the kernel) is counted per
  tick, and the exact time is split between the two in that proportion,
  rather than timing every system call and interrupt (see "Processor
  time and memory").
- Every 5 seconds the boot processor's clock interrupt (which comes for
  it even while that processor idles with its tick stopped) samples the
  number of threads running or ready and folds it into three
  exponentially decayed averages (1, 5 and 15 minutes, fixed point with
  11 fraction bits, as in Unix load averages). The run queues keep a count of their threads for this.
- User threads run at priority 8 for nice 0; every 4 nice steps move one
  priority (nice -20 is 13, nice 19 is 4). `SetThreadPriority` sets a
  thread's base priority (ending any boost) and moves a ready thread to
  the run queue of its new priority.
- Floating point and SSE registers belong to threads: the switch saves the
  old thread's (FXSAVE) and loads the new one's (FXRSTOR). The kernel
  itself uses no such registers (the build checks), so interrupts and
  system calls need not save them.

### Priority boosts

Priorities 1-15 are the *variable class*, 16-31 the *real-time class*
(`Kernel.PriorityBoosts`). A thread has a base priority (what
`SetThreadPriority` set) and a current one, which it is queued and run
at; only threads of the variable class are ever boosted, and a boost
never takes a thread past 15.

- **Wake boost.** A thread whose wait ends because what it waited for
  happened is raised above its base by an amount set by what woke it,
  the sizes other systems use: keyboard or mouse input +6
  (`Io.InputEvents`, terminal input), an audio stream's room to write
  +8, data from the network +2 (sockets), the display answering +2
  (virtio-gpu), an I/O completion +1 (`CompleteRequest`; drivers may
  pass another with `CompleteRequestWithBoost`), another thread's event,
  semaphore or address wake +1 (`SignalEvent`; `SignalEventWithBoost`
  for others). A boost never lowers a higher current priority. A wait
  that ends by its timeout or an alert gets nothing; nor does a mutex
  or shared lock handed over.
- **Decay.** Each time slice the thread uses up, its current priority
  drops one level, back to its base. A thread that waits again before
  its slice ends keeps its boost, so interactive threads (that wait
  often) stay ahead of computing ones of the same base priority: woken,
  they preempt them at once instead of after their time slice.
- **Starvation boost.** About once a second the dispatch interrupt looks
  through the run queues (at most 16 threads at a time) for threads of
  the variable class that have been ready for 4 seconds without running
  (`ReadySince`), and raises each to 15 for one time slice, after which
  it drops straight back to its base (also if it waits first). So a
  thread kept off the processor by busier ones of higher priority still
  makes progress, and releases what locks it holds.

The rules are pure functions checked on the host
(`tools/SchedulerPolicyTest`); the kernel self tests check that an event
wakes a thread beside a busy one at once, and `schedtest` (in coretest)
both that and the starvation boost from user mode.

### Locks and synchronization objects

All at `PassiveLevel`, all sleeping rather than spinning, and all built
on the dispatcher lock and its wait queues:

- **Events** (`Kernel.Events`): notification (stay signaled, release
  everyone) or synchronization (release one, reset). A thread may wait
  for any or all of up to 64. An event may have observers
  (`AttachEventObserver`): routines told of every signal (and of a
  semaphore's or mutex's release) under the dispatcher lock, before
  the waiters are released, which wait for nothing and consume nothing
  - how event polls hear of objects becoming ready.
- **Mutexes** (`Kernel.Mutex`): an owner, recursive, handed directly to
  the first waiter.
- **Semaphores** (`Kernel.Semaphores`): a count from 0 to a limit. A
  wait takes one; a release gives back one or more (failing, and
  changing nothing, past the limit) and releases waiters in the order
  they came. A semaphore is an event of kind `EventKindSemaphore`,
  signaled while its count is above zero, so it is waited on with the
  other events, in a wait for any or a wait for all (which takes one
  only when all are signaled); releasing works at DispatchLevel too.
- **Shared locks** (`Kernel.SharedLocks`): reader/writer locks. Any
  number of holders shared or one exclusively. Writers come first: a
  thread asking for the lock shared waits while a writer holds it or
  waits for it, so readers that keep coming cannot keep a writer out;
  and when a writer releases it, every reader waiting then gets it
  together before the next writer, so readers are not starved either.
  Ownership is handed over by the releasing thread. The exclusive
  holder may acquire the lock again either way (each counts as another
  exclusive hold); a shared holder must not acquire it again at all (a
  writer waiting in between would deadlock it, and holders are not
  recorded per thread to catch it). `TryAcquire...` versions never
  wait. The volume list (`FileSystem.Volumes`) uses one: every path
  lookup reads it shared, mounting and removing a disk change it
  exclusively. So do other tables that are read far more than changed:
  each process's handle table (`THandleTable.EntryLock`: changes hold
  the process's lock and the entry lock exclusively, only while the
  entries change, releasing the objects afterwards; lookups take only
  the entry lock shared, and `ReferenceHandleEntry` references under it,
  so the threads of a process look up handles side by side without the
  process's lock), the process registry (`LockProcessRegistryShared` for
  listing and finding processes; registering and changing groups and
  sessions exclusive) and the mount list (describing mounts and finding
  a volume's mount point shared). A volume's node cache stays under the
  volume's lock, which every file operation holds for its whole
  duration.

**Timing windows.** `Kernel.SchedulerLatencySelfTest` makes two windows
QEMU does not hit by chance happen on every boot, with test hooks. The
idle window hook (`SetIdleWindowHookForTest`) holds an idle processor
between its check for work and its wait, interrupts off: a thread
pinned there and woken inside the window must run at once, and so must
a thread left in a busy processor's queue whose lock the test holds
while the idle processor's dispatch interrupt arrives in the window
and is refused its steal (the case the one-step check and wait was
made for; with interrupts enabled in the window it sleeps with the
work, and the test fails). And with the time slice stretched beyond
any wait (`SetTimeSliceTicksForTest`), lowering a spinning thread's
priority below a ready thread's must hand over the processor at once
(without the reschedule `SetThreadPriority` asks for, it never would).

Kernel self tests (`Kernel.SynchronizationSelfTest`) run on every boot:
semaphore counts, limits and consumers in several threads; readers and
writers of a shared lock in several threads (no reader sees a write half
done, writers are alone, readers really share, a writer gets in while
readers keep coming); the wake boost; and a stress of threads in a ring
waking each other across processors while another thread keeps moving
them between processors and changing their priorities.

## The clock and timers

- **Time.** The kernel measures time with a fine clock from the HAL
  (`HalClockNanoseconds`): on x86-64 the time stamp counter, read on any
  processor without a lock (`Hal.TimeStampClock`), or where that cannot
  be trusted KVM's paravirtual clock or the HPET (`Hal.ClockSources`,
  below). Uptime, timers, timeouts and the tick count (`ClockTickCount`,
  in 10 ms ticks, which drivers still use for coarse deadlines) all come
  from it, in nanoseconds (`ClockNanoseconds`).
- **Calibration** (`Hal.ClockCalibration`, x86-64). The counter's rate is
  the first of: stated by the hypervisor (leaf 4000_0010h EAX, or KVM's
  paravirtual clock record's scale); stated by the processor (Intel CPUID
  15h: the core crystal times EBX/EAX, the crystal known by the model
  where ECX is 0 - 25 MHz Goldmont D, 19.2 MHz Goldmont and Goldmont
  Plus, else from CPUID 16h's base frequency and the ratio, else 24 MHz
  Skylake and Kaby Lake client; `Hal.TimerFrequencies`); measured over
  50 ms against the HPET; against the ACPI PM timer (3.579545 MHz, the
  FADT's port, 24 or 32 bits; `Hal.PowerManagementTimer`); against the
  PIT, which is probed first (channel 2's latched count must go down:
  many recent PCs gate it off, QEMU's `pit=off` leaves it out, and its
  busy wait gives up after a bound of reads); last CPUID 16h's nominal
  base frequency. A stated rate is checked against a 20 ms measurement
  where there is a reference: more than 1% apart and the measurement is
  taken. The local APIC timer (divided by 16): the hypervisor's leaf
  (EBX, the bus), on bare metal Intel the CPUID 15h crystal (the timer
  runs on it), else measured against the counter over 20 ms (so the two
  agree closely, which decides whether a clock interrupt comes early by
  the counter); a stated rate is checked the same way. The start-up busy
  waits (the processors' INIT and STARTUP delays) use the counter once
  its rate is known, else the HPET, the PM timer or the PIT. The boot
  log says which source gave each rate (`[hal] Time stamp counter
  2918.400 MHz (not invariant), rate: KVM paravirtual clock; stated ...,
  2918.410 MHz measured against the HPET`).
- **The HPET** (`Hal.Hpet`, `Hal.HpetTable`, `Hal.HpetMath`). The ACPI
  HPET table gives the register block (mapped uncached), the comparator
  count, the counter width and legacy replacement capability; the
  capabilities register the period in femtoseconds (at most 100 ns).
  The counter is enabled at start (the HAL looks the table up before the
  rates are measured: Kernel.Startup finds the ACPI tables before
  `InitializeHal`) with every comparator quiet and legacy replacement
  off, and runs in every power state. A 64-bit counter is read high,
  low, high; a 32-bit one is extended to 64 bits by counting its wraps
  (the last value kept with a compare-and-exchange; the clock reads it
  every few seconds at most, a wrap is 42.9 s at 100 MHz). Comparators
  are used in 32-bit mode, one-shot (at least 192 ticks ahead, written
  again further on while the counter may already be past it) or
  periodic (value-set, first match then period). `hpet=off` ignores it.
  Suspend to RAM loses its configuration: `SaveHpetState` and
  `RestoreHpetState` (before the clock continues) keep the general
  configuration, each comparator's configuration, value and FSB route.
  The PNP0103 device in the namespace is not used (it only repeats the
  table's address).
- **Clock sources and the watchdog** (`Hal.ClockSources`). The clock is
  the counter where it is invariant or in a virtual machine without
  kvmclock; kvmclock where the counter is not invariant and KVM offers
  it; the HPET on bare metal without an invariant counter
  (`Hal.HpetClock`: the counter's ticks times its period, paused and
  continued across suspend like the others). `clocksource=tsc`,
  `clocksource=hpet` or `clocksource=kvmclock` (`clock=` is the older
  spelling) chooses one that exists. While the counter is the clock and
  there is an HPET, `Kernel.ClockWatchdog` calls `HalWatchClock` once a
  second (a kernel timer's deferred call): the counter and the HPET are
  read together (again if the reads were more than 50 us apart) and the
  stretch each measured since the last check compared; more than 1%
  (at least 500 us) apart twice in a row and the clock moves to the HPET,
  continuing from the counter's time, logged (`[clock] time stamp
  counter drifts from the HPET ... the clock is the HPET from now on`),
  and the clock page is published again. With `clocksource=tsc` the
  drift is only logged. `clockdrifttest` makes the watchdog see the
  counter run 5% fast from its third check (the fallback's test). Deep
  idle states are used where the clock keeps counting in them
  (`HalClockRunsInDeepIdle`: an invariant counter, or the HPET).
- **The clock page and the HPET.** When the clock is the HPET (or
  kvmclock) the page says `ClockPageModeSystemCall` and programs make
  the system call. Mapping the HPET's register page read-only into
  programs (as Linux once did for its vDSO) would work, but the page
  also holds the comparators and the interrupt status, every read is
  an uncached device access (an exit to the hypervisor in a virtual
  machine) that is barely cheaper than the call, and the runtime and
  mlibc would need a second way of reading the page for a case that
  only old machines and `clocksource=hpet` reach: so it is not done.
- **One-shot clock interrupts.** Each processor's local APIC timer runs
  in one-shot mode (`Kernel.Clock`). Every time it interrupts, it is set
  again for the first of four things on that processor: its next 10 ms
  tick, its first timer, the first wake-up of the threads that began a
  timed wait there and, on the boot processor, the next load average
  sample. Whoever adds an earlier due time on a processor
  asks for an earlier interrupt (`RequestClockInterruptBy`, interrupts
  disabled). A late interrupt counts every tick it missed, and the ticks
  keep to their schedule (each is due 10 ms after the last was due).
- **Tickless idle.** The tick is only needed while a processor runs a
  thread: time slices (`QuantumTicks`) and the split of processor time
  between user mode and the kernel. The clock interrupt that finds a
  processor in its idle thread stops its tick (`NextTickTime` =
  `NeverDue`), so an idle processor sleeps until its next timer or
  wake-up, a device interrupt or another processor's dispatch interrupt,
  and at most 4 seconds (the longest the clock interrupt is set for at
  once). The switch to the idle thread stops it at once
  (`StopClockTick`, the clock interrupt moved to the next due time), so
  a thread that wakes, runs briefly and waits again costs no tick; the
  switch away from the idle thread starts the tick again
  (`RestartClockTick`), a whole tick later, so the thread gets a full
  time slice. Processor time stays exact (it is taken at every switch),
  the uptime and the timers come from the counter, and the load
  averages have a deadline of their own. Each processor counts its clock interrupts
  (`ClockInterruptCount`) and of those the ones that found a tick, a
  timer or a wake-up due: an idle QEMU guest takes about one a second
  per idle processor rather than 100; what is left is due work (in the
  test machine, netlog's 100 ms poll and the services' timers). Kernel option `tickless=off` keeps
  the tick on idle processors too.
- **Dynamic tick.** A busy processor whose running thread is alone
  (nothing in its run queues) has no time slice to end either. The
  clock interrupt that finds it so asks for the dispatch interrupt,
  which looks under the processor's scheduling lock (where the count is
  exact) and defers the tick (`DeferClockTick`, `TickDeferredUntil`) to
  a residual tick a second later. That one still charges the ticks that
  passed (the split of processor time between user mode and the kernel
  is sampled once a second then) and the next dispatch decides again.
  Whoever queues a thread on that processor sees the deferral under the
  same lock and sends it its dispatch interrupt, which starts the tick
  again a whole tick from then (`ResumeClockTick`), and so does any
  switch: the newcomer waits at most one time slice, as before. An
  alerted thread (asked to end, stop or take a signal) running on
  another processor is sent a dispatch interrupt too, so it reaches its
  safe point at once rather than at a tick that may be a second away.
  `TickDeferralCount` counts the deferrals. Kernel option
  `dynamictick=off` (or `tickless=off`) keeps the 100 Hz tick on busy
  processors.
- **The clock page** (`Kernel.ClockPage`): one physical page with the
  clock's parameters (`TAbiClockPage`: the counter value at an origin,
  the uptime then and the counter's rate, from `HalDescribeUserClock`;
  the wall clock's offset and gradual adjustment, from
  `ReadWallClockState`), mapped read-only into every program (a section
  region; its address is the auxiliary vector entry
  `AuxiliaryClockPage`). The runtime reads the uptime and the wall clock
  from it with the processor's counter and no system call
  (`System.ReadClockPageTime`: a copy under the page's sequence count,
  odd while the kernel changes it, and the counter - `LFENCE; RDTSC` on
  x86-64, `ISB; MRS CNTVCT_EL0` on AArch64, where `CNTKCTL_EL1.EL0VCTEN`
  is set on every processor as its clock starts or wakes); `Sys.Time`
  (`WallClockNanoseconds`, `MonotonicNanoseconds`, `UptimeMilliseconds`),
  `Now`, `GetLocalTime` and `GetTickCount64` use it. The arithmetic is
  one include (`shared/ClockPageMath.inc`) shared by the kernel's wall
  clock, the runtime and `tools/ClockPageTest`, and the HALs convert the
  counter the same way, so the page's time is to the nanosecond what the
  system call gives. The kernel publishes the page at start, whenever
  the wall clock is set or adjusted, and when the clock continues after
  suspend to RAM. Where programs cannot read the kernel's clock (KVM's
  paravirtual clock, chosen under KVM unless the counter is invariant or
  `clock=tsc`) the page says `ClockPageModeSystemCall` and the runtime
  makes the call.
- **Timers** (`Kernel.Timers`) go on the queue of the processor that
  sets them; each queue has a lock its clock interrupt takes, and
  setting or cancelling also takes one shared lock, so that two
  processors changing the same timer cannot put it on two queues. The
  clock interrupt queues the expired timers' deferred calls.
- **Timeouts.** A thread waiting with a timeout goes on the sleep queue
  of the processor it began the wait on (under the dispatcher lock).
  That processor's clock interrupt requests the dispatch interrupt when
  the first is due, which wakes the threads due and asks for the next
  wake-up's interrupt. A wake-up already due is left out when the
  interrupt is set again, so a processor kept above dispatch level for a
  while is not interrupted over and over.
- **Never early.** A timer or timeout due at T ends at T or later by the
  counter: the APIC timer is set a little long (rounded up, plus 1/1024),
  and an interrupt that still comes early only sets itself again.
- **Suspend to RAM** turns the counter off and may restart it from zero:
  the HAL pauses the clock before sleeping (`HalPrepareForSleep`) and
  continues it from the same time after waking, before any other
  processor runs, so the uptime leaves out the time asleep and every due
  time still holds. The HPET's registers are kept before and written
  back before the clock continues; its event timer is set again from
  the broadcast's deadline, the PIT's channel 0 silenced again, and the
  watchdog starts afresh. Each processor starts its clock interrupt again as
  it wakes (`StartClockOnThisProcessor` in `WakeEntry`).
- The counters of all processors are taken to run together, as they do
  on machines with an invariant counter and in virtual machines; under
  emulation (TCG) both the counter and the APIC timer follow the host's
  real time.
- **Invariant counter and kvmclock.** `Hal.TimeStampClock` checks that
  the counter is invariant (CPUID 8000_0007h EDX bit 8: the same rate in
  every power state) and the HAL logs it. One that is not may stop in
  deep idle states, so the idle states then stay at HLT; under KVM
  (which does not say its counter is invariant unless asked) the kernel's
  clock is then KVM's paravirtual clock instead (`Hal.ParavirtualClock`,
  kvmclock: MSR 4B564D01h, one record for every processor where KVM
  says it is stable, read with a version count). `clocksource=` (or
  `clock=`) chooses. It pauses and continues across suspend to RAM like
  the counter clock.
- **What programs see.** `CallGetClockInformation` (236) gives a
  `TAbiClockInformation`: the clock source, the counter's and the local
  timer's rates and where they came from, the HPET's period, width,
  comparators, vendor, address, the comparator in use, its route and
  interrupts, the broadcast timer and its wake-ups, the watchdog's
  checks and largest drift, and whether programs read the clock page.
  `powerstat --clock` prints it (and the default listing includes it),
  timetest checks it.
- **The wall clock** (`Kernel.WallClock`) is the uptime plus an offset:
  the battery backed clock's reading at start, to the nanosecond from
  then on. It can be stepped (`CallSetWallClock`, `CallAdjustWallClock`
  at once: the offset changes and the battery backed clock is written)
  or slewed (`CallAdjustWallClock` with `AdjustGradually`: the offset
  moves towards the target at 500 parts per million of the time
  passing, so the clock runs a little fast or slow but never jumps or
  goes back; a new adjustment replaces what is left of the last). A
  step that would take the clock outside 1970 to 2200, or a gradual
  adjustment over an hour, is refused (ErrorInvalidArgument), so the
  offset cannot overflow nor reach the battery backed clock. The
  state is read without a lock under a sequence count, so any level may
  read the time. `CallGetPreciseTime` gives the wall clock or the uptime
  as seconds and nanoseconds; `CallGetTime` still gives whole seconds.
  The runtime's `Now` and `GetLocalTime` use the precise call
  (milliseconds), `Sys.Time` has `WallClockNanoseconds` and
  `MonotonicNanoseconds`. Every change of the clock is a line of the
  kernel log (`[clock] stepped the wall clock by ...`). Whoever keeps
  wall clock times as uptime deadlines registers a step routine
  (`AddWallClockStepRoutine`, at most four), called below
  DispatchLevel after every step (not a slew, and not when the time is
  read again on resume, with the other processors still frozen): the
  timer descriptors' absolute real time timers work out their
  deadlines again or are canceled (`TimerCancelOnSet`).

## Power, idle states and temperature

**Idle states** (`Kernel.IdleStates`, `Kernel.Arch.IdleStates`). The idle
thread calls `IdleProcessor`, which picks the deepest of the
processor's idle states whose target residency fits in the time to its
next clock interrupt (with the tick stopped, its next due timer), and
counts each entry (`IdleStateEntries`). Checking and waiting are one
step: interrupts go off, the processor checks again that no steal was
refused since it last looked (work left in another queue), and the
state is entered with interrupts enabled only by the waiting
instruction (STI;HLT or STI;MWAIT, whose STI takes effect after the
next instruction; on AArch64 WFI or a PSCI standby state with
interrupts masked, which still wake for a pending one), so a wake-up
cannot fall between the check and the wait and leave a processor
asleep with work to steal. The table is shared and read without a lock;
a sequence number (odd while `SetFirmwareIdleStates` changes it) makes
a reader take its copy again if it changed meanwhile.
- x86-64: state 0 is HLT. MWAIT C-states come from CPUID leaf 5 (the
  sub-states of each C-state; hint `(n - 1) shl 4`) with typical exit
  latencies, or from ACPI's `_CST` once the namespace is loaded
  (`Firmware.AcpiProcessorIdle`): functional fixed hardware entries
  (class 2, whose address is the hint) and I/O port entries (the read of
  the chipset's P_LVLx port enters the state, with interrupts off; the
  next interrupt ends it). Before `_CST` every processor object is told
  what the kernel can do (`Firmware.AcpiProcessorControl`: `_OSC` with
  the processor UUID, else `_PDC`; Intel's capability bits for MWAIT
  C-states, P-states through the MSR, software coordination), since
  firmware loads its per-processor tables and answers only then. The
  deep states are used where the counter is invariant, CPUID 5 states
  its line size and the interrupt break (MWAIT), and not under a
  hypervisor (QEMU's emulated MWAIT does not sleep with several
  processors) unless `idle=mwait` (`idle=port` for port states). Where
  the local APIC timer does not keep running in them (no ARAT) every
  state deeper than C1 is marked as stopping it, and the broadcast
  timer below wakes the processors in them. `idle=halt` keeps to HLT,
  `maxcstate=N` stops at C(N).
- AArch64: state 0 is WFI. PSCI `CPU_SUSPEND` states come from the device
  tree's `arm,idle-state` nodes (`ListDeviceTreeIdleStates`: power
  state, latencies, minimum residency) where the firmware offers
  `CPU_SUSPEND` (`PSCI_FEATURES`, which also says the power state
  format). Standby states return like WFI. **Power-down states** lose
  the processor's registers, timer and GIC interface: its state is saved
  first (`Kernel.Arch.Suspend`, as for suspend to RAM) and `CPU_SUSPEND`
  gets the start-up entry and a start-up record of the processor's own
  (`PrepareIdleWakeEntry`: power-downs come and go on many processors at
  once, so the shared record will not do; each has a small wake stack
  too); an interrupt brings it back there, it sets itself up again
  (translation, vectors, block, GIC) and resumes the saved state inside
  `ArchEnterIdleState`. Firmware may take a shallower state and return
  instead, registers kept. Power-down states and standby states marked
  `local-timer-stop` stop the timer: the broadcast timer wakes them.
  QEMU's virt machine and the Pi 5's tree have none, so WFI it is there;
  with a tree that has one (tested with QEMU and a dumped tree given
  one) the standby state is entered. `idle=wfi` keeps to WFI.
  `idle=powerdown-test` tests the way back from a lost state on QEMU
  (whose `CPU_SUSPEND` is a WFI): a made-up power-down state turns the
  processor off with `CPU_OFF`, and whatever would wake it (its due
  time, a thread made ready for it, at least every 20 ms for the device
  interrupts it takes) starts it again with `CPU_ON` through the same
  entry (`WakePoweredDownProcessor`; a wake asked for while it was on
  its way off - a flag, or an interrupt pending in `ISR_EL1` - keeps it
  on; a resumed processor asks itself for a dispatch interrupt, since
  CPU_ON brings none; a refused CPU_ON is retried by the boot
  processor's clock a millisecond later). Tested on QEMU's virt machine
  (GICv3, 4 processors): the self tests, the broadcast self test and
  timetest pass; `powerstat --check-idle` does not, by design, as the
  boot processor then starts the others every 20 ms.

**The broadcast timer** (`Kernel.BroadcastTimer`). A processor about to
enter a state whose timer stops hands its next due time (its clock
interrupt time) to a table, one slot per processor, and marks its own
timer stale (`ClockInterruptTime` = never: whatever sets it next sets it
in full, `RearmClockInterrupt`, past due times included). If that time
is earlier than the boot processor's next clock interrupt, the boot
processor is asked (a flag and its dispatch interrupt,
`ServeBroadcastRequest`) to bring its interrupt forward; its clock
interrupt (`ServeBroadcast`) sends every processor whose time has come
its dispatch interrupt, and its next one is set for the earliest time
left in the table (part of its next clock deadline). The slot is written
before the boot processor's interrupt time is read, and a dispatch
interrupt sent before the processor waits stays pending, so no wake-up
is lost. The due time handed over is the clock interrupt time, so it
covers a deferred tick's residual tick (dynamic tick) as well as timers
and wake-ups; `ResumeClockTick` and `RestartClockTick` set a stale timer
again in full. The boot processor never enters these states (it keeps time),
nor does any processor when it is the only one - unless the platform
has a timer of its own (below).

**The HPET as the broadcast timer** (`Hal.HpetEventTimer`,
`Hal.HpetInterrupts`, x86-64). One HPET comparator is the kernel's
event timer, set up once device interrupts can be routed
(`HalStartPlatformTimers`, phase one, before the other processors
start) on vector 0xD1 (the clock's level) to the boot processor. Its
route, the first that works of: an FSB message where the comparator can
and interrupt remapping is off; an I/O APIC input its route capability
allows that nothing else uses (input 2, the PIT's, with channel 0
silenced; inputs above 23); legacy replacement (comparator 0 on IRQ 0);
input 8 or a free one of 16-23. The input is kept from drivers
(`RoutePlatformTimerInterrupt`). Each way is checked before it is kept:
three matches 1 ms ahead must interrupt no more than 2 ms late, else the
next way is tried (a second round takes any that interrupts at all).
KVM's in-kernel interrupt controller has no route for input 2 (it sends
ISA IRQ 0 there instead), so under KVM the check moves on to legacy
replacement. `hpetroute=message|ioapic|legacy` forces one way.

Where the event timer runs, `StartBroadcastDevice` makes it the
broadcast timer (`broadcasttimer=boot` keeps the boot processor's
clock): a single shared comparator rather than one per processor (that
would take as many comparators with FSB delivery as processors, which
few chipsets have, and saves only the wake-up's inter-processor
interrupt). `EnterBroadcastIdle` writes the slot, then (under a lock)
programs the comparator for the processor's due time if that is earlier
than the time it is set for (`DeviceDue`); the comparator's interrupt
sets `DeviceDue` to never under the same lock before it reads the
table, so either it sees the slot or the processor sees never and sets
the comparator itself. It wakes the processors due (`ServeBroadcast`,
from slot 0 on) and sets the comparator for the next due time. The boot
processor then may enter states whose timer stops too, and its clock no
longer takes the others' due times. Deferred ticks are covered the same
way: the due time handed over is the clock interrupt time, the residual
tick included. The HPET self test (`Kernel.Arch.TimerSelfTest`) pins a
thread to the boot processor with the broadcast forced and checks ten
20 ms sleeps there; it also checks the counter against the clock over
50 ms (2%), a fresh measurement of the counter's rate against the
reference (2%), a one-shot 5 ms ahead (under 40 ms late) and the
periodic mode (about one interrupt per 2 ms period). `idlebroadcast=off`
keeps to states whose timer runs; `idlebroadcast=force` treats every
state of the other processors as stopping the timer and really leaves
it at its longest (4 s), so only the broadcast wakes them on time: the
test on machines without such states. The kernel self test does that
for ten 20 ms sleeps on the last processor (each on time, the broadcast
counted).

**Performance states on PCs** (`Power.PerformanceStates`). Where the
processor has hardware P-states (HWP, `Hal.PerformanceControl`: CPUID 6
EAX bit 7) they are turned on on every processor (`IA32_PM_ENABLE`) and
given the whole range the processor reports (`IA32_HWP_CAPABILITIES`),
balanced energy preference; the processor picks its clock itself, and
the thermal limit lowers the top of the range instead of modulating the
clock. Otherwise ACPI's `_PSS` (frequencies, power, latency, control
values), `_PCT` (the performance control MSR, or an I/O port) and `_PPC`
(the fastest state allowed; read again on the processor's Notify 0x80):
a governor thread ("Performance") takes the fastest state allowed at
60 % busy or more and the slowest after three looks under 25 %, half a
second apart, as the Raspberry Pi's does; the thermal limit caps it (the
fastest state at or below that share of the top frequency), taking over
from clock modulation. The MSR is written only where CPUID says it is
there (Enhanced SpeedStep). `cpufreq=off|max|min` as on the Pi.
`CallListPerformanceStates` lists the states (the one in use, those not
allowed); the clock rate and range are in `CallGetProcessorPower`.

**Thermal zones** (`Power.ThermalZones`) are temperatures with a passive
and a critical trip point, read by a thread ("Thermal", with a large
stack for AML) as often as each says. Above the passive point the
processors are slowed a step (10 % of full speed) at every reading, to
30 % at most, and let up again a step at a time once 3 degrees below
(the lowest limit any zone asks for holds, `Power.Performance`); two
readings in a row at the critical point shut the machine down cleanly
(`RequestShutdown`). `thermal=off` only reads and shows them. The limit
is carried out by clock modulation on x86-64 (`Hal.ProcessorThrottle`,
MSR 19Ah, eighths of the time, written on each processor by the thread
moving itself from processor to processor, `Power.EveryProcessor`), or by
the Raspberry Pi's clock governor below.

- **Active cooling.** A zone's active trip points (`_AC0`, the hottest,
  to `_AC9`) each list the cooling devices that must run at or above it
  (`_ALx`: fans `PNP0C0B`, or power resources). The policy keeps the
  hottest trip point reached until the zone is 3 degrees below it, and
  the zone's routine runs the devices of that trip point and of every
  cooler one (`Io.AcpiPower`: each device once in `Power.Cooling`,
  running while any zone wants it; `Firmware.AcpiFans`: `_FSL` 100 or 0
  for a fan with fine control, else its power resources' `_ON`/`_OFF`
  and `_PS0`/`_PS3`; its speed from `_FST` or the power resource's
  `_STA`). `CallListCoolingDevices` lists them with their zone and trip
  point.
- **Notifications.** A Notify on a zone reaches the policy (it only
  notes it: AML is running): 0x80 reads the zone at once, 0x81 and 0x82
  read its trip points (and fans) again first.

**ACPI** (`Io.AcpiPower`, a thread with a large stack once the namespace
is loaded): every `ThermalZone` object (`Firmware.AcpiThermal`: `_TMP`,
`_PSV`, `_CRT`, `_HOT`, `_TZP`, tenths of a kelvin; readings outside
-73 to 177 C are refused) becomes a thermal zone; batteries (`PNP0C0A`,
`Firmware.AcpiBatteries`: `_STA` bit 4, `_BIX` or `_BIF`, `_BST`) are read
then and every 10 seconds, kept for `CallListBatteries` so that no AML
runs on a caller's small stack; `_OSC`/`_PDC`, `_CST`, `_PSS` as above;
the wake devices (see Suspend to RAM). It then waits for what the
firmware's notifications bring:
- **Processor hotplug.** A Notify 0 or 1 on a processor object (QEMU's
  `device_add` of a processor: its GPE, `\_SB.CPUS.CSCN`, the Notify):
  `_STA` says present and enabled, `_MAT` gives its local APIC or
  x2APIC entry (the id, the enabled flag); it is told the capabilities
  and brought up like the processors at start
  (`BringUpPluggedProcessor`, the start-up code prepared first if no
  processor needed it then). Removal (eject) is not done.
- **The embedded controller** (`Firmware.AcpiEmbeddedController`,
  `Io.AcpiEmbeddedController`), connected right after the tables load
  and before the devices' `_INI`: its ports from the ECDT where there is
  one, else from the `PNP0C09` device's `_CRS` (data, then command);
  the EmbeddedControl address space for AML (`RD_EC`/`WR_EC` byte by
  byte, every wait bounded so a dead controller fails the access instead
  of hanging); `_REG(3, 1)`; and its GPE taken from the method table
  (`RegisterGpeHandler`): each event's queries (`QR_EC`) run their
  `_Qnn`, which is where laptops Notify their zones, batteries and
  buttons. QEMU has neither
thermal zones nor batteries: `make acpi-power-test`
(`tools/AcpiPowerTest`) reads them from a table `make-table.py`
assembles (two zones, one with a nonsense `_TMP`; batteries with
`_BIF`, `_BIX` and an empty slot; a processor's `_CST`), and with
`--ssdt` the same zones and batteries go into QEMU through
`-acpitable file=...` (checked by hand: the zones and batteries are
listed, and a zone above its critical point powers the machine off).

**The Raspberry Pi** (`Power.BoardClocks`, untested on the board). The
firmware (VideoCore mailbox) tells the ARM clock now, its least and its
most (`arm_freq_min`, `arm_freq`: 1.5 and 2.4 GHz on a Pi 5) and the
temperature, and sets the ARM clock (and the voltage for it) when asked
(`SetClockRate`, tag 38002h); it keeps whatever clock it started with
otherwise. A thread ("BoardClocks") looks at the busiest processor
every half second: 60 % busy or more raises the clock to the most
allowed, three looks in a row under 25 % lower it to the least, in
between it stays. The temperature is a thermal zone ("soc", read every
second, passive at 80 C - `thermallimit=` - and critical at 90 C -
`thermalcritical=`); the passive limit caps the clock (never below the
firmware's least; the firmware's own 85 C limit stays beneath).
`cpufreq=off` leaves the clock to the firmware, `cpufreq=max` and
`cpufreq=min` fix it. The SD image's `config.txt` sets no `force_turbo`,
`arm_freq` or `over_voltage` (it never did).
- **The Pi 5's fan.** The firmware does not run it for the operating
  system: Linux drives it with RP1's PWM1 channel 3 on GPIO 45
  (`cooling_fan` in the tree, inverted: high stops it). `Drivers.Rp1Pwm`
  (untested on the board: built only) sets up RP1's clock generator for
  it (CLK_PWM1 from the 50 MHz crystal, undivided, enabled; offsets and
  fields as Linux's clk-rp1) and the channel (range for the tree's
  41566 ns period, inverted, trailing-edge mark/space, latched with the
  global update bit), and `Drivers.Rp1Fan` gives GPIO 45 its first
  function (PWM1 channel 3); the governor runs the fan at 30, 50, 70 and
  100 % from `fanon=` (55 C), 5, 12 and 20 degrees above it (the tree's
  cooling levels), each level held until 5 degrees below where it
  starts. Anything that does not read back as written leaves the PWM
  unused: GPIO 45 is then a plain output (function SYS_RIO, pad
  driving, no pulls) and any speed above 0 is full speed, as before; a
  wrong clock after all would leave the pin at one level, low being
  full speed, which errs on the cool side. `fan=on` keeps it at full
  speed, `fan=off` leaves it alone. It is the cooling device "fan".

**Calls and tools.** `CallGetProcessorPower` (154) gives the clock
source, whether idle is tickless, the idle states and, per processor,
clock interrupts, busy and idle time and idle state entries, the clock
rate and its range, the performance limit and the fan;
`CallListThermalZones` (155) and `CallListBatteries` (156) list the rest
(`Sys.Power`), and calls 228-232 the wake sources and their alarm
(`CallSetWakeAlarm`, `CallListWakeSources`, `CallSetWakeSource`), the
cooling devices and the performance states. `powerstat` prints them (and
the performance states, fans and wake sources; `--wake INDEX on|off`
changes one), with each processor's clock
interrupts per second over a second; sysinfo shows the clock rate, the
hottest temperature and the batteries; the kernel debug shell's `power`
writes the same to the log.

**Tests.** `make acpi-power-test` also reads, from its table, four wake
devices (`_DSW` and `_PSW` told, a power resource turned on), an
embedded controller played in memory (bytes, a 16-bit field, `_REG`, a
query running `_Q42`, a dead controller timing out, a zone reading its
temperature through it), active trip points with a fan by `_FSL` and
one by its power resource, `_OSC` and `_PDC` given the capabilities,
`_PSS`/`_PCT`/`_PPC`, `_MAT` entries and a port C-state. coretest runs
