**Volumes, mute and the default output.** Each output's volume (its
hardware's, `ControlAudioSetMasterVolume`) can be muted
(`ControlAudioSetMute`): the mixer then writes silence, whatever the
amplifier can do, and the volume is kept for when it is unmuted (the
monitor input records the silence too: it is what plays). One output is
the default (`ControlAudioGetDefaultOutput`, `...Set`, asked of or set
on any output; the first until another is chosen): where programs play
that name no output, since libaudio's `OpenAudioOutput(nil)` opens it.
The kernel keeps only the number, and says what each output is
(`ControlAudioGetKind`: HD Audio, AC'97, USB audio). Anyone may change
these, as anyone at the machine could turn its knobs (the devices are
open to everyone); the system settings service keeps them in the
system's settings (`Sound/N/Volume`, `Sound/N/Muted`,
`Sound/DefaultOutput`) and gives them to the kernel at every boot.

In user space, `libaudio` holds `Audio.Device` (format, volume, writing,
draining), `Audio.Outputs` (the outputs there are, their volumes, mutes
and kinds, the default one), `Audio.Wave` (PCM WAV files) and
`Audio.Synthesis` (sine tones from a quarter-sine table and a fixed
point phase).

### The voice engine

`Audio.Engine` mixes voices in a graph, in 32-bit float, the way XAudio2
does:
- **Voices.** A source voice plays the buffers queued on it, in any
  sample kind and rate. Submix voices take what others send them and pass
  it on, in the order of their processing stage. The one mastering voice
  ends the graph. Sound only flows down: to the mastering voice or to a
  submix voice of a later stage.
- **Buffers** (`Audio.Voices`). A buffer plays from its play start to
  its play end, jumping back round its loop region as often as it says
  (or until `ExitLoop`). Callbacks tell when buffers start and end, loops
  come round, the stream ends (the buffer flagged as its end) and passes
  start and end. The rate, times the voice's frequency ratio (its pitch),
  is converted by cubic Hermite interpolation.
- **Shaping.** Every voice has a volume, a volume per channel, a filter
  (`Audio.Filters`: state variable low, band and high-pass and notch, and
  one-pole low and high-pass) and a chain of effects. Each send to a
  destination has an output matrix (how the channels go into the
  destination's) and a filter of its own.
- **Effects** (`Audio.EffectChain`). An effect is a record of routines
  (process in place, parameters, reset, release, the length of its tail)
  and a state, so programs can write their own. A voice stopped with
  `StopPlayTails` keeps processing until its effects' tails have played.
- **Operation sets.** A change made with an operation set waits for
  `CommitChanges` with that set, so several changes land in the same
  pass; set 0 changes at once.
- **Running.** Passes of 10 ms run on the engine's own thread, which
  writes the mastering voice's float samples to `/dev/audio`; the kernel
  mixes them with other programs. Writing waits while the device's queue
  is full, and that paces the engine. Callbacks run on the engine's
  thread and may call back into the engine. An offline engine has no
  device or thread: `RenderAudio` processes passes for its caller, as the
  tests do. `GetPerformanceData` counts voices, passes and frames, and
  the frames queued in the device.

### Effects and 3D audio

The built-in effects implement the effect interface, so they go in any
voice's chain like a program's own:
- **Reverb** (`Audio.Effects.Reverb`): Freeverb's eight comb filters
  (damped feedback: the room's echoes) and four all-pass filters (the
  wash) for each channel, the right a little longer than the left. Room
  size, damping, wet and dry levels and width; its tail lasts until the
  longest comb falls to -60 dB.
- **Echo** (`Audio.Effects.Echo`): a delay line of up to two seconds with
  feedback and a wet/dry mix.
- **Equalizer** (`Audio.Effects.Equalizer`): four peaking bands
  (Bristow-Johnson biquads), each a centre, a gain and a width in
  octaves.
- **Volume meter and limiter** (`Audio.Effects.Dynamics`): the meter
  reports each pass's peak and RMS level per channel; the limiter holds
  the peak under a threshold, its gain dropping at once and recovering
  over the release time, shared by the channels.

`Audio.Spatial` works out what X3DAudio does for an emitter and a
listener (left-handed space: X right, Y up, Z forward):
- **Panning.** Each emitter channel is panned by its direction from the
  listener, with equal power between the two speakers on either side of
  it, over mono, stereo, quad, 5.1 or 7.1 (the LFE gets nothing). The
  channels of a multi-channel emitter sit at their azimuths round it;
  inside its inner radius the sound spreads over every speaker.
- **Distance and cones.** The volume follows a curve of distance (by
  default 1 / distance past the curve's scale), and a cone fades from
  its inner to its outer volume between its angles. Curves also give a
  low-pass coefficient and a reverb send level by distance.
- **Doppler.** The factor comes from the speeds of emitter and listener
  along the line between them, against the speed of sound.
- `ApplySpatial` puts the result on a voice: the output matrix, the
  frequency ratio and the filter.

### Programs and tests

The programs are `tone` (plays a tone, or writes it as a WAV file, in
any format), `play` (WAV files: integer, float and extensible, any of the
formats streams take), `record` (records an input into a WAV file),
`soundinfo` (a WAV file's format, length, peak and frequency), `mixer`
(an output's volume and mute, `-l` the outputs, `-D N` the default
output, `-r` keeping the change through the system settings service),
`voicetest` (the engine's tests) and `effecttest`
(the effects' and 3D audio's). The tests record what QEMU's HD Audio device plays (its
`wav` audio backend). coretest plays a 1000 Hz tone, a 440 Hz WAV file,
600 and 1500 Hz from two programs at once, then 800, 2000 and 300 Hz at
22.05, 96 and 11.025 kHz as u8, float mono and s24 six-channel samples,
then `voicetest play`: one cycle of 600 Hz at 24 kHz looped 600 times at
twice its pitch, 1200 Hz for half a second. Then two programs record the monitor
(16 kHz mono s16 and 96 kHz six-channel float) while 900 Hz plays, and
`soundinfo` checks both recordings in the guest. Last, 700 Hz on the
AC'97 output (`/dev/audio1`) and 500 Hz on a USB audio device
(`/dev/audio2`), each recorded into a file of its own. Another test
records half a second from `/dev/audioin`: QEMU's microphone codec
(`hda-micro` on the `none` backend) gives silence, at the right rate and
length. `scripts/check-audio.py`
measures each 50 ms of the recording at the expected frequencies
(Goertzel's algorithm) and checks the order, the tones together and the
lengths. `voicetest` on its own renders graphs offline and checks them:
resampling, pitch, volumes, matrices, every filter, the callbacks' order
and the frames played, loops, flushing, 8-bit samples, submix stages and
several sends, send filters, operation sets, a custom effect with its
parameters and tail, and the performance data. `effecttest` measures
each built-in effect (the meter's readings, the limiter's ceiling, the
echo's delays and levels from an impulse, the equalizer's gain in and
out of its band, the reverb's answer, decay and width), tails after
stopping, and the 3D calculations: panning in stereo, 5.1 and 7.1,
distance, curves, cones, emitter channels, the inner radius, Doppler,
and a voice placed and moving to one side.

## Media (libmedia)

`libmedia.so` (`userland/lib/media`, units `Media.*`) reads media files
and decodes their audio: the containers, the audio codecs, the records
decoded frames come in, colour conversion for video frames, resampling
and channel mixing to an output's format. Video codecs are libraries of
their own (libvideo for VP8 and VP9, libav1) that produce libmedia's
frame records and register themselves with it. Everything is Free
Pascal, pure CPU, royalty-free formats only (no H.264, HEVC or AAC
decoding; those are recognised so a file can say what it holds).

### Frames, packets and the decoder contract

`Media.Frames` is the contract with the video decoders: `TVideoFrame`
(display size, bit depth 8/10/12, layout 4:2:0, 4:2:2, 4:4:4 or
monochrome, three `TVideoPlane`s of 1 or 2-byte little-endian samples
with their stride, the H.273 colour primaries, transfer and matrix codes,
full or limited range, the presentation time) and `TAudioBuffer`
(rate, channels, interleaved floats -1..1 in the WAVE / SMPTE order:
front left, front right, centre, LFE, back left, back right, side left,
side right). `ConvertFrameToBgra` (`Media.ColorConversion`) turns a
frame into BGRA pixels: BT.601, BT.709, BT.2020, SMPTE 240M, FCC or the
identity matrix (unspecified: BT.709 above 576 lines), limited or full
range, 10 and 12-bit samples brought to 8, as integer arithmetic with 16
fraction bits; chroma is upsampled by repetition.

`Media.Packets` has the tracks and packets. A `TMediaTrack` carries its
kind, `TCodecId`, the container's codec name, a time base, rate and
channels or picture size, and the codec's setup in a form that does not
depend on the container (`Headers`): Vorbis' three header packets, the
OpusHead packet (an MP4 dOps box is turned into it), FLAC's 34-byte
STREAMINFO, the vpcC / av1C box bodies. `CodecDelay` is what the decoder
drops at the start (Opus pre-skip, MP3 encoder delay); a packet's
`TrimStart` / `TrimEnd` are what it drops from that packet (Ogg granule
positions, Matroska DiscardPadding, the last FLAC or MP3 frame). Times
are in the track's time base (`ToMicroseconds`, `ScaleTime` without
overflow for nanosecond bases).

`TMediaDemuxer` (`Media.Demuxers`): `Recognizes` (by signature, never by
name), `Open`, `ReadPacket` (all tracks, in file order), `SeekTo`
(microseconds; the next packets start at or before the target, video at
a key frame) and `Duration`. `Media.Containers.OpenMediaFile` shows the
first 64 KiB to each demuxer in turn. `TAudioDecoder`
(`Media.AudioDecoders`): `Configure(Track)`, `Decode(Packet, Buffer)`
(applying the delay and trims), `Reset` after a seek;
`Media.AudioCodecs.CreateAudioDecoder` makes the one for a track.
`TVideoDecoder` (`Media.VideoDecoders`): `Configure`, `SendPacket`,
`ReceiveFrame` (frames in presentation order), `Flush` and `Reset`, found
through `RegisterVideoDecoder` / `CreateVideoDecoder` since the video
libraries are separate. Broken input raises `EMediaError`
(`EMediaUnsupported` for valid files using what is not decoded); a
decoder can take the next packet after one it refused.

### Containers

- **WAV** (`Media.Wav`): RIFF and RF64 WAVE, PCM 8 to 32 bits, floats
  32 and 64-bit, WAVE_FORMAT_EXTENSIBLE, MP3 data (tag 0x55); packets of
  4096 frames, seeking by arithmetic.
- **FLAC** (`Media.FlacFile`): "fLaC" and the metadata blocks (an ID3v2
  tag in front is skipped); frames have no length, so a frame ends where
  the next valid header starts and the CRC-16 of the bytes before it
  comes out zero. Seeking uses the seek table, or bisects the file by
  frame headers' sample numbers, then steps to the frame holding the
  target.
- **Ogg** (`Media.Ogg`, RFC 3533): pages with their CRC-32 checked,
  packets across pages, multiplexed and chained streams (a chained link's
  tracks appear when its first page is reached, so `TrackCount` can grow
  while reading), the Vorbis, Opus and FLAC mappings (Theora recognised).
  Packet lengths are worked out without decoding (`Media.Ogg.Codecs`:
  the Opus TOC byte, FLAC frame headers, Vorbis block sizes from the
  setup header's modes, scanned backwards from its end as ffmpeg does,
  `Media.Ogg.VorbisModes`), so timestamps come from granule positions
  exactly: a first page granule smaller than what its packets decode to
  becomes `TrimStart`, a last one `TrimEnd`. Opus times count from the
  end of the pre-skip (the first packet is at minus the pre-skip, the
  decoder drops it as `CodecDelay`); a Vorbis stream's first packet sits
  at minus its own length since it decodes to nothing. Seeking bisects
  over pages, less the Opus pre-roll of 80 ms.
- **Matroska and WebM** (`Media.Ebml`, `Media.Matroska.*`): the EBML
  header (DocType webm or matroska), segments and clusters of known or
  unknown size (live streams), SeekHead, Info, Tracks (Vorbis' Xiph-laced
  CodecPrivate split into its three headers, OpusHead with CodecDelay and
  SeekPreRoll, FLAC's metadata blocks to STREAMINFO, MP3, integer PCM
  little and big-endian, float PCM, VP8, VP9, AV1 with av1C; AAC, H.264,
  HEVC and Theora recognised), header stripping, SimpleBlock and
  BlockGroup (BlockDuration, ReferenceBlock for key frames,
  DiscardPadding as `TrimEnd`), Xiph, EBML and fixed lacing; Cues for
  seeking, walking the clusters when there are none. Block times are less
  the codec delay. Frames compressed with zlib, bzip2 or LZO, or
  encrypted, are refused (that track's packets skipped).
- **MP4** (`Media.Mp4.*`, ISO BMFF): moov and its sample tables (stts,
  ctts, stsc, stsz/stz2, stco/co64, stss), edit lists (the first media
  edit shifts times; audio before 0 beyond the codec's delay becomes
  `TrimStart`; the end of the edit, or a last sample shorter than its
  codec frame, `TrimEnd`), 64-bit and to-the-end box sizes, the sample
  entries av01 (av1C), vp09 (vpcC), vp08, Opus (dOps to OpusHead's
  little-endian layout), fLaC (dfLa to STREAMINFO), mp4a (esds: object
  types 0x6B/0x69 MP3, 0x40/0x67 AAC recognised), .mp3, ipcm, fpcm, sowt,
  twos and lpcm (PCM in packets of up to 1024 frames), avc1/hvc1/hev1
  recognised; samples of all tracks in file order. Fragmented files
  (mvex/trex, moof/traf with tfhd defaults, tfdt and every trun flag)
  are read as they arrive: a moof or sample not yet wholly in the stream
  makes `ReadPacket` return False without losing its place and a later
  call goes on once more is appended, so an init segment followed by
  media segments appended to one stream (Media Source Extensions, later)
  plays. Seeking uses stss, or reads the remaining moof boxes (only
  those) and searches their index; mfra is not used.
- **MP3** (`Media.Mp3File`): ID3v2 tags in front (footers, several in a
  row) and ID3v1 / APEv2 at the end skipped; a stream is taken only when
  three more frames agree with the first; the Xing/Info and LAME tags
  (frame count, seek table, encoder delay as `CodecDelay` = delay + 529,
  padding as `TrimEnd` = padding - 529 on the last packet; the tag frame
  itself is not given out) and VBRI; one packet per frame; seeking by the
  Xing or VBRI table or, for constant bit rates, by position.

### Audio decoders

- **PCM** (`Media.Pcm`): integers of 8 to 32 bits and floats of 32 and
  64, little or big-endian; integers are divided by 2^(bits - 1), which
  is exact.
- **FLAC** (`Media.Flac`, RFC 9639): constant, verbatim, fixed (orders
  0-4) and LPC (orders 1-32) subframes, Rice partitions with escapes,
  wasted bits, the stereo decorrelations, 4 to 32 bits per sample (64-bit
  arithmetic, so the 33-bit side channel of 32-bit audio needs nothing
  special), 1 to 8 channels, the frame's CRC-8 and CRC-16 checked.
- **Vorbis** (`Media.Vorbis.*`, the Vorbis I specification): the three
  headers (a single Xiph-laced block from Matroska is split too),
  codebooks (a 10-bit lookup table and a fallback for longer codes; VQ
  lookup types 1 and 2), floors 0 and 1, residues 0, 1 and 2, channel
  coupling, windows and overlap for mixed block sizes, and the inverse
  MDCT as a DCT-IV through an N/4-point FFT in double precision;
  channels reordered from the Vorbis order to the WAVE order. Its output
  is within 2e-7 of libvorbis' (about 137 dB).
- **MP3** (`Media.Mp3.*`, MPEG-1, 2 and 2.5 Layer III; the structure and
  tables follow minimp3, public domain): every bit rate including free
  format, mono, stereo, mid/side and intensity stereo (MPEG-2's too),
  the bit reservoir, CRC frames, mixed and short blocks, alias reduction,
  the IMDCT and a DCT-II based synthesis filter bank. Packets can be
  whole frames or any pieces of the stream (MP3 in WAV): the decoder
  finds and assembles frames itself and resynchronises after damage. A
  frame whose reservoir reaches back past what it has (just after a
  seek) comes out silent, so timing holds. Layers I and II are refused
  (EMediaUnsupported). Its output is within ISO 11172-4's full accuracy
  of ffmpeg's floating point decoder (RMS 1e-7 to 3.5e-7 against the
  limit of 8.8e-6).
- **Opus** (`Media.Opus.*`, RFC 6716 with the RFC 8251 updates; the
  tables were generated from libopus 1.5.2 and the units carry its BSD
  notice): the range decoder, SILK (narrow, medium and wide band, mono
  and stereo, 10 to 60 ms, LBRR frames skipped as in normal decoding,
  its resampler), CELT (every band layout and frame size from 2.5 to 20
  ms, transients, spreading, PVQ, anti-collapse, energy finalisation,
  the pitch post-filter, de-emphasis), hybrid mode, redundancy frames
  and mode transitions, TOC codes 0 to 3 with padding, the classic packet
  loss concealment (an empty packet), multistream with channel mapping
  families 0, 1 (reordered to the WAVE order) and 255, the OpusHead
  output gain and the reference's soft clipper; output at 48 kHz
  (`ConfigureRaw` takes 8, 12, 16, 24 or 48 kHz for the raw API the test
  vectors use, with `DecodeRaw`, `DecodeRawInt16` and `FinalRange`).
  The neural concealment of newer libopus (deep PLC, DRED) is left out.

### Resampling, mixing and output

`TResampler` (`Media.Resampler`) is a polyphase windowed-sinc filter
(Kaiser window, beta 8.6): the output rate over the input rate, reduced,
is Up/Down; output sample j lies at input time j * Down / Up, whose
fraction picks one of Up phases (rounded to 1024 phases when Up is
larger, as for 44100 to 47999). It has 32 taps upsampling and
proportionally more downsampling (the cut-off just under the lower
Nyquist frequency), streams (what is fed in pieces gives the same
output), and `Flush` makes the output exactly ceil(input * Up / Down)
frames. `TChannelMixer` (`Media.ChannelMixer`) maps channel counts in the
usual layouts: downmixing folds centre and surrounds into the fronts at
-3 dB (ITU-R BS.775) without the LFE, each output row scaled so
full-scale input cannot clip; upmixing puts mono in both fronts and
stereo in the front pair. `TAudioConverter` (`Media.AudioConversion`)
chains both and writes 16 or 32-bit integers (rounded and clipped) or
floats, the audio devices' sample kinds 2, 4 and 5.

### mediaplay

`mediaplay FILE...` plays the first audio track of each file on the
audio device (libaudio's `Audio.Device`), as floats at the decoder's own
rate and channels when the device takes them (the kernel converts to
what the hardware plays), through `TAudioConverter` otherwise or when
`-r RATE` / `-c CHANNELS` ask; `-s SECONDS` seeks first, `-d PATH`
chooses the output. `-i` prints the container, length and tracks.
`-k` decodes every track and prints checksums instead of playing (in
the manner of ffmpeg's framemd5): `video TRACK FRAME PTS WxH MD5` per
decoded frame (the visible samples of its planes, row by row), `packet
TRACK N PTS SIZE MD5` per packet of a track without a decoder (video
until a video library registers its decoders), and `audio TRACK FRAMES
RATE CHANNELS MD5` per audio track (its samples as 16-bit
little-endian). A damaged packet is skipped; a hundred and the file is
given up.

### Tests

`make media-test` builds libmedia for the host (tools/MediaTest) and
checks it over fixtures the host's tools make at build time
(`tools/MediaTest/make-*-fixtures.py` into build/tools/media-fixtures;
each script skips, with a note in its manifest, what the host cannot
make; the synthetic signals are made by Python and are the same every
build):
- colour conversion (known colours in each matrix, range and depth),
  times, PCM decoding and trimming, WAV files of every sample kind
  against the floats they were made from, the resampler (length, a
  tone's accuracy, a tone above the new Nyquist frequency removed, an
  odd ratio, feeding in pieces), the mixer's matrices, the output
  encoding;
- FLAC: files the host's flac made in many settings (levels 0-8, 8 to
  32 bits, 1 to 8 channels, block sizes 192 to 65535, LPC order 32,
  odd rates, constant/verbatim subframes, wasted bits, an ID3v2 tag in
  front, with and without a seek table) decoded to exactly the WAV
  files they were made from, their integer samples' MD5 equal to
  STREAMINFO's, seeking landing on the frame holding the target with the
  WAV's samples there, and damaged frames refused (never a crash);
- Vorbis: Ogg Vorbis files libvorbis made through ffmpeg (qualities -1
  to 10, 8 to 96 kHz, 1, 2, 3 and 6 channels, one with digital silence)
  decoded through a test-only page splitter and through the Ogg
  demuxer, against libvorbis' own decoding: at least 100 dB, largest
  error at most 1e-4, the reference's length, no samples from the first
  packet; the inverse MDCT against its definition;
- MP3: files lame and ffmpeg made (MPEG-1 32 to 320 kbit/s, VBR, ABR,
  mono, joint, stereo, forced mid/side, CRC, no reservoir, transients
  for short blocks, MPEG-2 and 2.5 rates, ID3 tags, no LAME tag, MP3 in
  WAV, uneven pieces) against ffmpeg's mp3float (the same number of
  samples, so the gapless trims agree, and ISO 11172-4 full accuracy),
  free format against lame's own decoder, seeking, and damaged streams
  decoding without crashing;
- containers: 27 files ffmpeg muxed (Ogg Opus, Vorbis and FLAC, a
  chained Ogg, WebM with Opus, Vorbis, live, VP8 and VP9, Matroska with
  FLAC, MP3, PCM both ways, floats and AV1, MP4 with Opus, FLAC, MP3,
  PCM, AAC, VP9, AV1, fragmented, and H.264 with B-frames and an edit
  list) plus a Matroska file the script writes byte by byte (every
  lacing, header stripping, unknown sizes, a BlockGroup): every packet's
  size, MD5, time, duration and key flag against ffprobe's, the tracks'
  codecs, rates, sizes and setup data, seeking, a fragmented MP4 opened
  from its init segment and then appended to, and every file cut short
  and with bytes overwritten (only EMediaError may come out);
- end to end: the container fixtures decoded as a player would, the
  lossless ones exactly the source WAV, the lossy ones its length to
  the sample and without a shift;
- Opus: the RFC 8251 test vectors (01 to 12), decoded stereo and mono
  at 48 kHz: every packet's final range equal to the encoder's, and the
  output passing opus_compare's quality measure (ported; its band
  spectrum through an FFT) against `testvectorNN.dec` or `NNm.dec`, as
  the reference's run_vectors.sh allows; libopus fixtures (SILK at each
  band and frame size, with in-band FEC, hybrid, CELT low delay at 2.5
  to 10 ms, CBR, 40 and 60 ms, 5.1) against libopus' own decoding at
  over 60 dB; malformed packets, a lost packet, 16 kHz output. The
  vectors come from `OPUS_TEST_VECTORS` (default
  ~/Downloads/sources/opus_testvectors-rfc8251.tar.gz, checksum pinned)
  and are skipped without it; they add about 30 s.
coretest makes a WAV file with `tone` and checks `mediaplay -i` and that
`mediaplay -k`'s MD5 is the file's data chunk's (16-bit samples decode
to floats and back exactly), and that a file that is no media file is
refused.

## Networking

A TCP/IP stack in the kernel (`kernel/network`, units `Network.*`),
beneath BSD-style sockets that are handles like any other.

```
  the network service (DHCP, DHCPv6, settings, state files)   host nslookup hostname
  resolver: Sys.HostLookup > Sys.HostNames > Sys.DnsQueries (Sys.DnsCache) > Sys.DnsMessages
  programs: Sys.Sockets, Sys.NetworkInterfaces,    ping ifconfig route arp ndp
            Sys.AddressText                         netstat ss nc wget
=========== system calls 104-127 (Processes.SocketCalls, .NetworkCalls) ====
  Network.SocketOperations   bind listen accept connect send receive ...
  Network.Sockets            the socket object, readiness events, waits
  Network.TcpSockets | Network.Udp | Network.IcmpSockets
  Network.Tcp*  (connections, segments, input, output, timers, states)
  Network.IpOutput  Network.IpDatagrams   (either IP version, for the above)
  Network.Ipv4  Network.Fragments  Network.Icmp  Network.Routing
  Network.Ipv6  Network.Ipv6Headers  Network.Ipv6Fragments  Network.Icmpv6
  Network.Ipv6Routing  Network.Ipv6AddressList  Network.Ipv6Interfaces
  Network.NeighborDiscovery  Network.RouterDiscovery  Network.Mld
  Network.Ipv6Identifiers  Network.TemporaryAddresses  Network.Ipv6Redirects
  Network.Ipv6DestinationCache  Network.MulticastGroups  Network.Igmp
  Network.SocketMemberships   (privacy addresses, PMTU, redirects, multicast)
  Network.Arp   Network.NeighborCache   Network.Ethernet   Network.Loopback
  Network.Interfaces          (one per adapter; lo is number 1)
  Network.Statistics          the protocols' counters (netstat -s)
  Network.Core                the lock, the receive queue, the wake-ups
  Network.Thread              received frames and timers
=========== Io.NetworkAdapters (the driver interface) ======================
  Drivers.VirtioNet (and the e1000/e1000e/RTL8139 drivers)
```

**The adapter interface** (`Io.NetworkAdapters`). A driver registers each
card with `RegisterNetworkAdapter`: a `Transmit` routine (copies one
Ethernet frame, at dispatch level or below, never waits; False when it
has no room, and the driver later calls `NetworkTransmitReady`), a
`LinkUp` routine and the Ethernet address. The adapter is named `eth0`,
`eth1`... in the order of registration. Received frames come back
through `NetworkFrameReceived` from the driver's deferred routine (the
frame is copied there into a packet and queued), a changed link through
`NetworkLinkChanged`. Registering sets the network layer up the first
time (so the loopback interface is always first); frames that arrive
before the network thread runs wait in the receive queue. Drivers
handle their own suspend and resume and keep their adapter across S3.

**Threads and levels.** No protocol work is done in an interrupt or a
deferred routine: they only queue the frame (a spin-locked queue of at
most 512 packets; more are dropped and counted) or mark the interface
(`PendingEvents`, atomically) and signal the network thread's event.
The network thread (`Network`, priority 13) takes the frames a batch at
a time, sends what waited on the interfaces, and runs the timers. All
other protocol work runs on the threads of programs inside their
socket calls. Everything happens at passive level.

**Locking.** One mutex, the network lock (`Network.Core`), covers all
protocol state: interfaces, routes, the ARP cache, fragments, sockets
and connections. The network thread takes it per batch; each socket
operation takes it for its work and drops it while it waits
(`WaitOnSocket`). Drivers' `Transmit` is called with the lock held
(drivers never wait), so sending needs no queueing; the loopback
interface's "transmit" puts the datagram on the receive queue, so a
datagram sent to this machine is handled later by the thread and never
re-enters the protocols inside the sender's call. Lock order: process
lock, then network lock, then spin locks (the receive queue, drivers').
The DNS server list has a spin lock of its own. Timers: whoever needs
to be called by a time asks the thread for a wake-up
(`RequestNetworkWakeAt`); the thread sleeps until the earliest, then
runs the ARP, reassembly and TCP timer routines, each of which asks
again from its own state.

**Buffers.** A packet (`Network.Packets`) is one heap block with room
for a whole frame after 128 bytes of headroom: each layer on the way
down prepends its header without copying. Received data is handled in
place and copied only where it is kept: into a socket's datagram queue
(at most 64 datagrams or 128 KiB), into a TCP connection's receive ring
(64 KiB, growing up to 4 MiB), or into a reassembly buffer. TCP keeps
sent data in a send ring (likewise) until it is acknowledged and
retransmits from there.

**Ethernet and ARP.** Frames for another station are dropped, and so is
multicast but IP's (IPv6's 33:33 and a group's last four bytes, IPv4's
01:00:5e and its low 23 bits, which IP filters by the groups the
interface listens to). A driver may give `TNetworkDriverRoutines` a
`SetMulticastFilter` routine: `Network.MulticastGroups` then hands it
the Ethernet addresses of every group the interface listens to
(all-nodes, all-hosts, the solicited-node groups, what programs joined;
all multicast past 64) whenever they change. None does yet: every
driver takes all multicast (virtio-net is promiscuous in QEMU without
`VIRTIO_NET_F_CTRL_RX`, the e1000 family sets "multicast promiscuous",
the Realtek chips fill their multicast filter with ones) and sets the
routine to nil. The ARP cache (64 entries) keeps an answer for ten minutes;
a datagram to an unknown neighbour waits on its incomplete entry (up to
8 per entry) while a request is sent once a second, three times; then
the datagrams are dropped and each local sender gets an ICMP host
unreachable (sent to itself through lo, so ping shows "Destination Host
Unreachable"). Requests for our address are answered and the asker
remembered; a new address is announced with a gratuitous request.

**Martian addresses** (`Network.InputFilter`, RFC 1812 5.3.7, RFC 1122
3.2.1.3, RFC 4291 2.5). Before anything else, a datagram whose
addresses cannot be genuine is dropped (counted as an address error).
127.0.0.0/8 and ::1 come in only on lo, as source or destination: a
datagram to 127.0.0.1 or ::1 from an Ethernet interface never reaches a
service that listens only on lo (TCP included). Nor does a source that
is one of our own addresses, or the arrival interface's subnet
broadcast (an answer would reflect to the whole subnet), come in from
outside; a limited-broadcast, multicast or IPv4-mapped source, a
destination of 0.0.0.0, :: or an IPv4-mapped one, and 0.0.0.0 as the
source of anything but UDP and IGMP are dropped everywhere. Going out,
a loopback source never leaves by another interface than lo
(`ErrorNetworkUnreachable`). Self tests inject crafted datagrams on a
test interface that is not in the table (`Kernel.NetworkPacketCrafting`,
`Kernel.NetworkHardeningSelfTest`); Ipv6Test checks the rules on
crafted headers.

**IPv4.** Datagrams are checked (version, lengths, header checksum) and
taken if addressed to any of this machine's addresses (the weak host
model), to 255.255.255.255, to the arrival interface's subnet
broadcast, or - UDP to port 68 only - to anything on an interface with
no address yet (what a DHCP client needs). Identifications are a keyed
hash of the addresses and protocol plus a counter from a table picked
by a second hash (RFC 7739 5.3, `Network.UnpredictableNumbers`). Nothing is forwarded. Fragments are put
together (RFC 815: one buffer, a bitmap of 8-byte blocks, at most 8
datagrams at once for 30 s each). Nothing is sent in fragments: a
datagram larger than the interface's MTU (1500) fails with
`ErrorMessageTooLong`, and TCP sets "don't fragment". The routing table
(`Network.Routing`) has an interface route for each interface's network
(added and removed with the address) and routes added by hand (the
default gateway); a lookup takes the longest prefix on an interface that
is up, the lowest metric among equals. Datagrams to this machine's own
addresses go through lo; a broadcast goes out of the interface it
belongs to (the bound one, the subnet's, else the default route's).

**ICMP.** Echo requests are answered (not broadcast ones). Echo replies
and errors about echo requests go to the ICMP echo sockets with the
request's identifier; raw ICMP sockets get every message. Destination
unreachable and time exceeded about UDP or TCP go to the socket or
connection; errors are sent for an unknown protocol, a closed UDP port
and a failed ARP, never about an ICMP error, a broadcast or a later
fragment. An error that comes in is believed only about a datagram we
sent (its quoted source is ours), and a "fragmentation needed" about
TCP only if the sequence number it quotes is in flight on that
connection (RFC 5927 4.1). Token buckets (`Network.TokenBuckets`) limit
the errors sent to other machines (100 a second, bursts of 50), echo
replies to them (1000, 200) and the errors taken in from them (200,
50), for ICMP and ICMPv6 alike (RFC 1812 4.3.2.8, RFC 4443 2.4 (f));
this machine's own traffic over lo is not limited.

**UDP.** A datagram goes to the socket bound to its port that fits best
(bound to its address before bound to every address, a connected one
before an unconnected one); a broadcast to every socket bound to the
port; with none, the sender gets port unreachable. A connected socket
hears of a port unreachable that comes back (`ErrorConnectionRefused`
on its next call). Broadcasts need `SocketOptionBroadcast`. A datagram
to a multicast group (either version) goes to every socket bound to the
port and to every address or the group, whichever socket joined it (as
Linux's default `IP_MULTICAST_ALL`); over IPv6 a datagram without a
checksum is dropped. Over IPv4 a datagram must fit one frame; over IPv6
it may be up to `MaximumIpv6DatagramBytes` (65527) and is sent in
fragments when larger than the path MTU (one too large for a packet is
built in a buffer of its own, `SendLargeIpPayload`).

**Multicast sockets** (`Network.SocketMemberships`,
`Network.MulticastGroups`, `Network.Igmp`, `Network.Mld`). A UDP socket
joins a group with `SocketOptionJoinGroup` (and leaves it with
`SocketOptionLeaveGroup`): the value is the address of a
`TAbiMulticastMembership` (family, group, interface index, or an IPv4
interface address; none: the interface the routes give the group), at
most 8 per socket, all left when it closes (IPV6_JOIN_GROUP and
IP_ADD_MEMBERSHIP in one; an IPv6 socket may join IPv4 groups unless it
is IPv6-only). The interfaces count who joined each group: the first
join reports it - IPv6 by MLDv2 (the interface's whole state, twice),
IPv4 by IGMPv3 ("change to exclude", twice a second apart) - and the
last leave reports it gone ("change to include no sources", twice).
IGMP answers queries at once and speaks version 2 (membership reports
to the group, leaves to 224.0.0.2) for 260 s after hearing a v1 or v2
query; its messages go with time to live 1 and the router alert option.
Groups of interface-local scope, all-nodes and all-hosts are never
reported. IPv4 now takes datagrams for 224.0.0.1 and the groups joined
on the arrival interface (lo takes every group), and sends multicast
out of `SocketOptionMulticastInterface` (else the routes' interface) to
the group's 01:00:5e address. `SocketOptionMulticastHops` (1 at first)
is the hop limit of multicast sent; with `SocketOptionMulticastLoop`
(on at first) a copy of what is sent to a group the leaving interface
joined comes back through lo. `Sys.Sockets.ChangeMulticastMembership`
is the library's call.

**Both IP versions.** Endpoints (`TNetworkEndpoint`) carry the family,
an IPv4 address or an IPv6 one (`Address6`) with the scope id of a
link-local address; sockets and connections compare them with
`EndpointsEqual` and friends (`Network.Addresses`). Received datagrams
reach UDP, TCP and the ICMP sockets as a `TIpDatagram`
(`Network.IpDatagrams`), which gives their endpoints and pseudo-header
sum whichever version brought them; going out, `Network.IpOutput`
chooses the source address, the payload limit and the pseudo-header sum
and hands the packet to `Network.Ipv4` or `Network.Ipv6`. A socket is of
one family (`TSocket.Family`), but an IPv6 socket also carries IPv4 as
v4-mapped addresses (::ffff:a.b.c.d) unless `SocketOptionIpv6Only` is
set (off at first, as on Linux; set before binding): bound to :: it
takes IPv4 datagrams and connections too (`SocketTakesFamily`; a TCP
listener on :: is found for an IPv4 SYN after any IPv4 listener of the
port), and binding, connecting or sending to ::ffff:a.b.c.d means the
IPv4 address. Inside, such a socket's endpoints are IPv4 ones;
`Network.SocketOperations` maps every endpoint an IPv6 socket hands back
(accept, receive, local and peer addresses) and the socket listing to
::ffff:a.b.c.d. A dual-stack socket on :: has the port for IPv4 as
well, so an IPv4 socket on the same port gets `ErrorAddressInUse`; a
program that binds both sets `SocketOptionIpv6Only` on its IPv6 socket
(sshd does, as OpenSSH). An IPv6-only socket refuses v4-mapped
addresses (`ErrorNetworkUnreachable`, binding: `ErrorInvalidArgument`),
and a socket bound to an address of one family cannot reach the other.
`Sys.InternetAddresses` writes v4-mapped addresses as RFC 5952 says
(::ffff:127.0.0.1). The ICMP sockets of an IPv6 socket speak ICMPv6 (echo request 128,
reply 129; the kernel fills in every checksum, which covers the
pseudo-header).

**IPv6** (RFC 8200; `Network.Ipv6`). A datagram is checked (version,
payload length) and taken if it is for one of this machine's addresses
(not a tentative one) or for a multicast group the interface listens to
(all-nodes, and the solicited-node group of each of its addresses);
then its extension headers are walked (`Network.Ipv6Headers`):
hop-by-hop options (first only) and destination options are looked
through (padding and router alert known; an unknown option skipped or
the datagram dropped, with a parameter problem, as its two high bits
say), a routing header with segments left is refused, "no next header"
ends it, and a fragment goes to reassembly (`Network.Ipv6Fragments`: as
IPv4's, 16 datagrams at once for 60 s, at most 4 of them for the
senders of one /64, which then push out their own oldest; the whole
datagram is walked again; atomic fragments are passed over). RFC 5722:
a fragment that overlaps one that came, or disagrees about the end,
gives up the whole datagram silently (`Network.ReassemblyBlocks`); an
exact copy is dropped alone. RFC 8200 4.5 / RFC 7112: a first fragment
that does not hold the whole header chain up to the upper-layer header
is refused with a parameter problem (code 3). ICMPv6, UDP and TCP get what
is left; another protocol a parameter problem. Lo (::1) carries IPv6 as
it carries IPv4: its receive side looks at the version nibble. Going
out, a datagram to one of our addresses goes through lo; to a
link-local address or a multicast group by the interface its zone names
(the socket's interface, the address's scope id, else the first
Ethernet interface with IPv6); others by the routes
(`Network.Ipv6Routing`: interface routes for fe80::/64 and manual
prefixes, on-link prefixes and default routes from routers that expire
with their lifetimes, routes by hand; the longest prefix on an interface
that is up and running, the lowest metric among equals), or the first
hop a redirect gave. The source follows RFC 6724 (`AddressSelection`
in shared/, used by `Network.Ipv6AddressList`): of the ready addresses
of every interface (weak host) the rules pick the destination itself,
the appropriate scope, not deprecated, the outgoing interface's, a
matching label in the full policy table, a temporary address when the
outgoing interface makes them, the longest matching prefix; a
destination within the link only gets the link's own addresses, one
beyond it never a link-local one. Multicast goes to its 33:33 address,
the rest through the neighbour cache. A datagram larger than the path
MTU is sent in fragments (`Network.FragmentBuilder`: the IPv6 header
and a hop-by-hop header stay in front of each, pieces of a multiple of
eight bytes, one random identification); the hop limit is the socket's
(`SocketOptionTimeToLive`, `SocketOptionMulticastHops` for groups) or
what a router advertised (64).

**Path MTU and the destination cache** (RFC 8201, RFC 4861 5.1;
`Network.Ipv6DestinationCache` over `Network.DestinationTable`, 64
entries, the least recently used giving way). A Packet Too Big about a
datagram from one of our addresses lowers the path MTU to its
destination (never below 1280) for ten minutes, after which the link's
is tried again; `Ipv6PayloadLimit` (so TCP's MSS) and fragmenting use
it, and TCP's connections to the destination are told at once
(`TcpPathMtuChanged`) - but only by a Packet Too Big about TCP that
quotes a sequence number in flight (RFC 5927 4.1); one about anything
else lowers only the cache. A path MTU learned again after the old one
expired is kept (it used to be lost with the expired entry). A redirect (RFC 4861 8.1: link-local source, hop
limit 255, code 0, at least 40 bytes, a destination that is not
multicast, from the router that is the destination's first hop now, a
target that is link-local or the destination itself, options with
lengths) gives the destination a first hop of its own for ten minutes
(`Network.Ipv6Redirects`), and the target's link-layer address goes to
the neighbour cache. What was learned through an interface goes when
IPv6 stops on it.

**Addresses and Neighbor Discovery** (RFC 4861, 4862;
`Network.Ipv6Interfaces`, `Network.NeighborDiscovery`,
`Network.RouterDiscovery`, `Network.NeighborCache`, `Network.Mld`).
Each interface has an IPv6 mode: `Ipv6ModeAutomatic` (Ethernet's at
first), `Ipv6ModeLinkLocal` (lo's, with ::1; RAs ignored) or
`Ipv6ModeOff`. IPv6 starts on an interface when it is up with its link
and its mode is not off: the link-local address (fe80:: with the
interface's identifier) is made, and every
new address is tentative while duplicate address detection runs (one
solicitation from ::, a second's wait; an advertisement for it, or
another host's probe for it, removes it as a duplicate). The groups are
reported by MLDv2 (two unsolicited reports, a report for each query;
from :: while the link-local address is tentative, with the hop-by-hop
router alert) so that snooping switches pass solicitations on. Once the
link-local address is ready an automatic interface solicits routers
(three solicitations, 4 s apart, until an advertisement comes). An
advertisement (link-local source, hop limit 255) gives the default route
through the router for its lifetime (metric: the interface's index, so
eth0's router wins among equals), its hop limit, reachable time and
retransmission timer, the link MTU (option 5), on-link prefix routes
(L) and SLAAC addresses for 64-bit prefixes (A: the prefix and our
identifier, with the valid and preferred lifetimes and RFC 4862 5.5.3
e's two hours, and a temporary address beside it, below), DNS servers (RDNSS, RFC 8106; listed with the
interface for the network service) and its M and O flags (kept as the
interface's `Ipv6RouterFlags`, `Ipv6RouterFlagManaged` and
`Ipv6RouterFlagOtherConfiguration`, for the network service's DHCPv6
client). Addresses a DHCPv6 server leased come from the network service
with their lifetimes (`InterfaceChangeAddressLifetimes`, origin
`Ipv6OriginDhcp`, flag `InterfaceAddressFlagDhcp`; adding one again
renews its lifetimes) and bring no prefix route. Addresses past their
preferred lifetime are deprecated, past their valid one removed. When
the link or the interface goes, the link-local, automatic and DHCPv6
addresses, what routers gave and the neighbours are dropped; manual
addresses stay and are tested again. The neighbour cache (64 entries) is RFC 4861 7.3's:
INCOMPLETE (multicast solicitations once a second, three times; the
waiting datagrams' senders then get "address unreachable"), REACHABLE
for the reachable time after a solicited advertisement, STALE (still
used; the first use waits 5 s, then three unicast probes a second
apart, unanswered: forgotten; unused for ten minutes: forgotten).
Solicitations for our addresses are answered and teach us the asker's
address.

**Interface identifiers and temporary addresses**
(`Network.Ipv6Identifiers`, `Network.InterfaceIdentifiers`,
`Network.TemporaryAddresses`). An interface's `Ipv6Options` say how it
makes its addresses; Ethernet interfaces start with
`Ipv6OptionTemporaryAddresses` and stable-privacy identifiers, lo with
none. The link-local and SLAAC addresses take a stable-privacy
identifier (RFC 7217): the first 64 bits of SHA-256 over the prefix,
the Ethernet address, the DAD counter and a 32-byte secret
(`Network.Sha256`), skipping the identifiers RFC 5453 reserves; the
same on one network for ever, different on each. A duplicate is made
again with the next DAD counter (three times at most).
`Ipv6OptionEui64Identifiers` goes back to the modified EUI-64 one. The
secret is the network service's: it keeps one in
/var/lib/network/stable-secret (64 hex digits, readable by root alone,
made on the first start) and hands it over before it sets anything up
(`InterfaceChangeStableSecret`, `Sys.NetworkInterfaces.SetIpv6StableSecret`);
until then a random one stands in, and a new secret starts IPv6 again on
the interfaces that use it. With temporary addresses (RFC 8981) each
SLAAC address gets one beside it with a random identifier
(`Ipv6OriginTemporary`, flags automatic and `InterfaceAddressFlagTemporary`),
valid at most two days and preferred at most one day less a random
DESYNC_FACTOR (up to 0.4 day), never longer than its prefix; five
seconds before it is deprecated its successor is made, and the old one
stays, deprecated, until its valid lifetime ends (one is dropped to
make room if the table, now 11 addresses an interface, is full). A
router renewing the prefix renews them within those limits; a
duplicate is replaced (three times in a row at most). Source selection
prefers them (rule 7). `ifconfig eth0 inet6 tempaddr|notempaddr|stable|eui64`
changes the options (`InterfaceChangeIpv6Options`), and marks temporary
addresses "temporary". The listing's `MaximumInterfaceAddresses` is 12.

**ICMPv6** (RFC 4443; `Network.Icmpv6`). Echo requests are answered,
multicast ones too (from an address of the arrival interface). Echo
replies and errors about echo requests go to the IPv6 echo sockets with
the identifier, raw ICMPv6 sockets get everything; destination
unreachable about UDP or TCP reaches the socket or connection (no route:
`ErrorNetworkUnreachable`, address unreachable: `ErrorHostUnreachable`,
port: `ErrorConnectionRefused`). Errors are sent for an unknown next
header or option, a routing header with segments left, a closed UDP port
and a neighbour that never answered; never about an ICMPv6 error, a
datagram to a group or from a non-unicast address; they quote what fits
in 1280 bytes. Packet Too Big and redirects (137) are handled as the
destination cache says.

**TCP** (RFC 793 with RFC 1122, 5681, 6298, 7323, 2018, 6675, 6582).
Connections
(`TTcpConnection`) live apart from sockets: a listener makes a child in
SYN_RECEIVED for each SYN while the backlog has room (counting children
not yet accepted), and the child joins the accept queue when the
handshake completes; a connection outlives its socket while it closes.

- *Half-open children* get no buffers: their SYN-ACK offers the receive
  buffer they will have, and the buffers come with the handshake's last
  ACK. All listeners together keep at most 256 children in
  SYN_RECEIVED; when a listener's backlog (or that total) is reached,
  its oldest half-open child gives way to the new SYN (a flood pushes
  out its own), and with none to give way the SYN is dropped. No SYN
  cookies.
- *Input* follows "Segment Arrives": the window check
  (`Network.TcpAcceptance`; an unacceptable segment gets an ACK; a zero
  window still takes the ACK of a segment at RCV.NXT, cutting its data
  away and answering with the window), trimming to the window, then
  RFC 5961's defences against blind attacks: a reset ends the
  connection only at exactly RCV.NXT (elsewhere in the window it gets a
  challenge ACK, outside it nothing), a SYN never resets a synchronized
  connection but gets a challenge ACK wherever it falls, and an
  acknowledgment beyond SND.MAX or older than SND.UNA less the largest
  window the peer offered gets one and goes no further; challenge ACKs
  are limited to 10 a second per connection. A SYN for a connection in
  TIME_WAIT beyond its sequence numbers (and timestamps) opens a new one
  (RFC 1122 4.2.2.13, RFC 6191). The acknowledgment frees the send ring and moves FIN_WAIT_1,
  CLOSING and LAST_ACK on, the send window is updated by the RFC 793
  rule, data in order goes to the receive ring and segments that arrive
  ahead (as many bytes as the receive ring holds) wait to be joined, a
  FIN in order ends the stream.
- *Options* (`Network.TcpOptions`): our SYN carries the MSS, SACK
  permitted, timestamps and a window scale of 7; a SYN-ACK only what the
  peer's SYN had, and each is used only when both sides sent it
  (`SocketOptionTcpFeatures` shows which). Laid out as other stacks do
  (20 bytes on a SYN; 12 for timestamps and 4 + 8 per SACK block after,
  data and options within the MSS, RFC 6691).
- *Window scaling* (RFC 7323, `Network.TcpWindows`): windows we
  advertise are in 128-byte units (up to 8 MiB), rounded so that the
  right edge never moves back; the peer's are shifted by its scale.
  Without scaling windows stay at most 64 KiB.
- *Timestamps* (RFC 7323): every segment but a reset carries TSval (a
  millisecond clock) and echoes TS.Recent, kept from segments that reach
  back to our last acknowledgment; PAWS drops (with an ACK) a segment
  whose TSval is older than TS.Recent, unless the connection was idle
  for 24 days; RTTM takes a round trip sample from the echoed TSval once
  a round trip (retransmissions too, which Karn's rule otherwise
  excludes).
- *SACK* (RFC 2018, `Network.TcpReceivedBlocks`, `Network.TcpScoreboard`):
  an acknowledgment carries up to four blocks (three beside timestamps)
  of what waits out of order, the block holding the latest arrival
  first; the sender keeps a scoreboard of up to 32 SACKed ranges above
  its acknowledgment (blocks outside what was sent are ignored), cleared
  on a timeout. No D-SACK.
- *Output* sends what fits in the smaller of the peer's window and the
  congestion window, in segments of at most the MSS (the peer's MSS
  option, or 536, never more than our MTU allows; ours is advertised on
  the SYN) less 12 bytes with timestamps, then the FIN. Nagle holds back
  small segments while data is in flight unless `SocketOptionNoDelay`.
- *Retransmission*: one timer per connection while anything is
  unacknowledged; its timeout is the smoothed round trip plus four times
  its variance, at least 200 ms, at most 60 s, doubled on each expiry;
  one sample a round trip (from timestamps, else one segment at a time
  and never a retransmitted one, Karn); the 200 ms floor is Linux's
  rather than RFC 6298's second. A SYN sent again leaves the data a
  timeout of at least 3 s (RFC 6298 5.7). An expiry goes back to the
  first unacknowledged byte, halves the slow start threshold (once per
  loss, RFC 5681) and drops the congestion window to one segment, ends
  loss recovery and clears the SACK scoreboard. After 12 expiries (5 for
  a SYN) the connection is given up (`ErrorTimedOut`). A zero window is
  probed with one byte on each expiry.
- *Congestion control*: slow start from ten segments, then congestion
  avoidance (a segment per round trip), up to 16 MiB. Loss recovery
  (`Network.TcpRecovery`) starts at three duplicate ACKs, or with SACK
  as soon as RFC 6675's IsLost says the first unacknowledged segment is
  lost, at most once per window of data ("recover", RFC 6582): the
  threshold becomes half the flight and the first hole goes again at
  once. Without SACK it is NewReno (window inflation by duplicates,
  partial ACKs resend the next hole and deflate the window, the full ACK
  ends it). With SACK it is RFC 6675's: while the congestion window
  exceeds the pipe (unSACKed bytes not taken as lost, plus holes resent)
  by a segment, the next lost hole goes, else new data, else a hole not
  yet known lost - only missing segments are resent. No CUBIC.
- *Buffers* (`Network.TcpBuffers`): both rings start at 64 KiB. The
  receive ring grows (doubling, up to 4 MiB) to four times what the
  reader takes in a round trip (measured from echoed timestamps, else
  the sender's estimate, at least 4 ms), with window scaling only; the
  send ring grows when a writer finds it full and the connection could
  keep more in flight. `SocketOptionReceiveBuffer` and
  `SocketOptionSendBuffer` fix a size (2 KiB-4 MiB; set before connect or
  listen, an accepted connection takes its listener's).
- *Keep-alives* (`Network.TcpKeepAlive`, RFC 1122 4.2.3.6) with
  `SocketOptionKeepAlive`: after `SocketOptionKeepIdle` seconds (7200)
  without hearing from the peer, an ACK with the sequence number before
  the next goes every `SocketOptionKeepInterval` seconds (75); after
  `SocketOptionKeepCount` (9) unanswered the connection is reset and the
  socket gets `ErrorTimedOut`. Anything from the peer answers; while data
  waits the retransmission timer watches instead. An accepted
  connection takes its listener's settings. sshd turns them on
  (`TCPKeepAlive`).
- *Path MTU* (`Network.TcpPathMtu`): `TcpPathMtuChanged(Destination,
  PathMtu)` is the entry point for path MTU discovery: every
  synchronized connection to that address whose MSS no longer fits
  lowers it (never below 536, or 1220 over IPv6) and resends what is in
  flight in the new size, without touching the windows. ICMP
  "fragmentation needed" with a next-hop MTU calls it.
- *ACKs* of received data wait up to 40 ms, or go at once for every
  second segment, out of order data and FINs; reading that opens the
  window by two segments sends a window update.
- *Closing*: a socket closed with unread data resets the connection
  (RFC 2525); otherwise the FIN is sent and the connection finishes on
  its own. TIME_WAIT lasts 60 s (twice an MSL of 30 s); FIN_WAIT_2 of a
  connection without its socket ends after 60 s. A closed listener
  resets the children it had not handed out.
- *Unpredictable numbers* (`Network.UnpredictableNumbers` over the pure
  `Network.KeyedNumbers` and `Network.SipHash`, keys from
  `Kernel.Random` at first use): initial sequence numbers are a
  4-microsecond clock plus SipHash-2-4 of the four endpoints (RFC
  6528); every TSval carries a per-connection offset hashed from the
  endpoints (RFC 7323 7.1); a connection's dynamic port is found by RFC
  6056's algorithm 4 (a hashed offset plus a counter that moves on by
  the tries and a small random step), a port with no peer known yet
  (bind, listen, datagram sockets) from a random start.
- *Zero windows*: the probe goes in every state with data still to
  send, the closing ones too; a connection whose socket is gone gives
  up (with a reset) after 8 probes, answered or not.
- *Test hook*: `SocketOptionTestDropEvery` (root's) drops every Nth data
  segment that arrives on the connection, as if lost on the way;
  networktest uses it to make loss over lo.

**Sockets** (`Network.Sockets`) are objects of type `Socket`, so
`CallClose`, inheritance, `CallDuplicateHandle` and passing them in
messages work as for any handle (`HandleKindSocket` = 14). A socket
keeps two notification events in step with its state under the network
lock: Readable (data, a connection to accept, the end of the stream, an
error) and Writable (room to send, or a connection attempt that ended).
`CallWaitForHandles` waits on Readable; `CallWaitForSocket` on either.
`CallWaitForHandles` also takes a file (always ready, as poll says of
files) and a device whose driver keeps no readiness event, so a program
can wait on its standard input, whatever it is, and a socket together
(nc does).
`CallRead` and `CallWrite` work on sockets (a receive or send without
flags). Deleting the socket (its last handle closed) closes it.

Who may open what: TCP and UDP sockets, and **ICMP echo sockets**
(`SocketKindDatagram` with `ProtocolIcmp`), are everyone's - an echo
socket can only send echo requests, the kernel puts the socket's own
identifier in each and fills in the checksum, and it receives only the
replies (and errors) for that identifier, so ping needs no privileges
and nobody can forge other ICMP messages or read anyone else's (as
Linux's ping sockets with `ping_group_range` open to all). **Raw ICMP
sockets** (`SocketKindRaw`) are root's: they send any ICMP message and
receive a copy of every one. Binding a TCP or UDP port below 1024 and
binding a socket to an interface (`SocketOptionInterface`) are root's.

| Call | Number | Arguments |
|---|---|---|
| CreateSocket | 104 | family, kind (stream, datagram, raw; or'ed with non-blocking), protocol |
| BindSocket | 105 | handle, address |
| ListenSocket | 106 | handle, backlog (1-64) |
| AcceptSocket | 107 | handle, peer address out (or 0); returns a new handle |
| ConnectSocket | 108 | handle, address (non-blocking: `ErrorInProgress`) |
| SendSocket | 109 | handle, buffer, length, flags, address (0: the peer) |
| ReceiveSocket | 110 | handle, buffer, length, flags (peek, don't wait), address out |
| ShutdownSocket | 111 | handle, receive / send / both |
| GetSocketOption, SetSocketOption | 112, 113 | handle, option (, value) |
| GetSocketAddress | 114 | handle, local or peer, address out |
| WaitForSocket | 115 | handle, readable / writable, timeout |
| ListNetworkInterfaces | 116 | buffer, capacity (`TAbiNetworkInterface`) |
| ConfigureNetworkInterface | 117 | `TAbiInterfaceConfiguration` (root) |
| ChangeRoute | 118 | add or remove, `TAbiRoute` (root) |
| ListRoutes | 119 | buffer, capacity |
| ListArpEntries | 120 | buffer, capacity |
| ListSockets | 121 | buffer, capacity (every socket, and connections without one) |
| GetDnsServers, SetDnsServers | 122, 123 | `TAbiDnsServers` (setting: root) |
| SetNodeName | 124 | name (root) |
| WatchNetworkChanges | 125 | returns an event handle signaled after each change |
| GetNetworkStatistics | 126 | `TAbiNetworkStatistics` |
| ListNeighbors | 127 | buffer, capacity (`TAbiNeighborEntry`: IPv6's neighbour cache) |

A listing returns how many records there are, at most
`MaximumListedNetworkRecords` (1024): a longer list is cut short there
rather than reporting a count no buffer could be given. Each socket
records its **owner** (`TSocketOwner`): the user and the process that
made it, or that accepted its connection; the listing reports both
(`OwnerUserId`, `OwnerProcessId`, 0 for a connection whose socket is
gone), which `netstat -p` shows with the process's name.

Addresses (`TAbiSocketAddress`) carry a family, sixteen address bytes
(IPv4 in the first four, in the order written; IPv6 all sixteen), a
port in the machine's byte order and, for IPv6, the scope id (the
interface index of a link-local address). Sockets are made with
`AddressFamilyIPv4` or `AddressFamilyIPv6` (ICMPv6 echo and raw sockets
take `ProtocolIcmpv6` or `ProtocolIcmp`); an address of the other
family is `ErrorAddressFamilyNotSupported`. Options: receive and
send timeouts, broadcast, reuse address, time to live, non-blocking, the
pending error (how a non-blocking connect ended), no delay, the kind,
the received time to live (ping shows it), the interface, the bytes
readable, TCP's keep-alives and buffers, IPv6-only (22), joining and
leaving multicast groups (23, 24), the multicast interface, hops and
loop (25-27). Send and receive take five arguments; the dispatcher now
passes R8 on. The ABI is in `shared/Abi.Networking.inc`; the new error
codes (`ErrorConnectionRefused`, `ErrorAddressInUse`,
`ErrorNetworkUnreachable`...) take Linux's numbers. `CallGetTime`
gained `TimeUptimeNanoseconds`, for timing ping replies.

**Statistics** (`Network.Statistics`, `CallGetNetworkStatistics`): the
counters of RFC 1213's groups, kept under the network lock where the
protocols do their work. IP: datagrams received, with header or address
errors, of unknown protocols, delivered, forwarded (always 0), sent,
dropped on the way out (too large, no memory), without a route, and
fragments, reassemblies and failed reassemblies (timed out or pushed
out). ICMP: messages in and out, errors, and each type 0-18 counted
apart (outgoing ones counted in `SendIpv4`, whoever sent them). TCP:
active opens (connect), passive opens (a listener's new child), failed
attempts (SYN_SENT or SYN_RECEIVED to CLOSED), resets of established
connections (ESTABLISHED or CLOSE_WAIT straight to CLOSED), the
connections established now (counted when asked), segments in, out and
retransmitted (a segment that carries data, a SYN or a FIN from before
the furthest sequence number sent), bad segments and resets sent. UDP:
datagrams delivered, to no port, damaged or without room in the
socket's queue, and sent. TCP and UDP count both IP versions; IPv6 has
IP's counters of its own (`Ipv6`), and ICMPv6 its own (`Icmpv6`, with
the types counted in slots: the errors 1-4 and the informational
messages 128-143).

**Configuration.** Anyone may list interfaces (name, description,
Ethernet address, flags up/running/loopback/broadcast, MTU, addresses
- the IPv4 one first, then the IPv6 ones with their flags (tentative,
deprecated, automatic, link-local), eight in all - IPv6 mode, hop
limit, link MTU and the DNS servers routers advertised, packets, bytes,
errors and drops each way), routes of both families (IPv4's first), the
ARP cache, the neighbour cache and the sockets; only root may change an
interface (the IPv4 address and prefix, IPv6 addresses added and
removed one by one - a DHCPv6 lease's with its valid and preferred
lifetimes, `ValidSeconds` and `PreferredSeconds` with
`InterfaceChangeAddressLifetimes` -, the IPv6 mode, up/down, MTU), the routes (an IPv6
route through a link-local gateway names its interface) or the DNS
servers (IPv4 or IPv6 addresses). The kernel keeps the DNS
servers and search domain only for the resolver to read, as it keeps
the time zone's name. Changes are written to the kernel log.

**Startup.** `Io.Startup` starts the virtio-net cards (the other
drivers register theirs alike); `Kernel.Startup` then starts the
network thread (`StartNetworking`). The network service configures the
interfaces (below).

**Watching for changes** (`Network.ChangeWatchers`,
`CallWatchNetworkChanges`, `Sys.NetworkInterfaces.WatchNetworkChanges`).
A program that follows the network gets an automatic reset event that
is signaled after every change: an adapter registered, a link that came
or went, an interface turned on or off or given an address, a route, the
DNS servers. It then lists again. The kernel keeps the events in a
table of 32 with a reference each; one whose handle was closed (only the
table's reference left) is dropped the next time the table is looked
at. A user other than root holds at most 8 (`ErrorTooManyHandles`), and
such users together leave 8 entries for root. Likewise a user other
than root holds at most 32 multicast memberships over all its sockets
and cannot take the interface groups' table below 16 free entries
(`Network.SocketMemberships`); a datagram socket may share a port
(`SocketOptionReuseAddress`) only with sockets of its own user (root
with anyone), and only one of several TCP sockets sharing a port may
listen on it. The network service waits on it instead of polling.

**Ports and interfaces.** Two sockets may bind the same port when both
are bound to interfaces (`SocketOptionInterface`, root's), different
ones: the DHCP client has a socket on port 68 for each interface.

**The node name** (`Processes.NodeName`): the host name
`CallGetSystemInformation` reports, "freepascalos" until root sets
another with `CallSetNodeName` (124; 1 to 63 letters, digits, hyphens
and dots, starting with a letter or digit): `hostname NAME`, or the
network service from `HostName` in Network.settings. `Sys.Information`
has `GetNodeName` and `SetNodeName`.

**The desktop's side.** The settings file and the network service's
state files (`/var/lib/network/NAME.state`: `Method`, `State` - down,
no-link, configuring, configured, failed - `Address`, `Gateway`,
`DnsServers`, `Domain`, `LeaseSeconds`, `LeaseObtained`, `DhcpServer`,
`Ipv6Method`, `Ipv6Addresses`, `Ipv6Gateway`, `Ipv6DnsServers`,
`Dhcpv6`, `Dhcpv6Server`, `Dhcpv6DnsServers`, `Dhcpv6Domains`)
are read in one place, libconfiguration: `Configuration.NetworkSettings`
reads, checks and writes `Network.settings` (method names; a static
address needs a prefix of 1-30 and must be a host of its network, not
0/8, loopback, multicast, its network's address or broadcast; a
gateway must be another host on that network; `Ipv6Method` is auto,
dhcpv6, static or none, a static IPv6 address (`Configuration.Ipv6Checks`)
needs a prefix of 1-128 and must be unicast and not link-local, ::
or ::1, its gateway any unicast IPv6 address (link-local ones too) but
the address itself; DNS servers are IPv4 host addresses or unicast
IPv6 ones, at most four; the search domain a domain name; an empty
`DnsServers` means those DHCP and the routers give),
`Configuration.NetworkState` parses a state file, and
`Configuration.NetworkStatus` puts each interface's state beside the
kernel's facts (link, Ethernet address, MTU, counters, its IPv4
address, every IPv6 address with its flags, the IPv6 mode and default
router) as one record with a condition (disabled, not configured, no
link, failed, connecting, connected; IPv4's) and watches the state
folder. The Control Panel's Network page and the taskbar's
network icon show them (see "The Control Panel" and "The desktop
shell"). Changes go through the system settings service
(`SystemRequestSetNetworkInterface`, `SystemRequestSetDnsServers`,
`SystemSettings.Network`; the request's `NetworkIpv6Method`,
`NetworkIpv6Address` and `NetworkIpv6Gateway`, an empty method leaving
the interface's IPv6 settings as they are): administrators only, every value checked
again there, the interface one the kernel has (not loopback); it only
writes the file, which the network service watches and applies.

**virtio-net** (`Drivers.VirtioNet`): a receive queue that always holds
a 2 KiB buffer per descriptor and a transmit queue of one buffer per
frame (a 12-byte virtio header in front, short frames padded to 60
bytes); no offloads. Both queues and configuration changes (the link
status) interrupt through MSI-X entry 0 (`ConnectVirtioQueuesInterrupt`
in `Drivers.VirtioPci`, which now also offers many chains at once and
takes each finished one back by its head); without MSI-X a 10 ms timer
polls. Suspending marks the card (its frames wait in the network
layer); waking resets it, gives it its queues and receive buffers again
(`RestartVirtioDeviceQueues`) and reports the link and room to send.

### The network service

`/bin/network` (units `NetworkService.*` in `userland/network`), run by
`/etc/services/network.service` in both boot modes (root, `ready =
notify`, restarted on failure up to three times), runs as long as the
system does. Its main loop (`NetworkService.Supervisor`) waits at once
for its notifications (an end request ends it), the system's settings
watcher (`Configuration.Watcher` on `/etc/settings`, group `Network`:
when a value in Network.settings changes - the settings library's and
the system settings service's `.new` file renamed into place included -
it is read again whole and applied; a rewrite that changes nothing is
not), the kernel's network changes, and the DHCP and DHCPv6 clients'
sockets, and wakes at the clients' next deadline (at least every 5 s).

**Settings** (`/etc/settings/Network.settings`, `NetworkService.Settings`):

    HostName = "freepascalos"       optional: the node name
    DnsServers = []                 empty: those DHCP and routers give; a list
                                    (IPv4 or IPv6) overrides them
    SearchDomain = ""               empty: the domain DHCP gives
    DhcpStartWait = false           true: a cold start waits 1-10 s before
                                    the first DHCPDISCOVER (no key: true)

    [Interfaces/eth0]
    Method = "dhcp"                 dhcp, static or none (no Method: static)
    Address = "10.0.2.15/24"        static only
    Gateway = "10.0.2.2"            static only
    Up = true
    Ipv6Method = "auto"             auto, dhcpv6, static or none (no Ipv6Method: auto)
    Ipv6Address = "fd00::10/64"     Ipv6Method static only (no prefix: /64)
    Ipv6Gateway = "fd00::1"         Ipv6Method static only, optional

The default suits QEMU's user networking: eth0 by DHCP, the other cards
left alone. Address and Gateway are read only for `static` (the Control
Panel keeps them for a switch back). An interface with no section is
`none` with `Up = true`. Each interface (`NetworkService.Interfaces`) is
brought in line whenever the settings or the kernel's interfaces change:
if its settings changed, what was applied is undone first - a lease is
given back (DHCPRELEASE) and its address removed, an address the
service set is removed with its routes - then:

| Method | What the service does |
|---|---|
| static | the address, on (or off as Up says), the default route through the gateway (metric 0 for eth0, 1 for eth1, ...) |
| dhcp | on, and a DHCP client started (it waits for the link); `Up = false` gives the lease back and turns the interface off |
| none | nothing: the interface is left as it is, an address set by hand included; only `Up = false` turns it off. An address the service itself had set (static, or a lease) is removed when the method becomes none |

A link that comes or goes, or an interface turned off or on by hand, is
passed to its DHCP client; an adapter that appears later is taken in
like the others.

IPv6 (`NetworkService.Ipv6Settings`, `NetworkService.Ipv6Configuration`)
is applied apart from IPv4, so changing it leaves a lease alone; the
kernel does the protocol work itself (link-local address, router
solicitation, SLAAC, the default route and RDNSS from advertisements),
and the service only sets the interface's IPv6 mode:

| Ipv6Method | What the service does |
|---|---|
| auto | `Ipv6ModeAutomatic` (the kernel's own start, so usually nothing); DHCPv6 as the routers' M and O flags say (below) |
| dhcpv6 | `Ipv6ModeAutomatic` (routes, prefixes and SLAAC from the routers still), and stateful DHCPv6 whatever the routers say |
| static | `Ipv6ModeLinkLocal` (advertisements ignored), the address added, and a default route `::/0` through `Ipv6Gateway` on the interface (the IPv4 metric) |
| none | `Ipv6ModeOff`: the kernel drops every IPv6 address and route of the interface |

When the IPv6 settings change, a static address and its default route
are removed first. The mode is set only when the kernel's differs, and
whatever the kernel learns later (new addresses, routes, RDNSS) is
taken from its change notifications into the state files.

The DNS servers given to the kernel are the settings'
list if it is not empty, else every lease's servers, then the DNS
servers the interfaces' routers advertised, then those DHCPv6 gave
(each once, four at most); the search domain is the settings', else
the first lease's domain, else the first DHCPv6 domain; they are set
only when they change. Asked to end, the service
gives every lease back (the addresses go), writes the state files and
ends with status 0; static addresses stay. Its log is
`/var/log/network.log`.

**The DHCP client** (`NetworkService.DhcpClient`, RFC 2131 4.4; messages
in `NetworkService.DhcpMessages`, leases in `NetworkService.DhcpLeases`)
has a UDP socket per interface (port 68, bound to the interface,
broadcasts allowed) and this state machine:

    Init -DISCOVER-> Selecting -OFFER, REQUEST-> Requesting -ACK-> Probing -> Bound
    Probing -address answered by another host, DECLINE-> (10 s) Init
    Requesting -NAK, or 4 requests unanswered-> Init
    InitReboot (a previous lease) -REQUEST-> Rebooting -ACK-> Probing; -NAK, 3 unanswered-> Init
    Bound -T1-> Renewing (REQUEST to the server, unicast, ciaddr set)
    Renewing -T2-> Rebinding (REQUEST broadcast) -expiry-> address removed, Init
    Renewing, Rebinding -ACK-> Bound; -NAK-> address removed, Init
    any -link lost-> Paused (the lease kept until it runs out) -link back-> InitReboot

Selecting collects the offers for a second after the first
(`NetworkService.DhcpOffers`) and requests the one offering the address
had before, else the first that came; an offer of the address had
before is requested at once. A reply's options may go on in its file
and server name fields (option overload, 52: 1 the file, 2 the server
name, 3 both), read after the options field, the file first, an
overload inside them ignored (RFC 2131 4.1).

The first DHCPDISCOVER of a cold start - the service's first client for
the interface in this run, without a lease kept from before that has
not run out (the state file's address, `LeaseObtained` and
`LeaseSeconds`) - waits 1 to 10 s at random (RFC 2131 4.4.1), so that
machines powered on together do not all ask at once; a lease still
valid is confirmed at once (INIT-REBOOT), and an expired one's address
is asked for in the DISCOVER instead. `DhcpStartWait = false` in
Network.settings turns the wait off, and the shipped Network.settings
does: a clean stop gives the lease back, so every boot would be a cold
start, and the network should be up as soon as the system is. A later
client (the settings changed, the link came back) never waits.

Messages carry the client identifier (61: type 1 and the Ethernet
address), the host name (12: the node name), the address asked for
(50) and the server (54) where they belong, the parameter request list
(55: mask, router, DNS, domain, lease, T1, T2, server id) and the
largest message (57); the broadcast flag is set until there is an
address. Replies are taken by transaction id and hardware address; read
are the offered address, mask (else the address's class), routers, DNS
servers, domain name, lease time (none: for ever), T1 and T2 (else half
and seven eighths of the lease) and the server identifier.
Retransmissions wait 4 s, 8, 16, 32 and at most 64, each moved by up to
a second at random; while renewing and rebinding half the time left, at
least a minute. Times run on the uptime clock. A client with no lease a
minute after it began is "failed" in its state file and goes on trying.
The previous lease's address comes from the state file left by an
earlier run (a crash; a clean stop gives the lease back) or from this
run.

**The DHCPv6 client** (`NetworkService.Dhcpv6Client`, RFC 8415;
messages in `NetworkService.Dhcpv6Messages`, the DUID in
`NetworkService.Dhcpv6Duid`) has a UDP socket per interface (port 546,
bound to the interface) and sends to ff02::1:2 port 547 on the link. Its
mode follows the IPv6 settings and the kernel's `Ipv6RouterFlags`:
Ipv6Method dhcpv6 is stateful; auto is stateful once an advertisement
had M (losing M later stops nothing until the settings change),
stateless with O alone, off with neither; static and none are off, as
is an interface with IPv6 off. The routers still give the default route
and the on-link prefixes: DHCPv6 gives none.

    Soliciting -Advertise (best preference; 255 at once)-> Requesting -Reply-> Bound
    Bound -T1-> Renewing (to the server) -T2-> Rebinding (to any) -valid lifetimes end-> Soliciting
    Renewing, Rebinding -Reply-> Bound; -NoBinding-> Requesting; -NotOnLink-> Soliciting
    Requesting -NoAddrsAvail, NotOnLink, 10 requests unanswered-> Soliciting
    Informing (stateless) -Reply-> Informed -information refresh time-> Informing
    any -link lost-> Paused (the kernel drops the addresses) -link back-> Soliciting or Informing

Messages carry the machine's DUID (client identifier, 1), the server's
(2) where they answer one, the elapsed time (8), an IA_NA (3; IAID: the
Ethernet address's last four bytes) with the addresses had before as
hints, and the option request (6: DNS servers 23, domain search list
24; information refresh time 32 with an information-request). A reply
counts with the transaction id, the client's DUID and a server's DUID.
Advertises are collected during the Solicit's first retransmission time
(about a second); one without an address for the IA_NA is ignored. T1
and T2 of 0 (or T1 above T2) are half and four fifths of the shortest
preferred lifetime. Retransmissions follow RFC 8415 15 (IRT, doubled,
each moved by up to a tenth, at most MRT): Solicit 1 s/3600 s after a
random wait of up to 1 s; Request 1 s/30 s, 10 tries; Renew and Rebind
10 s/600 s until T2 and the end of the valid lifetimes;
Information-request 1 s/3600 s after up to 1 s, refreshed after the
server's refresh time (at least 600 s; 86400 s without one). RELEASE
goes once when the client stops (the service ends, the IPv6 settings
change), not retransmitted. The leased addresses go to the kernel as
/128s with their lifetimes (`AddInterfaceLeasedIpv6Address`), again at
every renewal; the kernel deprecates and removes them as the lifetimes
run out, and those the server stops giving are removed. The DUID is a
DUID-LLT of the first interface that asks, made once and kept in
`/var/lib/network/dhcpv6.duid` ("00:01:00:01:..."), or a DUID-LL when it
cannot be kept. Left out: Confirm after the link comes back (it
solicits again with the old addresses as hints), Reconfigure, rapid
commit, prefix delegation (IA_PD), temporary addresses (IA_TA), the
server unicast option, SOL_MAX_RT and INF_MAX_RT from servers, and
Decline (the kernel's duplicate address detection removes a duplicate
without telling the server).

**The address probe** (`NetworkService.AddressProbe`): before an
offered address is taken, an empty datagram goes to its discard port on
the client's socket. The interface has no address yet, so the kernel's
ARP request for it carries 0.0.0.0 as sender - RFC 5227's probe - and a
second later the ARP cache tells whether a host answered for the
address; then the client declines it. Nobody answering costs nothing:
the datagram is dropped after the kernel's three tries.

### Interface state files (the contract with the desktop)

For each interface but lo the service keeps `/var/lib/network/NAME.state`
(`NetworkService.StateFiles`), in the format of libconfiguration's
settings files (read it with `TSettingsDocument`):

| Key | Kind | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `Method` | string | `static`, `dhcp` or `none` |
| `State` | string | `down`, `no-link`, `configuring`, `configured` or `failed` |
| `Address` | string | `10.0.2.15/24`, or `""` |
| `Gateway` | string | `10.0.2.2`, or `""` |
| `DnsServers` | list of strings | the lease's servers (dhcp), the settings' (static) |
| `Domain` | string | the lease's domain (dhcp), the search domain (static) |
| `LeaseSeconds` | integer | the lease's length; 0 for static, none and an endless lease |
| `LeaseObtained` | integer | Unix time the lease was acknowledged (renewals too); 0 without one |
| `DhcpServer` | string | the server that gave the lease, or `""` |
| `Ipv6Method` | string | `auto`, `dhcpv6`, `static` or `none` |
| `Ipv6Addresses` | list of strings | the kernel's IPv6 addresses with prefixes (`fe80::5054:ff:fe12:3456/64`, `fec0::5054:ff:fe12:3456/64`, a DHCPv6 one as `2001:db8::100/128`), tentative ones left out |
| `Ipv6Gateway` | string | the gateway of the interface's IPv6 default route (`fe80::2`), or `""` |
| `Ipv6DnsServers` | list of strings | the DNS servers its routers advertised (RDNSS) |
| `Dhcpv6` | string | `off`, `no-link`, `configuring`, `configured` (an address leased) or `informed` (DNS servers only) |
| `Dhcpv6Server` | string | the DUID of the DHCPv6 server that gave the lease ("00:03:00:01:..."), or `""` |
| `Dhcpv6DnsServers` | list of strings | the DNS servers DHCPv6 gave (option 23) |
| `Dhcpv6Domains` | list of strings | the domain search list DHCPv6 gave (option 24) |

`State` is `down` while the interface is off (also for dhcp after the
service stopped, and for none without an address), `no-link` while it
has no link, `failed` when its settings cannot be applied or DHCP found
nothing for a minute, `configuring` while DHCP looks for a lease, and
`configured` once it has its address (none: an address set by hand). A
