file is written whole as `NAME.state.new` (0644) and renamed into place,
and only when its text changes, so a program watching the folder hears
of real changes only; the folder (0755) is made by the system disk and
by the service. The desktop watches the folder; the Control Panel
changes the settings by having the system settings service write
`/etc/settings/Network.settings`, which the service picks up through its
watch.

### The resolver

`Sys.HostNames` is the one place programs turn hosts into addresses
(`LookUpHost`: the first IPv4 address; `LookUpHostAddresses`: all, of
the families asked for, IPv4 first, with the canonical name;
`LookUpAddressName`: the reverse; `HostLookupErrorMessage`). A host is a
numeric address (IPv4, or IPv6 as RFC 4291 writes it), then a name in
`/etc/hosts` (`Sys.HostsFile`, read at each lookup), then a name asked
of the DNS servers; "localhost" is 127.0.0.1 even without the file. An
address is named by `/etc/hosts`, then by a PTR record. Errors:
`ErrorNotFound` (no such name, no address, no server), `ErrorTimedOut`
(no server answered), `ErrorWouldBlock` (the servers failed: "try
again").

Its DNS answers are kept in a cache of the process's own
(`Sys.DnsCache`, under a lock in `Sys.DnsQueries`, used with
`UseCache`, which only `Sys.HostNames` sets): 64 answers at most, kept
under the question (the name without case or final dot, and the type)
for the shortest time to live of the answer section (a day at most);
negative answers (NXDOMAIN, and NOERROR without a record of the type)
for the authority section's SOA, the smaller of its time to live and its
MINIMUM (RFC 2308 5, three hours at most), and not at all without an
SOA; server failures, refusals and truncated answers are never kept. A
cached answer comes back with its records' times to live lowered by the
seconds it was kept. A new answer pushes out those that ran out, else
the one that runs out soonest; the cache is emptied whenever the servers
asked differ from those it was filled from (`ClearDnsCache` empties it
by hand).

Below it, `Sys.DnsQueries` (which `host` and `nslookup` use directly)
asks the kernel's servers (or those given) over UDP: each server in
turn, `Attempts` rounds (2), `TimeoutMilliseconds` each (2.5 s). Every
query has a new random id and leaves from a random port of the dynamic
range (`Sys.RandomNumbers`, from `/dev/urandom`), the socket is
connected to the server so only its datagrams come in, and a reply
counts only if its id and question are the query's. A truncated reply
is asked again over TCP; SERVFAIL, REFUSED, NOTIMP and FORMERR pass on
to the next server, the last of them being the answer if none does
better. `QueryDnsSearching` tries a single-label name in the search
domain first. Aliases are followed through the CNAME records of an
answer, and asked for again when the answer stops at an alias, eight
steps at most. `Sys.DnsMessages` builds queries and reads answers into
records (A, AAAA, CNAME, NS, PTR, MX, SOA, TXT; others by length),
checking every length against the message; `Sys.DnsNames` reads names
with their compression pointers, only backwards and at most 64 of them,
so a pointer loop is refused, and makes reverse names (`in-addr.arpa`,
`ip6.arpa`). EDNS(0) (RFC 6891): queries carry an OPT record
advertising 1232 bytes (`EdnsPayloadSize`, `DefaultEdnsPayloadSize`; 0
leaves it out), so larger answers come over UDP (the reply buffer is
1500 bytes); a truncated answer still goes to TCP; a server answering
FORMERR without an OPT record of its own does not know EDNS and is asked
again without it. A reply's OPT record is not kept among the records:
it fills `HasEdns`, `EdnsPayloadSize`, `EdnsVersion` and `EdnsFlags`, and
its extended response code goes into `ResponseCode` (BADVERS); `host -v`
shows it as dig's OPT pseudosection. `Sys.InternetAddresses` reads and
writes IPv6 addresses too (RFC 5952 form).

**netstat** (`userland/netstat`, `Netstat.*`) in the manner of
net-tools: the sockets (`Netstat.Connections`: TCP, then UDP, then ICMP
with `-w`; `-l` servers, `-a` all, otherwise connected ones; `-p` the
owner as "pid/name" from a process snapshot), `-r` the routes with
net-tools' columns (the sorting and flags now in
`Sys.NetworkInterfaces`, shared with route), `-i` the interfaces and
their counters, `-s` the protocol counters in net-tools' words. Every
endpoint goes through `Netstat.Names`: without `-n` a host is named by
`/etc/hosts`, else by a reverse (PTR) lookup through the system's DNS
servers with a short timeout (one second, one try; answers are kept
for the run, and after a server fails to answer no more are asked);
the wildcard address stays a number. A port is named from
`/etc/ports` (`Netstat.Services`, the services(5) format: "name
port/protocol aliases"; it is not called /etc/services because that is
the service manager's folder of definitions), for the socket's
protocol. The routing table stays numeric.

**ss** (`userland/bin/ss.pas`, units in `userland/ss`, built on
netstat's units) in the manner of iproute2: the same list of sockets
(`Ss.Sockets`: netid tcp, udp, or raw for ICMP; ss's states, a UDP or
ICMP socket with a peer ESTAB, one without UNCONN), connected ones by
default (no LISTEN, UNCONN, TIME-WAIT or SYN-RECV), `-l` listening and
unconnected, `-a` all; `-t -u -w -x` the kinds (`-x`, local sockets:
there are none), `-4 -6`, `-n` ports as numbers, `-r` hosts by name
(ports are named by default, hosts not, as iproute2 has it), `-p`
`users:(("nc",pid=412))`, `-e` the owner's user id, `-H` no header,
`-s` the counts (`Ss.Summary`). The kernel keeps no TCP internals
(window, round trip time) to show, so `-i` adds nothing yet. The
table (`Ss.Table`) leaves out Netid when one kind is asked for and
State when one state is, and sizes each column to its widest cell. The
filter (`Ss.Filters`) is iproute2's: `state`/`exclude` with state names
and groups (connected, synchronized, bucket, big, all), then
`sport`/`dport` compared with = != < > <= >= (or eq, ne, lt, gt, le,
ge) against `:22` or a service name, `src`/`dst` against an address
with a prefix and a port (`10.0.0.0/8`, `[::1]:22`, `*:80`), joined
with and, or, not and parentheses, in separate words or one.

**nc** (`userland/nc`, `Netcat.*`) with OpenBSD's options. One thread
relays (`Netcat.Relay`): it waits on the standard input and the socket
together and moves whatever is ready, the input first, so a file is
sent whole before the peer's end is acted on. The peer ending its
stream ends nc; the end of the input shuts the sending side with `-N`,
ends nc after `-q` seconds, or otherwise leaves the socket open for
what the peer still sends; `-w` ends an idle connection and limits
connecting (the socket's send timeout). `-l` listens (TCP: one
connection, or one after another with `-k`; UDP: the first datagram's
sender becomes the peer); `-z` tries ports and ranges, and for UDP
waits for a port unreachable; `-v` writes OpenBSD's messages. Hosts go
through `Sys.HostNames`; `-n` takes numeric addresses only.

**Tools.** `ping` (an ICMP echo socket; per-reply lines and the summary
with loss and min/avg/max/mdev like iputils; `-c -i -W -s -t -q -n`;
the host is looked up by `Sys.HostNames`, and the first line shows the
name and the address, `PING name (addr)`), `ifconfig`
and `route` in the manner of net-tools (rather than an `ip` tool: their
output is what most people know to read, and each does one thing),
`arp`, `host` (BIND's: addresses and mail servers by default, `-t
TYPE`, a reverse lookup for an address, `-v` with the whole answers as
dig prints them, `-T` for TCP, `-W`, `-R`, a server to ask),
`nslookup NAME [SERVER]` (the non-interactive form, `-type=`,
`-timeout=`, `-vc`) and `hostname` (show, `-s`, `-i`, `-I`; set as
root).

**Tests.** `make tcp-test` (in `make test`) builds the TCP's pure units
on the host (`tools/TcpTest`): options written byte for byte and read
back (malformed ones too), scaled window fields and buffer growth, the
SACK scoreboard (merging, IsLost, the pipe and NextSeg over a loss
scenario near the sequence wrap) and the receiver's SACK blocks. A
kernel self test on every boot checks the Internet
checksum, sequence number comparison, a UDP datagram over lo, a refused
connection and a TCP connection's states from the handshake to
TIME_WAIT, with data both ways. coretest runs `networktest` (loopback
ping; UDP echo with the largest datagram and one too large; a refused
broadcast; port unreachable; a megabyte of TCP echo through many windows
with a sender and a server thread; a refused connection; non-blocking
connect and waits; the socket listing; window scaling, SACK and
timestamps agreed over lo, the keep-alive options set, refused and
inherited by an accepted connection, 512 KiB through a forced 4 KiB
receive window and 2 MiB with every 20th data segment lost; then the
network service, started
as a child: eth0 configured by QEMU's DHCP server within 20 s with
10.0.2.15/24, the default route through 10.0.2.2 and the DNS server
10.0.2.3, the whole of `eth0.state`; pings to and the ARP entry of
QEMU's gateway, a TCP echo through QEMU's `guestfwd` to `cat` at
10.0.2.100:7; eth1 made static (192.168.50.2/24) in Network.settings
and back to none, applied by the service at once; the service asked to
end giving the lease back, then started again and left running),
`networktest --unprivileged` as an ordinary user (raw sockets, low
ports, every change refused; ping allowed), and `dnstest`, which runs a
DNS server of its own on 127.0.0.1:53 with a fixed zone (`DnsTest.Zone`:
nothing needs the internet, QEMU's DNS forwards to a host that may have
none) and makes it the system's for a while: `/etc/hosts` both ways, A,
a CNAME answered whole and one asked again, the search domain, several
addresses, AAAA, NXDOMAIN, PTR, a truncated answer asked over TCP, a
compression loop refused, a reply with a wrong id ignored, a missing
server passed over, new ids and ports each time; the cache (a name
and a name that does not exist asked again without a query, a query from
the cache saying so with its time to live lowered, an emptied cache
asking again); EDNS (medium.test.example's 804-byte TXT whole over UDP,
the same truncated and asked over TCP without EDNS, old.test.example's
FORMERR to EDNS asked again without it - the test server answers a
query's OPT record with its own and truncates at the size advertised).
`dnstest --serve` and
`--wait` serve coretest's `host` and `nslookup` command lines; there
are also `ifconfig`, `route`, `arp`, `ping` (`localhost` from
`/etc/hosts`), `hostname` and eth0's state file, and netstat and nc ones:
a listener seen by `netstat -tln` (and its program with `-p`), files
sent both ways by nc over loopback with matching sha256 sums, a UDP
round trip, `nc -z` on an open and a closed port and a range, two
ESTABLISHED ends in `netstat -tn`, the default route in `netstat -r`,
lo and eth0 in `netstat -i`, and the ICMP counters of `netstat -s`
growing after a ping. The network protocol host test (`make network-protocol-test`,
`tools/NetworkProtocolTest`) checks the OPT record built and read (with
BADVERS, and one not owned by the root refused), the cache on a clock of
its own (times to live counted down and run out, RFC 2308's SOA times,
no data, no SOA, SERVFAIL and truncated answers not kept, case and final
dots, the bound of 64), DHCP replies with option overload (both fields,
one, an overload inside a field ignored, an option running past its
field refused) and the choice of offers, and DHCPv6: DUID-LLT and
DUID-LL, a Solicit and a Request byte for byte, an Advertise and Replies
read back (preference, IA_NA, lifetimes, status codes at both levels,
DNS servers, domain list, refresh time), damaged messages refused, T1
and T2 worked out. QEMU's user networking has no DHCPv6 server (and its
advertisements set neither M nor O, so DHCPv6 stays off in the QEMU
tests); DHCPv6 has host tests only. The session test checks
growing after a ping; names: a listener on 8080 shown as `http-alt` by
`netstat -tl` and `ss -tl` and picked by `ss sport = :http-alt`, a
connection over 127.0.0.1 shown as `localhost` by `netstat -t` and `ss
-r`, ss's state and port filters, its header, `-s` and `-x`, and a
filter it cannot read. `make netstat-test` checks the ports file's
parser (and the installed /etc/ports) and ss's filters on the host.
Reverse DNS is not checked in QEMU: dnstest's server answers PTR, but
netstat asks the system's DNS servers. The session test checks
that the network service configured eth0. The QEMU command lines of all
tests and `make run` have a virtio-net card on user networking.

### TLS and wget

**libtls** (`userland/lib/tls`, units `Tls.*`) is a TLS 1.3 client
(RFC 8446) that falls back to TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246) for servers without
1.3, with X.509 certificate checking (name constraints, OCSP stapling)
and session resumption; **wget** fetches over HTTP and, through it,
HTTPS. TLS 1.1 and older are not spoken ("protocol version").

```
  wget (userland/wget: Wget.Urls, .Transfer, .Sessions, .Observer,
        .Sinks, .Progress, .Files, .Settings, .Credentials, .Netrc;
        .Recursion, .Links, .Robots, .RobotsCache, .Patterns,
        .LocalPaths, .Downloads, .Converter, .LinkConversion, .FileText)
=========== libhttp (see "libhttp" below): URLs, HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 =====
=========== Tls.Sessions: over a socket, the system's roots and clock ======
  Tls.SocketTransport  Tls.SystemTrust (/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt)
  Tls.Client           create, handshake, read, write, close, errors, tickets
  Tls.ClientConnections  the same as an object      Tls.SessionCache
  Tls.Handshake (1.3)  Tls.Handshake12 (1.2)  Tls.HandshakeMessages
  Tls.ServerAuthentication  chain + OCSP for both   Tls.KeyShares
  Tls.RecordLayer      records, alerts, handshake reassembly
  Tls.RecordProtection AEAD per direction (1.3 and 1.2 formats)
  Tls.KeySchedule  Tls.KeySchedule12 (PRF, EMS)  Tls.Transcript
  Tls.ClientHello      Tls.ServerMessages  Tls.ServerMessages12  Tls.CipherSuites
  Tls.CertificateChains  Tls.NameConstraints  Tls.Ocsp  Tls.Signatures
  Tls.HostNames  Tls.TrustStore
  Tls.Certificates  Tls.CertificateExtensions  Tls.Asn1  Tls.Pem
  Tls.ByteBuffers  Tls.Errors  Tls.Constants  Tls.ObjectIdentifiers
=========== libcryptography ================================================
```

Everything below `Tls.Sessions` but the socket transport and the trust
store file is plain Pascal over a transport (two routines that send and
receive bytes), so it builds on the host and is tested there.

**Cryptography** (libcryptography). Secret data never decides a branch
or a memory address:

- *Poly1305* in five 26-bit limbs (every product fits in 64 bits), the
  final reduction chosen by masks; *ChaCha20-Poly1305* (RFC 8439 2.8)
  checks the tag in constant time before decrypting anything.
- *AES-GCM* (SP 800-38D, 96-bit nonces): AES on AES-NI
  (`Crypto.AesInstructions`, used whenever CPUID says so), the key
  expansion reading the whole S-box for every byte; GHASH bit by bit
  with masks (no tables). Without AES-NI the table driven AES is still
  there for files at rest, but TLS then offers only ChaCha20-Poly1305.
- *HKDF* (RFC 5869) over any digest; SHA-384 was already there.
- *X25519* (RFC 7748): sixteen 16-bit limbs in signed 64-bit integers, a
  Montgomery ladder with masked swaps and a fixed inversion chain; an
  all-zero result (a small-order point) is refused.
- *Signature checks*, on public data: `Crypto.BigNumbers` (32-bit
  limbs, Montgomery multiplication, up to 8192 bits), RSA PKCS #1 v1.5
  and PSS with MGF1 (`Crypto.Rsa`: exact DigestInfo and padding
  comparisons, a signature as long as the modulus and below it), ECDSA
  on P-256, P-384 and P-521 (`Crypto.EllipticCurves`: Jacobian
  coordinates in Montgomery form, the a = -3 doubling; `Crypto.Ecdsa`:
  r and s in [1, n-1], the digest cut to the order's length, public
  points checked to be on the curve; RFC 6979 nonces shifted for
  P-521's 521-bit order) and Ed25519 (`Crypto.Ed25519`).
- *Key exchange* besides X25519: ECDH on P-256, P-384 and P-521
  (`Crypto.Ecdh`): the private scalar made k + n or k + 2n so it has a
  fixed length, then a Montgomery ladder with masked point swaps (the
  big number arithmetic under it still takes value-dependent time; the
  keys are one-handshake keys); the peer's point must be on the curve.
  ML-KEM-768 (FIPS 203, `Crypto.MlKem` over `Crypto.MlKemPolynomials`
  and SHAKE/SHA-3 in `Crypto.Sha3`): key pairs from a 64-byte seed,
  encapsulation with the modulus check, decapsulation with implicit
  rejection, no secret-dependent branches or table indexes.

**The handshake** (`Tls.Handshake`, `Tls.ClientHello`). The
ClientHello offers TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2 (supported_versions; a program
may narrow it with MinimumVersion/MaximumVersion), the groups x25519,
X25519MLKEM768 (codepoint 0x11EC), secp256r1, secp384r1 and secp521r1
in that order with a key_share for the first only (x25519), the
signature schemes ECDSA P-256/SHA-256, P-384/SHA-384, P-521/SHA-512,
Ed25519, RSA-PSS (rsae and pss, SHA-256/384/512) and RSA PKCS #1 (for
certificates and TLS 1.2 only), server_name (unless the host is an IP
address), status_request (an OCSP staple), ALPN when the program names
protocols, in order, from a comma separated list (libhttp: "h2,http/1.1";
the server must choose one of them), psk_key_exchange_modes (psk_dhe_ke) when
resumption is on, and for TLS 1.2 ec_point_formats (uncompressed),
extended_master_secret and an empty renegotiation_info; a random
32-byte legacy session id and a dummy change_cipher_spec before the
client's second flight (middlebox compatibility, appendix D.4). TLS 1.3
suites: TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 and
TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 in that order with AES-NI, ChaCha20-Poly1305
alone without; TLS 1.2 suites after them (below); a program may choose
(wget `--ciphers`, IANA or OpenSSL names).

- A HelloRetryRequest is answered once: it may ask for another offered
  group (a new share is made: a server that wants secp256r1 or the
  hybrid gets it this way) and/or send a cookie; one asking for the
  group already shared, for a group not offered, or for nothing, is an
  illegal parameter; the transcript then starts with
  message_hash(ClientHello1). A second retry is an unexpected message.
- The ServerHello must echo the session id and pick an offered TLS 1.3
  suite (the retry's, after one), no compression and a share in the
  group that was shared; only offered extensions may come back, each
  once (in every server message). The shared secret (`Tls.KeyShares`:
  X25519, the x coordinate of ECDH, or ML-KEM-768's secret then
  X25519's for the hybrid) feeds the key schedule (`Tls.KeySchedule`:
  Derive-Secret, HKDF-Expand-Label with "tls13 "); the transcript hash
  (`Tls.Transcript`) keeps the ClientHello until the suite says which
  hash to use.
- EncryptedExtensions; a CertificateRequest is answered with an empty
  Certificate (the client has none); the Certificate (no request
  context, 1 to 16 certificates, a status_request staple on the first
  entry) is checked at once (below); CertificateVerify must use an
  offered scheme other than PKCS #1, fit the key's kind (and an ECDSA
  scheme its curve), and verify over 64 spaces, "TLS 1.3, server
  CertificateVerify", a zero and the transcript hash; the server's
  Finished is an HMAC of the transcript compared in constant time.
- Then the application traffic keys; the handshake secrets are wiped
  and the resumption master secret kept. After the handshake a
  KeyUpdate moves the read keys on and, when asked, the client answers
  with its own and moves its write keys; post-handshake authentication
  was not offered and is refused.

**Resumption** (TLS 1.3 PSK, RFC 8446 sections 2.2 and 4.6.1). With a
cache key (`TTlsClientOptions.SessionCacheKey`; `TTlsSocketSession`
uses "host:port") each NewSessionTicket becomes a ticket in
`Tls.SessionCache`: the ticket, its PSK (HKDF-Expand-Label of the
resumption master secret, "resumption", the nonce), the suite, age_add
and lifetime (seven days at most), kept in memory only, at most four
per key, behind a spin lock - only when the certificate was verified.
The next handshake to that key takes the newest live ticket (each is
used once) and offers it last in the ClientHello (pre_shared_key: the
identity, the obfuscated age, and a binder: HMAC with the "res binder"
key of the hash of the ClientHello up to the binders); after a
HelloRetryRequest the ticket goes again only with a suite of its hash.
A server that takes it (selected identity 0, a suite of the same hash)
skips Certificate and CertificateVerify; the early secret comes from
the PSK and a fresh (EC)DHE exchange still happens (psk_dhe_ke). No
0-RTT.

**TLS 1.2** (`Tls.Handshake12`, RFC 5246 with RFC 7627, RFC 5746 and
RFC 8422). A ServerHello without supported_versions and with version
1.2 goes on as TLS 1.2 unless the client wanted only 1.3, it follows a
HelloRetryRequest, or its random ends in the DOWNGRD sentinel (a TLS
1.3 server pushed down, RFC 8446 section 4.1.3). Suites, ECDHE and
AEAD only: TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA/RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256,
_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 and _CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 (no CBC, no RSA key
exchange). The server must take extended_master_secret and send an
empty renegotiation_info (else handshake_failure). Certificate (a
plain list), an optional CertificateStatus (the OCSP staple),
ServerKeyExchange (a named curve offered, not the hybrid; its signature
over both randoms and the curve parameters, by an offered scheme -
PKCS #1 allowed, ECDSA on any curve - with a key that suits the suite:
EC or Ed25519 for ECDSA suites, RSA for RSA ones), an optional
CertificateRequest (answered with an empty Certificate) and
ServerHelloDone; then ClientKeyExchange, the master secret from the
session hash (`Tls.KeySchedule12`: the P_SHA256/P_SHA384 PRF,
"extended master secret"), the key block, change_cipher_spec and
Finished (12 bytes of PRF), and the server's change_cipher_spec and
Finished. A HelloRequest later is answered with a no_renegotiation
warning; there are no session ids or tickets in TLS 1.2.

**Records** (`Tls.RecordLayer`, `Tls.RecordProtection`). A record's
length is checked before it is read (2^14 + 256 protected, 2^14
plain); protected records are opened with the AEAD (nonce = IV XOR the
64-bit sequence number, the header as additional data), the zero
padding stripped and the inner type found. TLS 1.2 records have no
inner type: the additional data is the sequence number, type, version
and plaintext length, AES-GCM's nonce a 4-byte implicit IV and the
8-byte explicit part sent in the record (the sequence number), and the
server's change_cipher_spec switches its keys on; warning alerts other
than close_notify are passed over. change_cipher_spec is
dropped only between the ClientHello and the server's Finished, and
only as the single byte 1; plaintext after the keys are set (but for an
alert), application data during the handshake, empty handshake records
and handshake messages straddling a key change are refused. Handshake
messages are put together across records, at most 256 KiB. Alerts:
close_notify ends the stream (reads return 0), user_canceled is
ignored, every other alert fails the connection. A failure sends the
matching alert (decode_error, bad_certificate, unknown_ca,
certificate_expired, decrypt_error...) once, encrypted when keys are
set; every later call returns the same error. Errors are negative codes
with messages (`Tls.Errors`); certificate errors say which certificate
or host they are about.

**Certificates** (`Tls.Asn1`, `Tls.Certificates`,
`Tls.CertificateExtensions`). The DER reader refuses indefinite and
non-minimal lengths, high tag numbers, elements running past their
parent, negative or padded integers, booleans other than 00/FF and set
unused bits; times are UTCTime (1950-2049) or GeneralizedTime, in Z,
calendar-checked. A certificate's inner and outer signature algorithms
must be the same. Kept: issuer and subject (DER, compared byte for
byte) and their first common names, the validity, the key (RSA,
RSA-PSS, EC P-256/P-384/P-521, Ed25519; others parse but cannot be
used) and the subjectPublicKey bytes (which OCSP hashes), and the
extensions basic constraints, key usage, extended key usage (server
authentication, OCSP signing), subject alternative names, key
identifiers, name constraints, the TLS feature list (RFC 7633: must
staple), certificate policies and authority information access
(recognized, not acted on). No extension twice; any other critical
extension makes the certificate unusable.

**The chain check** (`Tls.CertificateChains`, at the system clock's
time): the server's certificate must be valid, carry no unknown
critical extension and, where it says, allow digital signatures and TLS
servers. A path is then searched from it to a trust anchor: each step
to an anchor (first) or a sent certificate whose subject is the issuer
before and whose key verifies its signature, trying every candidate in
turn (cross-signed roots), at most 8 issuers; a sent certificate that
is itself an anchor ends the path (so a pinned server certificate
works). Each issuer must be an authority (basic constraints), may sign
certificates (key usage), must be valid, must allow the path below it
(path length) and, if it restricts extended key usage, must allow TLS
servers; anchors are trusted as they are (only their validity and path
length count). Then the name constraints (`Tls.NameConstraints`, RFC
5280 4.2.1.10) of every authority on the path, the anchor's too, over
every certificate below it but self-issued intermediates: its subject
(a directoryName, compared RDN by RDN as DER), any emailAddress in it
and its subject alternative names. dNSName "example.com" holds the
name and those below it, ".example.com" only those below; a wildcard
name must lie wholly inside a permitted subtree and is excluded when
anything it can stand for is; iPAddress by address and mask (another
family is outside); rfc822Name as a mailbox, a host or ".domain".
When the permitted subtrees hold a name's type it must lie in one; it
must lie in no excluded subtree. A constraint of a type that cannot be
checked (URI, other names) meeting a name of that type refuses the
certificate as unsupported. A path that breaks a constraint is given
up and the search goes on. Signatures (`Tls.Signatures`): RSA keys of
2048 bits or more, no SHA-1, the key's kind fitting the algorithm,
Ed25519 over the message itself. Last, the host
name (`Tls.HostNames`, RFC 6125/9525): subject alternative names only,
never the common name; an IPv4 literal matches only an iPAddress; DNS
names compare without case and without a final dot; a wildcard only as
the whole leftmost label, for exactly one label, with two more labels
after it. Without a path the most telling reason found on the way is
reported (an expired issuer, a bad signature), else "unknown issuer".
The errors: expired, not yet valid, unknown issuer, name mismatch, bad
signature, not an authority, malformed, unsupported, chain too long,
wrong usage, missing, name constraints (-51), revoked (-52), invalid
OCSP response (-53) and missing OCSP response (-54).

**Revocation** (`Tls.Ocsp`, `Tls.ServerAuthentication`). A stapled OCSP
response (RFC 6960; in the TLS 1.3 certificate entry or TLS 1.2's
CertificateStatus) must be a successful basic response signed by the
issuer the path went through, or by a responder certificate it carries
that the issuer signed, that has id-kp-OCSPSigning and is valid; the
responder id (name or SHA-1 key hash) must name the signer; a single
response must match the certificate (issuer name and key hashed with
SHA-1 or SHA-2, the serial) and be current (five minutes of skew;
without nextUpdate, at most four days old). Revoked fails the
connection (certificate_revoked); an invalid response fails it too
(bad_certificate_status_response); unknown is accepted. No staple is a
soft failure, unless the certificate carries must-staple: then only a
good staple will do. There is no CRL or OCSP fetching. With certificates not verified these errors are
only the ignored one.

**Roots.** `/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt` is the Mozilla CA list
as a PEM bundle (userland/etc/ssl/certs, MPL-2.0, see its README),
installed by `make system-disk`; `Tls.SystemTrust` reads it (or a file
the program names) into a trust store (`Tls.TrustStore`, `Tls.Pem`)
for each session. A root that does not parse is left out.

**The interface.** `Tls.Client` works over any transport:
`CreateTlsClient` (server name, trust store, whether to verify, the
time, ALPN, cipher suites, groups, minimum and maximum version, session
cache key), `TlsHandshake`, `TlsRead` (0 at the end;
`TlsClosedCleanly` tells a close_notify from the transport just
ending), `TlsWrite`, `TlsClose` (close_notify), `TlsErrorDescription`
("the certificate has expired (certificate: example.com)", "the server
sent an alert: handshake failure") and `TlsIgnoredCertificateError`
(what the chain check said when not verifying), and
`TlsProtocolVersionName`, `TlsKeyExchangeGroupName`, `TlsSessionResumed`
and `TlsCertificateStatus` for what was negotiated. `TTlsClientConnection`
(`Tls.ClientConnections`) owns such a connection as an object, and
`TTlsSocketSession` (`Tls.Sessions`) puts it over a connected socket
with a timeout, the system's roots and clock (`Open`, `Read`, `Write`,
`Close`, `DescribeError`), with the server name, trust file and ALPN as
strings, and `Port` and `ResumeSessions` (on) for the ticket cache. Names,
error details and the server's certificate list are strings and
dynamic arrays; the DER, keys and records stay bytes.

**QUIC mode** (`Tls.Quic`, for libquic; RFC 9001 section 4). With
`TTlsClientOptions.Quic` pointing at a `TTlsQuicCallbacks` the same
handshake runs without records: `SendHandshake(Level, Data)` takes each
handshake message with its encryption level (Initial, Handshake,
Application), `ReceiveHandshake(Level, Buffer)` waits for the server's
bytes of the level being read (QUIC pumps the connection meanwhile), and
`InstallSecret(Level, Direction, Suite, Secret)` hands over each traffic
secret as it is made (both handshake secrets at the ServerHello: the
client acknowledges Handshake packets before its Finished). The
ClientHello then offers TLS 1.3 only, leaves the legacy session id
empty, carries quic_transport_parameters (0x39) with the callbacks'
`TransportParameters`, and never resumes; no change_cipher_spec and no
alert is sent: `TlsQuicAlert` gives the alert a failure stands for
(QUIC's CRYPTO_ERROR 0x100 + alert). EncryptedExtensions must carry the
server's transport parameters (`TlsQuicPeerTransportParameters`) and an
ALPN protocol (else `TlsErrorApplicationProtocolMissing`, -22,
no_application_protocol). Without `Quic` nothing changes.

**wget** (`userland/bin/wget.pas`, units in `userland/wget`) is a
program on top of libhttp (below): each request goes through
`THttpClient.Execute`, which looks the host up (`Sys.HostLookup`,
numeric addresses need no DNS), connects within the timeout, runs TLS
for https offering HTTP/2 and HTTP/1.1 by ALPN (`--no-http2`: HTTP/1.1
only), or goes over HTTP/3 (libquic) once the server advertised it by
Alt-Svc (`--no-http3`: never; `--alt-svc-file=FILE` keeps the
advertised alternatives between runs, so even a one-URL run can use
HTTP/3 the next time; "Connecting to HOST:PORT over HTTP/3..." and,
after a failure, the TCP connection as usual), and returns the head with the body left to read; wget's own
units say what it does in GNU wget's words (`Wget.Observer`:
"Resolving...", "Connecting to...", "Reusing existing connection...",
"HTTP request sent, awaiting response..."), decide what each status
means, where the body goes and when to try again (`Wget.Transfer`). The
URL (`Wget.Urls`) is parsed and resolved by libhttp's URL Standard
parser, then wget refuses other schemes, user names and port 0 and
drops the fragment. The request carries Host, User-Agent, Accept,
Accept-Encoding, a Range when continuing, Authorization, Cookie and
"Connection: Keep-Alive"; the head is checked by libhttp (1xx skipped;
a Content-Length that is not a number, two that differ, and transfer
codings other than chunked are refused) and the body framed by it (by
length, chunked with extensions and trailers skipped, or to the end of
the connection; DATA frames over HTTP/2). `-S` shows an HTTP/2 head as
"HTTP/2 200" and its fields.
Redirects 301/302/303/307/308 are followed to http or https URLs only,
at most 20, the file keeping the first URL's name; the file is named
after the URL's last segment (index.html for a directory), with .1,
.2 ... when the name is taken, or as -O says (`-O -` is standard
output; several URLs go into one -O file). `-c` continues with a Range
(a 206 must start where asked; a whole file sent back is refused rather
than the file truncated; 416 means it is complete). A transfer that
breaks or times out is tried again (`-t`, 20 by default, waiting a
second more each time up to ten), continuing where it broke when it
can; unknown hosts, refused connections, certificate failures and
error responses are not tried again. `-S` shows the response heads,
`-q` nothing at all, `-T` limits every wait, `-U` sets the User-Agent,
`--no-check-certificate` warns instead of refusing, `--ca-certificate`
names other roots, `--ciphers` the suites. On a terminal a progress
line (`Wget.Progress`: name, percent, bar, size, speed, estimate) is
redrawn five times a second; elsewhere there is none. Messages and exit
statuses are GNU wget's (4 network, 5 certificate, 6 authentication,
7 protocol, 8 server error...).

What one run keeps from request to request is a `TWgetSession`
(`Wget.Sessions`): the settings, libhttp's client with its connection
pool, the cookie jar and the authenticator.

- **Keep-alive** (libhttp's pool, limited to one idle connection): as
  GNU wget, one connection is kept, for the scheme, host and port it went to; the next request
  there (a redirection, another URL of the command line, the next file
  of a recursion) uses it ("Reusing existing connection to host:80.").
  It is kept only when the response's body had a known end (a length
  or chunks) and the server did not close (HTTP/1.0 must say
  keep-alive); the bodies of redirections and errors are read and
  dropped for that (up to 1 MiB, else the connection is closed). A
  kept connection the server closed meanwhile shows as a failed send or
  no answer, and libhttp sends the request once more on a new one. An
  HTTP/2 connection is shared the same way.
  `--no-http-keep-alive` sends "Connection: close".
- **Cookies** (libhttp's `Http.Cookies`, `Http.CookieDates`,
  `Http.CookieFiles`): a jar as RFC 6265 (and 6265bis) has one: Set-Cookie with Expires (its date
  algorithm), Max-Age (which wins), Domain (domain-matching, no
  top-level domains, never inside an IP address), Path (the default
  path is the request's folder), Secure and HttpOnly; a request gets the
  matching cookies, longer paths first. `--load-cookies` and
  `--save-cookies` read and write Netscape's cookie file format (tabs,
  TRUE/FALSE, `#HttpOnly_`, expiry 0 for session cookies, which are
  written only with `--keep-session-cookies`); `--no-cookies` turns the
  jar off.
- **Authentication** (libhttp's `Http.Authentication`,
  `Http.Challenges`, `Http.Digest`; `Wget.Credentials` and
  `Wget.Netrc` for ~/.netrc): nothing goes until a 401; then the best
  challenge wget can answer is taken (Digest SHA-256, Digest MD5, Basic)
  and the request made again, once (again only for a stale nonce); a
  server that refuses ends with "Username/Password Authentication
  Failed." and status 6. Digest is RFC 7616's: MD5, MD5-sess, SHA-256,
  SHA-256-sess, qop auth or none, userhash, a random client nonce and
  the count going up on later requests with the same nonce, which carry
  the credentials at once (Basic too). The credentials are
  `--http-user`/`--http-password`, else `--user`/`--password`, else the
  host's line in `~/.netrc` (machine, default, macdef skipped; `-e
  netrc=off` turns it off).
- **gzip** (`Wget.Sinks`): bodies go into the file through a sink, with
  libhttp's decoders (`Http.ContentDecoding`) in front when wanted.
  `--compression=auto` or `gzip` asks for gzip (not when continuing)
  and decodes gzip, x-gzip or deflate on the way (libcompression's
  `TInflater`);
  auto leaves .gz and .tgz files as they are; `none` (the default, as
  GNU wget's) asks for identity. A decoded body that breaks starts
  again rather than continuing, and damaged data is status 7.
- **--trust-server-names** names the file after the URL the redirections
  end at.
- **Recursion** (`Wget.Recursion`): `-r` breadth first from each URL,
  into `host/path` files (`Wget.LocalPaths`: a folder's index.html, the
  query kept in the name, `-P` a folder in front, `-nH` no host folder,
  `-nd` no folders), overwriting what is there. A page's links
  (`Wget.Links`: a small tag scanner that skips comments, scripts and
  styles and decodes character references; followed links are a, area,
  link, frame, iframe and meta refresh, requisites img, script,
  stylesheet and icon links, input, embed, audio/video/source/track,
  object and backgrounds; <base> respected) are followed below `-l` (5;
  0 or inf: no limit), and requisites are fetched at any depth with
  `-p` (alone, `-p` fetches one page and what it needs). Only links to
  the same host are followed, with `-np` none above the starting
  folder. Each server's robots.txt is fetched first and kept
  (`Wget.Robots`, RFC 9309: the group naming wget, else *, the longest
  rule winning, * and $ in rules); `-e robots=off` ignores it. `-A`/`-R`
  (`Wget.Patterns`) take suffixes or wildcard patterns; a page they
  reject is fetched for its links and then removed. `-k`
  (`Wget.Converter`, `Wget.LinkConversion`) rewrites the links of every
  saved page at the end: to a relative path for what was fetched (with
  "?" and "#" escaped), to the absolute URL for relative links to what
  was not. `-O` cannot be used with -r or -p.

**Tests.** On the host: `make crypto-test` (RFC 8439's Poly1305 and
AEAD vectors with the reduction edge cases, the GCM specification's
test cases with and without AES-NI, FIPS 180 SHA-384, RFC 5869 HKDF,
RFC 7748 X25519 with 1000 iterations, RFC 6979's ECDSA P-256 and P-384
signatures, RSA PKCS #1 and PSS signatures of 2048 to 4096-bit keys
made by OpenSSL, each also tampered with; ECDH on P-256/384/521 and
P-521 ECDSA (deterministic signatures made the same) against OpenSSL
through Python's cryptography; SHA-3/SHAKE against hashlib and
ML-KEM-768 key pairs, decapsulation and implicit rejection against
OpenSSL), `make tls-test` (strict DER, the host name rules, RFC 8448's
whole 1-RTT handshake through the key schedule, transcript, record
protection, CertificateVerify and both Finished messages, its
HelloRetryRequest transcript, its resumption (sections 3 and 4: the
ticket's PSK, the early secret, the binder, the handshake secrets),
the session cache, retries (cookie, a new group, refused ones) and TLS
1.2 answers (downgrade sentinel, no extended master secret) against a
scripted server, the test certificates of tools/TlsTest/certificates
in good and failing chains, all 118 Mozilla roots parsed and their
self-signatures checked, and fixtures tools/TlsTest/make-fixtures.py
makes with Python's cryptography each run: chains under name
constraints of every kind, Ed25519 and P-521 chains, OCSP responses
(good, revoked, unknown, delegated, stale, for another certificate,
badly signed) and TLS 1.2 PRF outputs; then `run-interop.sh`: whole
connections to OpenSSL's s_server with every TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2
suite, ECDSA, RSA-PSS, Ed25519 and P-521 servers, servers that want
secp256r1, secp384r1 or X25519MLKEM768 (a HelloRetryRequest),
resumption, stapled OCSP responses (good, revoked, must-staple with and
without), a certificate request, key updates both ways and each
failure) and
`make http-test` (libhttp, below) and
`make wget-test` (URLs with RFC 3986's resolution examples, file names,
response heads with their repeated fields and keep-alive rules,
chunked bodies fed in pieces of every size, RFC 6265's dates, cookie
parsing, domain and path matching and ordering, Netscape cookie files
both ways, WWW-Authenticate challenges, Digest against RFC 7616's MD5
and SHA-256 and RFC 2617's examples, Basic against RFC 7617's, .netrc,
link extraction, robots.txt, accept and reject lists, local paths,
relative links and link conversion). In QEMU,
coretest runs `wgettest`, which fetches from test servers on the host
that QEMU's user network reaches through `guestfwd`
(scripts/test-web-server.py over HTTP and HTTPS with the test
certificates, and `openssl s_server -www`): contents by sha256sum,
every suite, redirects, chunked and close-delimited bodies, continuing,
-S, the user agent, a timeout, a 404, and a name mismatch, an unknown
authority and an expired certificate each refused (and accepted with
--no-check-certificate); the server keeps connections alive, so
wgettest also checks several requests over one connection (HTTP and
HTTPS, after redirections and a 404, and not with
--no-http-keep-alive), cookies across a redirection and through cookie
files, Basic and Digest (both algorithms, the credentials sent at once
the second time, ~/.netrc), gzip bodies (plain, chunked, a .gz left
alone, damaged data), --trust-server-names, and recursion over a small
site under /site/ (-r, -l 1, -np, -A, -R, -p, -k, robots.txt and -e
robots=off), and HTTP/2 against 10.0.2.107 (the same server in its
https-h2 mode: contents, -S showing "HTTP/2 200", requests sharing one
connection, redirects, gzip, Digest, continuing, and HTTP/1.1 with
`--no-http2`; checked against the test root, which names 10.0.2.107
too). HTTP/3 is not checked in QEMU yet: guestfwd forwards TCP only;
slirp does pass the guest's UDP to 10.0.2.2 on to the host's loopback,
but that needs a host HTTP/3 server serving many connections with a
certificate under the test root for the advertising origin (QuicTest's
serves one connection with a pinned Ed25519 certificate). test-qemu.sh says so and stops when python3
with ssl or openssl is missing on the host.

### libquic: QUIC and HTTP/3

**libquic** (`userland/lib/quic`, units `Quic.*`, `Qpack.*`, `Http3.*`,
`libquic.so` on libtls) is a QUIC version 1 client (RFC 9000, 9001,
9002) with QPACK (RFC 9204) and HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) on top, and libhttp's
HTTP/3: `Http3.HttpConnections` makes an HTTP/3 connection one of
libhttp's `THttpConnection`s, `Http3.SystemConnections` registers it
with libhttp's Alt-Svc factories. `h3get` fetches a URL with libquic
alone; wget (and every libhttp client that calls `EnableHttp3`) gets
HTTP/3 through libhttp.

**On libhttp, not the other way.** libquic links libhttp (HPACK's
Huffman code, which QPACK shares; header fields; the connection class
it implements) and libhttp knows nothing of QUIC: it only offers
`RegisterConnectionFactory`. A program that wants HTTP/3 links libquic
and calls `EnableHttp3` (or `CreateHttp3Client` in place of
`CreateSystemClient`); one that does not never loads libquic's 350 KB.
The other way (libhttp linking libquic) would have put libquic in every
HTTP program, and made one Huffman unit impossible without a third
library under both.

```
  libhttp's client       Http3.SystemConnections (the "h3" factory, EnableHttp3)
                         Http3.HttpConnections (THttpConnection over the below)
  h3get                  Http3.Requests (a request, its response)
                         Http3.Connections (control/QPACK streams, SETTINGS, GOAWAY)
                         Http3.FrameParser  Http3.Frames  Http3.Constants
                         Qpack.Decoder  Qpack.Encoder  Qpack.DynamicTable
                         Qpack.StaticTable  Qpack.Primitives
                         (libhttp: Http.HpackHuffman, Http.HeaderFields, Http.ByteBuffers)
=========== Quic.Sessions: host and port, the system's roots, NEW_TOKEN cache
  Quic.UdpSockets        a connected UDP socket (Sys.Sockets) as transport
  Quic.Connections       TQuicConnection: Connect, streams, Pump, Close
  Quic.ClientHandshake   libtls in QUIC mode over the CRYPTO streams
  Quic.ConnectionCore    start, keys, transport parameters, the pump
  Quic.PacketReceiving   Quic.FrameHandling   Quic.PacketSending
  Quic.LossRecovery      Quic.Congestion (RTT, NewReno, pacing)
  Quic.StreamTable       Quic.Streams  Quic.SendBuffers  Quic.ReceiveBuffers
  Quic.SentPackets       Quic.ConnectionState (one connection's state)
  Quic.PacketProtection  Quic.InitialSecrets (and the Retry tag)
  Quic.PacketHeaders     Quic.Frames  Quic.FrameWriter  Quic.TransportParameters
  Quic.RangeSets  Quic.ConnectionIds  Quic.Buffers  Quic.VariableIntegers
  Quic.DatagramTransports  Quic.Errors  Quic.Constants
=========== libtls (Tls.Quic), libcryptography ==============================
```

Everything but `Quic.UdpSockets` and `Quic.Sessions` is plain Pascal over
a datagram transport (two routines: send a datagram, wait up to a
timeout for one), so it builds and runs on the host (make quic-test).

**Driving it.** A connection has no thread: whoever waits runs it.
`PumpConnection` sends what is due, waits for a datagram until the next
timer (loss detection, an acknowledgement's delay, pacing, the idle
timeout, the end of closing) or the caller's deadline, handles what
came and the timers that ran out, and sends again. Every blocking call
(`Connect`, `OpenStream` waiting for MAX_STREAMS, `Write` waiting for
room, `Read`, `AcceptStream`) pumps until its condition holds or its
timeout (`TQuicConnection.Timeout`, 30 s) passes; `Pump(ms)` runs one
round for a caller that serves several streams (HTTP/3's control
streams). The TLS handshake is pulled the same way: libtls's
`ReceiveHandshake` callback pumps until CRYPTO bytes of its level are
there. Packets of a level whose keys TLS has not made yet (a Handshake
packet coalesced behind the Initial whose ServerHello makes its keys,
1-RTT data behind the server's Finished) are kept (at most sixteen) and
handled when `InstallSecret` brings the keys.

**Packets** (`Quic.PacketHeaders`, `Quic.PacketProtection`,
`Quic.InitialSecrets`). Long headers (Initial with its token, Handshake,
Retry, Version Negotiation; 0-RTT is dropped) and short headers with this
side's 8-byte connection ID; several packets per datagram, the 1-RTT one
last. Packet numbers go out in as few bytes as twice the unacknowledged
range needs and are expanded with RFC 9000 A.3's rule. Initial keys come
from the client's first Destination ID (HKDF with version 1's salt,
"client in"/"server in"); other levels' keys from the TLS secrets
("quic key", "quic iv", "quic hp") for AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM (SHA-384)
or ChaCha20-Poly1305; header protection masks from AES-ECB or ChaCha20
over a 16-byte sample. Reserved bits must be zero once a packet opens.
Datagrams with an Initial from the client (or an ack-eliciting one from
a server) are padded to 1200 bytes; datagrams are 1200 bytes until the
handshake is confirmed, then a single PING+PADDING probe of 1452 bytes
(`Options.ProbePathMtu`) raises them to 1452 when it is acknowledged
(its loss does not count as congestion).

**The handshake** (`Quic.ClientHandshake`, `Quic.ConnectionCore`). The
client picks a random 8-byte Destination ID, sends the ClientHello in a
padded Initial and takes the server's first Initial's Source ID as its
Destination from then on. A Retry (once, before any Initial, with a
valid integrity tag: AES-128-GCM with RFC 9001's fixed key over the
original Destination ID and the packet) gives a token, a new Destination
ID and new Initial keys, and the CRYPTO data goes again; a Version
Negotiation packet that does not list version 1 (and came before
anything else, echoing the IDs) ends the attempt
(`QuicErrorVersionNegotiation`). Transport parameters (`Quic.TransportParameters`:
duplicates, ranges and server-only parameters checked) go in the
ClientHello; the server's must confirm every ID seen
(original_destination_connection_id, initial_source_connection_id,
retry_source_connection_id exactly when there was a Retry), else
TRANSPORT_PARAMETER_ERROR. Initial keys are dropped when the first
Handshake packet goes out, Handshake keys when HANDSHAKE_DONE comes
(the handshake is then confirmed). A TLS failure closes with
CRYPTO_ERROR (0x100 + alert).

**Streams and flow control** (`Quic.StreamTable`, `Quic.SendBuffers`,
`Quic.ReceiveBuffers`). Each stream's sending side keeps what was
written until it is acknowledged (at most 256 KiB: writers wait), sends
lost ranges again first, then new bytes within the peer's
MAX_STREAM_DATA and MAX_DATA, then a FIN; its receiving side puts frames
together in a ring that grows up to the window this side gave (256 KiB
a stream, 1 MiB the connection), refuses data beyond it
(FLOW_CONTROL_ERROR) or beyond a final size (FINAL_SIZE_ERROR), and
gives the peer a new limit when half the window has been read. Peer
streams open when first named (with all lower ones of their kind) within
the MAX_STREAMS given (100 of each kind), and a forgotten one makes room
for the next; this side's wait for the peer's MAX_STREAMS (sending
STREAMS_BLOCKED). RESET_STREAM, STOP_SENDING (answered with a reset),
STREAM_DATA_BLOCKED and DATA_BLOCKED are handled; streams that are done
both ways are freed.

**Recovery and congestion** (`Quic.LossRecovery`, `Quic.Congestion`,
`Quic.SentPackets`): RFC 9002's appendix A. Ack-eliciting packets are
remembered in a ring per space (384 1-RTT, 32 Initial or Handshake) with
records of their frames (a stream range, a CRYPTO range, which control
frame) rather than copies; an ACK frees them (the ranges count as
delivered) and gives an RTT sample (the peer's ack delay taken off up to
max_ack_delay); a packet three behind an acknowledged one, or 9/8 RTT
older, is lost and its frames queued again (control frames with current
values). The PTO (smoothed RTT + 4 variances, + max_ack_delay for 1-RTT,
doubled each time) sends one or two probes carrying the oldest data in
flight again (or a PING), in Initial too while the handshake runs; a
client with nothing in flight before its address is validated probes
anyway. NewReno: 10 datagrams to start (at most 14720 bytes), slow start,
halving per recovery period, persistent congestion (losses over three
PTOs with nothing acknowledged between them) down to two datagrams; a
pacer lets 5/4 of the window go per smoothed RTT in bursts of ten. ACKs
go at once for Initial and Handshake and for packets out of order or
after a gap, else after two ack-eliciting packets or 25 ms; they carry up
to 32 ranges, and ranges below an acknowledged ACK are no longer sent.

**The rest of the transport.** CONNECTION_CLOSE (transport or
application; an application's close is APPLICATION_ERROR in Initial and
Handshake packets) is sent once and again in answer while closing (three
PTOs); a peer's close drains. The idle timeout is the smaller of both
sides' (at least three PTOs). A short packet that does not open but ends
in one of the peer's stateless reset tokens ends the connection
(`QuicErrorStatelessReset`). NEW_CONNECTION_ID frames are kept (up to
four, retire_prior_to honoured, RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID sent);
PATH_CHALLENGE is answered; NEW_TOKEN is kept and `Quic.Sessions` offers
it on the next connection to that host and port. Key updates (RFC 9001
section 6): `RequestKeyUpdate` (or `Options.KeyUpdateInterval` packets)
moves the send keys ("quic ku") once the previous update was
acknowledged; a packet with the other key phase bit is tried with the
next keys and, when it opens, moves the receiving side (and the sending
side, if the peer started); the previous keys open late packets for
three PTOs. Memory per connection is fixed but for the streams' buffers:
one datagram buffer each way, the sent-packet rings, sixteen buffered
packets.

**QPACK** (`Qpack.*`). The static table's 99 entries; HPACK's Huffman
code from libhttp's `Http.HpackHuffman` (one copy for HTTP/2 and HTTP/3:
its 257 code lengths only, the code being canonical), field lines as
libhttp's `THttpHeaderField` (so heads pass between the two without a
copy into another shape) and libhttp's byte buffers for output; prefixed
integers (62-bit, QPACK's own) and string literals. The decoder keeps
the dynamic table the server's encoder stream builds (capacity, inserts
with static or dynamic names, literal names, duplicates, eviction;
instructions may arrive in any pieces), decodes field sections (Required
Insert Count, Base, indexed, post-base, name-reference and literal
lines, a size limit), lets a section whose entries have not arrived wait
(at most 16 streams) and acknowledges on the decoder stream (Section
Acknowledgment, Stream Cancellation, Insert Count Increment). The
encoder uses the static table and literals only (Required Insert Count
0), so it never blocks the server and needs nothing back.

**HTTP/3** (`Http3.*`). `THttp3ClientConnection` opens this side's
control stream (SETTINGS: a 4 KiB QPACK table, 16 blocked streams, 64
KiB field sections) and QPACK streams, reads the server's: the control
stream must start with SETTINGS (H3_MISSING_SETTINGS) and may carry
GOAWAY (no new requests at or above its ID) and CANCEL_PUSH; the
encoder stream feeds the decoder; push streams are refused (no
MAX_PUSH_ID: H3_ID_ERROR), unknown types get STOP_SENDING
H3_STREAM_CREATION_ERROR, and a critical stream's end is
H3_CLOSED_CRITICAL_STREAM. `THttp3Request` sends HEADERS (:method,
:scheme, :authority, :path, then the caller's fields), the body in DATA
frames (`WriteBody`, `FinishRequest`), and reads the response:
`ReadHead` passes interim 1xx heads (kept in `InterimStatus`) and checks
the final one (one three-digit :status first, lower case names, no
connection-specific fields: else H3_MESSAGE_ERROR on the stream),
`ReadBody` streams the DATA payloads out as they arrive
(`THttp3FrameParser` collects only non-DATA frames, up to a limit, and
passes over unknown and reserved ones), checks Content-Length and takes
trailers. A frame in the wrong place is H3_FRAME_UNEXPECTED, a frame cut
by the stream's end H3_FRAME_ERROR; a request freed before its end is
cancelled (H3_REQUEST_CANCELLED), and so is one that failed on this
side (canceled, timed out) with its stream still open.
`SendPriorityUpdate` sends PRIORITY_UPDATE (0xF0700, RFC 9218) on the
control stream. Errors are libquic's QuicError* codes and Http3Error*
(-101 malformed response, -102 reset by the server, -103 connection
error, -104 GOAWAY, -105 incomplete, -106 not possible now, -107
canceled while waiting).

**HTTP/3 in libhttp** (`Http3.HttpConnections`, `Http3.SystemConnections`).
`THttp3Connection` is a libhttp `THttpConnection` (protocol
`HttpProtocol3`, multiplexed) over `THttp3ClientConnection`, each
`THttp3Exchange` a `THttp3Request`: Send writes HEADERS (the fields less
Host and the connection-specific ones, Priority when not the default,
content-type and content-length from the content) and the content in
16 KiB DATA frames (a server that sent STOP_SENDING has answered: the
sending stops and the response is read); ReceiveHead passes interim
heads and gives libhttp's head record with RawHead "HTTP/3 200" and the
fields (wget -S); ReadBody streams DATA; trailers are kept at the end.
Threads share one connection: QUIC has no thread and libquic is not
thread safe, so one lock guards it and every libquic call holds it. A
request that waits runs the connection itself in slices of at most 20
ms (`THttp3ClientConnection.WaitForProgress` is virtual for this): a
slice sends what is due, takes in what came for every stream, and lets
the lock go before the next, so other threads' requests go out and find
what arrived for them. `Abort` only sets a flag the waiting thread sees
within a slice; the stream is cancelled when the exchange finishes.
StartExchange first takes in, without waiting, what came while the
connection sat idle (a GOAWAY, a close, more streams), and refuses when
no stream is left within the server's MAX_STREAMS (the pool then opens
another connection). The connection is usable while QUIC is open, no
GOAWAY came and the idle timeout is over a second away. Results map to
libhttp's: GOAWAY for a request at or above its ID and
H3_REQUEST_REJECTED are retryable `HttpStreamReset`, an incomplete head
`HttpNoResponse`, an incomplete body `HttpBodyEndedEarly`, a waiting
timeout `HttpTimedOut`. A thread blocked in libquic's own waits (room
in a full 256 KiB send buffer, MAX_STREAMS) holds the lock until they
end. The factory (`OpenHttp3Connection`) opens a `TQuicSession` to the
alternative's host (the origin's when Alt-Svc named none) and port,
with the origin's host as the TLS server name (`TQuicSession.ServerName`:
the certificate must be good for the origin), the client's trust file,
certificate checking and suites, the handshake within
`AltServiceTimeoutMilliseconds` (3 s), then the client's timeout for
every wait; `EnableHttp3` registers it for "h3".

**h3get** (`userland/bin/h3get.pas`): `h3get [-v] [-s] [-I] [-k] [-o FILE]
[-X METHOD] [-d DATA] [-H 'NAME: VALUE'] [--cacert FILE] [--timeout S]
[--mtu BYTES] [--fail] https://HOST[:PORT]/PATH`; `-v` shows the address,
suite, response head, trailers, RTT and packet counts. Exit statuses as
wget's: 4 network, 5 TLS, 7 protocol, 8 an error status with --fail.

**Tests.** `make quic-test` builds libquic for the host (with libtls and
TlsTest's Crypto.Random) and checks: RFC 9001 appendix A (the Initial
secrets and keys, the header protection sample, the ChaCha20 short header
packet whole, the key update secret, the Retry tag), whole Initial and
AES-256-GCM packets against the same built by Python's cryptography
(tools/QuicTest/make-vectors.py, which also makes the test server's
Ed25519 certificate), RFC 9000's packet number and varint examples, every
frame written and read back, ACK ranges, malformed frames, transport
parameters; QPACK through RFC 9204 appendix B (B.1 to B.5, the encoder
stream fed a byte at a time, a section blocked until its inserts come)
and RFC 7541's Huffman strings (libhttp's unit); HTTP/3 frames and the frame parser. Then
whole connections over UDP on 127.0.0.1 and ::1 to a server written for
the test (`QuicTest.Server`: libquic's core in the server role, a
minimal TLS 1.3 server over libtls's key schedule and an Ed25519
certificate the client pins): each suite, IPv6, 3 MB both ways, 150
streams in a row, a tenth of the datagrams of both sides dropped, a
Retry, key updates from either side, the path MTU probe, Version
Negotiation without version 1, a stateless reset, the server's
application close, an untrusted certificate (the server gets CRYPTO_ERROR
unknown_ca); and HTTP/3 to the test's HTTP/3 server: GET, 1 MB, a POST
echoed with trailers, 204, 103 then 200, a head waiting 100 ms for the
encoder stream, five requests at once, a malformed :status, a reset
request, GOAWAY, the close. Then libhttp's client over HTTP/3
(`QuicTest.HttpClient`, with libhttp, libcompression and HttpTest's
pipes built in): the first request goes to an HTTP/1.1 server on pipes
whose response says Alt-Svc: h3=":PORT"; the next go over a factory
like the system's (UDP to the test server, its certificate pinned):
"HTTP/3 200" with its fields, one QUIC connection for everything, 1 MB,
a 200 KB POST echoed with trailers, 204, 103, a head waiting for the
encoder stream, six threads at once on the connection, a cancel from
another thread (the connection goes on), the request's fields (no Host,
no Connection), PRIORITY_UPDATE, GOAWAY; after it a new connection fails
and TCP answers (the alternative marked broken, not tried again); an
alternative whose UDP is dropped silently costs one handshake timeout
before TCP answers, then nothing; with AllowHttp3 off it is never
tried. Last, `run-curl-interop.sh` has the host's
curl (ngtcp2 and nghttp3, when it has HTTP/3) fetch from `QuicTest
serve`, an independent stack against libquic's core. Nothing has been
tried against servers on the internet yet.

### libhttp

**libhttp** (`userland/lib/http`, units `Url.*` and `Http.*`,
`libhttp.so` over libtls, libcompression, libcryptography and libsystem)
is the one HTTP client of the system: wget now, the browser engine
(libweb) next. Everything but the two socket units is plain Pascal and
builds on the host (`make http-test`).

```
  programs: wget, libweb (later), ...
=========== Http.Client: Execute (one request) and Fetch (the whole fetch)
  Http.FetchTasks   fetches on threads: OnHead, OnData, OnDone, Cancel
  Http.Messages     THttpRequest, THttpResponse (content read as it comes)
  Http.Redirects  Http.Authentication (Http.Challenges, Http.Digest)
  Http.Cookies (Http.CookieDates, Http.CookieFiles, Http.PublicSuffixes)
  Http.Cache (Http.CacheControl, Http.DiskCache)   Http.ContentDecoding
  Http.AltServices  Alt-Svc, and the connection factories (h3 plugs in)
  Http.ConnectionPool   Http.Connectors (Http.SocketConnector: the system's)
=========== Http.Connections: THttpConnection / THttpExchange =============
  HTTP/1.1: Http.Http1Connections (Http.ResponseHeads, Http.Chunks)
  HTTP/2:   Http.Http2Connections, Http.Http2Streams, Http.Http2Frames,
            Http.HpackEncoder, Http.HpackDecoder, Http.HpackTables,
            Http.HpackHuffman
  HTTP/3:   libquic's Http3.HttpConnections, from the "h3" factory that
            libquic's EnableHttp3 registers (libhttp does not link libquic)
=========== Http.Transports: a byte stream (Http.SocketTransports: TCP+TLS)
  Http.HeaderFields  Http.FieldValues  Http.Dates  Http.StatusCodes
  Http.Methods  Http.Priorities  Http.RequestBodies  Http.BodySinks
  Http.Results  Http.Observers  Http.ByteBuffers
=========== Url.*: the URL Standard =======================================
  Url.Parser  Url.Records  Url.Accessors  Url.Hosts  Url.IpAddresses
  Url.DomainNames  Url.Punycode  Url.PercentEncoding  Url.FormEncoding
  Url.SearchParams  Url.Origins
```

**URLs** (the WHATWG URL Standard). `Url.Parser` is the basic URL
parser's state machine, with a base URL and the state override the
URL class's setters use (`Url.Accessors`: href, origin, protocol,
username, password, host, hostname, port, pathname, search, hash, each
doing nothing where the standard says so). A `TUrlRecord` keeps the
scheme, credentials, host (null, empty, domain, IPv4, IPv6 or opaque),
port (null when the scheme's default), the path serialized ("/a/b";
an opaque path as it is), query and fragment. Input is UTF-8 and every
percent-encode set takes all bytes above 0x7E, so the machine works
byte by byte (`Url.PercentEncoding` has the C0 control, fragment,
query, special-query, path, userinfo, component and form sets).
Hosts (`Url.Hosts`): "[...]" is IPv6 (`Url.IpAddresses`: "::" once, an
embedded IPv4 address; serialized with the first longest zero run
compressed), a special URL's host is percent-decoded, put through
domain to ASCII and, when it ends in a number, must be IPv4 (decimal,
octal or hexadecimal parts, the last filling the remaining bytes);
other hosts are opaque. Domain to ASCII (`Url.DomainNames`): an ASCII
domain without "xn--" labels is lower cased; otherwise the code points
are mapped (the cased scripts' capitals, full-width ASCII, ideographic
full stops; joiners refuse the domain) and non-ASCII labels become
"xn--" Punycode (`Url.Punycode`, RFC 3492); "xn--" labels must decode
to something non-ASCII. This is the part of UTS #46's table that
matters for case, without NFC. `Url.SearchParams` is URLSearchParams
(append, delete, get, getAll, has, set, a stable sort by UTF-16 code
units, form serialization), over `Url.FormEncoding`
(application/x-www-form-urlencoded); `Url.Origins` gives tuple and
opaque origins (blob: URLs take their inner URL's), same-origin and
the serialization, and "potentially trustworthy".

**Messages.** Header fields (`Http.HeaderFields`) are an ordered array
of name-value pairs, names in lower case and shared strings for the
common ones; `Combined` joins a name's values (never Set-Cookie's).
`Http.FieldValues` reads lists, tokens, quoted strings and parameters;
`Http.Dates` HTTP dates (all three forms, through the cookie date
algorithm) and writes IMF-fixdate; `Http.StatusCodes` reason phrases
(HTTP/2 sends none), classes and heuristic cacheability;
`Http.Methods` safe and idempotent methods; `Http.Priorities` RFC
9218's urgency and incremental flag as the Priority field. A request's
content (`Http.RequestBodies`: bytes, a stream, or a producer routine)
says its length (unknown: chunked over HTTP/1.1) and rewinds for 307,
308, retries and 401. A response's content goes into sinks
(`Http.BodySinks`: memory, discard, stream, callback) as it arrives.

**Connections.** `Http.Connections` is what every version offers: a
`THttpConnection` starts `THttpExchange`s (Send, ReceiveHead with 1xx
skipped, ReadBody without framing, Finish, Abort from any thread,
Reprioritize). Requests and responses are the same records for every
version (`THttpRequestHead`, `THttpResponseHeadInfo`), so HTTP/3 needs
only a connection class of its own.

- **HTTP/1.1** (`Http.Http1Connections`, RFC 9112): one exchange at a
  time, no pipelining; the request line, Host, the fields (names written
  as "User-Agent"), Content-Length or chunked content; the head through a
  16 KiB buffer (`Http.ResponseHeads`); bodies by length, chunked
  (`Http.Chunks`), or to the end of the connection; none for HEAD, 1xx,
  204 and 304. The connection goes on only when the body had a known
  end, was read whole, and neither side said close (HTTP/1.0 must say
  keep-alive).
- **HTTP/2** (`Http.Http2Connections`, RFC 9113): the preface and
  SETTINGS (push off, a 1 MiB stream window, 100 streams,
  SETTINGS_NO_RFC7540_PRIORITIES) and a WINDOW_UPDATE to a 16 MiB
  connection window; the server's SETTINGS must come first and are
  acknowledged (header table size, concurrent streams, initial window
  with every stream's adjusted, frame size). The connection has no
  thread: an exchange that waits reads the connection itself when no
  other thread is, deals each frame to its stream (`Http.Http2Streams`)
  and wakes the exchange waiting on it, then hands reading over; a
  one-thread program simply reads. FWriteLock (writing, the HPACK
  encoder, stream id order) is taken before FLock (the rest), never the
  other way. Flow control both ways: DATA waits for both send windows;
  received data is given back half a window at a time as exchanges take
  it, so a slow reader slows the server instead of filling memory;
  padding and data for streams given up go back at once. SETTINGS,
  PING, GOAWAY (streams above its last id fail as retryable, no new
  ones), RST_STREAM (REFUSED_STREAM retryable), WINDOW_UPDATE (0 and
  overflow refused), header blocks across CONTINUATION (decoded even for
  streams gone, at most 1 MiB), PUSH_PROMISE refused, unknown frames
  skipped. Responses are checked (:status once and first, no other
  pseudo-headers, lower case names, no connection-specific fields,
  content-length against the data); a bad one resets its stream; a
  connection error sends GOAWAY. Requests drop connection-specific
  fields and Host (it becomes :authority), add Priority when not the
  default, and PRIORITY_UPDATE re-prioritizes. Frames
  (`Http.Http2Frames`) are built into reused byte buffers
  (`Http.ByteBuffers`).
- **HPACK** (RFC 7541): `Http.HpackHuffman` holds only appendix B's 257
  code lengths, the code being canonical (codes made on first use;
  decoding by first code per length; padding over seven bits, padding
  not all ones and EOS refused); `Http.HpackTables` the static table and
  the dynamic table, a ring bounded by its size; `Http.HpackDecoder`
  (integer overflow, bad indexes, size updates only first and within
  SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE, the header list limit reported per
  stream while the table stays in step); `Http.HpackEncoder` (indexed
  when in a table, never-indexed Authorization and short cookies,
  incremental indexing unless an entry would take half the table,
  Huffman unless longer, size updates at the next block, the smallest
  first).
- **HTTP/3** is libquic's (see "libquic: QUIC and HTTP/3"): a program
  that wants it links libquic and calls `EnableHttp3`, which registers
  a factory for "h3" (`RegisterConnectionFactory`), or makes its client
  with `CreateHttp3Client`. Once an https origin advertised h3 by
  Alt-Svc (and `AllowHttp3`, the default), new requests to it go to an
  HTTP/3 connection of the pool or a new one from the factory, leaving
  the origin's HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 connections; a factory that finds no
  connection, or a new HTTP/3 connection that fails a request before
  its answer when the request may go again (sending failed, refused, or
  an idempotent method with no answer), marks h3 broken for five
  minutes and the request goes over TCP. There is no racing of QUIC
  against TCP (happy eyeballs): a silently blocked UDP path costs one
  `AltServiceTimeoutMilliseconds` (3 s) every five minutes.
  HPACK's Huffman code (`Http.HpackHuffman`) and the header field record
  are QPACK's too.

**The client** (`Http.Client`). `Execute` is one request: a connection
from the pool (`Http.ConnectionPool`: a shared HTTP/2 connection with
room for a stream, an idle HTTP/1.1 one, at most 6 idle per origin and
32 in all, 60 s idle), else a new one (an Alt-Svc factory's, or the
connector's: `Http.SocketConnector` looks up, connects and runs TLS
with ALPN "h2,http/1.1" through `Http.SocketTransports`; the client
makes an HTTP/2 connection when "h2" was chosen); User-Agent, Accept,
Accept-Encoding, Authorization (once a server asked) and Cookie added;
Set-Cookie and Alt-Svc taken; a kept connection that turns out closed
(a failed send, or no answer) or a request refused unprocessed sends
the request again on a new connection (at most three tries). The
observer (`Http.Observers`) hears each step. `Fetch` adds the rest:
the cache, redirects (`Http.Redirects`: 301/302 POST and 303 non-HEAD
become GET without content and its fields, 307/308 keep both,
credentials only to the same origin, cookies worked out again, at most
20), 401 answered with credentials (once, again for a stale nonce),
content decoding (`Http.ContentDecoding`: gzip and x-gzip with
concatenated members, deflate as zlib or raw, br and zstd (several
frames), all through libcompression's streaming decoders, in pieces as
the body arrives; `SupportedAcceptEncoding`, "gzip, deflate, br, zstd",
names exactly the codings compiled in), and
the content handed to a sink as it comes; OnHead sees the final head
first and a cancel token stops it from another thread. `Get` is the
one-line form; `Http.FetchTasks` runs fetches on threads (OnHead,
OnData, OnDone on the task's thread; Cancel resets an HTTP/2 stream or
closes an HTTP/1.1 connection), many tasks sharing one client and its
HTTP/2 connections. The client, pool, jar, cache and authenticator are
thread safe.

- **Cookies** (`Http.Cookies`, RFC 6265bis): nameless cookies, 4096
  bytes for a name and value, 1024 for an attribute value, control
  characters refused, 400 days at most; a Domain that is a public
  suffix (`Http.PublicSuffixes`: the Public Suffix List's algorithm with
  wildcards and exceptions, over a compiled list of the main
  second-level and hosting suffixes, or
  /usr/share/publicsuffix/public_suffix_list.dat when there) only for
  that host itself; Secure only from secure requests and not shadowed
  by insecure ones; `__Secure-` and `__Host-` prefixes; SameSite (Strict,
  Lax, None needing Secure; unspecified as Lax) on storing and sending,
  from the request's `TCookieRequestContext` (secure, same-site,
  top-level navigation, safe method, HTTP or script); HttpOnly hidden
  from and kept from scripts (`DocumentCookie`, `SetDocumentCookie`);
  50 per domain and 3000 in all, least recently used first. Netscape
  cookie files (`Http.CookieFiles`) read and write the jar.
- **Cache** (`Http.Cache`, RFC 9111, a private cache): complete GET
  responses with a final status, unless no-store or Vary: *; matched
  by URL and the Vary fields; fresh by max-age, Expires - Date, or 10%
  of the time since Last-Modified (at most a day) for statuses
  cacheable by default, the age from Age, Date and the request and
  response times; no-cache, max-age, max-stale, min-fresh and
  must-revalidate honoured; stale responses revalidated with
  If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since, a 304 freshening the stored
  fields; unsafe requests invalidate; 32 MiB by default, the least
  recently used first; with a folder, each response also a file
  (`Http.DiskCache`: an FNV-1a name, written through a temporary file).
  The request's cache mode (default, no-store, reload, no-cache,
  force-cache, only-if-cached) is Fetch's.
- **Authentication** (`Http.Authentication`): as wget's was (above),
  per origin, with a credentials provider for what was not given.
- **Alt-Svc** (`Http.AltServices`, RFC 7838): values parsed (protocol
  ids percent-decoded, IPv6 alt-authorities, ma, persist, clear; ma=0,
  port 0 and bad authorities dropped, bad parameters ignored) and kept
  per origin until they expire, at most eight per origin and 512
  origins (the least recently updated go first); an alternative marked
  broken stays broken when advertised again; persist=1 is kept (no
  network changes are told to programs, so nothing is dropped for it
  yet); `SaveText` and `LoadText` keep the cache between runs (lines
  "ORIGIN PROTOCOL HOST PORT EXPIRES PERSIST"; wget's --alt-svc-file).
  HTTPS DNS records (RFC 9460) are not looked up: libsystem's resolver
  keeps no data of unknown record types.

Not here yet: proxies (wget had none), 100-continue, HTTP/2 PING
keep-alive, HSTS and CORS (libweb's), the full UTS #46 table.

**Tests** (`make http-test`, tools/HttpTest): the URL Standard (about
200 cases written from the standard's examples and rules: special and
other schemes, credentials, ports, dot segments, every percent-encode
set, IPv4 forms, IPv6 compression and embedded IPv4, IDNA with
Punycode, file URLs and Windows drive letters, relative references
with RFC 3986's examples, setters, URLSearchParams, origins), HPACK
against RFC 7541 appendix C (C.1 to C.6, each block decoded with the
table sizes checked and encoded again byte for byte, then malformed
blocks), HTTP/2 frames built and read back, HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2
exchanges with small servers in threads over in-memory pipes (every
body framing, interim responses, content of unknown length, HEAD; a
3 MiB response through a 1 MiB window, a 200 KB upload into a 64 KB
window, four threads and forty requests on one connection, an answer
after a later one, trailers, CONTINUATION, a refused stream, a
malformed response, priorities, GOAWAY), and the client over a
connector of pipes (keep-alive and a stale connection, gzip and
deflate, redirects with their method rules and limit, cookies, the
cache fresh and revalidated, Basic, Alt-Svc, eight fetch tasks on one
HTTP/2 connection, a cancel), RFC 6265bis's rules in the jar (public
suffixes, Secure, prefixes, SameSite both ways, HttpOnly against scripts,
400 days), RFC 9111's freshness and age arithmetic, the disk cache read
back by another cache, Alt-Svc parsing and its cache (expiry, choosing
an alternative with a factory, broken for five minutes and still broken
when advertised again, saved and read back, AllowHttp3, the bounds),
and HPACK in bounded memory over
5000 blocks. Then `run-interop.sh`: HPACK both ways
with libnghttp2 through Python's ctypes (libhttp's blocks with
evictions and every byte Huffman coded decoded by nghttp2, nghttp2's
blocks decoded by libhttp; skipped without libnghttp2), curl checking
that test-web-server.py's https-h2 mode speaks HTTP/2, and the client
over a host socket and libtls against that server (HTTP/2 by ALPN,
200000 bytes, one connection, gzip, a range, Digest, cookies across a
redirect, HTTP/1.1 when HTTP/2 is not offered). In QEMU, wgettest's
HTTP/2 checks (above). HTTP/3 through the client is checked by `make
quic-test` (above).

### The SSH server

`sshd` lets another machine log in, run commands and copy files with a
stock OpenSSH client (`ssh`, `scp`, `sftp` of OpenSSH 9 and later); the
use in mind is a Raspberry Pi 4 run from a Linux PC. The protocol is in
**libssh** (`userland/lib/ssh`, libsystem <- libcryptography <- libssh),
the server program in `userland/sshd`, the SFTP subsystem in
`userland/sftp-server`, the client programs `ssh`, `ssh-keygen` and
`ssh-add` in `userland/bin` (the client's units in `userland/ssh`).

**libssh** is both sides. Its protocol units do no input or output:
bytes go in, bytes and messages come out, so the host test drives them
from memory (and its client against its server) as the programs drive
them from sockets. A few units on top do input and output for both
programs (`Ssh.HandleWriters`, `Ssh.SocketChannels`,
`Ssh.AgentChannels`); the host test leaves them out.

| Unit | What it is |
|---|---|
| `Ssh.Wire` | byte, boolean, uint32, uint64, string, mpint, name-list (RFC 4251); `TSshReader` raises `ESshProtocolError` on short or bad data; byte strings are plain `string`s |
| `Ssh.PacketCiphers`, `Ssh.ChaChaPolyCipher`, `Ssh.AesGcmCipher`, `Ssh.CipherSuites` | what protects a direction: plain, `chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com` (two ChaCha20 keys, the length encrypted apart, Poly1305 over both; the original 64-bit nonce ChaCha20 is the IETF one with nonce 00000000 \|\| sequence number), `aes256-gcm@openssh.com` and `aes128-gcm@openssh.com` (RFC 5647: the length as additional data, the invocation counter in the nonce) |
| `Ssh.PacketLayer` | the binary packet protocol (RFC 4253 section 6): random padding of 4 or more bytes to whole blocks (the length left out for the authenticated ciphers), 32-bit sequence numbers, packets up to 256 KiB, counts for rekeying |
| `Ssh.Algorithms` | KEXINIT made and read; for each kind the client's first choice the server has, worked out the same on both sides |
| `Ssh.KeyExchange`, `Ssh.KeyExchangeMethods` | X25519 key pairs; the methods both ways: curve25519-sha256 (RFC 8731, K an mpint) and mlkem768x25519-sha256 (draft-ietf-sshm-mlkem-hybrid-kex: C_INIT = ML-KEM-768 encapsulation key \|\| X25519 key, S_REPLY = ciphertext \|\| X25519 key, K = SHA-256(ML-KEM secret \|\| X25519 secret) as a string); the exchange hash and the keys derived from K and H (RFC 4253 section 7.2) |
| `Ssh.HostKeys`, `Ssh.KeyFiles` | host keys `ssh-ed25519` and `ecdsa-sha2-nistp256`: blobs, signatures, new keys; OpenSSH's unencrypted private key format (`openssh-key-v1`) |
| `Ssh.PublicKeys` | client keys (`ssh-ed25519`, `ecdsa-sha2-nistp256`, `ssh-rsa`) and their signatures (`rsa-sha2-256`/`512`, not SHA-1 `ssh-rsa`), authorized_keys lines, SHA256 fingerprints |
| `Ssh.Transport` | what both sides' transports share: version lines, KEXINIT each way, NEWKEYS and the keys put to use, strict kex, rekeying, held messages, the transport's own messages |
| `Ssh.ClientTransport` | the client's half of each method, the host key's signature over H checked and the key handed to the program (`OnHostKey`: known_hosts), EXT_INFO read (server-sig-algs, publickey-hostbound) |
| `Ssh.ServerTransport` | the server's transport: version lines, the first key exchange and every rekeying, NEWKEYS, the transport's own messages, messages held back during an exchange |
| `Ssh.UserAuthentication` | RFC 4252: `none` (the list), `publickey` (PK_OK for a query, the signature over the session id and the request), `password`; who may log in is a `TSshAccountPolicy`'s to say; ten failures end the connection |
