| `Ssh.Connection` | RFC 4254 for either side: channels opened by either side (a peer's open may be answered later: `DeferOpenConfirmation`), windows and the largest packet each way, requests with and without replies, EOF on its own (`SendEofWhenFlushed`), global requests both ways (replies in order); programs derive their channels from `TSshChannel` |
| `Ssh.ClientAuthentication`, `Ssh.ClientIdentities` | the client's side of RFC 4252: `none` for the list, then each key (signed at once; as publickey-hostbound-v00 bound to the host key when the server offers it; RSA keys with rsa-sha2-512/256 from server-sig-algs), keyboard-interactive (the program answers the prompts), password |
| `Ssh.AuthorizedKeys` | authorized_keys lines and their options (`command=`, `from=`, `environment=`, `expiry-time=`, `permitopen=`, `permitlisten=`, `principals=`, `cert-authority`, `no-*`, `restrict` and what gives back) |
| `Ssh.Certificates` | OpenSSH certificates (PROTOCOL.certkeys) of ed25519, ecdsa-sha2-nistp256 and rsa keys: read, the CA's signature checked, a user certificate checked for a user and a time (principals, validity, critical options force-command and source-address, extensions as permissions) |
| `Ssh.AddressPatterns` | OpenSSH pattern lists (`*`, `?`, `!`) and address lists with IPv4 and IPv6 CIDR blocks (an IPv4 mapped address matched as IPv4) |
| `Ssh.KnownHosts` | known_hosts lookups (name lists, `[host]:port`, hashed names, `@revoked`) and new lines |
| `Ssh.AgentProtocol` | the agent protocol's messages (list keys, sign) and a reader putting a stream back into messages |
| `Ssh.PolledChannels` | how a program's one loop serves channels and listeners: each names the handles it waits on and what to do when one is ready, and is polled after every wait |
| `Ssh.HandleWriters`, `Ssh.SocketChannels`, `Ssh.AgentChannels` | (input and output) writer threads for pipes, terminals and sockets; channels joined to TCP connections (connecting without waiting) and TCP listeners for forwarding; the agent relay and the agent client over named ports |

Both sides offer `mlkem768x25519-sha256` first, then `curve25519-sha256`
and `curve25519-sha256@libssh.org`; the server offers the host key
algorithms it has keys (and certificates) for, the three ciphers and no
compression. The hybrid method stays secret against someone recording
the connection now to break it later with a quantum computer as long as
ML-KEM holds, and against everyone today as long as X25519 does; OpenSSH
9.9 and later choose it by default and OpenSSH 10 warns about a
connection without it. Every cipher is authenticated encryption, so no MAC is
chosen (as OpenSSH does for them); `hmac-sha2-256` is listed only so the
MAC lists are not empty. Two OpenSSH extensions matter to its clients:

- **ext-info** (RFC 8308): with `ext-info-c` in the client's first
  KEXINIT, SSH_MSG_EXT_INFO follows the server's first NEWKEYS with
  `server-sig-algs` = `ssh-ed25519,ecdsa-sha2-nistp256,rsa-sha2-512,rsa-sha2-256`,
  without which clients would sign with SHA-1 RSA, and
  `publickey-hostbound@openssh.com` = `0`, so that clients sign their
  publickey requests over the server's host key too
  (publickey-hostbound-v00@openssh.com; the server takes it only with
  one of its own host keys): a signature cannot be replayed to another
  server, which OpenSSH's agent restrictions build on.
- **strict key exchange** (`kex-strict-s-v00@openssh.com`, always
  offered; on when the client offers `kex-strict-c-v00@openssh.com`):
  during the first exchange only its own messages may come and the
  client's KEXINIT must be its first packet, and the sequence numbers
  start again at 0 after every NEWKEYS, sent and received. That closes
  the Terrapin attack (a man in the middle removing packets during the
  unprotected handshake by shifting sequence numbers).

The server starts a new key exchange after 1 GiB or 2^28 packets in
either direction and takes the client's whenever it comes; messages the
layers above send meanwhile wait until its NEWKEYS is out.

**sshd** runs as the `sshd` service (`/etc/services/sshd.service`, text
and graphical modes, `ready = notify`; `service stop|start|restart
sshd`). The listening process (`Sshd.Listener`) reads
`/etc/ssh/sshd_config` (`Sshd.Configuration`), makes missing host keys
(`Sshd.HostKeyStore`: the kind from the file's name, written with mode
0600 set before the key goes in, `PATH.pub` next to it; `/etc/ssh` by
default), listens on IPv4 and, when it can, IPv6, and starts itself
again as `sshd --connection -f CONFIG` for each connection, the socket
as its standard input (at most 32 at once). So each connection is a
process of its own in the service's session: one that fails takes
nothing else with it, and stopping the service ends them all.

`sshd_config` takes OpenSSH's keywords: `Port`,
`PasswordAuthentication`, `PubkeyAuthentication`,
`KbdInteractiveAuthentication` (yes), `PermitRootLogin`, `HostKey` (one
per key), `HostCertificate`, `TrustedUserCAKeys`, `AuthorizedKeysFile`
(`%h`, `%u`), `Subsystem sftp PROGRAM`, `LoginGraceTime` (seconds to log
in, 120), `MaxSessions` (session channels per connection, 8),
`AllowTcpForwarding` (yes/all, local, remote, no), `GatewayPorts` (no,
yes, clientspecified), `PermitOpen` (any, none, host:port ...),
`AllowAgentForwarding`, `PermitTTY`, `PermitUserEnvironment` (no),
`ForceCommand`, `ClientAliveInterval` (0) and `ClientAliveCountMax` (3),
`TCPKeepAlive` (TCP keep-alives on the connections, yes), and **Match**
blocks: `Match User`, `Group`, `Address` (CIDR too), `LocalPort` (all
given must match) or `All`, followed by the keywords that can differ per
connection (the authentication methods, PermitRootLogin, the forwarding
and agent settings, PermitTTY, ForceCommand, the keep-alives,
MaxSessions, TrustedUserCAKeys, AuthorizedKeysFile,
PermitUserEnvironment); for each keyword the first value that applies
wins, as in OpenSSH. Before the user is known (the method list of a
`none` request is the user's), only Address and LocalPort can match; the
connection's configuration is settled once it has logged in.
`sshd -t` checks it and the host keys.

A connection's process (`Sshd.ConnectionLoop`) waits on the socket, the
input writers' progress event and every session's output and program at
once (`WaitForHandles`), and with them whatever the channels and
forwardings wait on (`Ssh.PolledChannels`). Accounts (`Sshd.Accounts`):
an existing user whose password is not locked, whose shell is not
`/bin/false` (and root only with `PermitRootLogin yes`); a key from the
AuthorizedKeysFile, read as root, with its options - `from=` must match
the client's address, `expiry-time=` must not have passed, and the rest
go with the login (below); a user certificate whose CA is in
TrustedUserCAKeys or on an authorized_keys line with `cert-authority`
(and `principals=`), for this user, valid now, from an address its
`source-address` allows, its `force-command` and missing extensions
becoming options as authorized_keys ones would; the account's password
(`Util.Logins`), by `password` or by `keyboard-interactive` (one
`Password: ` prompt), never an empty one, a wrong one answered after a
second.

Each **session channel** (`Sshd.Sessions`) runs one program as the user
(`StartAsUserWithVariables` in `Util.Logins`, in a session of its own),
with the login environment plus `SSH_CONNECTION`, `SSH_CLIENT`, `TERM`,
`SSH_TTY` and the client's `LANG`/`LC_*`:

- `pty-req` then `shell` or `exec`: a pseudo-terminal of the size asked
  for, the program in a new foreground group with the terminal as its
  controlling terminal, as a terminal window starts its shell;
  `window-change` sets the terminal's size; `signal INT` types Ctrl-C.
  The terminal's output gets a carriage return before each bare line
  feed (`Ssh.TerminalOutput`): a pseudo-terminal passes a line feed on
  as written, for the terminal window to move to the next line's
  start, but the client's terminal (xterm, PuTTY) only moves down, as
  a Unix terminal's ONLCR would have added the return; without it every
  program's lines stepped to the right over SSH;
- without a terminal: three pipes, standard error sent as extended data;
- `subsystem sftp`: the configured `sftp-server`;
- `signal`: otherwise the program ends with 128 plus the signal number.

What the client sends goes to the program through an **input writer**
(`Sshd.InputWriters`), a thread per session: a pipe write waits until
every byte is in, and a program writing its own output (which the
connection has to keep reading) would otherwise stop the connection -
scp and sftp keep many requests in flight while replies come back. The
thread signals the connection after each write, and only then is the
channel's window opened again, so a client never has more in flight
than the program takes. The program's output is read only while less
than 64 KiB waits for the client's window. When the program ends (and,
on pipes, its output is read to the end), the channel sends EOF,
`exit-status` and CLOSE; whatever the program left running in its
session is ended, and on a terminal the master side is closed (hang-up).
Closing the channel or losing the connection ends the program too. The
log (`/var/log/sshd.log`) says who connected, logged in with what,
which key (fingerprint), what ran and how it ended; never a password.

**sftp-server** speaks SFTP version 3 (the draft OpenSSH follows) on its
standard input and output, as the user: open, close, read, write, stat,
lstat, fstat, setstat, fsetstat, opendir, readdir (with `ls -l` lines),
mkdir, rmdir, remove, rename (not over an existing file), realpath,
readlink and symlink (OpenSSH's argument order), and the extensions
`posix-rename@openssh.com`, `expand-path@openssh.com` (scp's `~/` paths),
`fsync@openssh.com` and `limits@openssh.com` (64 KiB reads and writes).
Since OpenSSH 9, `scp` uses SFTP; the old scp protocol (a remote `scp`
program) is not there.

**More of the server.** A key's options and the configuration act on
the session (`Sshd.Sessions`): a forced command - the key's `command=`,
a certificate's force-command, then ForceCommand - runs as `SHELL -c`
in place of the shell, command or subsystem asked for, which goes in
`SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND`; `no-pty` (or a certificate without permit-pty,
or PermitTTY no) refuses pty-req; `environment=` lines are set with
PermitUserEnvironment yes.

- **Forwarding** (`Sshd.Forwarding`): a `direct-tcpip` channel (ssh -L)
  is allowed by AllowTcpForwarding yes/all/local, PermitOpen and the
  key's `permitopen=`, refused by `no-port-forwarding`; the server
  connects without waiting and confirms the channel when the connection
  is made (a refused connection refuses the channel), the loop looking
  at connecting sockets every 20 ms. `tcpip-forward` (ssh -R) is allowed
  by AllowTcpForwarding yes/all/remote and `permitlisten=`; GatewayPorts
  no listens on the loopback address only, yes on every address,
  clientspecified where the client says; ports below 1024 only for
  root; port 0 takes any and the reply names it. Each connection to it
  opens a `forwarded-tcpip` channel to the client; `cancel-tcpip-forward`
  stops it. A forwarded socket's channel (`Ssh.SocketChannels`) writes
  what it receives through a writer thread (the window opening as the
  socket takes it) and reads the socket only while less than 64 KiB
  waits for the peer's window; end of file goes each way on its own (the
  socket shut down for sending, EOF on the channel) and the channel
  closes once both are done or the socket breaks.
- **Agent forwarding** (`Sshd.AgentForwarding`, `Ssh.AgentChannels`):
  OpenSSH makes a Unix domain socket for `auth-agent-req@openssh.com`;
  the system has none, and the nearest local IPC is a named port
  (`Processes.Channels`), which also tells who connected. A session that
  asks (AllowAgentForwarding, no `no-agent-forwarding`) gets a port
  `sshagent-PROCESS-N` and `SSH_AUTH_SOCK=port:sshagent-PROCESS-N`; a
  connection to it from the session's user (or root; others are turned
  away by `GetChannelPeer`) opens an `auth-agent@openssh.com` channel to
  the client, and the agent protocol's bytes pass unchanged: local
  messages (up to 16 KiB) one way, channel data the other. The system's
  `ssh` and `ssh-add` connect to such an `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`.
- **Host certificates**: each HostCertificate (a line as `ssh-keygen -s
  -h` writes it) for one of the host keys is offered as its own host key
  algorithm (`ssh-ed25519-cert-v01@openssh.com`, ...), first; the
  certificate goes as K_S and the key signs.
- **Keep-alives**: with ClientAliveInterval, a client silent that long
  gets a `keepalive@openssh.com` global request (any reply, even a
  refusal, answers it); after ClientAliveCountMax unanswered ones the
  connection ends ("Timeout, client not responding"). TCPKeepAlive sets
  the socket option (`SocketOptionKeepAlive`) on the listening sockets.

**The client.** `ssh` (`SshClient.*` in `userland/ssh`) parses OpenSSH's
command line (options stop at the destination; `-o` takes the usual
ssh_config names; no ssh_config file is read), connects, and runs one
loop like the server's over the socket, standard input, the -L
listeners and the forwarded sockets:

- the host key is checked against `~/.ssh/known_hosts`
  (`SshClient.HostKeyCheck`, StrictHostKeyChecking ask/accept-new/no/yes;
  a changed or revoked key is always refused, with OpenSSH's warning);
- identities: the agent's keys (SSH_AUTH_SOCK), then `-i` files or
  `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` and `~/.ssh/id_ecdsa` (unencrypted OpenSSH key
  files), then keyboard-interactive and the password, asked on the
  terminal (standard input if it is one, else `/dev/tty`; never with
  BatchMode);
- a session channel unless -N: pty-req when -t is given or the session
  is interactive on a terminal (the local terminal then in raw mode,
  its size sent again when it changes), `auth-agent-req` with -A, LANG,
  then exec or shell; standard input to the channel, data to standard
  output, extended data to standard error, the exit status as ssh's own
  (255 for an error). On a terminal `~.` at the start of a line
  disconnects, `~?` lists the escapes, `~~` sends a `~`;
- -L listens (on the loopback address unless a bind address is given)
  and opens a direct-tcpip channel per connection; -R asks
  tcpip-forward and connects each forwarded-tcpip channel to its local
  target; with -A, agent channels go to the local agent.

`ssh-keygen` makes ed25519 and ecdsa key pairs in OpenSSH's format
(mode 0600, `.pub` next to it; no passphrase: `-N` must be empty), and
prints fingerprints (`-l`) and public keys (`-y`); `ssh-add -l`/`-L`
lists an agent's keys. Not there yet: sntrup761x25519-sha512, scp in the
system, encrypted key files, ssh_config files, a local agent.

**libcryptography** gained what the host keys need: Ed25519 (RFC 8032,
`Crypto.Ed25519`; extended coordinates, a ladder that swaps by masks,
reduction mod L by folding bytes) on the field arithmetic now shared
with X25519 (`Crypto.Curve25519Field`); ECDSA signing (`SignEcdsa`,
`EcdsaPublicKey` in `Crypto.Ecdsa`) with k made by RFC 6979 from the key
and the digest, so no random numbers are needed (the P-256 arithmetic
takes time that depends on k); and `Crypto.KeyGeneration` for new
Ed25519 seeds and ECDSA keys.

The post-quantum exchange uses the ML-KEM-768 that came with TLS's
X25519MLKEM768 (`Crypto.MlKem`, `Crypto.MlKemRandom`, on `Crypto.Sha3`).
ECDSA signing on P-256 and making a P-256
public key are now constant time (`Crypto.P256`): 8 fixed 32-bit limbs
mod p and mod n in Montgomery form, subtractions kept or dropped by
masks, inverses by Fermat (a public exponent), projective points added
with the complete formulas of Renes, Costello and Batina (a = -3, so the
point at infinity and doubling need no case), and k G by a Montgomery
ladder swapping by masks; P-384 still uses the variable time code.

**Tests.** The crypto host test checks Ed25519 against RFC 8032's
vectors (and refuses changed signatures and S + L) and ECDSA signing
against RFC 6979 A.2.5 and A.2.6. `make ssh-test` (`tools/SshTest`)
checks libssh on the host: RFC 4251's mpint examples, base64, the
packet layer of every cipher (sizes from 1 to 40000 bytes, a byte at a
time, the padding rules, changed packets and bad lengths refused), a
chacha20-poly1305 and two AES-GCM packets, the curve25519-sha256 hash
and derived keys, host key signatures, OpenSSH key files, RSA
signatures and authorized_keys lines against answers
`make-vectors.py` works out with Python and OpenSSL when the test is
built; and the server's layers against a small client in memory (the
host key's signature over H, strict kex, EXT_INFO, passwords, publickey
with PK_OK and the signed request, a channel with a request, data, a
rekeying and its orderly end, a stray packet before KEXINIT refused).
`scripts/test-ssh.py` (the last part of `make test`) boots the system
with QEMU forwarding a free port to port 22 and uses the host's
OpenSSH: exec with each cipher, host key and client key kind (ed25519,
ecdsa, rsa-sha2-512), 300 KB through `cat`, `ssh -tt` (tty, `stty
size`, the exit status), two channels over one connection
(ControlMaster), `scp` both ways, an `sftp` batch, password logins for
the user and root, and a wrong key, a wrong password and a locked
account refused. Then the additions: mlkem768x25519-sha256 as the
default (`ssh -v` names it; OpenSSH's post-quantum warning is gone) and
forced, `-L` and `-R` to an echo server on the host, agent forwarding
with the host's ssh-agent (`ssh-add -l` in the guest, and the guest's
own `ssh` logging in to its sshd over loopback with the forwarded key),
the guest's `ssh-keygen` and `ssh` (a new key, exec with its exit
status, a pseudo-terminal), a `command=` key, keyboard-interactive, and
after a restart with a new sshd_config a user certificate
(TrustedUserCAKeys), a host certificate checked against
`@cert-authority`, an idle session kept by keep-alives, and a
`Match User root` block. The SSH host test also checks the
mlkem768x25519 exchange (its K, H and keys against Python and OpenSSL),
the authorized_keys parser, certificates made by `ssh-keygen -s` (all
three key kinds, a bare and an expired one, a host certificate, a
publickey signature by a certificate's key), address and pattern lists,
known_hosts (hashed names, `@revoked`), Match blocks, the agent framing,
and libssh's client against its server in memory with each method and
cipher (hostbound publickey, keyboard-interactive, password, a refused
login, a session, global requests, a rekeying the client starts). The
crypto test checks the constant time P-256 against RFC 6979's
signatures and the public keys.

### Compression

**libcompression** (`userland/lib/compression`, units `Compression.*`)
is deflate (RFC 1951) both ways, with the zlib (RFC 1950) and gzip
(RFC 1952) wrappers and their checksums, and brotli (RFC 7932) and
Zstandard (RFC 8878) decompression. It needs only libsystem. libimage
uses it for PNG and TIFF, gzip for .gz files, libhttp for content
codings.

```
  Compression.Buffers   CompressZlib, DecompressGzip, ... on TBytes (raise)
  Compression.Streams   TDecompressionStream, TCompressionStream over a TStream
=========== streaming, any piece sizes, errors as codes ====================
  Compression.Inflater  TInflater: raw, zlib, gzip (several members), or
                        whichever the header says; checks every checksum
  Compression.Deflater  TDeflater: levels 0-9, raw, zlib or gzip
  Compression.InflateEngine   blocks, codes, history; fast loop
  Compression.HuffmanDecoding two-level lookup tables
  Compression.DeflateEngine   greedy and lazy matching, stored blocks
  Compression.MatchFinder     hash chains over two windows
  Compression.DeflateBlocks   stored, fixed or dynamic, the smallest
  Compression.HuffmanEncoding lengths limited to 15 (7), canonical codes
  Compression.BitWriter  Compression.ZlibFormat  Compression.GzipFormat
  Compression.Checksums (Adler-32, CRC-32)  Compression.DeflateFormat
  Compression.Formats  Compression.Errors
=========== streaming decoders, one interface ==============================
  Compression.StreamingDecoders  TStreamingDecoder (TInflater's contract)
  Compression.InflatingDecoders  TInflatingDecoder: a TInflater behind it
  Compression.BrotliDecoder   TBrotliDecoder: steps, undone at a short read
  Compression.BrotliMetaBlocks  BrotliPrefixCodes  BrotliContextMaps
  Compression.BrotliBitReader  carry for the bytes of an unfinished step
  Compression.BrotliDictionary (+ BrotliDictionaryData.inc, checked in)
  Compression.BrotliTransforms  BrotliTables (lengths, context lookup)
  Compression.ZstdDecoder     TZstdDecoder: frames, skippable, blocks
  Compression.ZstdLiterals  ZstdHuffman  ZstdSequences  ZstdFrames
  Compression.FiniteStateEntropy  ZstdBitReaders  XxHash64
  Compression.OutputWindows   the ring both write into, grown on demand
=========== libsystem ======================================================
```

**Decompressing.** `TInflater` is fed with `SetInput` and emptied by
`Decompress(Output, Capacity, Written)`, which says why it stopped:
it needs input, the output is full, the data has finished, or it
failed (`Error`, a `TCompressionError`). The decoder
(`Compression.InflateEngine`) is a state machine that can stop
wherever the input runs out - in a block header, among a dynamic
block's code lengths, between a length and its distance, in the
middle of a copy - and go on with the next piece. Output goes into a
96 KiB history (32 KiB that matches reach back into, 64 KiB of room)
that the caller empties; the last 32 KiB slide to the front once all
of it is taken. While 8 bytes of input and a whole match's room are
left, a tight loop decodes: it refills a 64-bit bit buffer eight bytes
at a time (56 bits, enough for a length and a distance with their
extra bits) and looks codes up in two-level tables
(`Compression.HuffmanDecoding`: 10 bits for literals and lengths, 8
for distances; longer codes in subtables), without a check per bit.
Codes are checked as zlib checks them (no over-subscribed code; an
incomplete one only as a single one-bit code), as are the code length
repeats, symbols 286, 287, 30 and 31, the end of block code, stored
lengths and every distance against the output so far; the first error
stops the decoder. The wrappers are checked as they arrive: the zlib
header (with a preset dictionary only when one was given: see below)
and Adler-32; the gzip header byte by
byte (extra field, name, comment, header CRC; `GzipHeader` has them),
CRC-32 and length; members follow one another as one output, and
anything else after a member is trailing data.

**Compressing.** `TDeflater` takes input with `SetInput` and gives
output with `Compress(Output, Capacity, Written, Finish)`. Input goes
into a buffer of two windows (`Compression.MatchFinder`); each
position is put on a hash chain of its next three bytes, and a search
walks back along it (comparing eight bytes at a time) as far as the
level allows. The levels are zlib's, with its limits: 0 stores, 1 to 3
take the longest match greedily, 4 to 9 take a match only when the
next position does not start a longer one. 32768 symbols make a block,
which `Compression.DeflateBlocks` sends stored, with the fixed codes
or with codes of its own (Huffman lengths limited to 15, the code
lengths run-length coded and limited to 7), whichever is smallest
counted to the bit. A block of incompressible data goes out before the
window slides away from its start, so that it can still be stored.

**Dictionaries and flushes.** `SetDictionary` before the first byte
gives raw or zlib data a preset dictionary: the deflater puts its last
32 KiB into the window as if they had just been coded (and zlib's
header gets FDICT and the dictionary's Adler-32), the inflater puts it
into the history before the first block. A zlib stream that asks for a
dictionary fails with `CompressionErrorPresetDictionary` when none was
given (`DictionaryId` names it) and `CompressionErrorDictionaryMismatch`
when another was. `Compress` with a `TDeflateFlush` flushes: `FlushSync`
codes everything taken so far and ends it with an empty stored block
(00 00 FF FF), so the receiver can decompress all of it now;
`FlushFull` also empties the hash chains, so nothing after refers to
anything before and decompression can start there; asking again
without new input adds nothing. The inflater needs nothing for them:
everything before a flush point comes out as soon as the input up to it
is in. `TCompressionStream.Flush` does the same for streams.

**The convenience layer.** `Compression.Buffers` does whole arrays in
one call and raises `ECompressionError` (with the code): decompression
is strict about cut off data and trailing bytes and can be bounded
(`MaximumSize`). `Compression.Streams` puts both directions behind a
`TStream`.

**Brotli and Zstandard.** `TBrotliDecoder` and `TZstdDecoder` decompress
with `TInflater`'s contract behind `TStreamingDecoder` (`SetInput`,
`Decompress`, `Finished`, `Error`, `InputRemaining`), as does
`TInflatingDecoder` around a `TInflater`, so libhttp drives all four
codings alike. Both write into a `TOutputWindow`: a ring that is a
power of two of at least the stream's window, starting at 64 KiB and
doubling with the output (only while it has not wrapped, so growing is
one reallocation), never beyond the window, so a short response never
takes the 16 MiB a brotli stream may ask for; output leaves it as far
as the caller's buffer goes, and decoding stops when what is not taken
would be overwritten.

Brotli is decoded in steps small enough to read again whole: the window
size, a meta-block header, each block category's type count, codes and
first count, the distance parameters and context modes, a context map,
one prefix code, a block switch, a command (its code and both extra
fields), one literal, a distance. `Compression.BrotliBitReader` reads a
64-bit buffer refilled eight bytes at a time; a read past the input
marks the step overrun and gives zeros, and the decoder then puts the
reader back where the step began and keeps the bytes it had begun on in
a carry (fewer than one step takes), so the caller's piece is let go
and the step is read again when more input comes. A literal is decoded
without that mark while 15 bits are at hand. Copies, dictionary words
(transformed into a 37-byte buffer) and uncompressed meta-blocks (taken
straight into the ring) carry on across calls by their remaining
length. Prefix codes use `Compression.HuffmanDecoding`'s two-level
tables (8 root bits), all the trees of a group end to end in one array;
the code length code is a fixed canonical code built once. Checked: the
window size pattern, reserved and padding bits (after uncompressed and
metadata headers and at the end of the stream), nibbles and metadata
lengths without needless zeros, complete codes, repeats within the
alphabet, context map runs, block types, distances (a special distance
of 0 or less), copy and insert lengths within the meta-block, and
dictionary references (length 4 to 24, transform below 121).

The static dictionary (122,784 bytes) is
`Compression.BrotliDictionaryData.inc`, checked in: it was written once
by `userland/lib/compression/make-brotli-dictionary.py`, which takes it
from the host's brotli library (libbrotlicommon's
`BrotliGetDictionary()` through ctypes) and refuses it unless its size
and CRC-32 are the RFC's (0x5136cb04); `--check` reads an include back
and checks it again. It is checked in rather than made at build time
because a build machine need not have brotli, and every host test that
compiles libhttp would otherwise need the generated file. The 121
transforms are a table written from the RFC's appendix B; the test
checks its CRC-32 (0x3d965f81) as the RFC gives it.

Zstandard: frames follow one another as one output; skippable frames
are passed over; anything else after a frame fails. The frame header
is gathered byte by byte (the window size, with the 128 MiB that zstd
itself allows by default, `MaximumWindowSize`; a dictionary id fails
with `CompressionErrorDictionaryNeeded`). A raw block is copied as its
bytes come, an RLE block written at once, a compressed block (at most
128 KiB) decoded when it is all at hand - straight from the caller's
piece when that holds all of it, else gathered first - and only once
the output before it is taken. Literals are raw (used where they are),
RLE, or Huffman coded (`Compression.ZstdHuffman`: weights direct or FSE
coded with two states, a single lookup table of up to 11 bits, one or
four streams, treeless blocks reusing the last tree);
`Compression.ZstdSequences` reads the three FSE tables (predefined,
built once per decoder; RLE; sent; repeat), then decodes each sequence
from the backward bitstream and carries it out at once: literals, then
the match from the offset (the three repeat offsets kept across the
frame's blocks). Every length, offset (against the frame's output and
the window), table and stream end is checked; so are the content size
when the header gives it and the XXH64 content checksum
(`Compression.XxHash64`) unless `VerifyChecksum` is off.

On the host (built without range checks) the decoders give roughly 250
MiB/s (brotli) and 330 MiB/s (zstd) on text at high levels, and over 1
GiB/s on repetitive data.

`make compression-test` (part of `make test`) builds the library on the
host as `tools/CompressionTest`, with vectors that
`tools/CompressionTest/make-vectors.py` makes with Python's zlib when
the test is built: zlib's output of five kinds of data at several
levels (stored, fixed only, Huffman only, run length, small windows
and small blocks, raw, zlib and gzip, several members, empty data, a
match exactly 32768 back), each decompressed whole, a byte at a time
and in varying pieces; broken streams of every kind, each refused with
its own error, whole and a byte at a time; every vector damaged forty
ways, which must be refused or decompressed but never crash (the test
is built with range checks); round trips at every level in every
format, whole and in pieces; sizes within a tenth of zlib's on the
same data; the stream adapters; gzip header fields. The samples it
compresses are then decompressed by Python's zlib and gzip
(`check-with-zlib.py`). Preset dictionaries and flushes are checked
both ways: zlib's data made with `zdict` (zlib and raw, levels 0 to 9,
a dictionary longer than the window) decompressed with the dictionary,
refused without it or with another; zlib's sync and full flushes
giving all the input before them at once, and the data after a full
flush decompressing on its own; the same of the library's own
dictionaries and flushes at every level, whose samples Python's zlib
then checks (`zdict`, decompressing up to each flush point). The brotli
and zstd decoders are checked over fixtures that
`tools/CompressionTest/make-fixtures.py` makes when the test is built,
with the host's `brotli` and `zstd` programs and Python's
`compression.zstd`: eight kinds of data (empty, one byte, text, UTF-8
in several scripts, binary records, noise, zeros, 3 MiB of repetition)
at brotli qualities 0 to 11 and windows of 2^10 and 2^24, zstd levels
1 to 22, without a checksum, a 1 KiB window, long distance matching and
streamed without a content size; several frames, skippable frames, a
metadata block (a brotli comment); streams made bit by bit (the empty
stream 06, metadata, an uncompressed meta-block, one-symbol codes,
dictionary words with and without a transform), each checked with the
host's decoder first; and broken ones: cut short, changed (brotli has no
check, so changed brotli data must only not crash), a bad window, bad
padding, trailing bytes, a bad checksum, magic or reserved bit, a
dictionary id, a 2 TiB window, a wrong content size. Each is decoded
whole, in varying pieces and a byte at a time in and out, and the
dictionary, transforms and context tables are checked against the RFC's
CRC-32s, XXH64 against known answers; the decoding speed is printed. On
the system, `gzip` (`-c`, `-d`, `-f`, `-k`, `-1` to `-9`) compresses and
decompresses files; started as `gunzip` it decompresses and as `zcat`
it decompresses to standard output (copies made by
make-system-disk.sh); coretest checks it.

### Archives (libarchive)

**libarchive** (`userland/lib/archive`, units `Archive.*`) reads zip,
tar, tar.gz, tar.zst and tar.xz files, writes zip files, extracts archives into folders
and lists an archive's folders for browsing. It is built over
libcompression (deflate, gzip, CRC-32, Zstandard, xz) and libsystem,
and its core units also build on the host. The file manager uses it for
compressed folders, pkg for packages (tar.zst).

```
  Archive.Readers     TArchiveReader (Count, Entries[], IndexOf,
                      ExtractToStream/ToFile), OpenArchive,
                      DetectArchiveFormat, IsArchiveFile
  Archive.Extraction  ExtractAll: safe names only, links last
  Archive.Folders     ListArchiveFolder: children, implied folders too
  Archive.ZipWriter   TZipWriter: AddFile/AddStream/AddFolder/AddLink, Finish
=========== formats =========================================================
  Archive.ZipReader   central directory, ZIP64, stored/deflated, CRC check
  Archive.ZipEndRecord  Archive.ZipExtraFields  Archive.ZipFormat
  Archive.TarReader   ustar, v7, GNU 'L'/'K', pax; hard links as copies
  Archive.TarFormat   Archive.RewindingStreams (tar.gz, tar.zst, seekable forward)
  Archive.XzStreams   tar.xz, decompressed into memory
  Archive.Detection   by content, not by name
=========== shared ==========================================================
  Archive.Entries (TArchiveEntry, SafeEntryPath)  Archive.Times
  Archive.Progress  Archive.Cp437  Archive.FileSystem (Sys.Files / host)
```

**Entries.** A member is a `TArchiveEntry`: its UTF-8 name with '/'
between the parts (a folder's ends with '/'), whether it is a folder or
a symbolic link (and its target), sizes, the modification time in Unix
seconds (UTC), Unix mode bits with the file type (0 when the archive
has none), whether it is encrypted, the method and the CRC-32. Zip
names are UTF-8 when flag 11 says so, else Info-ZIP's Unicode path
field when its CRC matches, else code page 437; the time is the
extended timestamp field's when there is one, else the DOS time taken
as UTC; modes come from the external attributes of members made on
Unix. Errors are `EArchiveError`; a progress callback
(`TArchiveProgressEvent`, uncompressed bytes so far) can cancel, which
raises `EArchiveCancelled`.

**Reading.** `OpenArchive` tells the format by content: a zip by a
local header at the start or its end of central directory record
(searched for backwards past a comment; data before the zip is allowed
for), gzip magic with a tar header inside, or a tar header ("ustar" or
a right checksum). The zip reader lists members from the central
directory (ZIP64 locator and extra fields included), so data
descriptors need nothing special; extraction inflates through
`TInflater` while computing the CRC-32 and refuses a wrong CRC or
size, encrypted members (flag 0 or AES) and other methods. The tar
reader walks the headers once when opened (pax `path`, `linkpath`,
`size`, `mtime`; GNU long names and links; base-256 numbers). A
.tar.gz or .tar.zst is read through `TRewindingDecoderStream`, which
decompresses forwards through libcompression's streaming decoders
(`TInflatingDecoder`, `TZstdDecoder`; several gzip members or zstd
frames read as one) and starts again only to go back, so listing and
extracting in order decompresses it once per pass. libcompression's xz
decoder works on whole buffers (it is the one the kernel unpacks RAM
disks with), so a .tar.xz is decompressed into memory when it is opened
(at most 512 MiB, `Archive.XzStreams`). A zstd file is taken for a
.tar.zst when its first block decodes to a tar header; an xz file for a
.tar.xz by its magic and, for small files, a size in its index that is a
whole number of tar blocks.

**Writing.** `TZipWriter` streams each member through `TDeflater`
(level 6) while computing its CRC-32, then writes the local header again
with the sizes (the output must be seekable); data that deflate does
not shrink is written again stored when the source can be reread. Names
get the UTF-8 flag when they are not ASCII, every member the extended
timestamp, "made by" Unix with the mode. A member expected near 4 GiB
gets a ZIP64 local header, and the central directory and end records
use ZIP64 when sizes, offsets or more than 65535 members need it, or
always with `ForceZip64`. Without `Finish` the file has no directory:
the caller deletes it.

**Extracting.** `SafeEntryPath` gives the relative path a name may be
extracted to: '\' taken as '/', '.' and empty parts dropped, and ''
for absolute names, drive letters, '..' parts and control characters.
`ExtractAll` leaves those out (and counts them), creates folders, writes
files, makes symbolic links only after every file (so nothing is written
through a link a member made), and sets folder times last. Times, modes
and links go through `Archive.FileSystem`, which calls libsystem on the
system and the host's Unix calls in the host test.

**Tests.** `make archive-test` builds the core units on the host with
range checks. `tools/ArchiveTest/make-fixtures.py` makes zip files with
Python's zipfile (stored, deflated, folders, a Unicode name, an empty
file, a link, data over 64 KiB, an extended timestamp, data
descriptors, forced ZIP64, 65540 members) and patches some by hand (a
CP437 name, the encrypted flag, a wrong CRC, unsafe names), and tar
files with tarfile (ustar, GNU, pax, tar.gz) plus an old v7 one. The
test checks every member's fields and data, extraction into folders
(modes, times, links, nothing outside), random access in a .tar.gz,
folder listing and cancelling; then writes zips (an empty file, folders,
a Unicode name, big and incompressible data, a link, a time before
1980; forced ZIP64; from files on disk; 65537 members), reads them back
and has `check-written.py` check them with Python's zipfile (testzip,
names, data, modes, DOS and extended times, ZIP64 end records).
The pax fixture is also read as .tar.zst (two Zstandard frames) and
.tar.xz. 7z is not read (TODO.md).

### Video: the AV1 decoder (libav1)

**libav1** (`userland/lib/av1`, units `Av1.*`) decodes AV1 (the AOMedia
Video 1 bitstream, royalty free): all of the Main profile in 8 and
10 bits, and the High (4:4:4) and Professional (4:2:2, 12-bit)
profiles' formats too, with every coding tool, film grain synthesis,
and tiles decoded on several threads. It needs only libmedia and the
runtime library, so it builds and is tested on the host as well.
Programs give `TAv1Decoder` the OBUs of a stream a temporal unit at a
time (an IVF frame, a Matroska block, an MP4 sample) and take the
frames it shows as libmedia's `Media.Frames` `TVideoFrame` records: one
plane each for Y, U and V, bytes for 8-bit streams and little-endian
words otherwise, cropped to the coded size (UpscaledWidth by
FrameHeight; the render size is only a hint), with the stream's colour
description. Or they go through libmedia: `Av1.MediaDecoder` registers
`TAv1VideoDecoder` (a `TVideoDecoder`: Configure with the track's av1C
configuration OBUs, SendPacket, ReceiveFrame, Reset) for codecAv1 when a
program uses it, as mediaplay does, so `mediaplay -k` checksums the AV1
frames of WebM, Matroska, MP4, IVF and OBU files (the last two read by
libmedia's `Media.Ivf` and `Media.ObuStream`).

```
  Av1.Decoder         TAv1Decoder: Decode (OBUs, a presentation time),
                      TakeFrame, Reset; operating point 0
  Av1.FrameDecoding   after a frame header: CDFs, previous segment ids,
                      motion field estimation; tile groups (tiles on the
                      worker pool); the wrapup: post filters, motion field
                      storage, the reference update; show_existing_frame
  Av1.Output          the output process: crop, film grain, TVideoFrame
  Av1.MediaDecoder    TAv1VideoDecoder, libmedia's decoder for codecAv1
  Av1.WorkerPool      workers that share a job's indices (tiles, rows)
=========== headers ========================================================
  Av1.SequenceHeader  Av1.FrameHeader (TFrameHeader)  Av1.FrameHeaderParsing
  Av1.BitReader (f(n), uvlc, le, leb128, su, ns)  Av1.References (the slots)
=========== tiles and blocks: syntax ========================================
  Av1.TileDecoding    init_symbol, decode_tile, read_lr, exit_symbol
  Av1.BlockDecoding   decode_partition, decode_block, compute_prediction
  Av1.BlockFlagsSyntax (segment ids, skip, CDEF, delta q/lf, is_inter)
  Av1.IntraModeSyntax Av1.PaletteSyntax Av1.InterModeSyntax
  Av1.ReferenceFrameSyntax Av1.MotionVectorSyntax Av1.TransformSyntax
  Av1.CoefficientSyntax  Av1.ResidualDecoding (transform blocks and trees)
  Av1.SymbolDecoder   the arithmetic decoder (64-bit window)  Av1.CdfContext
=========== prediction and reconstruction ===================================
  Av1.MvPrediction Av1.MvCandidates Av1.WarpSamples   find_mv_stack ...
  Av1.MotionField     motion field estimation (projection) and storage
  Av1.IntraPrediction Av1.IntraEdges Av1.PalettePrediction Av1.ChromaFromLuma
  Av1.InterPrediction Av1.BlockInterPrediction Av1.MotionVectorScaling
  Av1.Warp (local and global warp, shear, warp estimation)  Av1.Obmc
  Av1.CompoundMasks (wedge, difference, inter-intra, distance weights)
  Av1.Reconstruction  Av1.InverseTransform (DCT/ADST/flip/identity 4-64, WHT)
=========== post filters ====================================================
  Av1.PostFilters  Av1.LoopFilter Av1.LoopFilterSamples  Av1.Cdef
  Av1.SuperRes  Av1.LoopRestoration Av1.Wiener Av1.SelfGuided
  Av1.RestorationWindow  Av1.FilmGrain Av1.FilmGrainNoise Av1.FilmGrainScaling
=========== state and tables ================================================
  Av1.FrameContext (frame-wide arrays)  Av1.TileContext (a tile's block)
  Av1.Picture (planes of 16-bit samples)  Av1.Common  Av1.ToolStatistics
  Av1.Constants Av1.Tables Av1.DefaultCdfs Av1.QuantizerMatrices (generated)
```

**Following the specification.** The decoder is the decoding process of
the AV1 Bitstream and Decoding Process Specification written out in
Pascal: the routines carry the specification's names
(`DecodePartition` is decode_partition, `ReadCoefficients` is coeffs( )),
the state keeps its variable names (MiRow, YMode, RefFrame, Mv,
`TBlockInfo` for the per 4x4 arrays YModes, RefFrames, Mvs, MiSizes,
...), and every constant table (scan orders, default CDFs, filter
kernels, quantizer lookups and matrices, Gaussian sequence) is generated
from the specification's own Markdown sources by
`userland/lib/av1/make-tables.py` into checked in include files
(`Av1.Constants.inc`, `Av1.Tables.inc`, `Av1.DefaultCdfs.inc`,
`Av1.QuantizerMatrices.inc`, and the record of adaptive CDFs
`Av1.CdfFields.inc` with its initialization). Where the specification
writes a slow but simple formulation the code takes a faster one with
the same results: the symbol decoder keeps a 64-bit window of inverted
bits instead of reading bit by bit (running out of data shifts in ones,
the specification's zero padding), the coefficient contexts work out
the transform class once per block, CDEF filters a padded copy of each
8x8 block with an "unavailable" value no strength lets through,
unscaled inter prediction inside the reference skips clamping and does
zero fractions as plain scaling.

**State.** A `TFrameContext` holds the frame being decoded: its headers,
CurrFrame, the CDFs it started with and those saved from the tile
context_update_tile_id, and the frame-wide arrays indexed by mode info
position (with room to the next 128 samples and a superblock more,
since blocks reach past the frame's edges and the specification stores
them whole). Each tile is decoded with a `TTileContext` (its symbol
decoder and CDFs, the above and left contexts, the block's variables,
scratch for prediction and reconstruction); tiles write disjoint parts
of the frame's arrays, so several decode at once on the worker pool,
one context per worker. Samples are 16-bit everywhere (8, 10 and
12-bit streams take the same code), in `TPicture` planes with padding
past the right and bottom. A decoded frame becomes one
`TReferenceFrame` (the picture after loop restoration, its sizes and
order hints, the motion field and segmentation map stored compactly,
its CDFs, global motion, loop filter deltas, segmentation features and
film grain parameters) that every slot refresh_frame_flags names shares,
counting references.

**Post filters.** After the last tile group the frame wrapup runs the
deblocking filter (in place: all vertical edges of a plane, then all
horizontal ones), CDEF (into a copy), superres upscaling and loop
restoration (into another copy), each on the worker pool by superblock
rows or restoration stripes: within one pass of the deblocking filter
no two edges touch the same samples (filter lengths follow the
transform sizes on both sides), so rows can go in any order. Film grain
is added to the output frame only, as the specification's output
process does, never to the reference.

**Threads.** `TAv1Decoder.Create(ThreadCount)` makes a pool of
ThreadCount workers (the calling thread and ThreadCount - 1 threads,
`Av1.WorkerPool`); the tiles of a tile group and the rows of each post
filter are shared between them. A stream of one tile still gets its
post filters spread over the workers.

**Tests.** `make av1-test` builds libav1 on the host with range checks
(`tools/Av1Test`) and decodes the streams `tools/Av1Test/make-fixtures.py`
makes at build time with the host's encoders: aomenc with each tool and
format switched on (intra only, inter at several speeds, global and
local warp, OBMC, compound modes, 10 and 12 bits, 4:4:4 and 4:2:2,
monochrome, palettes and intra block copy, film grain, superres,
uniform and non-uniform tiles, 128x128 superblocks, lossless, quantizer
matrices, delta q and loop filter, segmentation, error resilience with
switch frames, reference scaling from resize mode, forward key frames),
SvtAv1EncApp and rav1e through ffmpeg; some of them also in WebM, MP4
and Matroska files (ffmpeg, without re-encoding) and as OBU files, read
through libmedia's demuxers and decoder registry. Every frame must equal what
aomdec, libaom's reference decoder, gives, sample for sample, on one
thread and with four, and damaged copies of the streams (bytes changed,
temporal units cut short or dropped) must be decoded or refused with
EAv1Error, never anything worse; the test lists how often each coding tool came up
(`Av1.ToolStatistics`, compiled in only for the test). On the system,
coretest runs `av1check`, which decodes four small streams built into it
(`userland/av1check/Av1Check.Streams.inc`, written by
`tools/Av1Test/make-system-check.py`) on one thread and four and
compares each frame's hash with aomdec's, then decodes the first again
from a WebM file through libmedia; a second coretest line has av1check
write that WebM file and checks mediaplay -k's MD5 of each frame.

**Not done.** Large scale tile decoding (Annex D: tile list OBUs, for
light fields) is not supported, and the scalability metadata's
operating point choice is fixed at 0. Speed comes from tables, integer
arithmetic and threads; there are no SIMD paths yet, and frames are not
decoded in parallel with each other.

## Ports and packages

Software from elsewhere comes to the system as **ports**, as on
FreeBSD: a tree of descriptions (`ports/CATEGORY/NAME/port.toml`), each
with the patches that make the software build and work here and files
of its own, built on the build machine by `scripts/ports.py` into
**packages**, which **pkg** installs, checks and removes on the system.
`ports/README.md` is the reference for port.toml, the commands and the
package format; this section is how the parts fit.

```
  build machine                                    the system
  ports/CATEGORY/NAME/port.toml, patches/, files/
        |  scripts/ports.py (scripts/portstool/)
        v
  fetch -> verify -> extract -> patch -> configure -> build -> stage -> package
        |                                                       |
  DISTDIR (~/Downloads/sources)            build/ARCH/ports/packages/*.pkg.tar.zst
                                                   |          |
                         install-to-image (image.list)    repo DIR --key
                                   |                          |  INDEX, INDEX.sig
                     build/ARCH/ports/image-root     HTTP(S) or a folder
                                   |                          |
                     system disk: /usr/local,        pkg update / install NAME
                     /var/db/pkg, /var/cache/pkg     pkg install FILE, remove,
                                                     verify, which, upgrade ...
```

**The prefix.** Ported software lives under `/usr/local` and nowhere
else (staging refuses anything outside it): the base system owns `/bin`,
`/lib`, `/app` and `/etc` and is replaced as a whole, so no package can
overwrite or break it, and replacing the base leaves packages alone;
`/usr/local` is also every build system's default. `/usr/local/bin` is
on the default PATH everywhere it is set (the kernel's first process,
`sh`, logins, the service manager's services, line completion,
`FindProgramPath`), and the program loader looks for libraries in
`/usr/local/lib` after `/lib` (see "Executables and shared libraries").

**The tool** is Python (it drives the build machine's own tools, and
Python's standard library reads TOML, tar in every compression, zip and
HTTP), split by concern under `scripts/portstool/`:

```
  cli.py          the commands; phases.py  PortBuild: phases, cookies, fingerprint
  portfile.py     Port: port.toml read, schema-checked, defaults, options, flavours
  schema.py       a JSON Schema subset, over ports/port.schema.json
  licenses.py     SPDX expressions against ports/licenses.txt
  tree.py         PortsTree: find, provider, search;  resolver.py  build order, cycles
  versions.py     version order and dependencies (as Pkg.Versions)
  fetch.py        download with mirrors, SHA-256, gpgv or Ed25519 signatures
  extract.py      archives unpacked safely;  patching.py  patch -pN, makepatch
  context.py      the clean environment and ${VARIABLES};  logs.py  a log per port
  toolchain.py    the C cross toolchain, meson cross files, cmake toolchain
                  files, the Free Pascal settings make writes
  builders/       autotools, meson, cmake, make, fpc, custom (and none)
  stage.py        the stage completed, tidied, checked, listed
  manifest.py     +MANIFEST;  package.py  writing and reading packages
  database.py     /var/db/pkg on a root;  image.py  install-to-image
  repository.py   INDEX and INDEX.sig;  ed25519.py  RFC 8032 in Python
```

A phase runs every phase before it that has not run; each leaves a
cookie in `build/ARCH/ports/NAME/.cookies`, and a fingerprint of the
port's folder (with the options, and for Pascal ports the runtime
library and libsystem it links against) sends a changed port back to
extract. Builds are reproducible: an environment of PATH and what the
tool sets (LC_ALL=C, TZ=UTC, SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH from the port's last
commit), a fresh stage, normalized permissions and times, sorted tar
members owned by 0:0, a fixed Zstandard level. A port that needs what
this machine lacks (the C toolchain, cmake, a host tool, another
architecture) is skipped, not failed, so `make ports` and the system
disk build work before the C toolchain exists.

**C ports** use the cross toolchain of `make c-toolchain`
(`build/toolchain/TRIPLET/bin/TRIPLET-gcc`, TRIPLET
`x86_64-freepascalos` or `aarch64-freepascalos`, with mlibc in
`build/sysroot/ARCH`). Each port builds against a sysroot of its own:
the toolchain's, hard linked, with the packages of its build
dependencies unpacked into it, pkg-config pointed there
(`PKG_CONFIG_SYSROOT_DIR`, `PKG_CONFIG_LIBDIR`). autotools gets
`--host=TRIPLET --build=... --prefix=/usr/local`, meson a cross file
(host_machine system `freepascalos`), cmake a toolchain file. zlib,
lua, sqlite3 and bash are committed with checksums verified against
upstream (zlib's and bash's signatures with the keys in their folders)
and status "untested" until the toolchain exists.

**Pascal ports** are compiled exactly as userland.mk compiles a /bin
program: make writes the build's compiler, USER_FLAGS, runtime and
library folders and link flags into `build/ARCH/user/ports-fpc.settings`
(`make ports-fpc-settings`, `ports/ports.mk`), and the fpc builder links
each program with `si_prc.o` against libsystem, libcryptography,
libcoreutils and the libraries the port names. hello is built from the
port's own files; ptop comes from the Free Pascal 3.2.2 source release
(fcl-base's CustApp and bufstream compiled in from the same tree) with
one patch, made with makepatch, that lets it read standard input and
write standard output; it is checked on the system (x86-64), installed
from a signed repository over HTTP.

**Packages** are `NAME-VERSION[_REVISION]-ARCH.pkg.tar.zst`: a pax tar
compressed with Zstandard whose first member is `+MANIFEST` (name,
version, origin, architecture, prefix, summary, SPDX licence,
dependencies, provides, conflicts, scripts, test commands, licence
files, then a `dir`, `file MODE SIZE SHA256 PATH` or `link PATH TARGET`
line per path), then `+DESC`, the scripts, and the payload. libarchive
reads tar.zst for pkg (and tar.xz; see "Archives").

**On the system disk.** `ports/image.list` names the ports the disk
carries installed: `make system-disk` builds their packages and their
run dependencies, `install-to-image` installs them into
`build/ARCH/ports/image-root` with their `/var/db/pkg` entries (pkg
treats them like any other package; their install scripts do not run),
adds `pkg-selftest`'s package to `/var/cache/pkg` for coretest, and
`scripts/make-system-disk.sh` copies the folder onto the disk with
empty `/var/db/pkg`, `/var/cache/pkg` and `/etc/pkg/keys`.

### pkg

`pkg` (`userland/bin/pkg.pas`, units `userland/pkg/Pkg.*`) installs
package files and packages from repositories, and removes, describes,
lists, finds (`which`), verifies, searches, updates, upgrades and tests
them. It links libarchive (tar.zst), libhttp (repositories),
libcryptography (SHA-256, Ed25519) and libsystem.

```
  pkg.pas           the command line, the lock
  Pkg.Commands      install, remove, info, list, which, verify, search, update,
                    upgrade, test over a context
  Pkg.Installer     one install or upgrade as a transaction
  Pkg.Remover       removal;  Pkg.Verification  an installed package checked
  Pkg.Repositories  /etc/pkg/repositories, INDEX fetched and its signature
                    checked, packages fetched and checked
  Pkg.Database      /var/db/pkg;  Pkg.Archives  a package file opened and checked
  Pkg.Manifests  Pkg.Index  Pkg.Versions  Pkg.Hashing  Pkg.Paths
  Pkg.Context       root, database, messages, and two services:
  Pkg.System        ... the system's: scripts by /bin/sh, URLs by libhttp
  Pkg.FileSystem    links, modes, renames, the lock (libsystem, or the host's)
```

**The database** is a folder per installed package,
`/var/db/pkg/NAME/`: `+MANIFEST` as it came in the package, `+DESC`,
the removal scripts, and `+INSTALLED` (`installed UNIXTIME`, `automatic
yes|no`: installed only as a dependency). An entry is written into a
temporary folder and renamed into place. `pkg -r ROOT` (or `PKG_ROOT`)
works on another root. Commands that change anything hold an exclusive
lock on `/var/db/pkg/.lock`.

**Installing** is a transaction (`Pkg.Installer`):

1. Checks before anything is touched: the architecture; the version
   against what is installed (the same or an older one is refused
   without `-f`); every dependency installed (a version requirement is
   checked against the package of that name; another package providing
   the name meets it); no conflicting package either way; no path that
   belongs to another package, is a folder, or (without `-f`) is there
   and belongs to no package.
2. The pre-install script (a failure stops it).
3. Staging: every file unpacked beside its place as `NAME.pkg-new`,
   its size and SHA-256 checked against the manifest while it is
   written, its mode set; links made the same way; the manifest's
   folders made. A failure removes everything staged and the folders
   made for it.
4. Commit: an existing file is moved aside to `NAME.pkg-old` and the
   staged one renamed into place; a failed rename puts back everything
   committed so far (and removes the staging).
5. The files of the previous version that the new one lacks are
   removed, the `.pkg-old` copies deleted, the database entry written,
   and the post-install script run (its failure is only reported).

A package named instead of a file comes from the repositories: the
newest version for this architecture in the cached indexes (a package
of that name before one that only provides it), its missing
dependencies installed first as automatic ones, each fetched into
`/var/cache/pkg` and used only when its size and SHA-256 are the
index's (a cached copy that matches is not fetched again). `pkg
upgrade` installs every newer version the indexes have (upgrades keep
whether a package was automatic).

**Removing** refuses a package another installed package needs (unless
that one goes in the same command, or `-f`), runs the pre-remove script
(a failure stops it), removes its files and links (saying which had
changed since they were installed), its folders left empty (deepest
first, never the prefix's own `bin`, `lib`, `share`, ...), its
database entry, then runs the post-remove script. **verify** checks
every folder, file (size, SHA-256, permissions) and link of a package,
and its dependencies. **Scripts** run as `/bin/sh FILE` with
`PKG_NAME`, `PKG_VERSION`, `PKG_ROOT` and `PKG_PREFIX` set; `pkg test`
runs a package's test lines the same way.

**Repositories** (`/etc/pkg/repositories`, `NAME URL [key=PATH |
signature=none]`): `pkg update` fetches `URL/INDEX` and `URL/INDEX.sig`
(http and https through libhttp with the system's certificates, or
`file:///path` and plain paths), checks the Ed25519 signature with
`/etc/pkg/keys/NAME.pub` (`ed25519 HEX`; refused without a key unless
`signature=none`), parses the index and only then replaces the cached
one in `/var/cache/pkg/repos/NAME/`. `scripts/ports.py repo DIR --key
SECRET` writes both on the build machine (`make ports-repo`).

**Tests.** `make ports-test` (tools/PortsTest, Python unittest) checks
the tool: port.toml and the schema, licences, versions, the resolver,
extraction, patches and makepatch, manifests, packages (layout, byte
for byte reproducibility, damaged ones found), install-to-image,
repositories, Ed25519 against RFC 8032 and OpenSSL, and whole builds
through `scripts/ports.py` in a ports tree of its own, including
autotools, meson and cmake cross builds with the build machine's gcc behind
x86_64-freepascalos names and a build dependency unpacked into the
sysroot, the skip without a toolchain, signatures, and refusals.
`make pkg-test` (tools/PkgTest) builds pkg's units on the host (all but
`Pkg.System`, with the host's Unix calls in `Pkg.FileSystem` and
`Archive.FileSystem`) over packages, an index and an image database
that `make-fixtures.py` makes with the ports tool: versions in the
ports tool's order, manifests, indexes, archives, then install,
refusals that change nothing (the same version, a file of another
package, an unmet version, a conflict, another architecture, a damaged
package, a failing pre-install script), forcing over a file of no
package, an upgrade, verify finding changes, which, info, list, and
removal leaving nothing; and repositories over file:// (update, search,
install by name with a dependency, a damaged cached package fetched
again, a bad signature and a missing key refused). coretest installs
`pkg-selftest` from `/var/cache/pkg`, checks its files, link, scripts
and test line, verifies it, sees two refusals and a changed file, and
removes it, leaving `hello` alone.

## JavaScript engine

libjavascript (`userland/lib/javascript`, units `Js.*`, built as
`libjavascript.so` for amd64 and arm64 on libsystem alone) is an
ECMAScript engine made for speed and a small footprint, with an
embedding API for libweb's DOM bindings. `js` (`userland/bin/js.pas`,
units in `userland/js`) runs a file, `-e` code or a REPL.

**Values** (`Js.Values`) are 64-bit NaN-boxed words: every double but
NaN is its own bit pattern, the negative quiet NaN space above the one
canonical NaN carries tagged values (top 16 bits: FFF9 int32, FFFA
undefined/null/false/true/the hole/the exception mark, FFFB object,
FFFC string, FFFD symbol, FFFE BigInt; pointers in the low 48 bits).
Numbers, booleans, null and undefined never allocate; integral doubles
in the int32 range are kept as integers so loops and indexing take
integer paths. A routine that has thrown returns `JsException`; the
thrown value waits in the runtime (no Pascal exception per JS throw).

**Strings** (`Js.Strings`) are immutable UTF-16 sequences stored with one
byte per unit when Latin-1 and two otherwise; concatenations longer than
40 units make ropes, flattened (iteratively, never recursively) on first
read. Property keys are atoms (`Js.Atoms`: interned strings, compared by
pointer; the table is weak) or symbols, or int32 values for array indices
below 2^31. Case mapping (`Js.CaseMapping`: toLowerCase, toUpperCase,
localeCompare's folding, case-insensitive regular expression classes)
maps runs of well-formed text and leaves lone surrogates as they are
(the run-time library raises on them).

**Objects** (`Js.Objects`, `Js.Shapes`) have a shape (hidden class: a
parent plus one property, with transitions to children that are weak and
die with their last object), four inline slots and a slot buffer, a
prototype, and dense elements in an array of their own (holes marked;
sealed and frozen elements by a flag, not by moving them). Many
properties, a delete or a reconfiguration turn an object's shape into a
dictionary of its own that it changes in place, bumping a generation
number. The internal methods are virtual: arrays (length), String
objects, arguments, proxies and host objects override them; the fast
paths read shapes and elements directly.

**Compiler.** `Js.Lexer` → `Js.Parser` (recursive descent, precedence
climbing, cover grammars for arrows and destructuring; scopes and
references recorded while parsing; nesting bounded) → `Js.Scopes`
(resolves each identifier to its variable; a variable used by a nested
function is captured; this/new.target/super/arguments used from arrows
become captured implicit variables of the enclosing function) → the
compiler in four layers (`Js.CodeBuilder`, `Js.ExpressionCompiler`,
`Js.StatementCompiler`, `Js.Compiler`) emitting register bytecode
(`Js.Bytecode`). Locals live in registers, captured variables in
per-scope environments (a scope only gets one when something in it is
captured; a for-let loop copies its environment per iteration).
finally blocks are copied in front of each jump out of them and compiled
once more as an exception handler; their copies are gaps in the
protected ranges. The temporal dead zone is checked only where a read
can precede initialisation. A script's own declarations are global
bindings found by name (var/function on the global object, let/const/
class in the global lexical environment).

**Lazy compilation.** A function of 160 source characters or more
(not class constructors, field initializers or functions using private
names) gets a stub TJsCode: its flags, name, length and source range,
and a TJsLazyFunction holding the position of its parameter list and
the chain of scopes around it (`Js.EvalScopes`, shared per scope). The
first parse still checks its early errors and marks the outer variables
it uses as captured; its bytecode is made on the first call
(EnterFrame), by parsing the function again from its parameters inside
scopes rebuilt from the chain, so its identifiers resolve to the same
environment hops and slots. The closures keep the TJsCode, which is
filled in place.

**Direct eval, with, arguments** (`Js.Scopes`, `Js.EvalScopes`,
`Js.DirectEval`, `Js.Arguments`). A call `eval(...)` marks every scope
around it exposed: their variables live in environments, and the
function keeps its this, new.target, home object and arguments as
implicit variables. The call site keeps a TJsEvalChain (each scope's
kind, environment size and variables with their slots); at run time,
when the callee is %eval%, the source is parsed inside scopes rebuilt
from it and compiled like an arrow's body, then run as a closure on the
caller's environment at the call - no lookup by name. Sloppy var and
function declarations go to an existing binding of the function, to
the global object at a script's top level, or to the function's eval
var object, which the names of the function and of everything nested
in it look in before the scopes outside. A with statement keeps its
object (ToObject) in a scope's environment; every identifier inside it
records the with objects (and eval var objects) on its way out and
compiles to lookups in them first (opLookupDynamic and kin, honouring
@@unscopables; a found function is called with the object as this).
A sloppy function with simple parameters that uses arguments gets a
mapped arguments object: its parameters are kept in the environment
and arguments[i] reads and writes their slots until unmapped. None of
this costs anything in functions that use none of it.

**Interpreter** (`Js.Interpreter`): one value stack of fixed capacity
holds every frame's registers (so pointers handed to natives stay
valid) and a fixed frame array bounds recursion (RangeError beyond). A
call passes callee, this and arguments in consecutive registers and the
callee's frame begins at its arguments; JS-to-JS calls continue in the
same loop, calls from Pascal re-enter it. Property access sites have
inline caches: own slot (shape + generation), direct prototype slot,
and property addition (shape transition, guarded by a prototype epoch
bumped when a prototype gains a setter or read-only property or a
prototype changes). Globals have their own caches. Exceptions look up
the frame's handler table (innermost first); a generator's return() is
a return completion that only finally handlers take. Generators, async
functions and async generators run in frames copied into and out of
their suspension object at each yield or await. A property site that
sees several shapes keeps up to three more cache entries (polymorphic,
the oldest replaced after four). Indexed reads and writes of typed
arrays and their length (while %TypedArray%.prototype's length getter
is the original) and for-of over them take direct paths.

**Collector** (`Js.Heap`): precise, tracing mark-and-sweep with an
explicit mark stack; the marking stops the world, the sweeping is
incremental. It runs only at safe points (loop back edges, frame
entries), so no allocation ever collects; native code keeps values it
holds across calls into JavaScript in the runtime's temporary roots.
The few cells with weak links of their own (shapes, collection
iterators) are kept on a list of their own and swept in the pause;
the rest is swept a slice (4096 cells) per safe point afterwards, the
safe point threshold dropping to zero until it is done, while new cells
go to a fresh list. An explicit collection, or one near the memory
limit, sweeps at once. LongestPause, TotalPause, MarkTime and SweepTime
are measured (TJsEngine.CollectorStatistics). Marking remains a pause
proportional to the live heap (8 ms for the 85 MB gc-large-heap
benchmark): making it incremental needs a write barrier on every store
of a reference into a cell (object slots and elements, environments,
the built-ins' direct element writes), which is the next step. Weak structures: the atom table, shape transitions,
WeakMap/WeakSet (ephemerons: values marked to a fixpoint for live keys),
WeakRef, FinalizationRegistry (cleanup queued as jobs). The next
collection is due at twice what survived (at least 4 MiB by default);
the memory limit and interrupts are checked at safe points and stop the
script with an uncatchable InternalError.

**Binary data** (`Js.ArrayBuffers`, `Js.Builtins.ArrayBuffer`,
`Js.Builtins.TypedArrays`, `Js.Builtins.Atomics`, `Js.Builtins.Base64`):
ArrayBuffer (resizable, transfer and transferToFixedLength moving the
memory without a copy, detached), SharedArrayBuffer (growable; one
agent), DataView with Float16, the twelve typed array kinds with
Float16Array (integer-indexed exotic objects: canonical numeric keys are
elements or nothing; fixed or length-tracking windows, out of bounds
after a shrink or detach), %TypedArray% with all its methods working on
the bytes (moves between same kinds, numeric sort without a comparator),
Atomics (single agent: wait throws as on a main thread), Math.f16round,
and Uint8Array base64/hex. A buffer's block counts towards the heap and
may be the host's memory (freed through the host's procedure).

**Modules** (`Js.ModuleRecords`, `Js.Modules`): every import and
export form, import attributes (`with { type: "json" }` for JSON
modules), namespace objects, live bindings (an import reads the
exporter's environment slot through opGetImport), cycles (module
environments exist from compilation; linking runs each module's
initializer, which makes its hoisted functions), top-level await (the
body of a module that awaits is an async function; evaluation follows
the specification's asynchronous module steps), import.meta (url,
resolve, plus what the host adds) and import(). The host resolves
specifiers (default: "./" and "../" against the referrer) and fetches
sources (TJsModuleFetch.Succeed or Fail, at once or later); the module
map fetches each key once. Linking and evaluation run as a job after a
graph has loaded. The js shell runs `.mjs` files and `-M` as modules,
reading imports from files.

**Embedding** (`Js.Engine`): `TJsEngine` (one realm) with Evaluate /
TryEvaluate, Call, Construct, RunJobs (the microtask queue), host
functions (plain callbacks with a magic number, or methods of objects),
host classes (`DefineClass`: constructor, prototype, instances carrying
native data with a finalizer and a trace hook for the JavaScript values
the host keeps alive), Protect/Unprotect for values held across calls,
MemoryLimit, Interrupt (any thread), CollectGarbage and heap statistics;
binary data without copies (NewArrayBuffer, NewArrayBufferFrom,
NewExternalArrayBuffer, NewTypedArray, NewUint8Array, BufferSourceData,
DetachArrayBuffer, IsArrayBuffer, IsTypedArray; natives use
Js.ArrayBuffers and Js.Builtins.TypedArrays.NewTypedArray); modules
(EvaluateModule, ImportModule, ModuleNamespace, and the ModuleResolver,
ModuleFetcher and ModuleMetaHook hooks).
Uncaught exceptions reach the host as `EJsError` with the stack text.
`Js.Platform` holds the clock and time zone hooks; `Js.SystemClock`
fills them on FreePascalOS from the kernel's clock and the time zone
database (the host tests keep the runtime's).

**Built-ins**: Object, Function (and the generator/async function
constructors), Array, String, Number, Boolean, Symbol, BigInt, Math,
JSON, Error and its kinds (with causes and V8-style stack traces),
Map/Set (ordered hash tables whose iterators survive deletions; the Set
methods), WeakMap/WeakSet/WeakRef/FinalizationRegistry, Promise (all,
allSettled, any, race, withResolvers, try), Array.fromAsync (written in
JavaScript, `Js.Builtins.SelfHosted`), iterator helpers
(Iterator.prototype.map and the others, Iterator.from), Reflect, Proxy,
Date (proleptic Gregorian arithmetic, ISO and toString/toUTCString
parsing, en-US locale strings), RegExp (`Js.RegExpCompiler` and
`Js.RegExpMatcher`: a backtracking matcher with an undo stack; named
groups, back references, lookahead and lookbehind, the u, v, y, s, d, i,
m, g flags, \p general categories and 38 scripts by their blocks),
globalThis, the URI functions, parseInt/parseFloat, eval,
queueMicrotask, console, Error.captureStackTrace and stackTraceLimit.
Annex B: escape/unescape, the String HTML methods, __defineGetter__ and
its kin, the RegExp statics ($1-$9, input, lastMatch...).
String.prototype.normalize (`Js.Normalization`): UAX #15 over tables
written by hand - Latin-1, Latin Extended-A, pinyin, Romanian and
Vietnamese letters, basic Greek, Cyrillic, Hangul (computed), the
combining marks' classes, and the common compatibility forms; Greek
Extended, other Latin Extended Additional letters and other scripts'
marks are left as they are. Intl (`Js.Builtins.Intl`), one locale
(en-US): NumberFormat (decimal, percent, currency, unit; digits,
grouping, signs; formatToParts), DateTimeFormat (fields and
date/timeStyle, local zone or UTC), Collator (code point order;
base/accent sensitivity, numeric), PluralRules, Segmenter (graphemes,
words, sentences), ListFormat; Number, BigInt and Date toLocaleString
use them. `Js.Inspect` prints values as Node's util.inspect does, on
one line.

**Several realms.** `TJsEngine.CreateSharing(Parent)` makes another
realm in a runtime (an iframe's window): one heap, objects passed
freely. Closures and native functions carry their `Realm` and every
call is dispatched to it (the interpreter's fast paths fall back to
`Call` for a foreign function; the callee realm notes the caller in
`CallerRealm`, which postMessage takes as its source). `Detach` stops a
sharing realm's roots (its window closed; its functions then run in the
caller's realm); a sharing engine is freed after the runtime's owner, or
its realm and host classes are kept until then.
`EvaluateBuiltin` compiles an embedder's built-ins written in
JavaScript (their sources are marked `Builtin`: Function.prototype.
toString gives native code). A not-a-function error names the callee
as V8 does ("a.b.c is not a function"), from the source text at the
call. Math.floor, ceil and round work on the whole double range (the
runtime's Floor gives 32 bits), and assigning an object or array
literal that reads the variable no longer builds it in that variable's
register first (`b = {x: b}`).

Not there yet: structuredClone (a host matter), private names inside
direct eval code, locales other than en-US, the full Unicode tables for
normalization and RegExp scripts; there is no JIT, and the collector's
marking is neither incremental nor generational.

`make javascript-test` (tools/JavaScriptTest) runs each
`scripts/*.js` (and each `scripts/*.mjs` as a module, its imports in
`scripts/modules`) against the output written in its trailing
`/* expected` comment, checks the embedding API (host functions and
classes, finalizers, protected values, the memory limit, interrupts,
buffers without copies, modules fetched later) and runs
`benchmarks/*.js`, reporting time, the heap's peak, the process's peak
bytes, the collections and the longest pause; `JS_GC_STRESS=1` collects
every 16 KiB to find missed roots.

## Network drivers

Network card drivers (`kernel/drivers/network`) register each card as a
network adapter (`Io.NetworkAdapters`: `RegisterNetworkAdapter` with
the routines that send a frame and say whether the link is up; the
driver calls `NetworkFrameReceived`, `NetworkLinkChanged` and
`NetworkTransmitReady`). Frames are Ethernet II without the check
sequence; adapters are named `eth0`, `eth1`, ... in the order they
register. What the drivers share is in `Drivers.NetworkCards`: it
registers the adapter, follows the link (a change is logged and the
network layer told), keeps the statistics, and writes the lines the
tests look for:

    [net] eth1: Intel 82574L, address 52:54:00:12:34:56, link down, interrupts by MSI
    [net] eth1 (Intel 82574L): link up, 1000 Mbit/s full duplex
    [net] eth1 (Intel 82574L): link up after waking

The kernel debug shell's `netcards` writes every card's link and
statistics (frames and bytes each way, damaged and missed frames,
failed sends, collisions, link changes).

**Probing.** `Io.Startup` starts the drivers after sound
(`InitializeE1000Adapters`, `InitializeRtl8139Adapters`,
`InitializeRtl8168Adapters`, `InitializeRtl8125Adapters`); each walks
the PCI functions for its IDs, maps the registers, resets the card,
reads its station address, takes its DMA memory, connects its
interrupt, registers the adapter and its power handler, and only then
enables receiving and the interrupt mask, so nothing arrives for an
adapter that does not exist yet.

**DMA memory** (`Drivers.NetworkBuffers`) is kept below 4 GiB for every
card: descriptor rings are one page; frame buffers are 2 KiB, two to a
page, so none crosses a page. The RTL8139's receive ring is one 32 KiB
buffer, from `AllocateZeroedContiguousPhysicalPages` (`Memory.PhysicalPages`:
a run of free frames below a limit, found in the free-frame bitmap; see
"Contiguous physical runs").

**Rings.** Receive and transmit rings of 128 descriptors with a buffer
each. Received frames are handed to the network layer from the buffer
(it copies them) and the descriptor given straight back; frames bigger
than one buffer are dropped whole. A frame to send is copied into the
next descriptor's buffer and padded to 60 bytes; when the ring is full
`Transmit` returns False and the driver calls `NetworkTransmitReady` once
it reclaimed descriptors. A receive lock and a transmit lock keep the
two sides apart (the deferred routine can run on two processors at
once).

**Interrupts.** MSI where the card has it (the PCI Express parts), else
the PCI interrupt line (shared: the handler checks and clears the
card's cause register), else a 10 ms polling timer. The handler only
records the causes and queues the deferred routine, which takes the
received frames, reclaims sent ones, and reads the link after a link
change interrupt. A second timer reads the statistics and the link
every two seconds, so a lost link interrupt is caught too.

**Suspend to RAM.** Each driver's power handler (devices stage) stops
its rings (frames offered meanwhile are refused, and the network layer
told when there is room again), masks the interrupts, turns receive and
transmit off and cancels its timers and deferred calls. Waking, the card
is reset and set up again from what memory holds, with the same adapter
record, and `NetworkCardWoke` makes the next link-up be announced as
"link up after waking".

The tests run QEMU with an e1000e, an e1000 and an RTL8139, each on its
own user-mode network (`-netdev user`); `make test` checks each card's
boot line (its interrupts: MSI on the e1000e, the line on the others)
and that its link came up, and the input test that each link is up
again after waking from suspend to RAM.

### Intel e1000 and e1000e

`Drivers.E1000` (with `.Registers`, `.Models`, `.Hardware`, `.Rings`)
drives Intel's gigabit family with one queue of legacy descriptors:
reset (CTRL.RST), the station address from receive address register 0
(loaded from the EEPROM/NVM by the reset) or else the EEPROM read
register (two layouts: 82540/82545/82546, and the later parts), "set
link up" with automatic speed detection (the PHY negotiates), receive
with broadcasts and every multicast (adapters keep no filter list; the
network layer filters), the check sequence stripped, 2 KiB buffers;
transmit with short packets padded, the copper inter-packet gap, at most
8000 interrupts a second. Statistics come from the clear-on-read
counters (CRC, alignment, receive and length errors, missed packets,
collisions, excessive and late collisions).

| Family | Parts (PCI device IDs, vendor 8086) |
|---|---|
