| 8254x | 82540EM/EP (100E, 1015, 1016, 1017, 101E: QEMU `e1000`), 82545EM/GM (100F, 1026), 82546EB/GB (1010, 101D, 1079, 1099, 10B5), 82541EI/ER/GI/PI (1013, 1018, 1014, 1078, 1076, 1077, 107C), 82547EI/GI (1019, 101A, 1075) |
| 8257x | 82571EB (105E, 10A4, 10BC), 82572EI (107D, 10B9), 82573E/V/L (108B, 108C, 109A), 82574L (10D3, 10F6: QEMU `e1000e`), 82583V (150C) |
| I217/I218/I219 | I217 (153A, 153B), I218 (155A, 1559, 15A0-15A3), I219 (156F, 1570, 15B7-15BE, 15D6-15E3, 0D4C-0D4F, 0D53, 0D55, 15F4, 15F5, 15F9-15FC, 1A1C-1A1F, 550A-5511, 57A0, 57A1) |

The 8257x parts get bit 22 of the transmit descriptor control their
manuals require. The I217/I218/I219 sit in the platform controller hub:
the reset is taken under the software flag (which keeps the management
engine off the MAC), the driver waits for "LAN init done", reads the
address only from the receive address registers (their NVM is the
platform's flash) and leaves the PHY as the firmware set it up; their
transmit arbitration and NFS filter bits are set as their
initialisation sets them. Not done for those parts: leaving the PHY's
ultra low power mode and the LANPHYPC toggle, the I219's descriptor
ring flush before a reset, K1/EEE workarounds, the management engine
handshake, and reading the flash. Fibre and SerDes parts, the
82543/82544, 80003ES2LAN, ICH8-ICH10 and 82577-82579 are not taken. The
82574L is driven by MSI, not MSI-X. Only the 82540EM and 82574L run in
the tests (QEMU); the rest is untested.

### Realtek RTL8139

`Drivers.Rtl8139` (with `.Registers`) drives the 10/100 RTL8139 (QEMU
`rtl8139`; also the Accton, D-Link, Planex, AboCom, Allied Telesyn,
Delta and Addtron cards built on it) through its I/O ports. The card
writes received frames one after another into the 32 KiB ring, each
behind a status/length header; "wrap" mode lets a frame run on past the
end, so frames are never split. The driver reads while the card says
the ring is not empty and writes back how far it read (minus 16, as the
card wants); a broken header restarts the receiver. Four transmit slots
are used strictly in turn, each with its own buffer; writing a slot's
length starts it. Interrupts come on the PCI line; the link is the
PHY's basic mode status (read twice: it latches a loss), and a link
change raises the "packet underrun / link change" interrupt. The
missed-packet counter feeds the statistics.

### Realtek RTL8168/8111 and RTL8125/8126

The Realtek gigabit (RTL8168/8111) and multi-gigabit (RTL8125, RTL8126)
chips share the descriptor format (an "owned by the card" bit and an
"end of ring" bit, no head or tail registers), the station address,
command, configuration and descriptor address registers, and the tally
counters. `Drivers.RealtekGigabit` (with `.Registers` and `.Rings`)
holds that: the card record, the rings, interrupts by MSI or line, the
deferred routine, the statistics (the chip dumps its tally counters to
a page when asked; the driver asks every two seconds and reads the
answer on the next round, so nothing waits), and suspend to RAM. A chip
unit gives it a `TRealtekChip`: where its interrupt registers are and
how wide, how to ring its transmit poll register, how to bring the chip
from any state to running, and how to read its link. QEMU emulates
none of these chips: they are untested.

`Drivers.Rtl8168` (10EC:8168, 10EC:8161): 16-bit interrupt registers at
3Ch/3Eh, transmit poll at 38h; reset, the station address (or its
power-on copy at 19E0h), the largest frame, the rings, receive and
transmit configuration; the link from the PHY status register. Not
done: the per-version PHY tuning and PHY firmware patches Linux applies
to some RTL8168 versions, and the RTL8169 (PCI) parts.

`Drivers.Rtl8125` (10EC:8125 RTL8125, 10EC:3000 Killer E3000, 10EC:8126
RTL8126, 10EC:5000 Killer E5000): 32-bit interrupt registers at
38h/3Ch, transmit poll at 90h (only the first of the chip's queues is
used), and the MAC's and PHY's internal registers reached through the
OCP windows (`Drivers.RealtekOcp`: B0h for the MAC, B8h for the PHY,
each access under a spin lock and with a bounded wait). The version is
read from the XID bits of the transmit configuration
(`Drivers.Rtl8125.Versions`), as the reference drivers do:

| XID | Version | PHY firmware patch |
|---|---|---|
| 609 | RTL8125A | rtl_nic/rtl8125a-3.fw |
| 641 | RTL8125B | rtl_nic/rtl8125b-2.fw |
| 688, 689 | RTL8125D | rtl_nic/rtl8125d-1.fw, rtl8125d-2.fw |
| 681 | RTL8125BP | rtl_nic/rtl8125bp-2.fw |
| 649, 64A | RTL8126A | rtl_nic/rtl8126a-2.fw, rtl8126a-3.fw |

A chip with another XID is logged and set up as the RTL8125B (or, on an
RTL8126 ID, the RTL8126A). `Drivers.Rtl8125.Setup` brings the chip up
in the order and with the values of Linux's r8169 (`rtl_hw_init_8125`,
`rtl_hw_start_8125`, `rtl_hw_start_8125_common`): receive gated off,
out-of-band mode left, the link list FIFO, a reset; the PLL and PHY
powered up and waited for ("LAN on"); with the configuration unlocked,
ASPM and clock requests off in the chip and on its PCI Express link
(those link states cause drops and stalls on these chips), interrupt
coalescing, receive side scaling and the extra queues off, the legacy
transmit descriptor format, the MAC's FIFO and timing values, EEE off
in the MAC, receive ungated; the largest frame, the station address
(from the power-on copy at 19E0h, else the address registers), the
rings, receive and transmit on. Then the PHY: the firmware patch if one
was loaded, advanced link-down power saving and EEE off, 10/100/1000
and 2.5G (5G on the RTL8126) advertised, autonegotiation restarted. The
link (up to 5000 Mbit/s, duplex) comes from the MAC's PHY status
register; while it stays down, the PHY status, BMCR, BMSR, the
PHY-specific status and the PHY state are logged after 10 and 60
seconds. The boot log names the version, its XID and the PCI revision.
Not done: the per-version PHY tuning tables and the PCI Express PHY
(EPHY) values Linux writes.

**Firmware patches.** Linux loads a PHY patch for every RTL8125/8126
version but treats it as optional (it carries on without the file);
this driver does the same: every version is set up without one, and
the patch, when it arrives, is applied on top. The driver asks for the
file through `Io.Firmware` (`RequestFirmware`); drivers start before any
volume is mounted, so `Io.Startup` calls `DeliverRequestedFirmware`
once the volumes are, which reads `/lib/firmware/<name>` from the
system volume (`make system-disk` installs `firmware/` there) and calls
each driver back at passive level with the contents (or nil: the
missing file is logged and the driver goes on without it); later
requests are answered at once. `Drivers.RealtekFirmware` reads the file
in Linux's rtl_fw format (r8169_firmware.c): an optional header (zero
magic, version string, the operations' offset and count, a checksum
making the bytes add to zero), then 32-bit operations that read and
write PHY registers - or, after "change to MAC", MAC registers through
the MCU window - in MDIO-style pages, keep the last value read,
compare, skip, jump back, and wait. Every operation and jump is checked
before anything runs, and a run stops after a million steps. The patch
is applied with the card's configuration lock held (the PHY is set up
again, and autonegotiation restarted, right after), and again on every
set-up after that (waking from suspend to RAM).

### Broadcom GENET v5 (untested)

The Raspberry Pi 4's Gigabit Ethernet (`Drivers.Genet`, registers in
`Drivers.Genet.Registers`, its MDIO bus in `Drivers.Genet.Phy`, the PHY
handling shared with the Pi 5's GEM in `Drivers.EthernetPhy`), an ACPI
platform device (`BCM6E4E`). **It has never run**: QEMU has no GENET,
and it was written from the register layout of Linux's bcmgenet driver
(used as documentation) without a Pi at hand.

- Start-up: the version register must say v5 (major field 6); the UMAC
  is reset and set up (2-byte receive alignment, no status blocks,
  promiscuous: the network layer filters), the port set for an external
  RGMII PHY, the PHY found on MDIO (address 1 first, then a scan) and
  reset, autonegotiation advertising 10/100/1000.
- The station address: `_DSD` `local-mac-address` (or `mac-address`),
  else the VideoCore mailbox's board address, else what the MAC
  registers hold.
- DMA: the default queue (ring 16) each way, 256 descriptors (in the
  controller's own register space, so they are MMIO writes), each with a
  2 KiB streaming buffer below 4 GiB with cache maintenance around every
  frame (`Io.Dma`).
- Interrupts from `_CRS` interrupt 0 (receive and transmit done); a
  deferred call takes received frames and reclaims sent ones; without
  the interrupt a 10 ms timer polls. The link is read from the PHY every
  second; UMAC speed and duplex follow it.
- Uncertain (check first on hardware): the per-ring and DMA engine
  register offsets, the reset sequence, the RGMII delay setup for
  `rgmii-rxid` (receive delay in the PHY through its shadow registers,
  transmit delay by the MAC), and whether the receive length counts the
  2-byte pad. No suspend to RAM handling.

### Cadence GEM, the Raspberry Pi 5's Ethernet (untested)

The Ethernet controller inside RP1 (`Drivers.CadenceGem`, registers in
`.Registers`, descriptors in `.Descriptors`, the MDIO bus in `.Mdio`), a
device tree platform device (`raspberrypi,rp1-gem`, `cdns,macb`) that
`Drivers.Rp1` gave its memory and interrupt. Written from Linux's
macb_main.c; **it has not run**: QEMU has no Pi 5.

- Start-up: the module id must say GEM and design config 6 must offer
  64-bit DMA (RP1 sees RAM at bus address 10_0000_0000). Reset (receive
  and transmit off, statistics cleared, all interrupts off), then the
  network configuration (MDC = 200 MHz / 96, bus width from design
  config 1, 2-byte receive offset, check sequence dropped, promiscuous,
  1536-byte frames), RGMII in the user I/O register, the management port
  on, the AXI pipeline from `cdns,aw2w-max-pipe`/`cdns,ar2r-max-pipe`/
  `cdns,use-aw2b-fill`, 50 us interrupt moderation, DMA configuration (2
  KiB receive buffers, bursts of 16, full packet buffers, 64-bit
  addresses, no timestamp words, no checksum offload).
- The address: `local-mac-address` (the firmware fills in the zeros of
  the .dtb), else the specific address 1 registers the firmware's
  network boot left.
- The PHY (`Drivers.EthernetPhy`, shared with GENET): the address of the
  node `phy-handle` names (1 on the Pi 5: the BCM54213PE), else a scan;
  reset, the RGMII delays of `phy-mode` (`rgmii-id`: both in the PHY,
  through the Broadcom shadow registers), autonegotiation for
  10/100/1000.
- Rings: 128 descriptors each way, 16 bytes (address low with the
  used/wrap bits, control or status, address high), in one shared DMA
  buffer (uncached for this non-coherent device) with an idle pair for
  the GEM's other queues; 2 KiB streaming buffers. Turning the MAC off
  rewinds its queue pointers, so each link up fills both rings afresh
  (frames queued while the link was down are dropped). Receiving takes
  descriptors the GEM marked used; transmitting writes the control word
  last and sets "start transmission".
- The interrupt is RP1's 6 (level), a MIP vector; the handler reads and
  clears the interrupt status, a deferred call does the work, RP1's
  IACK follows. Without it a 10 ms timer polls. The link is read every
  second.
- Diagnostics: if the link has been up 10 s and nothing was received,
  one `[gem] ... nothing received` line gives the controller's frame,
  FCS, no-buffer and overrun counters, receive and transmit status,
  control, configuration and interrupt mask and the bus errors seen;
  `gemdebug` logs that line every 10 s.
- `make gem-descriptor-test` checks the descriptor words on the host.
- Uncertain: whether RP1's clocks for the GEM are running as the
  firmware left them (no RP1 clock driver), the PHY reset line (RP1 GPIO
  32) being released, and the interrupt moderation units.

## File systems

The VFS (`kernel/filesystems`) has three parts:

- `FileSystem.Types` defines the driver contract: a `TFileSystemDriver`
  record of routines (probe, mount, lookup, read directory, read file, read
  symbolic link, release node) and the node, volume and status types.
- `FileSystem.Volumes` keeps the driver list and the mounted volumes.
- `FileSystem.Files` resolves paths and implements open files (objects of
  type `File`).

Nodes are shared: every node a driver hands out goes through a node cache
(keyed by a per-volume node number), so all opens of one file see the same
size and each other's writes, and a file that is open cannot be removed.
Every driver call holds the volume's lock.

The namespace is a single tree. The root lists the mounted volumes, each a
directory named after its block device: `/disk1p7/docs/readme.txt`. Paths
are absolute; `.` and `..` are resolved textually first. Symbolic links are
followed up to 8 deep, and an absolute link target is resolved from the
root of the link's own volume (for a volume mounted at a directory: of
the volume at the top of its chain of mounts, normally the system
volume, so `/bin/sh` in a link on `/tmp` means the system's). The system
volume is also found by the name `system` (`/system/...` in the kernel,
`/volumes/system/...` for programs), an alias that is not listed.

Drivers (each split into Structures / Volume / Write units plus a main
unit; ext also has Blocks and Directories):

| Driver           | Formats               | Notes                                                  |
|------------------|-----------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| `FileSystem.Fat`   | FAT12, FAT16, FAT32 | VFAT long names with generated `~N` short names, NT lower-case flags, all FAT copies kept in sync, FSInfo free count |
| `FileSystem.ExFat` | exFAT               | contiguous ("no FAT chain") and chained files, allocation bitmap, entry set checksums and name hashes, up-case table lookup, volume dirty flag |
| `FileSystem.Ext`   | ext2, ext3, ext4    | block maps and extent trees (writing up to depth 1), 64-bit, flex_bg, META_BG, all metadata checksums, fast and slow symlinks, holes |

FAT long names and exFAT names are UTF-16 on disk; `Runtime.Unicode`
converts. Malformed UTF-8 in a name (overlong forms, surrogates, code
points past U+10FFFF, stray or missing continuation bytes) becomes
U+FFFD, so no lone surrogate reaches the disk (`make unicode-test`, on
the host).

Removing a file that is still open removes only its name: the open file
goes on reading and writing, and its storage is freed when it is closed
for the last time (the driver routines `RemoveOpenNode` and
`FinishRemoval`; the node leaves the node cache at once, so a new file
with the same node number is not confused with it). On ext3/ext4 such a
file goes on the orphan list in the superblock in the same transaction,
and mounting frees orphans a crash left behind (`FileSystem.Ext.Orphans`).
The orphan list is linked through the inodes' deletion-time field, so
e2fsck reads a deletion time smaller than the inode count as a link of a
damaged list: a freed inode's deletion time is the wall clock but never
earlier than the inode count or the volume's creation or last write time
(`EarliestDeletionTime`), as the clock starts at zero on machines without
a real-time clock (an AArch64 machine whose firmware does not tell the
time: see `TBootInformation.FirmwareTime`).
Renaming onto an existing name replaces it as on Unix (a file replaces a
file, a directory an empty directory); on ext3/ext4 the removal and the
rename are one transaction (`BeginAtomicChange` / `EndAtomicChange`). In a
directory with the sticky bit (`/tmp`), only the owner of a name, of the
directory or root may remove or replace it.

**Advisory locks** (`FileSystem.Locks`), as flock gives them: a shared
or an exclusive lock on a whole file or directory, asked for with
`CallControlHandle` (`ControlLockFile` with `FileLockShared` or
`FileLockExclusive`, and `FileLockNoWait` not to wait;
`ControlUnlockFile`; `LockFile` and `UnlockFile` in `Sys.Files`). A
lock belongs to the open file - every handle duplicated from it - and
lasts until it is given up or the open file's last handle is closed, so
a program that ends gives its locks up. Any number of shared locks or
one exclusive lock; asking for the other kind first gives up the one
held. Locks only hold back other lock requests, not reads or writes. A
shared lock needs read permission on the node, an exclusive one write
permission, so programs that may only read cannot hold writers up. The
state lives with the node (shared by every open of it through the node
cache), made with the first lock and freed when nobody holds or waits
for one; one mutex covers every lock state. Waiting is alertable (an
ended program stops waiting, `ErrorInterrupted`); each release signals
a synchronization event that wakes one waiter, which looks again; one
let in to a shared lock passes the signal on. The request references
the open file while it runs, since another thread may close the handle
during a long wait. The settings library takes its writers' lock this
way (see "Settings").

### The block cache

**Syncing one file.** Every dirty line carries a tag: whose change
dirtied it (`CachedWriteTagged`). The VFS names the node a driver call
changes (`BeginNodeChange`/`EndNodeChange` in `FileSystem.Types`, the
volume's `ChangeTag`, read by `VolumeWrite`): a file for writes, size
changes and attribute changes, the directory for creating and removing
names, and "shared" for renames and hard links (two directories, or a
directory and an inode). A line dirtied by a second change becomes
shared too. `FlushCachedTag` writes back only the dirty lines of one
tag and the shared ones (those dirty when it began), then flushes the
device; `SyncFile` (CallSyncHandle, fsync and fdatasync) first writes
the file's pages kept by shared writable mappings back to it (the file
sync hook of `Processes.MappedFileChanges`), so one program's fsync
leaves other files' dirty blocks to the background writer. The ext3/4
journal flushes the disk at every commit anyway; ext2, FAT and exFAT
gain the most. Memory volumes have nothing to write.

**Size.** The block cache (`Io.BlockCache`, 4 KiB lines) starts at its
minimum and takes a new line for a miss, instead of reusing the least
recently used one, while it is below its maximum and twice the low
watermark of memory is free (see "Memory pressure and running out"). By
default the maximum is half the memory free when the cache starts and
the minimum 4 MiB (a sixteenth of the free memory on a machine with very
little, at least 256 KiB); the kernel options `blockcache=MIB`
(maximum), `blockcachemin=MIB` and `blockcacheshare=PERCENT` change
that, and the maximum stays below 90% of the free memory
(`Io.BlockCacheSizing`, checked on the host by `CachePolicyTest`). Under
memory pressure its shrinker gives clean lines back, least recently used
first, down to the minimum; asked hard it writes the dirty ones back
first. Line records come in chunks of 256 (`Io.BlockCacheLines`), a
chunk freed once none of its records holds a page; the hash table is
sized for the maximum. No kernel heap memory is allocated with the cache
lock held, so an allocation that must reclaim never finds the cache
locked by itself. None of the file systems relies on the cache's size:
they hold lines only for the length of a call, and the ext journal keeps
its own copies.

**Pages for mappings.** `PinCachedPage` hands out a line's page itself,
pinned and locked (for file mappings that page in through the cache): a
mapping takes a reference to the physical page, and the cache never
reuses a page someone else holds - such a line gets a fresh page and the
cache drops its own reference.

**Reports.** The kernel shell's `cache` shows the size, its bounds, the
dirty lines, hits and misses with the hit rate, lines grown, given back
and discarded; `CallGetBlockCacheStatistics` (169) gives the same as a
`TAbiBlockCacheStatistics` (with the bytes the file systems queued for
discarding and the disks were told to discard), which `free` and
`sysinfo` ("Disk cache") show.

The block cache writes back:

- **Writes** only dirty a line. Dirty lines reach the disk when
  `FlushCachedDevice` is called (which then also sends the disk a flush),
  when the background writer (the `CacheWriter` thread) finds them dirty
  for more than a second, before their line is reused, or when the
  shrinker needs their memory. Dirty lines are kept on a list in the
  order they became dirty, so the writer looks at no clean line, and a
  flush writes only the lines dirty when it began (never waiting on
  lines dirtied while it runs). A batch is one device's lines in
  ascending order, which is also the order their locks are taken in.
  Everything
  that needs data durable or ordered flushes: the ext journal around its
  commit blocks, exFAT after marking the volume dirty, syncing (including
  before `test-exit`), and raw disk access.
- **Locking.** The cache lock only covers the hash table, the recency list
  and which part of a device each line holds, and is never held across
  I/O. Each line has its own mutex for its data and I/O, so different
  disks (and different lines) are read and written in parallel. A line's
  mutex is only taken while the line is pinned, so choosing a line to
  reuse never waits.
- **Reading ahead.** Read misses on consecutive lines of a device read up
  to 16 more lines in the same request.

### Discarding freed space

When the ext, FAT or exFAT driver frees blocks or clusters it queues their
byte range (`FileSystem.Discards`); ranges are batched per volume, merged
when they touch (`FileSystem.DiscardRanges`, 128 a batch), and sent by
the cache writer each round (about twice a second), when volumes are
synced, and when a batch fills. A block must never be discarded while
the disk could still name it in use after a crash, so a batch goes out
only after the cache was flushed (the metadata that freed it is durable),
and on a journaled ext volume a range waits until the transaction that
freed it has committed (a failed transaction drops it). A block freed
and allocated again before its discard went out must not be discarded:
every allocation cancels its range first, under the volume's discard
lock, which is held while a batch goes out (sending never takes a volume
lock). Before the disk gets a range, the cache forgets the lines lying
wholly inside it, dirty or not. Volumes discard if their disk can and
the kernel option `discard=off` is not given (`TVolume.Discards` is nil
otherwise).

`fstrim [-v] MOUNTPOINT...` (`CallTrimVolume`, 168, root only;
`FileSystem.Trim`) discards all of a volume's free space: with the
volume locked, synced and the cache flushed, the driver walks its free
space (`TFileSystemDriver.TrimFreeSpace`: the ext block bitmaps, groups
whose bitmap is still uninitialized left alone; the FAT; the exFAT
allocation bitmap) and every free run goes to the disk.
`scripts/test-memory-pressure.sh` checks that the sparse image files of
an NVMe disk (ext4, batched discards) and a virtio disk (FAT16, fstrim)
attached with `discard=unmap` shrink back after a 24 MiB file was
written and removed.

ext volumes are mounted read-only if they use features the
driver cannot keep consistent (bigalloc, quota, encryption, case folding,
multiple-mount protection). htree indexed directories are read but not
modified.

**Damaged disks.** USB sticks are mounted as soon as they arrive, so the
drivers take whatever is on a disk as untrusted: a damaged or hostile
volume may be refused, mounted read-only or answer `StatusCorrupted`,
never more. In particular:

- ext: the superblock's geometry is checked at every mount (also the one
  after a journal replay): blocks of 1 to 64 KiB, block and inode
  bitmaps of one block (blocks and inodes per group at most 8 x the
  block size), the first ordinary inode at least 11, inode and block
  counts that fit the groups and the device. Directory names are at most
  255 bytes (also on volumes without the file type feature, whose name
  length has 16 bits); extent headers hold no more entries than their
  node and no deeper trees; bitmap blocks and inode numbers are range
  checked; sizes past the last 32-bit block are refused rather than
  truncated. The orphan list is measured first (tortoise and hare, at
  most 65536 entries) and never names a reserved inode such as the
  journal. Journal recovery looks revoked blocks up in a hash table and
  log blocks by binary search, and refuses journals past 16M blocks.
- FAT: tables too small for the clusters, a FAT32 active table that does
  not exist and cluster counts reaching the FAT32 end-of-chain values are
  refused; a long name part numbered 0 starts no name. exFAT: the boot
  sector's sector and cluster sizes, cluster count, FAT length and the
  cluster heap's end on the device are checked at mount, and so is the
  allocation bitmap's size; contiguous runs are summed in 64 bits and
  files are no larger than the cluster heap.
- Both: a cluster chain longer than the volume is `StatusCorrupted`, as
  is a FAT folder past 65536 records or an exFAT folder past 256 MiB, so
  a chain that loops without an end marker no longer holds the volume
  lock for ever. exFAT clears its dirty mark only between two cache
  flushes.

`make file-system-image-test` (`tools/FileSystemImageTest`) builds the
three drivers for the host on stand-ins for the block cache, heap, clock
and mutexes, and runs them on disk images `make-images.py` makes with
`mke2fs`, `mkfs.fat`, `mtools` and `mkfs.exfat`: valid ones, copies with
one specific kind of damage each (expected to be refused, read-only or
`StatusCorrupted`), and copies damaged at random (`--fuzz`, aimed at
the bytes that are not zero, the images' metadata). Each image is
mounted, walked, written to, unmounted and mounted again; the heap
stand-in's guard areas catch writes outside a block, and its count of
blocks leaks; the cache stand-in reports a loop as a hang.

### The ext3/ext4 journal

ext3 and ext4 volumes are written through their journal (JBD2, the file of
inode 8), in "ordered" mode:

- **Transactions.** Every driver call that changes the volume is one
  transaction (`FileSystem.Ext` wraps the write entry points). All of the
  driver's disk accesses go through `ExtRead`, `ExtWriteMetadata` and
  `ExtWriteData`. While a call runs, metadata blocks (inodes, bitmaps,
  group descriptors, the superblock and its free counters, directory,
  extent and block pointer blocks, symbolic link targets) are not written
  in place: each changed block is copied into the transaction, and reads
  see the copy. File data is written in place right away.
- **Commit.** When the call ends (`FileSystem.Ext.Transactions`) the
  blocks go to the log after a descriptor block, followed by a revoke
  block if needed. Then the disk is flushed, the commit block written and
  flushed again; from then on the change survives a crash. Then the blocks
  are written in place. Because data was written before the flush, a
  committed file never points at stale data.
- **The log** holds transactions one after another and is reset to its
  start when the next one does not fit. Recovery replays everything since
  the reset, so freeing a block that is in the log adds a revoke record:
  the old metadata copy must not overwrite whatever the block holds now.
  While the log holds anything, the superblock carries the needs-recovery
  feature and the journal superblock names the log's start. Syncing or
  unmounting empties the journal and clears the mark; the kernel syncs
  every volume before `test-exit` leaves the emulator.
- **Recovery** (`FileSystem.Ext.JournalRecovery`) runs when a writable
  volume that needs it is mounted. It makes three passes: scan for the
  last valid commit, collect revoke records, replay the logged blocks.
  The volume is then mounted afresh. A volume mounted read-only is not
  replayed.
- **Formats** (`FileSystem.Ext.JournalFormat`): plain journals and
  journals with v3 checksums (CRC32C on every descriptor, revoke and
  commit block and on every logged block), 32 or 64-bit block numbers, and
  escaped blocks that start with the journal's magic number.
  `FileSystem.Ext.Journal` switches on the revoke feature, and 64-bit
  block numbers on 64-bit volumes, as Linux does. Version 1 superblocks,
  v1 and v2 checksums, fast commits and external journals are replayed
  where possible, but the volume stays read-only.
- **Limits.** A call that changes more blocks than a transaction holds (a
  quarter of the log, at most 2048 blocks) commits part way, so a crash in
  between can leave it half done (as Linux does for long truncates).

The flush is a new I/O request, `IoFunctionFlush`. AHCI sends it as FLUSH
CACHE EXT, and `FlushBlockDevice` sends it to the disk holding a
partition. The disk statistics filter counts flushes.

`make test` builds a GPT test disk (`scripts/make-test-disk.sh`) with one
partition per format and the same files on each. The kernel reads every one
of them (`Kernel.FileSystemTest`), then writes to each one
(`Kernel.FileSystemWriteTest`). The writing only happens with the kernel
option `fstest`, which the main test passes; other boots leave test
volumes alone, since the write test changes them and leaves journaled
ones read-only until the next boot (the simulated crash below).
Afterwards `scripts/verify-test-disk.sh`
checks every partition on the host with the format's own consistency
checker and reads the written files back through independent
implementations.

### Watching for changes

Programs watch folders and files for changes (`FileSystem.Watches`,
`FileSystem.NodeTrails`; `CallCreateWatch`, `CallReadWatch`). A watch is
an object behind a handle of its own kind, ready for
`CallWaitForHandles` while change records wait in it, so a window
program's message loop waits on it like on any handle
(`Windowing.HandleWatches`).

- **What is reported.** The VFS reports every change once it worked,
  whoever made it and whichever driver carried it out, so every file
  system reports the same way: names created (files, folders, links,
  hard links, named pipes), removed and renamed (with both names), file
  contents written or resized (`WatchContents`), and permissions,
  owners and times changed (`WatchAttributes`). Moving a name into a
  watched folder is reported as created, out of it as removed. A watch
  asks for any of the three groups; with `WatchSubtree` a folder's watch
  also reports every folder below it, the names being paths from the
  watched folder (`sub/file`). Records about the watched item itself
  have an empty name: written, attributes, moved (renamed, and the
  watch follows it), removed (the watch ends), and its volume gone (the
  watch ends).
- **Finding the watch.** A watch knows its folder or file by node
  number, not by path: a path may go through a symbolic link, use
  another letter case on FAT and exFAT, or one of several hard links,
  and a folder above may be renamed while it is watched. Every name
  change is reported with the trail of its folder: the node numbers and
  names the path resolution passed through from the volume's root
  (`ResolveInVolume` fills it). A watch finds its node anywhere on the
  trail and takes the names below it for the record. FAT and exFAT
  number nodes by their directory entry, which a rename changes, so a
  rename reports the number before and after, and the watch follows.
  Trails are only built while some watch exists; an open file on a
  writable volume always keeps the trail of its node (a compact copy),
  since its writes are reported in the folder it was opened in, under
  the name it was opened by.
- **The queue.** Up to `MaximumQueuedWatchRecords` (64) records wait;
  when it is full the last place goes to an overflow record, and
  nothing else is queued until the program has read it: it must look
  at the folder again. A write or attribute change repeating the newest
  record waiting (a file written in many pieces) is not queued again.
  `CallReadWatch` moves whole records (`TAbiWatchRecord`: size, kind,
  flags, the name and for renames the old name) into the program's
  buffer and never waits.
- **Permission.** A watch needs read permission on what it watches
  (and search permission on the folders of its path, as any path does).
  A subtree watch reports names in folders below that the watcher could
  not list itself.
- **Volumes.** `/volumes` (the namespace root) is the list of volumes: a
  watch on it reports a volume arriving (created) and going away
  (removed), named after it; with `WatchSubtree`, everything on every
  volume. Devices under `/dev` are not files of any volume and are not
  watched (`ErrorUnsupported`).
- **Locking.** One mutex guards every watch; changes are reported with
  the volume's lock held, and watches are made with it held too, so a
  change cannot slip by between resolving the path and watching it.

A watch may belong to a watch group (inotify, `FileSystem.WatchGroups`):
its records then go to the group's queue as Linux's inotify events (see
"Event descriptors (260-269)"); a rename reported to several watches
gives them one cookie, and a name created or removed by a rename carries
`WatchRecordMoved`.

`watchtest` (run by coretest) checks it with a shell making the changes
in another process, on the system volume (ext4) and on the FAT16,
exFAT and ext2 test volumes; `watch` prints the changes of any path and
`volumes -w` the volumes coming and going.

### Mount points

A volume may also be mounted on a directory of another one
(`FileSystem.Mounts`, the table in `FileSystem.MountTable`): a memory
volume on `/tmp`, a USB disk on `/mnt/usb`. It stays in `/volumes` as
well.

- **Resolution.** The table names the volume holding the mount point,
  the mount point's node number (the record keeps a reference to the
  node, so its volume is busy and the folder can be neither removed nor
  renamed: `StatusInUse`, and neither can a folder above it, as the
  record keeps the path as text), the volume mounted there, and the mount
  point's path from the root of the volume at the top of the chain
  ("/tmp"). `ResolveInVolume` looks each directory it passes up in the
  table (only on volumes with `MountsOnVolume` > 0) and goes on at the
  mounted volume's root, moving the operation's lock from one volume
  to the other: two volume locks are never held at once, and the
  operation goes on with the volume it ended on (`var Volume`). Being
  by node number, letter case, symbolic and hard links lead in as
  well. `..` of a path is textual, so `/tmp/x/../..` leaves the mounted
  volume; a symbolic link is resolved afresh from the top volume's root
  with the mount point's path in front of a relative target, so `..` in
  a link leads out just the same.
- **Two names at once.** Rename and hard links locate both parents first
  (`LocatePath`, `LocateParent`: the volume and the path there) and
  refuse with `StatusCrossesVolumes` (`ErrorCrossVolume`, 18; `mv`
  copies then) when the volumes differ; then they resolve on that one
  volume without crossing. A folder moved below itself is recognized by
  the nodes the target's parent was found through (its trail, under the
  volume's lock), so a symbolic link in the target's path does not hide
  it.
- **Mounting** (`MountAtDirectory`) needs a folder that is not a
  volume's root, nothing mounted on it already, and the volume not
  mounted elsewhere nor above the folder (no cycles); mounting a volume
  where it is mounted already only changes its options. 32 mounts at
  most.
- **Unmounting** (`UnmountVolume`) is refused while a node of the volume
  besides its root is in use (an open file or folder, a mount point of
  another volume on it) or its root is open, and (`CallUnmountVolume`)
  while a program's current directory is in it, unless forced. The idle
  check, writing the volume back (driver `Sync`) and marking it gone
  happen in one hold of its lock (`RetireVolume`), then the disk is
  flushed; it
  takes it off the list and from its folder, and marks it gone as an
  unplugged disk's volumes are (below): a forced unmount's open files
  fail with `ErrorNoDevice` from then on, and the driver data goes
  when the last is closed (an open root included: the volume's root
  node stays until no handle names it). Its device cannot be mounted again until
  then (`DeviceHasLingeringVolume`). The system volume is never
  unmounted. A disk unplugged takes its volumes' mounts, and the mounts
  on them, with it (`ForgetMountsOfVolume`).
- **Options** (`FileSystem.MountOptions`, kept in `TVolume.Options`):
  `ro`/`rw`, `noexec` (programs on it do not start: `OpenProgramFile`
  sees `TNodeInformation.VolumeFlags`), `nosuid` (set-id bits ignored
  when they start), `discard` (kept for drivers that tell the disk
  which blocks were freed), `uid=`, `gid=`, `umask=`, `fmask=`,
  `dmask=` (below), `size=` and `mode=` (memory volumes), and
  `defaults`, `atime`, `noatime`, `relatime` (ignored). New options on a
  mounted volume apply at once; `ro` writes it back first; a read-only
  volume stays read-only until it is unmounted (ext replays its journal
  only when mounted writable).

The calls (172-175): `CallMountVolume` (a `TAbiMountRequest`: a device
`/dev/disk1p2`, a volume `/volumes/NAME` or `tmpfs`, the folder, the
type, the options; root only), `CallUnmountVolume` (a mount point or
`/volumes/NAME`; `UnmountForce`), `CallListMounts` (a
`TAbiMountInformation`: name, device, type, where programs see it, the
options as `mount` lists them) and `CallGetFileTimes` (below);
`Sys.Mounts` wraps them. `mount` lists the mounts, mounts (`-t`, `-o`,
`LABEL=NAME`, `-a` for `/etc/fstab`) and `umount [-f]` unmounts; `df`
shows each volume where it is mounted.

**/etc/fstab** (`Sys.MountTable`: `SOURCE DIRECTORY TYPE OPTIONS [DUMP
PASS]`, `#` comments, `LABEL=`, the table's own `noauto` and `nofail`)
is mounted by the first service manager before any service starts
(`Services.Mounts`), by coretest, which runs as the first program in
the tests, and by `mount -a` (`Sys.MountAll`: an entry whose folder has
a volume mounted on it already is left alone). The system's table
mounts a memory volume on `/tmp` (`mode=1777,size=50%`); before that,
and on a system without the table, `/tmp` is the system volume's own
sticky folder.

### Memory volumes (tmpfs)

`FileSystem.Memory` keeps a volume in RAM: files, folders, symbolic and
hard links, named pipes, owners, permissions and the four times to the
nanosecond (reading does not move the access time). A file's contents
are whole pages from the physical page allocator
(`FileSystem.Memory.Storage`: a page map per file, holes read as zeros),
counted against `size=` (bytes, k, m, g, or a share of the RAM; half by
default; `StatusNoSpace` past it; no file reaches past it either,
holes included, since a page map is as long as its file), and counted
by the kernel as
drivers' memory. Folders are lists of entries with a serial number each,
which a listing's cursor keeps (`FileSystem.Memory.Nodes`). A file's
pages go back when it is shortened, when its last name goes (or, if it
is open, when it is closed for the last time) and when the volume is
unmounted. Memory volumes are made by `MountMemoryVolume`
(`CallMountVolume` with type `tmpfs`), named `tmpfs1`, `tmpfs2`, ...;
the root gets `mode=` (rwxrwxrwt by default).

### Owners on FAT and exFAT

FAT and exFAT have no owners or permission bits
(`TFileSystemDriver.HasNoOwners`). Every node gets the owner and group of
the mount options (`uid=`, `gid=`; root without them) and rwxrwxrwx less
`fmask=` (files; 0133 by default, so rw-r--r--) or `dmask=` (folders;
0022, rwxr-xr-x); `umask=` sets both (as on Linux, files then get the
execute bits too). The read-only attribute takes a file's write bits
away (not a folder's: Windows marks customized folders read-only), and
chmod without write bits sets it (`FileSystem.OwnerMapping`,
`FileSystem.Security.MapOwnerlessNode`, applied as nodes enter the node
cache and after every attribute change; options changed on a mounted
volume remap the cached nodes). chown and chgrp succeed only to the
owner and group the node shows already. So with `uid=1000`, user 1000
may write there, and without it others may only read.

### File times

`TNodeInformation` has the access, modification and change times and
the time a node was made (birth, 0 where the format does not keep it),
each with nanoseconds. ext reads the extra fields of large inodes
(nanoseconds and two more bits of seconds after each time, `i_crtime`);
FAT has the creation time to 10 ms and the access date; exFAT the
creation and access times and 10 ms steps; memory volumes keep all
four exactly. `TAbiFileInformation` is unchanged (whole seconds);
`CallGetFileTimes` (175) gives a `TAbiFileTimes` for a path or a handle.
`TAbiAttributeChanges` takes nanoseconds with `ChangeFieldNanoseconds`
(two more fields; programs built before pass the shorter record, which
the kernel copies alone without the flag): ext writes them to a large
inode's extra fields (with the two bits of seconds past 2038), memory
volumes keep them, FAT and exFAT round down. "Now" times are filled in
to the nanosecond. C programs: `stat` gives `st_atim`/`st_mtim`/
`st_ctim` from CallGetFileTimes, `utimensat` and `futimens` set them
(`UTIME_NOW`, `UTIME_OMIT`).
`stat` shows the times to the nanosecond and the birth (`%w`, `%W`),
`ls -l --time=atime|ctime|birth` (`-u`, `-c`) shows and sorts by
another time, `touch -a` and `-m` set one of them.

### Volumes going away

When a disk is unplugged, `FileSystem.Volumes.RemoveVolumesOfDisk` takes
its volumes off the list (they leave `/volumes`), marks each gone
(`MarkVolumeGone`: under the volume's lock, so it waits for the
operation running), and tells the watchers: watches on the volume get
"volume gone" and end, watches on the list of volumes "removed". From
then on every operation on the volume fails with `StatusVolumeGone`
(`ErrorNoDevice`, "No such device"), except closing: open files go on
existing until their programs close them. The driver's data is given
back (its `Unmount`) once no node of the volume besides the root is in
use (`TVolume.NodesInUse`), which may be right away or when the last
open file is closed. The volume record itself is never freed: open
files, named pipes and image sections name volumes by address, and none
of them must take a later volume for it.

The ext3 and ext4 partitions are built needing journal recovery: debugfs
leaves committed transactions in their journals (plain on ext3; v3
checksums and 64-bit block numbers on ext4). These hold a replayed block,
a block logged and then revoked, and an escaped block, which the kernel's
read test checks after the replay at mount. Each write test ends with a
simulated crash (`SimulateCrashAfterNextCommit`): its last rename is
committed but never written in place. The host checks that the rename is
only in the journal, replays it with `e2fsck`, and requires the result to
be clean. That checks the kernel's journal format, revoke records
included, against e2fsprogs. The system disk, written by the user mode
tests, must pass `e2fsck` too.

## Objects

Every object has a header (signature, reference count, type, name record)
followed by its body; callers only ever see body pointers. An object is
deleted, through its type's delete routine, when its last reference is
dropped. Thread objects embed the scheduler's thread control block.

### The object namespace

Named objects live in a tree of directories (`Objects.Namespace`),
written as paths from the root with backslashes:

| Directory | What is in it |
|---|---|
| `\Device` | every device listed under /dev (`Io.Manager` names each one it lists, with its owner and mode, and takes the name away with `UnlistDevice`) |
| `\Storage` | the disks and partitions (`TBlockDevice`) |
| `\Kernel` | the console (`Console`) and the system process (`System`) |
| `\Ports` | the ports of `CallCreatePort`, owned by their creator, mode 0666 (connecting is the server's to judge) |
| `\Shared` | what programs name: events, semaphores, mutexes, sections, timers (mode 1777, like /tmp) |

A directory is an object of type `Directory` holding a list of entries;
an entry is the name record in the header of the object named there
(`TObjectNameRecord`: the directory, the link in its list, the name of
up to 63 characters, owner, group, mode, flags). A named object holds a
reference to its directory, so a directory lives while anything is named
in it. The namespace holds none to an ordinary object: its name goes
when the object is deleted (`DetachObjectName`, called only for objects
that were ever named, so most deletions never touch the namespace) or
when removed (`RemoveObjectName`); the object goes on unnamed. Directories
are permanent: the namespace holds a reference until the name is removed,
which needs an empty directory that a program made (the kernel's stay;
programs may make 1024 in all). A lookup takes a reference only if the
object is not already being deleted (`TryReferenceObject`): a count that
reached zero still has its entry until its deletion takes it out. One
spin lock guards the tree (lookups are short walks, and names go at
DispatchLevel too). `CreateObject(Type, Path)` names a kernel object
(root, 0600); `CreateNamedObject` takes the owner and mode;
`LookupObjectByName(Path, Type)` finds one without checks.

Permissions work as for files, through the caller's `TNamespaceCaller`
(the kernel's own calls are unchecked; a program's carries its
credentials and the routines that judge them, `Processes.ObjectNameCalls`):
search (x) on every directory on the way, write (w) on a directory to
name or remove in it (in a sticky one, removing needs the name's or the
directory's owner, or root), read (r) to list one, read and write on an
object to open it; chmod by the owner, chown by root, the group by the
owner to one of its groups. Root passes every check.

System calls (200-205; `Sys.NamedObjects` in libsystem):

| Call | Does |
|---|---|
| 200 `CallCreateObjectDirectory` (Path, Mode) | a directory of the caller's (umask applied) |
| 201 `CallNameObject` (Handle, Path, Mode) | names an unnamed event, semaphore, mutex, section or timer: `ErrorExists` if taken, `ErrorBusy` if named already |
| 202 `CallOpenNamedObject` (Path, Kind) | a new handle to it (Kind 0: any that opens; directories, devices and ports do not: `ErrorUnsupported`) |
| 203 `CallListObjectDirectory` (Path, Buffer, Capacity, FirstIndex) | `TAbiObjectDirectoryEntry` records (name, type, the kind it opens as, flags, owner, group, mode, entries, references); returns how many there are |
| 204 `CallRemoveObjectName` (Path) | the name goes; the object stays while handles hold it |
| 205 `CallSetObjectSecurity` (Path, Mode, Owner, Group; -1 leaves one) | chmod and chown |

A process restricted from port connections can use none of them. The
library's `CreateNamedEvent`, `CreateNamedSemaphore`, `CreateNamedMutex`
and `CreateNamedSection` create or open: a new object is named, and if
the name is taken the existing one is opened instead (trying again if it
went away in between), so two programs agree on one object by its name
alone. `objls [-l] [-R] [PATH]` lists the namespace (mode, owner, group,
references, type, name). `objtest` (in coretest) checks it from user
mode, the self test `Kernel.ObjectNamespaceSelfTest` from the kernel
(as root and as a checked user with id 1000).

A reference count never wraps: one that reaches
`ObjectReferenceCountLimit` (2^40, which only a reference leak gets to)
stays there, the log says so (`[object] Warning: the reference count of
... saturated`), and the object is never deleted - a leak instead of a use
after free. A self test takes a count to the limit
(`SetObjectReferenceCountForTest`) and checks it stays.

## User mode

### Processes and address spaces

Each user process has its own top level page table. The kernel half is
copied from the kernel's table when the process is created, so kernel
addresses stay valid in every process; the scheduler loads a thread's
`AddressSpaceRoot` into CR3 when it switches between processes.

User memory is described by regions (`Processes.AddressSpace`):
the program image, shared libraries, heap allocations, thread stacks and
an 8 MiB main stack, each at a random place of its own (see "Address
space layout randomization" below; with `aslr=off` the program is at
0x400000, libraries from 0x7F00_0000_0000, allocations from
0x1000_0000_0000 and the stack below 0x7FFF_FFFF_F000). Pages are only
mapped when first touched: the page fault handler asks the address space
whether the address belongs to a region and, if so, maps a zeroed page. A
fault anywhere else in user mode ends just that process (exit status 139,
as a segmentation fault on Unix). The threads of a process share its
address space; region changes, page commits and the copies the kernel
makes in and out of it are serialized by a spin lock in the address space.

The regions are kept in a region tree (`Processes.RegionTree`): an AVL
tree ordered by start address, one kernel heap node per region, each
node also holding its subtree's lowest start, highest end and largest
gap between neighbouring regions. Finding the region of a faulting
address, checking that a new region overlaps none (only the region
starting last below its end can) and first-fit search for free room
above a base (subtrees whose largest gap is too small are skipped
whole) all take time logarithmic in the number of regions. Nothing
bounds the number but the address space and the process's region
limit (65536 by default, see "Process limits"); the tree code depends
on nothing else in the kernel and is tested on the host against a plain
list (`tools/RegionTreeTest`, `make region-tree-test`).

What goes with what: a thread's stack, the stack's guard and its thread
data go when the thread exits, however it ends (an exit call, the
process ending, `CallTerminateThread` while it waits); an allocation
made with `AllocateForThread` (the runtime's threadvar block, its
dynamic TLS vector and blocks) goes with its thread too unless freed
before (the region remembers its owner's id, so an address freed and
handed out again is never taken by mistake; a thread that made more
than one has all of them looked for when it ends); device mappings and
sections go with `CallFreeMemory`;
libraries are never unloaded, and everything goes with the address
space.

#### Address space layout randomization

Every process gets its own layout (`Processes.AddressLayout`, chosen in
`CreateAddressSpace` and kept in the space's `Layout`), each part at a
random page of a window of its own, so the parts stay out of each
other's way and each keeps room to grow:

| Part | Where | Entropy |
|---|---|---|
| program image | [1 TiB, 2 TiB) | 28 bits |
| run time allocations (heap chunks, mappings) | first fit upwards from a random page of [16 TiB, 17 TiB) | 28 bits |
| each thread's stack and thread data | first fit from a random page of [48 TiB, 64 TiB), chosen per thread | 32 bits |
| each library | a random page of [126 TiB, 127 TiB), chosen the first time its image section is loaded and kept for every process (see below) | 28 bits |
| main stack top | a random page of the 64 GiB below 0x7FFF_FFFF_F000; the initial stack pointer a random 16 bytes into a page | 24 + 8 bits |

A range that does not fit above its random start is looked for from the
start of its window, so randomization never makes memory run out
sooner. Programs are position independent (`ld -pie`, ET_DYN) and the
loader relocates them like libraries; an ET_EXEC program would still go
to its fixed address. The kernel option `aslr=off` gives every process
the old fixed layout (for debugging: the same addresses in every run).

Libraries are placed as Windows places DLLs: the first load of a library
since its image section was made (a boot, or the file changed) puts it
at a random page of the library window, which its section remembers
(`PreferredStart`); later loads, in any process, put it there again if
that range is free in the process. So a library is at the same address
in every process, and its relocated pages are the same: they are kept
with the section and mapped by later loads instead of relocating again
(see "Relocated copies" below). The program, the heap, the stacks and
the thread data stay random per process. The kernel option
`aslr=process` gives each process random places of its own for its
libraries too (and no relocated copy is ever used for them).

The random numbers come from `Kernel.Random`: ChaCha20 (RFC 8439,
`Kernel.ChaCha20`) with fast key erasure - each block gives the next key
and 32 bytes of output - seeded at boot from RDSEED or RDRAND (RNDRRS or
RNDR on AArch64 with FEAT_RNG), cycle counter jitter, the boot
information and the device tree's `/chosen` `rng-seed` and `kaslr-seed`
(the Raspberry Pi firmware fills them from its hardware generator), with
a fresh hardware number and the counter stirred into every block. The
network stack (temporary addresses, stable-privacy secrets, fragment
identifications, TCP initial sequence numbers), `/dev/random` and made-up
virtio MAC addresses use it too. `tools/AslrTest` (`make aslr-test`)
checks ChaCha20 against the RFC's vector and many layouts against their
windows on the host; `aslrtest` (a coretest line) runs a program twice
and checks that its code, its stack, a heap block and a thread's stack
all moved - and a library's too when booted with `aslr=process`
(booted with `aslr=off`, the same command prints "aslrtest: aslr=off,
the addresses are the same").

#### Relocated copies

Relocating a library writes into some of its pages (the GOT, data
pointers, text relocations). Those pages are made by the kernel, not in
the process (`Processes.ImageLoader`, `Processes.RelocatedCopies`):

- When a module is mapped, the loader notes which pages of its image
  its relocations write (`PlanRelocatedPages`) and leaves them out of
  the mapping: their regions get no pages until the module is relocated.
- Relocating starts by resolving every symbol the relocations name, once
  each (`BuildResolutionTable`). The resolutions - each symbol's address
  and size, the TLS placement of its module - with the load bias, the
  module's own TLS placement and the TLS descriptor resolvers are the
  key.
- If the module's image section keeps a relocated copy with that bias
  and key, its pages are mapped (copy on write, like the section's
  built pages) and nothing is relocated. Otherwise the relocations are
  applied into fresh kernel pages - each starting as what the page
  holds before relocation: the file's page, a built page or zeros - the
  pages are mapped, and they are kept as a copy of the section under the
  key (up to `MaximumRelocatedCopies` = 4 per section, the least
  recently used going first). A program is kept only when it is not at a
  random address (it would never be there again).
- A module with copy relocations (a program linked for a fixed address)
  is relocated in the process as before, after the others, so what it
  copies is relocated data.
- Copies go with their section, and a shrinker ("relocated image
  copies") drops them, oldest first, when memory is short; pages a
  process maps stay its.

Two loads with equal keys would write exactly the same bytes, so a copy
is never used where its contents would be wrong; with libraries kept at
their place (above) every process after the first gets libsystem and
the others relocated for nothing, sharing the pages until it writes
them. `CallGetImageCacheStatistics` (208) gives a
`TAbiImageCacheStatistics`: the sections kept, the copies and their
pages, the loads that reused a copy, kept a new one or kept none, the
libraries placed at their section's place, and the copies dropped.
`latelibtest` (a coretest line) runs two children loading
libdynpascal.so and checks that relocated copies were reused and that
both found it at the same address.

Where the program and its libraries went is kept in the process's module
list (`Process^.Modules`, a `TModuleList` of `TLoadedModule`): each
module's file name, its `Base` (the load bias: an address in the process
is the module's link address plus `Base`) and the span of its segments
(`ImageStart`, `ImageEnd`). The debug shell's `modules ID` lists them;
`scripts/symbolize.py` takes them (`--base NAME=HEX`, `--start
NAME=HEX`, or `--modules FILE` with lines of that listing or of a crash
report naming a module and its base) and assumes the fixed layout for
the modules it is not told about.

#### Hardening: crafted programs and racing callers

Nothing in a program or library file is trusted (`Processes.ImageLoader`):
loadable segments must lie in user space (their sizes no larger than an
image may be, so no address computed from them wraps), relocation tables
must be whole 24-byte records (`DT_RELASZ`, `DT_PLTRELSZ`), string
tables are copied with a terminating zero, and every address the file
names must lie in the module's own image `[ImageStart, ImageEnd)`: the
bytes a relocation writes, the TLS initialization image, the
initializer and finalizer arrays, and for a copy relocation the source
in the defining module's image. A needed library is a name, never a
path. Each image region carries the tag of the load that mapped it
(`TUserRegion.LoadTag`), so a load that fails takes back exactly what it
mapped (`ReleaseImageRegions`), and a library that fails to load leaves
no half relocated module behind for the next load to trip over.

The window through which the kernel reads and writes another address
space (`WriteIntoAddressSpace`, `ReadFromAddressSpace`, `WriteIntoImage`,
`WritablePageWindow`) checks on its own, whatever the loader did: user
addresses only, inside a region (no guard, no device memory); reads need
a readable region; writes a writable one - or, for the loader's
`WriteIntoImage`, a program image's read-only pages, relocated in place -
and never a shared file mapping. A write first makes the page the
process's own: a copy on write page, a file's page, an image section's
built page or any page someone else holds a reference to is copied, so
the kernel never writes a page other processes see (a set-user-ID
program's cached pages, say). `MapSharedPage` maps only into a region
that is already there. Fork marks every page of a private region copy
on write in both spaces whatever its protection, and changing a
protection never makes a page others hold writable (it is marked copy
on write instead).

The program's file is opened once (`OpenProgramFile`, for exec and
spawn; `OpenLibraryFile` for `CallLoadLibrary`): the caller's permission
(execute; for a library read and execute; a `noexec` volume refuses
both) and the set-user-ID owner are taken from that open file, and the
loader loads that same file, so a symbolic link swapped in between
cannot get another program run as the first one's owner. A program
needs no read permission: `OpenProgramFile` opens it with
`OpenForExecution`, which makes the file system check execute instead
of read permission (the path's directories still need search), and the
kernel reads it on its own authority, so a program of mode 0711 runs
while its user cannot read it. The open file never reaches the program
(programs cannot pass `OpenForExecution`: their open flags are masked
to the Abi ones). If the new program's user may not read it
(`ImageUnreadable`), it runs with `AT_SECURE` set, so a dynamic linker
ignores `LD_PRELOAD` (which could load code to read it), and the
process is marked (`TProcess.ImageUnreadable`, kept by fork, set anew
by exec): there is no ptrace or core dump, and anything added that
shows a process's memory or image to another program must refuse such
a process. Exec loads
into an address space of its own through a `TLoadTarget` (the space and
its module list), which becomes the process's only at the switch.
Address spaces are reference counted: the process's slot changes only
with `PublishAddressSpace`, under a lock readers of other processes take
too (`ReadPublishedSpaceUsage` for ps and the out-of-memory scores,
`ReferencePublishedSpace` for `CallGetProcessResources`), and the last
reference destroys the space. The auxiliary vector carries the
credentials the program runs with and `AT_SECURE` (set when the real and
effective user or group differ), so mlibc's dynamic linker ignores
`LD_PRELOAD` and `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` in a set-user-ID program.

Fork obeys `RestrictProcessCreation` and the user's process limit like
any start, copies handles even above a limit lowered since, and gives
the child's thread the forking thread's stack (with its overflow
handling), thread data and, in the kernel's thread block, its own id; a
child that cannot start gives its memory and handles back at once. A
thread's handle is reserved before the thread starts, so a full table
refuses the thread rather than leave one running nobody can wait for.
Thread handles never travel through a channel. kill applies stop
signals per process by each one's dispositions, `kill(-1, ...)` reaches
every process the caller may control (never "group 1"), and the lowest
Int64 is no target. Exec keeps pending signals. A section is charged
to its creator's commit limit and counted in its footprint for as long
as it exists. A mapped file is joined under its volume's lock, which a
change of the file holds from its first hook to the end of the write,
so a private user never joins in between; a snapshot reads the pages
each later change touches before it lands.

`loadertest` (two coretest lines) runs the crafted files of
`/usr/lib/loadertest`, written at build time by
`scripts/make-crafted-elves.py`: programs with a segment in kernel
space or wrapping, a relocation into kernel memory, TLS outside the
module, a relocation table of part records; libraries with relocations
into kernel memory, outside the module and into a gap of the module
where the test mapped `/bin/su` (shared and private: the mapped page and
the file must be unchanged), a copy relocation from kernel memory, an
unterminated string table, an initializer array in kernel memory; and a
relocation into a read-only page two processes share, which each must
see with its own value. Good files of the same make show the rest is
well formed. It also checks a forked child's thread id and stack
overflow, a thread refused for lack of a handle, a thread handle not
sent, a section over the commit limit, and a private mapping of a file
rewritten meanwhile. Run as a user (`--unprivileged`) it races spawn
against a link swapped between a set-user-ID copy of `true` and itself,
and checks a lowered limit stays lowered. ctest's `security` group does
the same for the C library: fork and `mprotect`, exec through a swapped
link to the set-user-ID helper `/usr/bin/ctest-suid`, `AT_SECURE` with
`LD_PRELOAD`, `kill(-1, SIGSTOP)`, a handled group `SIGTSTP`, pending
signals across exec, fork's restriction and process limit, and process
details read while another process execs in a loop.

#### Process limits

Every process has a region limit and a handle limit (by default 65536
regions and 16384 handles, at most 1048576 and 65536), inherited by the
processes it starts. `CallSetProcessLimit(Limit, Value)` (131) changes
the caller's (`ProcessLimitRegions`, `ProcessLimitHandles`; lowering is
always allowed, raising is root's alone: a limit a user's process lowered
stays a ceiling for it and what it starts, as a hard limit does). Two more settings
go through it, inherited the same way: `ProcessLimitProcesses` (4), the
most processes the caller's real user may run at once when this process
starts one (default 4096, at most 65536; root's are not counted; one too
many fails with `ErrorWouldBlock`), and `ProcessLimitOomScoreAdjust` (5),
how willingly the process is ended when memory runs out, passed as the
adjustment plus `OomScoreAdjustOffset` (1000) so it is never negative
(see "Memory pressure and running out"). `ProcessLimitRestrictions`
(6) is a sandbox a process puts itself in: flags only ever added,
inherited by what it starts (see "Browser process model", the sandbox).
And `CallGetProcessResources(ProcessId, Address)` (130) reports what a
process holds as a `TAbiProcessResources`: regions, handles and threads
against the limits, the regions' size and its committed, peak and
shared pages (`Processes.LimitCalls`). `ps -o regions,handles` shows the
counts. `limittest` (a coretest line) starts and joins 2000 threads,
ends 200 more from outside while they wait, holds 5000 regions and 3000
handles (pipes, events, sockets) at once, lowers both limits, passes
600 handles to a child, and checks every count comes back to its
baseline.

Run time allocations, reservations and file mappings may be split into
several regions - pieces committed, decommitted or protected apart from
the rest (`Processes.RegionEditing`), all carrying the allocation's
start as their `AllocationBase` so freeing that start frees every piece,
and joined again once alike. See "Virtual memory: reserving, committing,
protecting, mapping files" below.

Device memory is mapped into a process with `CallMapHandle(Handle,
Offset, Length)`: the handle's driver says which physical memory that is
and whether writes may be combined (the I/O function IoFunctionMap), and
the pages go into a region of their own, mapped at once, writable if the
handle was opened for writing. The program unmaps it with
`CallFreeMemory`. The page table entries of device pages carry a
software bit (MappingDevice), so neither unmapping nor destroying the
address space hands them to the page allocator, and the kernel never
reaches them through its physical memory window. Write-combining is the
page attribute table's entry 4, which the kernel sets at start (and
every processor takes on as it starts or wakes).

### Virtual memory: reserving, committing, protecting, mapping files

Programs manage their address space with six calls (160-165,
`Processes.VirtualMemoryCalls`, the work in `Processes.VirtualMemory`; libsystem's
`Sys.Memory`: `ReserveMemory`, `CommitMemory`, `DecommitMemory`,
`ReleaseMemory`, `ProtectMemory`, `QueryMemory`, `AllowDynamicCode`,
`MapFile`):

- **`CallReserveMemory` (Length, Flags)**: address space without memory,
  in the run time allocation area: a region with no access that is not
  committed. Freed whole with `CallFreeMemory`.
- **`CallCommitMemory` (Address, Length, Protection)**: pages of one
  reservation (or allocation) become ordinary on-demand pages with a
  protection (`MemoryRead`, `MemoryReadWrite`, `MemoryReadExecute`,
  `MemoryNoAccess`, any of them with `MemoryGuard`), zero when first
  touched, counted against the commit limit first (all or nothing).
- **`CallDecommitMemory` (Address, Length)**: their pages go, they are
  reserved again.
- **`CallProtectMemory` (Address, Length, Protection)**: committed pages
  of reservations, allocations and file mappings get another protection;
  returns the first page's previous one.
- **`CallQueryMemory` (Address, InformationAddress)**: a
  `TAbiMemoryInformation`: the run of alike pages around the address,
  its allocation's start, state (free, reserved, committed), protection
  and kind (private, image, file mapping, stack, thread data, device,
  section, stack guard).
- **`CallSetMemoryPolicy` (Flags)**: `MemoryPolicyAllowDynamicCode`.

Committing or protecting part of a region splits it where the change
begins and ends and joins alike neighbours again
(`Processes.RegionEditing`, tested on the host by `RegionTreeTest`
against a model of every page). Run time allocations (`CallAllocateMemory`)
are reservations committed whole, so the heap's memory may be decommitted
and protected in parts too. Protection is per region: changing it maps
the pages already there again. A page the program may not touch (no
access, a guard) stays where it is, mapped for the kernel only
(`MappingNoAccess`: no user bit on x86-64, EL1-only with UXN and PXN and
an ASID on AArch64), so making it accessible again finds its contents;
`ValidateUserRange` refuses system call buffers in such pages, as in
reserved ones.

**User W^X.** No user page is writable and executable at once
(`ErrorAccessDenied`), and anonymous memory becomes executable only in a
process that asked for it (`CallSetMemoryPolicy` with
`MemoryPolicyAllowDynamicCode`, for a compiler at run time: write the
code into read-write pages, then protect them read-execute). Program
images, and files mapped executable and read-only (`MapExecutable`), are
code from files and need no permission. The policy is not inherited.

**Guard pages.** `MemoryGuard` makes a one-shot trap: the first touch by
the program raises `ExceptionGuardPage` (the fault resolver takes the
guard off just that page and marks the thread, `GuardPageHit`, for the
exception dispatcher) and the page is an ordinary one from then on. The
runtime raises it as an access violation (runtime error 216,
`EAccessViolation`); an exception filter sees the code.

**Commit charge.** Each address space counts the pages of private memory
it may come to use, touched or not (`RegionChargePages`): committed
allocations and reservation parts, stacks, thread data, writable image
regions and writable private file mappings. It is checked against the
process's commit limit (`CallSetProcessLimit(ProcessLimitCommit,
Pages)`, 0 = none, the default; inherited by children; only root may
raise it or take it away) and added to the system's total
(`Memory.CommitCharge`). For a policy on running out of memory the
kernel API is `CommitChargeOf(Space)` (per process) and
`SystemCommittedPages` (all of them); `CallGetProcessResources` shows
both (`CommitChargePages`, `CommitLimitPages`,
`SystemCommitChargePages`). The out-of-memory policy
(`Processes.MemoryCharges`) gets them through `SetCommitCounters`
(`InitializeVirtualMemory`): a process's commitment beyond its resident
private pages, and the system's total.

**File mappings.** `CallMapHandle(Handle, Offset, Length, Flags)` on a
regular file opened for reading maps it (Length 0: to its end):
read-only shared by default, `MapWritable` for a shared writable mapping
(only through a handle opened for writing, else `ErrorAccessDenied`),
`MapPrivate` for copy on write (writable with `MapWritable`),
`MapExecutable`. `CallMapMemory` (mmap) does the same with the Linux
`MAP_SHARED`/`MAP_PRIVATE` and `PROT_*` values; a shared mapping made
through a writable handle may also be made writable later
(`CallProtectMemory`; the region's `BackingIsWritable`). The pages are a
**mapped file**'s (`Processes.MappedFiles`): it holds the pages of the
file read so far in a two-level table, each read once - `ReadFromFileAt`
through the file system and its block cache - when some process first
touches it. Reading sleeps, so the fault resolver leaves the address
space's spin lock for it (with a reference to the mapped file) and lets
the touch happen again; a fault that may not sleep (a copy at raised
level) fails instead, and `WaitOnAddress` reads the word once before its
spin lock. Every mapping, in every process, maps those same pages, each
with a reference of its own taken under the mapped file's lock
(`AcquireResidentMappedFilePage`); the region holds a reference to the
mapped file. A mapped file keeps an open file of its own
(`DuplicateOpenFileForReading`, and `DuplicateOpenFileForWriting` once a
shared writable mapping is made), so the mapping outlives the program's
handle and the file's name. Unmapping (`CallFreeMemory`, munmap) and the
end of the process give the references back; the last one writes the
dirty pages back and destroys the mapped file, deferred
(`DrainMappedFileReleases`) when it goes under a spin lock or on the
thread reclaiming memory. A node with mapped files counts them
(`TNode.MappedFileCount`).

Page table entries carry flags (`Processes.MappedPageEntries`): *dirty*
(written through a shared writable mapping, not written back yet) and
*preserved* (a snapshot's page, see below). There are two kinds of
mapped file, each found again by later mappings of the same file in a
registry (a spin-locked list, volume and node number):

- **Shared** ones, for shared mappings, always show the file. A shared
  writable mapping maps the pages read-only at first; the first write
  faults, marks the page dirty and maps it writable
  (`MarkMappedFilePageDirty`; the kernel's own writes through the
  physical window do the same). Dirty pages are written back
  (`WriteBackMappedFile`, one at a time per mapped file) through
  `WriteToFileWithinSize`, which never makes the file longer, on
  `CallSyncMemory` (msync; `SyncMemoryWait` also flushes the volume),
  when a writable mapping is unmapped or its process ends
  (`MarkMappedFileWriteBackPending`, then
  `FlushPendingMappedFileWriteBacks`), before a volume is written back
  (`sync`, `AddVolumeSyncHook`), on the block cache's background writer
  once a page has been dirty for 5 s, and when the mapped file goes.
  Before a batch is written, its pages lose write access in every
  mapping (the page protector of `Processes.MappedFileMappings`), so a
  later write marks the page dirty again and is never lost.
- **Private** ones, for copy on write mappings and program images, keep
  what the file held when they were mapped. Before the file changes for
  the first time while they have users, they become **snapshots**
  (`IsStale`: later mappings get a new mapped file), and before each
  change from then on every snapshot reads the pages the change touches
  - only those - and marks them preserved; pages no change touched are
  still read from the file when first needed. Writing a few bytes of a
  large file another program maps privately costs a page, not the file,
  and writing a running program's file does not change the program. A
  snapshot that cannot read a page it must keep (memory ran out) is
  damaged: its missing pages fail. Before a private mapped file is found
  or made, the shared one's dirty pages are written back, so a copy on
  write mapping starts from what shared mappings wrote.

The file system reports changes around the write with the range
(`Processes.MappedFileChanges`): before it (`AddFileChangingHook`, volume
lock held, Offset and Length - `WriteToFile`, `ChangeFileSize` from the
shorter size, truncation on open from 0) for the snapshots, and right
after it with the lock still held (`AddFileWrittenHook`), when the
resident pages of the mapped files that are not snapshots get only the
changed bytes read into them, so what a shared writable mapping wrote
elsewhere in the same page stays; a mapped file's own write-back is not
read back into it. A page read while the file changed is read again
(`ChangeCount`). `read()` of a file with mapped files copies what lies
in their resident pages (the shared one first) instead of going through
the file system (`SetResidentFileReader`, `ReadThroughMappedPages`): it
sees a mapping's writes before they are written back, and a page held
twice - mapped and in the block cache - is read from neither. A mapped
file's page that the block cache holds too is still two copies; what
`read()` reads from mapped pages no longer pulls lines into the cache.

Each mapped file lists the region nodes mapping it, with their address
spaces (`AttachMappedFileMapper` from `AddRegionRecordLocked` and
`SplitRegionLocked`, detached in `FreeRegionNode`; the links are in
`TRegionNode`, whose address never changes). `VisitMappings`
(`Processes.MappedFileMappings`) takes a reference to each live space on
the list (`TryReferenceAddressSpace`) and, holding one space's lock and
the mapped file's at a time, hands every region to a visitor: taking
write access before a write-back, or removing the entries that map
pages being evicted. Fork holds the child's lock as well as the parent's
while it copies, since the child's regions are on those lists already.

**Eviction.** The shrinker "mapped files"
(`Processes.MappedFileEviction`, `Memory.Pressure`) drops clean pages
that can be read again - not dirty, not preserved, not of a damaged
snapshot - from each mapped file's eviction cursor on: gently only those
nobody maps (nothing but the mapped file holds them: a library nobody
runs, pages an image section keeps), hard also mapped ones, whose
mappings are removed first so the next touch reads them again
(`TakeEvictionCandidates`, `UnmapMappedPages`, `DropEvictionCandidate`,
which frees a page only when the mapped file and the shrinker are its
last holders). It never takes a volume lock or writes anything.
`CallTrimMappedFiles` (root) runs it on demand.

**System calls 214-217.** `CallSyncMemory(Address, Length, Flags)`
(msync, `SyncMemoryAsync`/`Invalidate`/`Wait`, the Linux values),
`CallQueryMemoryResidency(Address, Length, Vector)` (mincore: a byte per
page, `PageResidencyResident`, `-Mapped`, `-Dirty`),
`CallGetMappedFileStatistics` (`TAbiMappedFileStatistics`: mapped files,
snapshots, resident and dirty pages, pages written back, evicted,
mappings dropped, snapshot pages read, bytes `read()` copied from mapped
pages) and `CallTrimMappedFiles(PagesWanted, Flags)`
(`TrimMappedPagesToo`); 218-219 are kept. In `Sys.Memory`: `SyncMemory`,
`QueryMemoryResidency`, `GetMappedFileStatistics`, `TrimMappedFiles`.

Tests: the mapped file self test (`Kernel.MappedFileSelfTest`, every
boot, on a memory volume of its own: a dirty page seen by `read()` and
not by the file system until written back, a `write()` into a dirty page
keeping the mapping's bytes, a private mapped file becoming a snapshot
that reads only the written page, eviction dropping clean unmapped pages
but not a preserved one); `filemaptest` (a coretest line: shared
writable mappings only through writable handles, seen at once by other
mappings and `read()`, dirty until msync, written back on unmap and
munmap, `write()` into a dirty page, a snapshot of a 1 MiB file reading
one page, trimming unmapping clean pages that read the same again and
leaving a dirty one); `MappedFileTest` on the host (`make
mapped-file-test`: entry flags, change spans and in-page byte ranges
against a byte model, write-back lengths, mapping overlaps). `maptest`
checks the rest: protection faults are catchable `EAccessViolation`s at
the byte touched, commit and decommit (and the charge), W^X and the
policy (a `ret` written and run), guard pages, a file seen through a
mapping and through `read()`, a `write()` seen through a shared mapping,
two private mappings keeping their writes apart and a private one
keeping the old contents, the commit limit, and that the library pages
it maps are mapped by other processes too (`PagesMappedElsewhere` in
`CallGetProcessResources`: resident file pages with more holders than
the mapped file and this mapping).

The runtime's heap still takes its chunks with `CallAllocateMemory`:
those pages are already provided only when touched, so reserving and
committing would only add system calls. The page heap uses the new calls
(see "Heap checking").

### Threads

A user process has one or more threads (`Processes.UserThread`). Each has
its own kernel stack (system calls and interrupts run on it; the scheduler
points the TSS and the system call entry at it on every switch), its own
user stack (a region with an unmapped guard page below it) and its own
thread data region (`Processes.ThreadStorage`) with the thread control
block and static thread-local storage. The thread pointer, the FS base
(MSR 0xC0000100), is part of each thread's state and is loaded by the
scheduler whenever it switches to a thread with a different one.

`CreateThread` (40) starts a thread at an entry point with one argument
and returns a thread handle; `WaitForThread` (42) waits for its exit
