configure, build, targets with stamps in `build/toolchain/work/llvm`, as
in the GCC script; `JOBS` and `LINK_JOBS` limit the parallelism). The
patches, one concern each:

| Patch | What |
|---|---|
| 0001-triple-freepascalos-os | `Triple::FreePascalOS` (OS name `freepascalos`, `isOSFreePascalOS()`) in LLVM's target triple, with a unit test |
| 0002-clang-freepascalos-target-info | `FreePascalOSTargetInfo` for x86-64 and AArch64: `__freepascalos__`, `unix`, `_REENTRANT` with `-pthread`, `_GNU_SOURCE` for C++, `__float128` on x86-64 - what GCC's `freepascalos.h` defines; the default include paths left to the driver |
| 0003-clang-freepascalos-driver | the toolchain class `toolchains::FreePascalOS` and its linker (`clang/lib/Driver/ToolChains/FreePascalOS.cpp`) |

The driver does what the GCC specs do. Headers: Clang's resource
directory, then `<sysroot>/usr/include`; for C++ libstdc++'s headers
from the GCC installation (`<gcc>/<triple>/include/c++/16.2.0` and its
target directory). Programs are PIE by default (`-fPIE`, `-pie`).
Linking (GNU ld from the binutils beside the GCC by default, `ld.lld`
with `-fuse-ld=lld`): `-m elf_x86_64` / `aarch64linux`, `-z
max-page-size=4096 --hash-style=both --eh-frame-hdr`, `-dynamic-linker
/usr/lib/ld.so`; `crt1.o` (for PIE too - mlibc has no `Scrt1.o`),
`crti.o`, `crtbegin.o`/`crtbeginS.o`/`crtbeginT.o` (normal, PIE or
shared, static) from the GCC installation, ..., `-lgcc --as-needed
-lgcc_s --no-as-needed -lc`, `crtend*.o`, `crtn.o`; `-static` takes
`--start-group -lgcc -lgcc_eh -lc --end-group`, `-static-pie` and
`-shared` as with GCC, C++ adds `-lstdc++ -lm`. The runtime defaults are
libgcc and libstdc++ from the GCC build; `-rtlib=compiler-rt`,
`--unwindlib=libunwind` and `-stdlib=libc++` select LLVM's runtimes
(their crtbegin/crtend and `<sysroot>/usr/include/c++/v1`), which are
not built here.

Where the system root and the GCC are comes from configuration files
beside the binary, which Clang reads for the target:
`build/toolchain/llvm/bin/x86_64-freepascalos.cfg` (and `aarch64-...`)
hold `--sysroot=<CFGDIR>/../../../sysroot/<arch>` and
`--gcc-toolchain=<CFGDIR>/../../<triple>`, with the normalized names
(`x86_64-unknown-freepascalos.cfg`, what `--target=x86_64-freepascalos`
looks for) linked to them; `x86_64-freepascalos-clang` and `-clang++`
are links to `clang` that pick the target from their name. So:

    build/toolchain/llvm/bin/clang --target=x86_64-freepascalos -O2 -o hello hello.c
    build/toolchain/llvm/bin/aarch64-freepascalos-clang++ -o test test.cpp -fuse-ld=lld

When Clang is there, `make c-runtime` also builds `ctest-clang` (the C
suite, GNU ld), `cxxtest-clang` (libstdc++) and `hello-clang-static`
(static, `ld.lld`) into `/usr/bin`, which `ctest` runs (next sections).
`make clang-driver-test` (part of `make test`; skipped without Clang,
`scripts/test-clang-driver.sh`) checks the driver on the host for both
targets: the predefined macros, the compiler's and the linker's command
lines with `-###` for the default PIE, `-no-pie`, `-static`,
`-static-pie`, `-shared`, C++, `-pthread`, `-fuse-ld=lld` and the
prefixed name, and - where the system root is built - real programs
linked by ld.bfd and ld.lld whose interpreter is `/usr/lib/ld.so`.

### How a C program starts

A C program is a PIE (ET_DYN) linked against `libc.so` with
`PT_INTERP` = `/usr/lib/ld.so`. The kernel's loader
(`Processes.ImageLoader`), seeing PT_INTERP, maps the program and the
interpreter and nothing else: it neither relocates them, nor loads
`DT_NEEDED` libraries, nor lays out TLS, nor collects initializers (it
does all of that for Pascal programs, which have no PT_INTERP). The
first thread starts at the interpreter's entry with the usual initial
stack plus `AT_BASE`, `AT_RANDOM` (16 random bytes), `AT_EXECFN`,
`AT_SECURE` and the user and group ids. mlibc's `ld.so` relocates
itself, maps `libc.so` and the other libraries from `/usr/lib` (and
`LD_LIBRARY_PATH`) with `mmap` - reserving each library's span, then
mapping its segments into it with `MAP_FIXED` - makes the static TLS
area and the main thread's TCB (its own layout: `%fs:0x28` is the stack
protector's canary), sets the thread pointer (`CallSetThreadPointer`),
runs the initializers and jumps to `_start` (`crt1.o`), which calls
`__mlibc_entry` and `main`. `dlopen` is the same `ld.so` at work (no
`CallLoadLibrary`), and `dl_iterate_phdr` - what C++ exceptions unwind
with - knows every object. A static program (`-static`) is an
ordinary ET_EXEC at 0x400000 the kernel starts directly; mlibc's static
startup does the same work for itself.

Libraries for C programs live in `/usr/lib` (the C runtime) and
`/usr/local/lib` (ported software, see `ports/README.md`): mlibc's
`ld.so` looks in `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, then in those two (its default
paths, `-Ddefault_library_paths` in `toolchain/build-toolchain.sh`), and
an rpath a port links with is honoured too. The kernel's loader, for
Pascal programs, looks in `/lib` and then `/usr/local/lib`; it never
loads a C library for a C program.

### Ports

The ports tool (`scripts/portstool`) builds a port with `toolchain = "c"`
with this toolchain and a sysroot of its own (a copy of
`build/sysroot/<arch>` with the build dependencies' packages unpacked
into it). Before an autotools port is configured
(`autotools_target.py`), every `config.sub` of its tree (and autosetup's
`autosetup-config.sub`) is replaced by `toolchain/config.sub` (from the
patched binutils), and its libtool learns the target: `freepascalos*`
joins libtool's Linux cases in `configure`, `libtool.m4`, `ltmain.sh`
and `aclocal.m4`, so shared libraries are built and named as on Linux.
zlib, lua, sqlite3, bash and binutils are built this way and tried on the system
(their `[test]` commands through `pkg test`, and a few uses of each);
`C_TEST_INIT=/usr/bin/PROGRAM scripts/test-c-runtime.sh` boots a disk with
another first program for such tries.

### The sysdeps

`toolchain/mlibc/sysdeps/freepascalos` is mlibc's view of the kernel,
one file per concern in `generic/` (`core.cpp`: logging, exit, the
thread pointer, futexes over `WaitOnAddress`/`WakeAddress`, clocks over
`CallGetPreciseTime`, or for `CLOCK_REALTIME` and `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` the
clock page with no system call, `clockpage.cpp`; `memory.cpp`; `files-core.cpp` and `files.cpp`;
`directories.cpp`; `threads.cpp`; `process.cpp`; `signals.cpp`;
`sockets.cpp`; `polling.cpp`; `terminal.cpp`; `system.cpp`), the start
files and the thread entry in `arch/<cpu>/`, and the ABI headers:
mlibc's Linux ABI (errno values, `struct stat`, `O_*`, signal numbers,
`termios`, socket constants) - the kernel's error codes already are the
Linux errno numbers - with the call numbers and records in
`include/freepascalos/syscall.h` (installed, for programs that want the
native calls). mlibc's "linux" option is off (it needs Linux's kernel
headers); posix, glibc and bsd are on (`madvise` and `mincore` are
built for the bsd option too, `toolchain/patches/mlibc`), and so are its separate
linux-epoll, linux-eventfd, linux-timerfd and linux-signalfd options
(their headers need nothing of Linux's), over the kernel's event
descriptors (`event-descriptors.cpp`, `event-polls.cpp`); inotify, which
mlibc keeps in the linux option, is the sysdeps' own (`inotify.cpp` and
an installed `<sys/inotify.h>` with Linux's values). See "Event
descriptors (260-269)".

- **Descriptors** are the kernel's handles, same numbers. What POSIX
  keeps per descriptor and the kernel does not - close-on-exec,
  `O_NONBLOCK`, the path a directory was opened with (for `openat` and
  the other `*at` calls, `fchdir`) - lives in a table in the process
  (`descriptors.cpp`), so fork copies it and exec drops it.
  `O_NONBLOCK` on pipes and terminals is a zero-timeout
  `CallWaitForHandles` before the read; on sockets the kernel's own
  non-blocking option. `O_CREAT` opens first and creates exclusively
  only if the file is missing, then sets the mode less the umask.
  `pread`/`pwrite` are `CallReadAt`/`CallWriteAt` (the descriptor's
  offset untouched, so threads sharing it do not race), `preadv` and
  `pwritev` gather into one of them (an mlibc patch; mlibc had none).
  `fsync`/`fdatasync` are `CallSyncHandle`: only that file's blocks. `flock` and `fcntl` record locks are the kernel's
  whole-file locks.
- **Memory**: `mmap`, `munmap` and `mprotect` pass the Linux `PROT_*`
  and `MAP_*` values to `CallMapMemory`, `CallUnmapMemory` and
  `CallProtectMemory`; mlibc's allocator takes its pages the same way.
  `msync` and `mincore` are `CallSyncMemory` and
  `CallQueryMemoryResidency` (ENOMEM for memory not mapped; `mincore`
  gives bit 0, resident).
  W^X holds: anonymous memory never becomes executable without
  `CallSetMemoryPolicy`, a file mapped executable needs no permission.
- **Threads**: mlibc makes the TCB and TLS; `PrepareStack` maps the
  stack with a guard page below and leaves the start routine, the TCB
  and the argument on it; `Clone` starts a kernel thread there with
  `CallCreateThreadOnStack`, which loads its thread pointer and runs the
  routine.
- **Processes**: `fork`, `execve` and `waitpid` are the kernel's
  (`CallForkProcess`, `CallExecuteProgram` with the close-on-exec list,
  `CallWaitForChild`), and so `posix_spawn`, `system` and `popen`
  work; process groups and sessions too.
- **Signals**: `sigaction` keeps the handlers here and tells the kernel
  the disposition and the handler's mask (`CallSetSignalDisposition`);
  the kernel continues a thread in `signal_dispatcher` with a
  `fpos_signal_record`, which calls the handler (with a `siginfo_t`:
  the sender, or the faulting address) and returns through
  `CallReturnFromSignal`. Processor exceptions come to the exception
  dispatcher (`CallSetExceptionDispatcher`) and become SIGSEGV, SIGFPE,
  SIGILL, SIGBUS or SIGTRAP: a handler runs and the instruction is
  tried again (or the handler `siglongjmp`s out); without one the
  program says where it faulted and ends as killed by the signal.
  Writing to a pipe nobody reads raises SIGPIPE. `sigaltstack` is
  accepted and ignored (handlers run on the thread's stack).
  `setitimer(ITIMER_REAL)` and `alarm` are a kernel thread of the
  process (`timers.cpp`, started with the first timer, all signals
  blocked, system calls only) sleeping on a word until the timer is due
  and then sending SIGALRM; a child of fork has none.
- **Sockets** are the kernel's IPv4 and IPv6 sockets: addresses
  translated from `sockaddr_in`/`sockaddr_in6` (ports in host order in
  the kernel's record), the common `SO_*`, `TCP_*`, `IP_TTL`,
  `IPV6_V6ONLY` options mapped (unknown ones are accepted and do
  nothing). `AF_UNIX` sockets are the kernel's local sockets
  (`localsockets.cpp`, see "Local sockets"): `sockaddr_un` paths and
  abstract names, `socketpair`, `SCM_RIGHTS`, `SCM_CREDENTIALS` with
  `SO_PASSCRED`, `SO_PEERCRED`, `SO_ACCEPTCONN`, `SOCK_SEQPACKET`;
  listen, accept, shutdown, the common options and send/recv without
  names are the same kernel calls for both kinds.
- **poll/select** look at every descriptor without waiting (files are
  always ready, sockets through `CallWaitForSocket`, event descriptors
  through `CallQueryHandleReadiness`), then wait in
  `CallWaitForHandles` on those it can wait for (at most 64), checking
  every 10 ms for what it cannot (a socket's room to write, a full
  eventfd's). epoll has no such limit (the kernel's event polls).
- **Terminals**: `termios` maps `ECHO`, `ICANON` and `ISIG` onto the
  console's modes and keeps the rest of the structure;
  `TIOCGWINSZ`/`TIOCSWINSZ`, `TIOCGPGRP`/`TIOCSPGRP`, `FIONREAD` and
  `FIONBIO` are there, and `TIOCGPTN`/`TIOCSPTLCK`. `posix_openpt` opens
  `/dev/ptmx` (one descriptor for the master), `ptsname` asks it for N
  (`/dev/pts/N`), `unlockpt` checks it is one (`pseudoterminals.cpp`),
  so `openpty` and `forkpty` work through mlibc's own code.
- **The rest**: `uname` and `gethostname` from `CallGetSystemInformation`,
  `sysconf`, `getentropy` from `/dev/urandom`, users and groups from
  `CallGetCredentials`/`CallSetUserIds`/`CallSetGroupIds` (and
  `getpwnam` from `/etc/passwd`, which mlibc reads itself), resource
  limits as constants.

### The POSIX block of system calls (180-199)

What the C library needs that the kernel did not have, added in the
kernel (`Processes.PosixMemoryCalls`, `Processes.MemoryMapping`,
`Processes.Fork`, `Processes.AddressSpaceCopy`, `Processes.Execution`,
`Processes.ChildWaits`, `Processes.Signals`, state in
`Processes.PosixState`):

| Number | Call | |
|---|---|---|
| 180 | `CallMapMemory` (Address, Length, Protection, Flags, Handle, Offset) | mmap: anonymous or a file's pages (shared read-only or private copy on write); `MAP_FIXED` replaces run time allocations and mappings in the range (inside a reservation the mapping becomes a piece of it); never images, stacks or devices |
| 181 | `CallUnmapMemory` (Address, Length) | munmap of allocations and mappings, splitting them |
| 182 | `CallForkProcess` () | a copy of the caller (see below); the child gets 0 |
| 183 | `CallExecuteProgram` (TAbiExecution) | execve in place: the new program is loaded into a new address space first, so a failure leaves the caller as it was; then the calling thread moves into it, the old space goes, the close-on-exec handles are closed, handled signals become default (ignored ones and the mask stay), set-user-ID applies; the same process id; the process's other threads end first (once the program is known to be there) |
| 184 | `CallWaitForChild` (ProcessId, StatusAddress, Flags) | waitpid with the Linux status word, `WNOHANG`, `WUNTRACED` |
| 185 | `CallCreateThreadOnStack` (Entry, Argument, StackPointer) | a thread on the caller's stack |
| 186 | `CallSetSignalDispatcher` (Address) | where handled signals are taken |
| 187 | `CallSendSignal` (Target, Signal) | kill (a process, a group, the caller's group, everyone it may) |
| 188 | `CallSetSignalMask` (How, Mask, OldMask) | sigprocmask (per thread) |
| 189 | `CallSetSignalDisposition` (Signal, Disposition, HandlerMask, Flags) | default, ignore or handle; `SA_RESETHAND` |
| 190 | `CallReturnFromSignal` (Record) | back from a handler: registers and mask |
| 191 | `CallSuspendForSignal` (Mask) | sigsuspend |
| 192 | `CallPendingSignals` () | sigpending |
| 193-195 | `CallSetProcessGroup`, `CallCreateSession`, `CallGetProcessGroupOf` | setpgid, setsid, getpgid/getsid (setpgid, and `CallCreateProcess` with a group id, join only a group of the caller's session: `ErrorNotPermitted` for another session's group, a number no process has, or a new session) |
| 196 | `CallGetParentProcessId` () | getppid |

**fork** makes a process object with the caller's credentials,
directories, group, session, terminal, limits, restrictions, exception
dispatcher and signal dispositions, every handle under the same number
(thread handles left out; open files are shared, offsets and all), and
a copy of the address space (`Processes.AddressSpaceCopy`): the same
layout and regions, each page the caller may write privately mapped
copy on write in both (the first write of either side copies it,
`BreakCopyOnWriteLocked`), read-only and shared pages mapped again with
a reference more, untouched pages left for both to fault in; device
memory is not copied. Its one thread is a copy of the calling thread:
it starts in the kernel and enters user mode with the caller's
registers at the system call (`ArchEnterUserModeWithContext`, an
`iretq` or `eret` with every register), the result register 0, the
caller's thread pointer and signal mask. The kernel's module list is
not copied (a C program's `ld.so` keeps its own). The parent keeps a
reference to each child (`Posix.Children`) until it waits for it: an
ended child is a zombie until then.

**Signals** (`Processes.Signals`): a process says per signal what
happens; a signal sent to it is then ended (status 128 plus the
signal; waitpid sees the signal), stopped or continued (`SIGSTOP`,
`SIGTSTP`, `SIGTTIN`, `SIGTTOU`, `SIGCONT`, through job control),
dropped (`SIGCHLD`, `SIGURG`, `SIGWINCH` by default - unless every
thread blocks it: then it waits, for a signal descriptor or sigwait -
and ignored ones),
or - handled, or blocked by every thread - left pending, and one thread
that does not block it is alerted (its wait ends with
`ErrorInterrupted`, which becomes `EINTR`; there is no `SA_RESTART`),
unless the sending thread takes it itself (`raise`). The alert is given
up when that thread is back in user mode, whoever took the signal.
At the thread's next return to user mode (`DeliverPendingSignals`, at
the end of every system call and in the interrupt return hook) the
kernel writes a `TAbiSignalRecord` below the red zone, adds the
handler's mask and enters the dispatcher; a pending signal that is not
handled takes its default action then. `SIGKILL` and `SIGSTOP` cannot
be caught or blocked. The system's own mechanisms meet signals where
they overlap: an end request (kill's TERM, a terminal's hang-up,
Ctrl-C) to a process that handles or ignores SIGTERM, SIGHUP or SIGINT
becomes that signal (`EndRequestTakenAsSignalLocked`, in
`Processes.EndRequests`), otherwise the process ends as before and its
parent's waitpid sees the signal; a child that ends sends SIGCHLD to a
parent that handles it; a process ended by a processor exception
nobody took counts as killed by SIGSEGV.

### Files and local sockets (250-259)

| Number | Call | |
|---|---|---|
| 250 | `CallReadAt` (Handle, Buffer, Count, Offset) | pread of a file or block device, the position untouched; each 16 KiB piece one VFS call under the volume's lock; `ErrorIllegalSeek` for pipes, sockets, terminals |
| 251 | `CallWriteAt` (Handle, Buffer, Count, Offset) | pwrite (the file grows as needed; an appending handle writes at Offset too) |
| 252 | `CallSyncHandle` (Handle, Flags) | fsync/fdatasync of one file (`SyncHandleDataOnly`), see "The block cache"; `ErrorInvalidArgument` for pipes and sockets |
| 253 | `CallCreateLocalSocket` (Kind, Flags, PairAddress) | a local socket (`LocalSocketStream`, `LocalSocketDatagram`, `LocalSocketPackets`; `LocalSocketNonBlocking`), or with PairAddress a connected pair (socketpair) |
| 254 | `CallBindLocalSocket` (Handle, NameAddress) | to a `TAbiLocalSocketName`: a path (a socket node is made there), an abstract name (first byte 0), or with Length 0 one picked by the kernel |
| 255 | `CallConnectLocalSocket` (Handle, NameAddress) | to a listener (waits while its backlog is full) or a datagram socket's destination; a path needs write permission on its node |
| 256 | `CallSendLocalMessage` (Handle, MessageAddress, Flags) | a `TAbiLocalMessage`: bytes, handles to pass, for datagrams the name to send to |
| 257 | `CallReceiveLocalMessage` (Handle, MessageAddress, Flags) | bytes, passed handles installed as the receiver's, the sender's name and credentials; `LocalMessageTruncated`, `LocalMessageHandlesCut` |
| 258 | `CallQueryLocalSocket` (Handle, Which, Buffer) | the name, the peer's name, the peer's credentials, the kind |

**Local sockets** (`Processes.LocalSockets`, the names in
`Processes.LocalSocketNames`, the calls in `Processes.LocalSocketCalls`)
are a handle kind of their own (`HandleKindLocalSocket`), told to
programs as `HandleKindSocket`; listen, accept, shutdown, the options,
`CallWaitForSocket`, `CallRead` and `CallWrite`, and send and receive
without names take them through the network socket calls (the
dispatcher sends them on, `PerformSocketCallOnLocalSocket`), and
`CallWaitForHandles` waits for them to be readable. Each socket queues
the messages sent to it: one send is one message - its bytes, the
objects it passes (each held as an open handle while in flight, as a
channel message's are) and who sent it (credentials and, for
datagrams, the sender's name). A datagram or packet socket receives
messages whole (cut to the buffer, `MSG_TRUNC`); a stream joins them
but never reads past a message that passes objects, so they come with
their bytes. connect makes the server's end at once and queues it in
the listener's backlog; accept takes it. Senders wait for room in the
receiver's queue (256 KiB, or 128 messages; `SO_RCVBUF` changes it);
readers for the `Readable` event. One mutex guards every local socket
and is never held while waiting. A socket's open handles are counted
(`NoteHandleOpened`): when the last closes, its peer sees the end of
the stream (reads 0, writes `ErrorBrokenPipe`, which the C library
turns into SIGPIPE), its backlog's connections are released, its name
is given up and what was queued is dropped, closing what it passed. A
socket passed in a message queued on itself is never collected (Linux
has a collector for such cycles). Names: a path is a socket node
(`NodeKindSocket`, `KindSocket`; ext and memory volumes have them, FAT
and exFAT do not) known by its volume and node number, so any path to
it connects; it stays after the socket closes (programs remove it
before binding again); abstract names go with their socket. Credentials
(`SO_PEERCRED`) are those of whoever made the peer: the connecting
process for a server's end, the listener's maker for the client, each
other's for a pair.
### Event descriptors (260-269)

eventfd, timerfd, signalfd, epoll and inotify are kernel objects behind
handles of their own kinds (`Processes.EventDescriptorCalls`), each
ready for `CallWaitForHandles` (so for poll and select) and for event
polls like every other waitable object, and read with `CallRead`; their
records are Linux's, so the C library passes them through. Their
constants and records are in `shared/Abi.EventDescriptors.inc`. A
handle made non-blocking (`EventDescriptorNonBlocking` when made, or
`CallControlHandle`'s `ControlSetNonBlocking`, which fcntl's `O_NONBLOCK`
sets) fails with `ErrorWouldBlock` instead of waiting.

| Number | Call | |
|---|---|---|
| 260 | `CallCreateEventCounter` (InitialValue, Flags) | eventfd (`Objects.EventCounters`): a 64-bit count; a read of 8 bytes takes it all (or one, `EventCounterSemaphore`) and waits at zero; a write adds, waiting while the sum would pass 2^64-2 |
| 261 | `CallCreateTimerDescriptor` (Clock, Flags) | timerfd (`Objects.TimerDescriptors`) on the real time, monotonic or boot clock (Linux's ids; the last two are the uptime) |
| 262 | `CallSetTimerDescriptor` (Handle, Flags, New, Old) | timerfd_settime and (New 0) timerfd_gettime: `TAbiTimerSpecification` (struct itimerspec), `TimerAbsolute`, `TimerCancelOnSet` |
| 263 | `CallQueryHandleReadiness` (Handle) | what poll says of any handle now (`PollReadable`, `PollWritable`, `PollError`, `PollHangUp`; `Processes.HandleReadiness`) |
| 264 | `CallSetSignalDescriptor` (Handle or -1, Mask, Flags) | signalfd (`Processes.SignalDescriptors`), or a new mask |
| 265-267 | `CallCreateEventPoll`, `CallControlEventPoll`, `CallWaitEventPoll` | epoll (`Processes.EventPolls`) |
| 268-269 | `CallCreateWatchGroup`, `CallChangeGroupWatch` | inotify (`FileSystem.WatchGroups`) |

**Readiness without looking at everything.** Kernel events can have
observers (`Kernel.Events`): routines told of every signal of the event
(and of a semaphore's release) under the dispatcher lock, before its
waiters are released; they wait for nothing and consume nothing. Each
object kind names at most two readiness events (`HandleReadinessEvents`:
a pipe end's Readable or Writable, a socket's Readable and Writable, a
device's ReadyEvent and WritableEvent, an event counter's Readable and
Writable, the single event of the others) and says what it is ready for
from its state (`HandleReadiness`), without its locks.

**Event polls** (epoll). An entry per handle number and object added
holds a reference to the object and an observer on each of its
readiness events; a signal puts the entry on the poll's ready list and
signals the poll's Ready event, from any level. A wait takes entries off
the list, asks each object what it is ready for and reports what was
asked for (`PollError` and `PollHangUp` always): a level triggered entry
still ready goes back on the list, an edge triggered one waits for the
next signal (every write to an eventfd or a pipe signals again, as on
Linux), a one shot one is disabled until modified; a wait finding
nothing resets Ready (only while the list is empty, under the event
lock) and waits on it, alertable. Entries are found by number in 64
buckets; any number of them, unlike `CallWaitForHandles`' 64 handles.
Files are refused (`ErrorNotPermitted`: always ready), a poll inside
itself or in a loop too, and polls nest at most four deep.
`PollExclusive` is accepted (every waiter wakes). A registration lasts
until removed, until the poll goes, or until the object's last handle
is closed in any process: object headers count the handles that name
them (`NoteObjectHandleOpened`/`Closed`, kept by `Processes.Handles`),
and the last close takes the object's entries out of every poll
(`ForgetObjectInEventPolls`, before the handle's reference goes), so
closing a socket's last descriptor closes it even while it is in a poll.
The entries on an object are listed in its header too. One mutex guards
the entries; the ready lists are the event lock's.

**Timer descriptors.** Armed with a first time (relative, or a time of
its clock) and a period, in nanoseconds; each time it goes off (a
deferred call at DispatchLevel, under the timer's spin lock) the count
of expirations grows by every period gone by, and Ready is signaled; a
read takes the count. An absolute real time timer follows the wall
clock: `Kernel.WallClock` calls its step routines after every step (not
a gradual adjustment, and not on resume, when the other processors are
still frozen), and its uptime deadline is worked out again - or, armed
with `TimerCancelOnSet`, it is stopped and reads fail with
`ErrorCanceled` (and it is ready) until it is armed again.

**Signal descriptors.** A program blocks the signals and reads them: a
read takes the lowest waiting signal of the mask - the process's or the
reading thread's - as a `TAbiSignalDescriptorRecord` (struct
signalfd_siginfo: the signal, the sender and `SignalCodeUser` or
`SignalCodeKernel`), as many as fit. A descriptor reports the signals
of the process that made it: `Processes.Signals` tells it of every
signal made to wait (`NoteSignalWaiting` signals its Ready), and Ready
is brought up to date before every wait on it and after every read, so
a signal taken some other way leaves nothing stale. For it (and
sigwait) a signal ignored by default that every thread blocks (SIGCHLD,
SIGWINCH, SIGURG) now waits instead of being dropped, as on Linux; once
unblocked it is dropped.

**Watch groups** (inotify). Members are ordinary watches
(`FileSystem.Watches`) whose records go to the group's queue instead of
their own, translated into Linux's events: names created and removed
(`GroupWatchMovedTo`/`MovedFrom` when moved in or out - native watch
records carry `WatchRecordMoved` for that now), renamed in a folder (both
halves with one cookie, the same for every watch that sees the rename),
written, attributes changed, the item itself removed (then
`GroupWatchIgnored`), moved, or its volume gone (`GroupWatchUnmount`,
then ignored); `GroupWatchIsDirectory` for folders. The file systems
report no opening, closing or reading, so those events are accepted
and never come. Adding a path watched already (same volume and node)
changes that member's mask (`GroupWatchMaskAdd`, `GroupWatchMaskCreate`
as Linux's); `GroupWatchOnlyDirectory`, `GroupWatchDontFollow`,
`GroupWatchOneShot` as Linux's. Up to 4096 records wait, then one
overflow record. The group's state is guarded by the watch lock.

**In the C library.** `epoll_create1`, `epoll_ctl`, `epoll_wait` and
`epoll_pwait` (the mask set around the wait, as ppoll's; at most 64
events per call; `struct epoll_event` is packed on x86-64 and copied
over), `eventfd`, `eventfd_read`/`eventfd_write`, `timerfd_create`/
`settime`/`gettime` (`CLOCK_REALTIME`, `CLOCK_MONOTONIC`,
`CLOCK_BOOTTIME`), `signalfd`, `inotify_init`/`init1`/`add_watch`/
`rm_watch`, with `*_CLOEXEC` and `*_NONBLOCK`.

The kernel self tests (`Kernel.EventDescriptorSelfTest`, every boot)
check observers, event counters, event polls (level and edge triggered,
one shot, modifying, a wait woken by another thread, nesting and loops,
entries forgotten with the last handle) and timer descriptors (periods
counted, stopping, a past absolute time, cancel on set and a timer that
follows a step of the clock, stepped by nothing); ctest's "event
descriptors", "epoll" and "inotify" groups check them from C, and a
coretest line runs the last two as an ordinary user.

### Tests

`toolchain/ctest`: `ctest` (C: stdio, malloc and mmap, strings, math,
time, files and directories with `*at` calls, the environment, pthreads
with mutexes, condition variables, `__thread` and once, fork/exec/waitpid,
`posix_spawn`, several children, process groups, pipes with `dup2` and
`popen`, Unix domain sockets of all three kinds (paths, abstract names,
autobind, `SCM_RIGHTS` across fork, `SCM_CREDENTIALS`, `SO_PEERCRED`,
shutdown, poll, non-blocking), pseudo-terminals through `/dev/ptmx` and
`openpty`, pread/pwrite from four threads on one descriptor, preadv and
pwritev, fsync and fdatasync, nanosecond times, msync and mincore, the
clock page against the system call, signal handlers, masks and pending signals, SIGCHLD, SIGPIPE,
SIGSEGV caught with `siglongjmp`, signals between processes, TCP over
loopback between threads with `poll`, UDP with `select`, `dlopen`, exec from a process with a thread running, exec of a Free Pascal program (`/bin/echo`), `alarm` and a periodic `setitimer`;
eventfd, timerfd, signalfd, epoll (a hundred pipes, a TCP server,
nesting, fork) and inotify; 569 checks), then `hello-static` and `cxxtest` (iostreams, containers,
exceptions through ten frames and across threads, `std::thread`,
mutexes, atomics, chrono) as programs of their own; with Clang (`make
clang-toolchain`) also `ctest-clang --groups-only` (every group again,
compiled by Clang), `cxxtest-clang` and `hello-clang-static` (printed as
skipped when the disk lacks them). `make c-test` boots
(QEMU, `ACCEL=kvm` for speed; with `ARCH=arm64` QEMU's virt machine) with
`init=/usr/bin/ctest` and passes when
every check did (`scripts/test-c-runtime.sh`, log in
`build/amd64/c-test-serial.log`); a coretest line runs `ctest` when the
system disk has it.

## Style engine (libcss)

libcss (`userland/lib/css`, units `Css.*`, `libcss.so`) is the style
engine of the web platform: CSS syntax, selectors, values, the property
table, style sheets, media queries, the cascade and computed styles. It
depends on libsystem only and knows no document model: it sees elements
through an adapter the host implements (libweb for its DOM, the tests
for a toy tree). `cssdump` (`/bin/cssdump`) parses style sheets with it
and prints them back normalized.

**Atoms and the element adapter.** Every name the engine compares is an
atom of one process wide table (`Css.Atoms`): a LongWord, interned once,
never freed, with its ASCII lowercase atom at hand. The table is seeded
with the keywords of `Css.Keywords` in enum order, so a keyword's atom is
its ordinal and keyword tests compare integers; a keyword's spelling
comes from its identifier (`kwInlineBlock` is `inline-block`). A host
refers to elements by opaque handles (`TCssElement`, any pointer) and
implements one `TCssElementAdapter`: local name and namespace (atoms),
whether it is an HTML element in an HTML document (case-insensitive
names and some attribute values), id and classes (atoms), attribute
lookup (by namespace and name, and by index for `[*|x]`), element-only
navigation (parent, previous and next sibling, first and last child),
`:empty`, the root, the state flags (`TCssElementState`: hover, active,
focus, focus-visible, focus-within, link, visited, target, checked,
disabled, enabled, placeholder-shown, open, modal and the others), the
language and direction, the quirks mode, and the parsed style attribute
and presentational hints (declaration blocks the host keeps). The
cheapest arrangement, the one libweb is meant to use, is to intern the
DOM's element and attribute names, ids and classes in libcss's table:
the adapter then returns stored integers and the engine allocates
nothing per element.

**Syntax.** The tokenizer follows CSS Syntax Level 3 exactly on UTF-8
(preprocessing, escapes decoded, every byte from 0x80 up an ident code
point, numbers with their integer flag and sign). A token list is one
dynamic array ending in EOF, in which every opening bracket and function
token knows the index of its closer: a component value is a token or a
range, skipping one is a jump, and the parsers walk `TCssTokenCursor`
ranges without building trees of component values. `Css.Parser` has the
rule and declaration algorithms with their error recovery, the @import
and @namespace ordering rules, and CSS Nesting: in a style rule's block
"ident : ..." is tried as a declaration and re-read as a nested rule
when its value holds a {} block among other things; declarations after
a nested rule become a nested declarations rule (they behave like "&").
The object model (`Css.Stylesheets`) has style rules with child rules,
@media, @supports (decided when parsed), @container (parsed and kept,
not evaluated yet), @layer blocks and statements, @import (the host
loads the sheet and hangs it on the rule), @namespace, @font-face (its
descriptors parsed, unicode-range from the source text), @keyframes,
@page and @property. Each serializes as CSSOM says; `Css.Serialization`
escapes identifiers, strings and numbers and writes token runs back
with the comments that keep tokens apart.

**Selectors.** Selectors Level 4 (`Css.Selectors`, `Css.SelectorParser`):
type and universal selectors with namespaces, id, class, attribute
selectors with all operators and the i/s flags, every pseudo-class of the
level (state ones from the adapter's flags; structural ones including
`:nth-child(An+B of S)` and the -of-type family; `:is`, `:where`
(forgiving), `:not`, `:has` with relative selectors, `:lang` with
wildcards, `:dir`, `:root`, `:scope`, `:empty`), the pseudo-elements
::before ::after ::marker ::placeholder ::selection ::first-line
::first-letter ::backdrop ::file-selector-button (unknown ::-webkit-
ones are valid and never match), the four combinators and the nesting
selector '&'. A complex selector keeps its compounds right to left;
specificity is (a, b, c) packed in ten bits each. Matching
(`Css.SelectorMatching`) starts at the subject and walks left; a failure
says how far back to restart (later sibling, closest descendant, or
give up), the WebKit/Servo scheme, so descendant combinators do not
backtrack quadratically. Sibling positions for `:nth-*` are cached per
element. `:has` searches the subtree or following siblings of its
element.

**The bloom filter and the rule index.** While a tree is styled
top-down, the names (lowercased local name, id, classes) of the
ancestors are counted in a 4096 entry counting bloom filter
(`Css.BloomFilter`, two 12 bit hashes per name). Each selector carries
up to four hashes of names its ancestor compounds need; a selector one
of them is missing for is rejected without touching the tree. The rule
index (`Css.RuleIndex`) holds every style rule selector that applies in
the current environment (its @media, @supports and @import conditions
hold), hashed by the subject compound's id, else class, else type, else
into the universal list; an element is matched only against its id's,
classes' and type's buckets and the universal one. The index also ranks
cascade layers (per origin, by first declaration, sublayers before the
layer's own rules, unlayered last; anonymous layers are unique) and
collects @keyframes, @font-face and @property rules.

**Values and the property table.** Specified values (`Css.Values`) are
immutable reference counted nodes: keyword, number, integer,
percentage, dimension (every unit of Values 4: absolute, font-relative,
viewport including s/l/d variants, container, angles, times,
frequencies, resolutions, fr), color, string, URL, custom identifier,
math function, list (space, comma or slash), function (gradients,
transforms, counters, attr(), basic shapes ...), and the raw tokens of
a value that still has var() (and of custom properties). Math functions
(`Css.Calc`) are full Values 4: calc, min, max, clamp, round, mod, rem,
abs, sign, the trigonometric and exponential functions, the constants;
the tree is type-checked with exponents per base type and simplified
(like units combined, absolute units made canonical, number-only
functions computed). Colors (`Css.Colors`, `Css.ColorParser`) are CSS
Color 4 and 5: named, hex, rgb/hsl (legacy and modern syntax), hwb, lab,
lch, oklab, oklch, color() in every predefined space, color-mix() (with
hue methods, premultiplied), currentcolor and the system colors (a
light and a dark table the host can replace); conversions go through
CIE XYZ with the specification's matrices, and drawing gets sRGB
clipped to the gamut. Images (`Css.Images`) are url(), image-set() and
linear, radial and conic gradients (repeating too, with an
interpolation color space), checked and kept as typed function values;
`Css.Transforms` checks every transform function.

The property table (`Css.PropertyIds`, `Css.PropertyTable`) has one row
per property: about 220 physical longhands, 34 logical ones, 55
shorthands and `cpCustom`. A row gives the group the computed value
lives in, the initial value as text (parsed once with the property's own
grammar), the grammar, how the value is computed and how it animates.
A property's name comes from its identifier. Grammars are table driven
(`Css.Grammar`): alternatives of keywords and basic types
(`<length-percentage+>` is non-negative), keyword sets in braces, comma
lists with a leading '#', or `@name` for a routine of the value parsers
(`Css.BoxParsers`, `Css.GridParsers`, `Css.TextParsers`: display in its
full multi-keyword syntax, sizes with fit-content(), the alignment
values, track lists with repeat() and line names, template areas
checked to be rectangles, grid lines, font families, shadows, cursors,
content and counters, easing functions, filters, clip paths, background
layers and the rest). `Css.Shorthands` expands margin, padding, inset,
every border shorthand (physical and logical), border-radius with its
slash, border-image, outline, background (layers), background-position,
font (system fonts too), font-variant, flex, flex-flow, grid,
grid-template (both forms), grid-row/column/area, gap, place-*,
overflow, list-style (with its 'none' rule), text-decoration, transition,
animation, columns, column-rule and container; what a shorthand leaves
out gets its initial value, and `all` takes the CSS-wide keywords.

**Declarations.** A declaration block (`Css.Declarations`) is an array
of small records (property, importance, the shorthand it came from,
custom property name, value). Shorthands are stored as their longhands;
serialization folds them back where the shorthand can be written (box
sides, pairs, border sides, flex, grid lines, and any shorthand whose
longhands all came from one var() value). A later declaration of a
property replaces an earlier one, except that a normal one does not
replace an !important one.

**The cascade.** For an element (or one of its pseudo-elements) the
engine collects the matching rules' blocks, the presentational hints
and the style attribute. Each block takes part with its normal and its
important declarations, ordered as Cascade 5 says: origin and
importance (user agent, user, author normal; author, user, user agent
important), element-attached declarations over rules, cascade layer
(later wins for normal, earlier for important; presentational hints
below every author layer), specificity, order of appearance. Walking
them from the highest priority, the first declaration of a property
wins; `revert` skips the rest of its origin, `revert-layer` the rest of
its layer. Writing mode and direction are cascaded first so that
logical properties are mapped to the physical ones in the same pass.
Custom properties cascade by name.

**Computed styles.** A computed value (`Css.ComputedValues`) is a 24
byte record: kind, keyword, px and percent as singles (or a 16 bit per
channel sRGB color), and a reference to a value tree for what does not
fit. Lengths are made absolute: em against the element's font size (the
parent's for font-size), rem against the root's, ex, ch, cap and ic as
fractions of the em, lh and rlh, viewport units against the media
environment, container units falling back to the small viewport.
Percentages stay until layout gives a basis (`ResolveComputed`), and a
calc() that is not px plus percent (min(10px, 5%)) stays a calculation
with px leaves. currentcolor stays except in `color`, font-weight's
bolder and lighter follow the parent, line-height in units becomes a
length, border, outline and column-rule widths snap to device pixels and
are 0 when their style is none or hidden, display is blockified for
floats, absolutely positioned boxes and the root, and a float is none
when the box is absolutely positioned. var() is substituted before
anything is computed: custom properties are resolved in dependency
order with cycle detection (a property in a cycle is invalid; one that
refers to it uses its fallback), env() knows the safe-area and titlebar
variables (the host can set them), a value that fails after
substitution is invalid at computed-value time and acts as unset, and a
shorthand with var() is expanded once its tokens are known. Registered
custom properties (@property) can be non-inherited and give initial
values. A style serializes any property (`SerializeProperty`, what
getComputedStyle answers): a logical longhand as its physical one in
the style's writing mode and direction, a shorthand from its longhands
when they can be written as it (the box sides, pairs, a border side,
flex), else as their common value or empty.

Computed values are stored in style structs (`Css.StyleStructs`): one
reference counted block per property group, like Gecko's and Servo's
(font, inherited text, inherited box, inherited user interface, lists,
inherited table; box, position and sizing with flex and grid, margins,
padding, borders, outline, backgrounds, effects, text decoration,
generated content, table, columns, user interface, animations). A group
is all inherited or all not, so a child inherits a group by taking its
parent's pointer; a group nothing was declared for is the shared
initial struct; every rebuilt struct is interned in the struct cache, so
elements with equal values in a group share one struct. A computed
style (`Css.ComputedStyle`) is a pointer per group, the custom property
set (shared with the parent when the element declares none) and its
pseudo-element.

**The style engine.** `TCssStyleEngine` (`Css.StyleEngine`) keeps the
sheets (the HTML user agent sheet of the HTML Standard's rendering
section, its quirks mode additions in quirks mode, user sheets and the
document's author sheets, which stay the host's), the media environment
(`TCssMediaEnvironment`: viewport in CSS pixels, resolution from the
system's DPI scale, color scheme, motion, transparency and contrast
preferences, forced colors, hover and pointer, scripting, color gamut,
dynamic range, update; set by the host), the rule index, the struct
cache and the style sharing cache. `ResolveStyle(Element, ParentStyle)`
gives a new reference; `ResolvePseudoStyle` gives nil when no rule
targets the pseudo-element; `StyleTree` styles a subtree top-down with
the bloom filter (`AnonymousStyle` gives an anonymous box's style:
inherited values from the parent, initial ones for the rest; hosts
walking themselves call PushAncestor and
PopAncestor). Elements with the same parent style that match the same
rules, with no style attribute or presentational hints and no attr()
in their declarations, get the same computed style from the sharing
cache without cascading again. `TreeChanged` forgets sibling positions
and shared styles; `Invalidate` rebuilds the index (sheets changed,
media changed).

Media queries (`Css.MediaQueries`) are Level 4 and 5: media types, not
and only, and/or/not conditions, the range syntax (`400px <= width <
700px`), min-/max- prefixes, and the features width, height,
aspect-ratio, device-*, resolution (with `infinite`),
-webkit-device-pixel-ratio, orientation, color, color-index, monochrome,
grid, prefers-color-scheme, prefers-reduced-motion,
prefers-reduced-transparency, prefers-reduced-data, prefers-contrast,
forced-colors, inverted-colors, hover, any-hover, pointer, any-pointer,
scripting, display-mode, color-gamut, dynamic-range, update, scan and
overflow-*; evaluation is three-valued and an unknown feature is false
at the top. em in a query is the environment's initial font size.

**Memory.** On the test's synthetic page (1767 elements, the user agent
sheet and a typical author sheet) the engine makes 44 distinct computed
styles (40 elements per style; 1723 of the elements come from the
sharing cache), 66 distinct structs (each used by 13 styles), about 17
bytes of computed style per element; a style with nothing shared would
be 5480 bytes. libcss.so is about 0.9 MB.

**Tests.** `make css-test` (tools/CssTest) builds libcss on the host and
checks tokenizer cases, parse-and-serialize round trips of values,
shorthands and style sheets, specificity, matching against a small tree
through the test adapter (with and without the bloom filter, quirks
mode), cascade order with origins, layers, !important, the style
attribute and revert, computed values (em, rem, %, calc, var() with
fallbacks and cycles, viewport units, border snapping, blockification),
the user agent sheet, media query evaluation, @supports, color
conversions against answers computed by `make-color-vectors.py` from
the primaries and white points (not from the matrices libcss uses), and
memory and sharing on the synthetic page, which it reports. coretest
runs cssdump on three inputs in the system.

**Not done yet.** Container queries are parsed but not evaluated (no
container matches, so their rules do not apply); :visited is matched
from the adapter's flag, with no privacy split of styles; relative color
syntax (`rgb(from ...)`), light-dark(), @scope, @counter-style,
@font-feature-values are not supported (of SVG's properties only the
painting ones are: fill, stroke and their parts, stop-color and
stop-opacity, text-anchor, paint-order, vector-effect, clip-rule, in two
groups of their own, one inherited); transitions
and animations are parsed and stored but not run; gamut mapping is
clipping; computed colors are 16 bit sRGB; the cascade's sort is an
insertion sort (fine for the dozens of rules that match one element).

## SVG (libsvg)

libsvg (`userland/lib/svg`, `Svg.*`) draws SVG 2 documents with
libdrawing. One renderer serves both uses: an SVG file shown as an
image (an `<img>`, a CSS `url()`, a favicon, the image viewer), parsed
and styled by libsvg itself, and inline `<svg>` in HTML, whose DOM
libweb copies into libsvg's nodes with the styles it computed.

**Documents.** `Svg.Xml` reads the XML (UTF-8, UTF-16 by its byte order
mark; comments, CDATA, processing instructions; a doctype whose
internal subset declares general entities, expanded with limits on
depth and size; namespaces with prefixes in scope; a root without a
namespace taken as SVG) into `TSvgNode`s (`Svg.Nodes`): elements with
their kind (from the name in the SVG namespace; others are not drawn),
attributes, text, the computed style and, for an embedder, its own
node. Malformed XML keeps what came before the error. `Svg.Styling`
styles a file with libcss: an element adapter over the nodes, the
`<style>` sheets, the style attribute, and the presentation attributes
(`Svg.Presentation`, shared with libweb: fill, stroke-width, font-size
... as declarations below every author rule, a bare number allowed
for lengths) as presentational hints. libcss knows SVG's painting
properties (fill, fill-rule, fill-opacity, stroke, stroke-width,
-linecap, -linejoin, -miterlimit, -dasharray, -dashoffset,
-opacity, clip-rule, text-anchor, paint-order, stop-color,
stop-opacity, vector-effect). `TSvgDocument` (`Svg.Document`) keeps the
tree, the elements by id, the natural size (the root's absolute width
and height, the viewBox's ratio), the pictures its `<image>`s refer to
(`Svg.ImageReferences`: data: URLs, decoded by libimage, SVG
included), how to restyle content a `<use>` instantiates (the styler
resolves it again with the use's style as the parent, as SVG 2's shadow
trees inherit from their use) and where its text's glyphs come from
(`Svg.Fonts`: the system's DejaVu Sans and Sans Mono, bold from 600,
read once under a lock, for files; libweb's font matching for inline
SVG). An embedder may also resolve ids the tree does not have.

**Rendering** (`Svg.Renderer`): a walk from the root with the current
transform, the viewport (percentages) and the parent's style.
display: none skips a subtree, visibility: hidden an element's own
painting; transform attributes compose. Shapes (`Svg.Geometry`: rect
with rx and ry, circle, ellipse, line, polyline, polygon, path with
the whole path data grammar, `Svg.PathData`) fill under their fill-rule
and stroke with every stroke property (non-scaling strokes in device
space), in paint-order, each with a colour (currentColor resolved), a
linear or radial gradient (gradientUnits, gradientTransform,
spreadMethod, the attributes and stops inherited along href; a
bounding-box gradient on a flat shape draws nothing) or a pattern
(patternUnits, patternContentUnits, patternTransform, viewBox, href;
the tile drawn at the device's resolution), or the paint's fallback
colour. Text (`Svg.Text`) lays out text, tspan, a and textPath (as a
tspan) with x, y, dx, dy and rotate lists, white space collapsed,
text chunks anchored by text-anchor, kerning, letter- and
word-spacing, and slants italic type without an italic face; its glyph
outlines are filled and stroked as paths. `<image>` draws its picture
by preserveAspectRatio, sampled between pixels (pixelated on request),
an SVG picture drawn again at the size shown. Groups, `<a>` and the
first suitable child of `<switch>` draw their children; nested `<svg>`
and a `<use>` of a symbol open a viewport (viewBox and
preserveAspectRatio; clipped to its rectangle when the transform keeps
it one); `<use>` draws its target restyled under it, refusing cycles.
opacity below 1 (unless a shape paints only one of fill and stroke,
which then takes it), clip-path and mask draw the element into a
layer the size of its bounds, put down through the union of the clip
path's children's coverage (clipPathUnits, clip-rule, a clip path's
own clip path) and the mask's luminance (maskUnits,
maskContentUnits, its region; mask-type alpha). Symbols, defs, paint
servers, clip paths and masks draw nothing themselves.

**As an image** (`Svg.Images`): `TSvgImage` is a scalable image over a
document; its natural size is the root's width and height, a missing
one following the viewBox's ratio, and without either CSS's default
300 x 150 (the ratio contained in it). Drawn at another size, the
viewport stretches over it and a root with a size but no viewBox
scales as if its viewBox were 0 0 width height, as browsers draw SVG
images. Its codec in libimage's registry recognizes SVG by content
(the first element is svg, after any declaration, comments and
doctype). Inline SVG makes its images deferred: drawn only when
painted, at the size shown.

**Not done yet.** Markers; text along a textPath's path, text
decorations, vertical text and bidirectional reordering; filters;
SVG animation (SMIL) and CSS transforms or animations on SVG elements;
external references (other files' elements, `<image>` of other URLs);
foreignObject's HTML; gzip-compressed files (.svgz served without
Content-Encoding); `context-fill`/`context-stroke`; miter-clip and
arcs joins are miters.

**Tests.** `make svg-test` draws small documents and probes the pixels
each feature decides (172 checks: shapes, path data with arcs and
implicit commands, fill rules, caps, joins, miter limits, dashes,
paint order, transforms, viewBox and preserveAspectRatio, nested
viewports, group and paint opacity, currentColor, the cascade with
sheets, style attributes and presentation attributes, use and symbols
with inheritance from the use, gradients and their spreads and
inheritance, patterns, clips, masks, text and its anchors, images
from data: URLs including SVG ones, entities and namespaces) and checks
natural sizes, renderings at other sizes and the sniffing. `SvgTest
FONTS IN.svg OUT.png W H` draws a file for looking at.

## Web engine (libweb)

libweb (`userland/lib/web`, `libweb.so`, units `Web.*`) is the browser
engine that both the browser application and the web view control will
use: the WHATWG Encoding Standard, the HTML parser and the DOM; the
event loop, fetching through libhttp (the Fetch Standard's rules),
loading documents and their subresources, and navigation with session
history; styling through libcss, text through libfont, layout and
painting through libdrawing and libimage (sections below). The script
bindings put the DOM in front of libjavascript. `htmldump` and
`webrender` (in /bin) are its command line front ends.

### Atoms and namespaces

Names are atoms (`Web.Atoms`): a process-wide table interns element and
attribute local names, namespaces, prefixes, event types and class
names once, and they compare as 32 bit integers. The well-known HTML,
SVG and MathML names are predeclared constants (`AtomDiv`,
`AtomForeignObject`, `AtomSvgNamespace`, ...), generated at build time
from `data/well-known-names.txt` by `make-tables.py`; the table only
grows and is not locked (the documents' thread makes atoms). A node
keeps its namespace and prefix together as a 16 bit `TNamespaceId`
(`Web.Namespaces`), an index into a table of (namespace, prefix) pairs
whose common ones are fixed (`NamespaceHtml`, `NamespaceSvg`,
`NamespaceXLink` with the xlink prefix, ...).

### Encodings

`Web.Encoding.*` implements the Encoding Standard: all encodings and
their labels (from `data/encoding-labels.txt`), "get an encoding",
streaming decoders that take bytes in any number of pieces and append
UTF-8 to a `TTextBuffer` (UTF-8 with the standard's maximal-subpart
replacement, UTF-16LE/BE with lone surrogates replaced, the 27
single-byte encodings from index tables in `data/single-byte-indexes.txt`,
x-user-defined, replacement), the BOM sniff, the meta prescan with its
"get an attribute" algorithm, the extraction of a charset from a
Content-Type pragma, and the HTML encoding sniffing algorithm (BOM,
transport charset: certain; prescan of the first 1024 bytes: tentative;
windows-1252). The UTF-8 encoder (lone surrogates to U+FFFD) and UTF-16
helpers are in `Web.Encoding.Utf8`. The multi-byte CJK encodings (GBK,
gb18030, Big5, EUC-JP, ISO-2022-JP, Shift_JIS, EUC-KR) are recognized
but not decoded yet: the parser reads them as windows-1252 and says so
(`UnsupportedEncoding`).

The data files were written once from the standards' tables (the named
references and the single-byte indexes with Python's own copies of
them, patched where WHATWG differs: KOI8-U is KOI8-RU, windows-1255
0xCA, the C1 bytes of the windows-* encodings); nothing is downloaded.

### Text: UTF-8 inside, UTF-16 at the API

The DOM keeps text and attribute values in UTF-8 (`string`). The DOM's
offsets and lengths (`length`, `substringData`, `splitText`, later
ranges and JavaScript's view of strings) are in UTF-16 code units;
`TCharacterData` converts them with `Web.Encoding.Utf8`, and a text node
remembers whether its text is all ASCII (a flag computed on first use),
in which case offsets are the same and no scan is needed. A lone
surrogate set from JavaScript is kept as generalized UTF-8 (WTF-8, the
surrogate's three bytes); the parser never makes one. The tokenizer can
work on bytes because every character HTML's syntax looks at is ASCII:
non-ASCII bytes only ever pass through as data.

### The DOM

`Web.Dom` holds the node classes (they refer to each other, so one unit,
its code spread over `Web.Dom.*.inc` by concern): `TNode`,
`TContainerNode` (documents, fragments, elements: only these have child
links), `TCharacterData` with `TText`, `TCDataSection`, `TComment`,
`TProcessingInstruction`, `TDocumentType`, `TElement`, `TAttr`,
`TDocumentFragment` and `TDocument`; `TNodeList` (live child lists that
remember their position, fixed lists), `THtmlCollection` (live, cached
until the global DOM version moves: `children`, `getElementsByTagName`,
`...TagNameNS`, `...ClassName`, `namedItem`), `TDomTokenList`
(`classList`), `TNamedNodeMap`. `Web.Dom.Exceptions` has DOMException
(`EDomException` with the WebIDL error name and legacy code).

- The mutation algorithms follow the DOM Standard: ensure pre-insertion
  validity, pre-insert, insert (fragments insert their children),
  append, replace, replace all, pre-remove, remove and adopt, and the
  Node, ParentNode and ChildNode methods on them (`insertBefore`,
  `replaceChildren`, `before`, `replaceWith`, ...), with
  HierarchyRequestError and NotFoundError where the standard throws.
  Element and attribute names are checked with the relaxed 2025 rules
  ("valid element local name"), and `createElementNS`/`setAttributeNS`
  use "validate and extract". Live ranges and node iterators are marked
  in the code for the Range work of a later phase.
- Attributes are an array of 16 byte records (value, local name atom,
  namespace id) on the element; `Attr` nodes are made only when asked
  for and keep their identity while the attribute lives. Ids are in a
  per-document map (each id's connected elements, the first in tree
  order found when several share it and kept until they change); class
  names are cached as atoms for selector matching (`HasClass`).
- `TDocumentObserver` is the hook for later phases: it gets exactly the
  tree mutation records MutationObserver queues (`TreeMutated`), the
  children changed steps, each node becoming connected (after the
  insertion, like the insertion steps scripts need) or disconnected,
  attribute and character data changes with old values.
  `TDocument.ElementClassFor` picks the element class (the bindings pick
  an element's interface from a table by local name instead, so all
  elements stay TElement); `LayoutData` and `ScriptWrapper` are slots for
  layout and the bindings; `DefaultView` is the window, the document's
  parent in event paths (but for load events).
- Templates have their contents in a fragment of the document's
  inert "template contents owner" document; cloning copies them and
  adoption moves them, as the HTML Standard says.

Events (`Web.Dom.Events`): `TEventTarget` (no fields of its own; nodes
keep their listeners in the rare data), `TEvent`, `TEventListener`
objects owned by the target's list. Dispatch builds the path through
"get the parent", runs capture listeners from the top down, the
target's capture and then other listeners, and bubble listeners back
up; stopPropagation, stopImmediatePropagation, preventDefault
(cancelable only, not in passive listeners), once, listeners added or
removed during dispatch, and exceptions in listeners (reported, the
others still run) behave as the standard says. Shadow trees,
retargeting and activation behavior come with the later phases; the
event loop too.

### Node size and lifetime

A node object is small: after the VMT, 8 bytes hold its kind, flags,
namespace id and local name atom; then the parent and sibling links,
its document, a layout data slot and a pointer to rare data (script
wrapper, reference counts, listeners, cached lists, Attr objects,
template contents), made only when needed. On x86-64 an element is 88
bytes (96 with the heap's header; the size was chosen to fit that heap
class) and a text node 72 (80). On the test's generated document
(3.4 MB of HTML, 380,000 nodes) the whole document costs about 150
bytes of heap per node, text and attributes included; whitespace-only
texts between tags are shared strings.

Nodes are kept alive by their parent and by references (Retain/Release:
the bindings will hold one per wrapper). A node counts the references
in its whole subtree, so a detached subtree knows at once whether
anything in it is referenced; a referenced detached subtree keeps its
document alive; a document lives while referenced (its creator holds
the first reference) or while anything of it is. Detached unreferenced
subtrees (removed nodes, nodes created and never inserted) are listed
and freed by `CollectGarbage`, which the owner calls between tasks,
never in the middle of an algorithm, so a removed node stays valid
until then; a document frees its listed nodes when it goes. Trees are
freed, cloned, compared and serialized without recursion, so a parsed
tree may be any depth.

### The HTML parser

`Web.Html.*` is the HTML Standard's parsing algorithm, complete:

- The input stream (`Web.Html.InputStream`) keeps decoded text with CR
  and CR LF normalized (also across pieces) and counts the input
  stream preprocessing errors.
- The tokenizer (`Web.Html.Tokenizer`, states in
  `Web.Html.Tokenizer*.inc`) has every state of the standard, with the
  parse errors by their codes. It stops wherever the input runs out and
  carries on with the next piece; lookaheads ("DOCTYPE", "[CDATA[",
  named references) wait until enough input is there. Plain runs of
  text are copied in one move and reach the tree builder as one token.
  The 2231 named character references (`data/named-character-references.txt`)
  are matched longest first by narrowing the sorted names one character
  at a time.
- The tree builder (`Web.Html.TreeBuilder`, modes in
  `Web.Html.TreeBuilder*.inc`) has all 23 insertion modes, the stack of
  open elements with the scope checks, the list of active formatting
  elements with the Noah's Ark clause, the adoption agency algorithm,
  foster parenting, template contents and the template insertion modes,
  foreign content with the SVG and MathML name and attribute adjustments
  and integration points, the document mode from the DOCTYPE
  (`Web.Html.Quirks`), and the fragment case. Parse errors are counted
  (and listed with `CollectErrors`), never fatal.
- `Web.Html.Parser` joins them: bytes in, with sniffing and decoders; a
  meta charset met later while the confidence is tentative switches the
  decoder when everything so far was ASCII and otherwise asks for a
  restart, which `ParseHtmlDocument` does. For scripts (phase 2) the
  parser calls a `TScriptHost` at each script end tag with the insertion
  point set and the script nesting level raised; the host can call
  `DocumentWrite`, which tokenizes the written text at once up to the
  insertion point, and can pause the parser for a parsing-blocking
  script (`Resume` carries on). With scripting off (the default)
  noscript is parsed as markup. `ParseHtmlFragment` is the fragment
  parsing algorithm.
- `Web.Html.Serializer` is the HTML fragment serialization algorithm
  (attribute values escape `<` and `>` too, as since 2025),
  `Web.Html.Markup` innerHTML, outerHTML and insertAdjacentHTML, and
  `Web.Html.TreeDump` the html5lib test format.

Not yet: the 2025 customizable `<select>` parser changes (the classic
"in select" modes are implemented), declarative shadow roots on
`<template shadowrootmode>`, form owners of form-associated elements.

### The event loop

`Web.EventLoop` is a page's event loop (HTML 8.1.7), single threaded:
everything of its documents runs on the thread that drives it.

- Task queues per task source (`Web.EventLoop.Tasks`: user interaction,
  DOM manipulation, networking, navigation, history traversal, timer,
  posted message, rendering). A turn takes the user interaction queue's
  first task if there is one, otherwise the oldest task of all queues,
  then does a microtask checkpoint. A task has a group (its document,
  window or loader); `DiscardTasks` drops a group's tasks when it goes.
- The microtask queue; the JavaScript engine's jobs go in as
  microtasks, and `OnMicrotaskCheckpoint` runs after each emptied queue.
- Delayed tasks (`Web.EventLoop.DelayedTasks`): a binary heap by due
  time and then by the order set; cancelling by handle leaves the slot
  to be skipped, and the heap is compacted when cancelled slots
  outnumber live ones.
- Timers (`Web.EventLoop.Timers`): setTimeout, setInterval and clear*
  for a global, with the standard's timer nesting level: above 5 a
  timeout below 4 ms becomes 4 ms; an interval schedules itself from
  its own task, so it clamps from its sixth run on; a timer cleared
  after its task was queued does nothing. Handlers are `TTimerHandler`
  objects (the bindings will wrap functions and strings).
- `requestAnimationFrame` (`Web.EventLoop.AnimationFrames`): the
  callbacks present when a frame starts run, each followed by a
  microtask checkpoint; ones requested meanwhile wait for the next
  frame, cancelled ones do not run.
- Rendering opportunities: the web view calls `RenderingOpportunity`
  when it can paint; each `TRenderingClient` (a window) runs its frame
  callbacks and then its `OnUpdateRendering` (layout and paint).
  `RequestRendering` asks for a frame (`OnRenderingRequested`).
- Other threads (network completions, image decoders) hand work over
  with `PostTask`, which is locked: tasks wait in an inbox, and
  `OnWake` (called on the posting thread) lets a GUI thread post itself
  a message; `WaitForWork` blocks a dedicated page thread until a task
  comes or a timer is due. The clock can be replaced (tests drive time
  by hand).

`Web.IdMaps` is the id to object hash map they use (the system's
runtime has fgl, not Generics.Collections).

### Fetching

`Web.Fetch.*` is the document side of the Fetch Standard over libhttp,
decided on the page thread:

| Unit | What it is |
|---|---|
| `Web.Fetch.Requests` | `TFetchRequest` (method, URL, fields, body, destination, mode, credentials, redirect and cache modes, referrer and policy, initiator, parser metadata, fetchpriority and the RFC 9218 priority, URL list, tainting) and `TFetchClient` (a document's URL, origin, referrer policy, CSP list, secure context, top-level origin) |
| `Web.Fetch.Responses` | `TFetchResponse`: type (basic, cors, opaque, opaqueredirect, error), status, fields, URL list, MIME type and the sniffed one |
| `Web.Fetch.Fetcher` | main fetch, scheme fetch, HTTP fetch, redirects, sniffing before delivery |
| `Web.Fetch.HttpHops` | one exchange on a libhttp fetch task thread; its head, data and outcome posted back as networking tasks; at most 12 run at once, the others wait (documents, style sheets, scripts and fonts ahead of images); a hop whose thread cannot be made fails like a network error |
| `Web.Fetch.Monitors` | `TFetchMonitor`: told of each fetch's start, response, failure, end or cancel (a network log; webbrowse -n) |
| `Web.Fetch.Jobs` | a fetch in progress and its consumer (`ProcessResponse`, `ProcessBody`, `ProcessEndOfBody`, always in later tasks). The two know each other: a consumer that is freed, even from inside one of its own calls, cancels its running jobs and detaches all of them (nothing more reaches it); a job that is freed tells its consumer (`JobReleased`) so a kept job pointer is cleared; `TFetchJob.Cancel` stops a job without the fetcher at hand |
| `Web.Fetch.NetworkContexts` | a profile's libhttp client (connections, cookies, cache), HSTS store, preflight cache, Accept-Language; shared by its pages |
| `Web.Fetch.MimeTypes` | MIME Sniffing's parser and serializer, Fetch's "extract a MIME type", the type groups |
| `Web.Fetch.Sniffing` | the MIME type sniffing algorithm, the image context, the Apache bug |
| `Web.Fetch.DataUrls` | data: URLs with forgiving-base64 |
| `Web.Fetch.ReferrerPolicy` | the policies, parsing, stripping, "determine request's referrer", potentially trustworthy URLs |
| `Web.Fetch.Cors` | safelisted methods and headers, preflight decisions and checks, the CORS check, exposed headers, the preflight cache |
| `Web.Fetch.MixedContent` | upgrades (images, audio, video; everything under upgrade-insecure-requests) and blocking |
| `Web.Fetch.Hsts` | RFC 6797: the field, known hosts with includeSubDomains, upgrades, saving to text |
| `Web.Fetch.ContentSecurityPolicy` | CSP 3 policies parsed and stored (field, report-only, meta) |
| `Web.Fetch.LocalFiles` | file: URL paths, MIME types by extension, folder index pages |

Main fetch computes the Referer (the request's policy, else the
client's, else strict-origin-when-cross-origin), applies
upgrade-insecure-requests and the mixed content upgrade, HSTS, then
blocks the insecure requests left on a secure page (top-level
navigations excepted). By scheme: about:blank (an empty UTF-8 HTML
document), data:, file: (only from a file: document or the browser
itself, read in 64 KiB pieces, folders as an index page), http and
https. By mode: same-origin requests to another origin fail; no-cors
ones get an opaque response, which the engine still reads inside
(images, style sheets) though scripts never will; cors ones need the
CORS check and, for unsafe methods or headers, a preflight (OPTIONS
with Access-Control-Request-Method/-Headers, the answer checked and
cached per origin, URL and credentials for Access-Control-Max-Age, at
most 7200 s). HTTP fetch adds Accept by destination, Accept-Language,
Origin (CORS requests and other unsafe methods), Sec-Fetch-Dest, -Mode,
-Site and -User on trustworthy URLs, cookies and authentication as the
credentials mode says for that hop, the SameSite context for libhttp's
jar (top-level navigation, same site as the top-level document, user
initiated), and the cache mode. libhttp follows no redirect: each one
is decided here (at most 20, http and https only, no credentials in a
CORS request's location, the CORS check of a redirect and the origin
becoming opaque after a cross-origin one, RFC 9110's method changes, a
Referrer-Policy on the redirect applied) and the new URL goes through
main fetch again. A response's Strict-Transport-Security is taken
(https, domain names only), X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff blocks
scripts and style sheets of the wrong type, the MIME type is extracted,
and when the request asks (navigations, images) the first 1445 bytes
are sniffed before the consumer sees the response - only when sniffing
can change the type (none or unknown, the Apache defaults, images), so
a typed HTML page streams from its first byte. CSP is parsed into the
client's list; only upgrade-insecure-requests acts yet.

### Loading documents and subresources

`Web.Loading.Documents` loads one document (`TDocumentLoader`, a
`TLoadingContext`: the document, window, fetcher, sink, client, base
URL, settings and the load event delay count that every loader shares):

- HTML streams into the parser as it arrives; a transport charset lets
  the parser start after three bytes (otherwise it waits for its 1024
  byte prescan). While the encoding is tentative the bytes are kept; a
  late meta charset that changes what was decoded empties the tree and
  parses the kept bytes again in the new encoding (`Restarts`,
  `OnRestarted`). text/plain and the text-like types become a `<pre>`
  the decoded text is appended to; images an image document.
- The end: readyState interactive (readystatechange), the deferred
  scripts, DOMContentLoaded (bubbling to the window), then, once
  nothing delays the load event and no async or in-order script waits,
  readyState complete, load at the window, pageshow. `Abort` stops it
  all. The DOM's document gained `ReadyState`, `DefaultView` (the window
  is the parent of its events, except load), `TargetElement` (:target)
  and a `BrowsingContext` slot.
- `Web.Loading.Observers` turns tree changes into loads: links, images
  and picture sources, scripts, base (the base URL is the first base
  href, kept current), meta (Content-Security-Policy, referrer,
  refresh), title (title changes are reported once per task).

Subresources, each delaying the load event while it loads:

- Style sheets (`Web.Loading.StyleSheets`): `<link rel=stylesheet>`
  without alternate or disabled, with its media (non-matching sheets
  are still fetched, at a low priority), crossorigin and referrerpolicy.
  The response must be text/css outside quirks mode, is decoded by the
  CSS fallback rules (`Web.Loading.TextDecoding`: BOM, charset,
  @charset, the document's encoding), parsed by libcss, and its @import
  chain loaded (supports() honoured, cycles cut, 16 levels) and hung on
  the rules before the sink gets the sheet; load or error fires at the
  link. Parser-inserted sheets block scripts until loaded.
  `LoadImportsOf` loads the imports of a `<style>` sheet for the style
  side.
- Images (`Web.Loading.Images`, `Web.Loading.Srcset`): srcset with x and
  w descriptors, sizes (media conditions; px, em, rem, vw, vh, vmin,
  vmax), `<picture>` sources by media and type, chosen for the device
  pixel ratio; fetched with image sniffing, decoded by libimage on a
  worker thread (at most 3 at once, the rest waiting; on the page thread
  when no thread can be had) (orientation, sRGB), scaled down there when larger than
  twice the width and height attributes at the pixel ratio (or than
  MaximumImageSide); the natural size is the original's over the chosen
  density. load or error at the element; loading=lazy waits for
  `LoadLazyImage` or the load event. The first six images get the
  urgency of visible ones. SVG files (found by content, libsvg's codec)
  come back as scalable images and are never scaled down; srcset and
  `<picture>` accept image/svg+xml. AVIF is not decoded, and neither
  the Accept header nor the supported types claim it, so pages fall
  back to the formats that are.
- Fonts (`Web.Loading.Fonts`): @font-face src lists (url() and format();
  local() is the sink's), the first supported source fetched in CORS
  mode, the next tried on failure; the bytes go to the sink.
- The favicon (`Web.Loading.Icons`): after parsing, the link rel=icon
  whose sizes fit 16 CSS pixels at the pixel ratio best (else any, else
  the last), or /favicon.ico; decoded and handed to the observer (an
  SVG icon as a scalable image, which the browser's tabs draw again at
  their size).
- Scripts (`Web.Loading.Scripts`): "prepare the script element" without
  running anything - a `TScriptExecutor` (the JavaScript engine) runs
  them; without one scripting is off and noscript parses as markup.
  Classic, module and importmap types, nomodule, external fetches
  (classic ones no-cors or by crossorigin, decoded by charset or the
  document's encoding; modules in CORS mode, UTF-8), and the standard's
  lists: the pending parsing-blocking script (the parser pauses until it
  is fetched and no style sheet blocks scripts), deferred scripts and
  parser-inserted modules after parsing in order, async ones as they
  come, script-inserted ones in order. load and error at the element.
  `FetchScript` is for the executor's module imports.
- `Web.Loading.Preloads`: `<link rel=preload>` and the preload scanner,
  which reads the bytes that arrive while the parser waits for a script
  (link stylesheet and preload, script src, img src and srcset, base)
  and starts their fetches at urgency 6; the real loader claims such a
  fetch (done or still arriving) instead of fetching again.
- Priorities (`Web.Loading.Priorities`): the document 0; render-blocking
  sheets and parser-blocking scripts 1; fonts and other sheets 2;
  visible images and async scripts 3; deferred scripts 4; other images
  and non-matching sheets 5; speculative fetches 6; icons 7;
  fetchpriority moves one step; documents and images are incremental.

The style and layout side gets the results through `TResourceSink`
(`Web.Loading.ResourceSink`): `StyleSheetLoaded` (the sink owns the
sheet, imports in place), `StyleSheetRemoved`, `ImportsLoaded`,
`ImageLoaded` (the sink owns the image; natural size, density, URL),
`ImageFailed`, `ImageRemoved`, `FontLoaded`, `FontFailed`,
`FontFormatSupported` and `MediaEnvironment` (viewport, pixel ratio,
preferences). `TNullResourceSink` drops everything.

### Navigation

`Web.Navigation.Navigables` is a top-level navigable (a tab, a web
view): its active document, window (`Web.Navigation.Windows`: the event
target the bindings will wrap, owner of the timers and frame callbacks)
and session history (`Web.Navigation.SessionHistory`: entries with URL,
title, scroll position, document id and a pushState slot; at most 50).
`Navigate` only scrolls for a fragment change (a new entry of the same
document, :target, hashchange); otherwise it fires beforeunload (asking
the observer when the page wants to stay), fetches the navigation
request (navigate mode, credentials included, sniffed) and makes the
response the new document - HTML, text, an image, a network error page
(`Web.Navigation.ErrorPages`), nothing for 204 and 205, a download for
attachments and types it cannot show - after pagehide and unload of the
old one, whose timers and fetches stop. `Back`, `Forward` and
`Traverse` go between entries (same-document ones without loading:
popstate, hashchange; others load again preferring the cache), `Reload`
revalidates (or bypasses the cache), `Stop` stops, and a meta refresh
navigates after the load, replacing the entry. The first document is
about:blank, replaced by the first navigation. `TNavigableObserver`
tells the browser or web view: `LocationChanged`, `TitleChanged`,
`LoadingStateChanged` (requesting, receiving, interactive, complete),
`DocumentChanged`, `FaviconChanged`, `HistoryChanged`,
`ScrollToFragment`, `RestoreScrollPosition`, `ConfirmUnload`,
`DownloadRequested`, `NavigationFailed`; the web view saves the scroll
position with `SaveScrollPosition` before leaving.

`Web.Navigation.Pages` (`TWebPage`) puts a loop, a fetcher over a shared
`TNetworkContext` and the navigable together for an embedder: set
`OnWake` (called on any thread: post yourself a message) and
`OnRenderingRequested`, call `ProcessPendingWork(BudgetMilliseconds)` on
that message, on a timer after `MillisecondsUntilNextTimer`, or when
idle, and `RenderingOpportunity` when a frame can be painted. `Run`
waits for work itself (programs without a GUI loop).

Not yet: CSP enforcement and Subresource Integrity (both are stored on
the request), ORB, bfcache, pushState/replaceState (the entries have the
slot), `<object>`/`<embed>` documents, form submission, Service
Workers, blob: URLs, animated images (the first frame is shown).

`htmldump [-s] [-e] [-c CHARSET] [-f CONTEXT] FILE` parses a file and
prints its tree in the html5lib format (`-s` the serialization, `-e`
the parse errors, `-c` the transport charset, `-f` a fragment in an
HTML context element).

### Script bindings

`Web.Bindings*` and `Web.Script*` give page scripts the DOM and the
window through libjavascript's embedding API (host classes; plus the
engine's object model for exotic objects and a weak processor of its
heap; libjavascript gained several realms per runtime and built-ins written
in JavaScript for them).

**Tables from WebIDL.** The interfaces are written in WebIDL
(`userland/lib/web/bindings/*.webidl`, close to the standards' text) and
`make-bindings.py` turns them into constant tables at build time
(`Web.Bindings.Tables.inc`: types, arguments, overloads, members,
interfaces, dictionaries, enums, the HTML element interface of each
local name) and, per file, the declarations of the routines its
`Web.Bindings.<File>` unit implements (`Node_appendChild`,
`Node_get_firstChild`, `Event_constructor` ...; mixin members are named
after the mixin and shared). A routine missing on either side does not
