   `PI_FIRMWARE=path`). Then
   ```
   make pi-sd-image                      # SERVER=<PC address> if the guess is wrong
   lsblk                                 # find the card: /dev/sdX or /dev/mmcblkN
   xzcat build/arm64/pi-sd.img.xz | sudo dd of=/dev/sdX bs=4M conv=fsync status=progress
   ```
   Check the device name with `lsblk` before and after inserting the
   card: dd overwrites whatever it is given. Raspberry Pi Imager works
   too ("Choose OS" → "Use custom" → `pi-sd.img.xz`). The image
   (`scripts/make-pi-sd-image.py`, Python and mtools, no root, no
   download) is 257 MiB: an MBR partition table with one bootable FAT32
   partition (type 0Ch, 256 MiB) holding the firmware zip's files as
   they are (`RPI_EFI.fd`, `start4.elf`, `fixup4.dat`, the device trees,
   `overlays/`, `firmware/`, its `config.txt` with `enable_uart=1`),
   `EFI/BOOT/BOOTAA64.EFI`, `FreePascalOS/kernel.elf` (used only if the
   network boot fails) and `FreePascalOS/options.txt` with
   `netboot=http://SERVER:8000/` and `netlog=SERVER`, SERVER being the
   PC's address on its default route when the image was made. The rest
   of a larger card (a 128 GB one, say) stays unused. SDXC cards come
   formatted exFAT, which the Pi's boot ROM cannot read; the image
   brings its own FAT32 partition, so no formatting is needed. Since the
   partition is FAT32, `options.txt` can be edited later on any PC (one
   line or several; the loader joins them). `PI_IMAGE=standalone` makes
   a card that needs no server instead: no `netboot=`, and a second
   (ext4) partition with the system volume.

   By hand instead: unzip the firmware onto a FAT32 partition (MBR,
   type 0Ch), copy `build/arm64/esp/EFI` and `build/arm64/esp/FreePascalOS`
   to it, and write the `netboot=` line into `FreePascalOS/options.txt`.
2. **The server, on your PC.** `make pi-netboot-serve` builds the arm64
   loader, kernel and system image and serves them over HTTP on port
   8000 (no root needed); it prints the PC's addresses and the
   `netboot=` line the card should have. Let TCP port 8000 in through the
   PC's firewall (`sudo ufw allow 8000/tcp`, or `sudo firewall-cmd
   --add-port=8000/tcp`), and UDP 5140 for the log (step 6). Leave it
   running; in another terminal, `make ARCH=arm64 esp served-system-image` after
   each change, then reset the Pi. Options for the Pi's kernel go in a
   file on the PC, `make pi-netboot-serve NETBOOT_OPTIONS=pi-options.txt`
   (read at each boot; if the server has an options file it replaces
   the card's, so repeat `netlog=` there). The Pi gets its address from
   the network's DHCP server; nothing needs changing there. The loader
   prints its steps on the HDMI screen and the serial console: `Network:
   address ...`, `Loading http://.../FreePascalOS/kernel.elf`, `Loading
   .../system.img` with a dot per 8 MiB, `RAM disk: 4773 KiB at ...` (the
   compressed image; the kernel unpacks it).
   TFTP works too (`TFTP=1`, root for port 69, `netboot=tftp://PC/`, the
   PC on the Pi's own network), and so does a PXE or HTTP boot by the
   firmware itself, the card then holding only the firmware (the DHCP
   server must name the PC and `EFI/BOOT/BOOTAA64.EFI`; untested).
3. **Firmware settings.** The firmware's defaults are what the system
   needs (v1.53: ACPI, 3 GB), so normally nothing is set; they live in
   `RPI_EFI.fd` itself and there is no `config.txt` switch for them. To
   check (Esc at the Raspberry Pi logo, Device Manager → Raspberry Pi
   Configuration):
   - Advanced Configuration → System Table Selection: **ACPI** (not
     "Device Tree", not "ACPI + Devicetree");
   - Advanced Configuration → Limit RAM to 3 GB: **enabled** (the
     default; the 1 GiB DMA limits are handled, but leave it);
   - SD/MMC Configuration → uSD/eMMC Routing: **eMMC2** (the default on
     the Pi 4: the SD card on EMMC2, `BRCME88C`);
   - Save (F10), reset, and boot from the SD card (Boot Manager, or let
     it find `\EFI\BOOT\BOOTAA64.EFI`).
4. **The serial console.** A 3.3 V USB serial adapter on the GPIO
   header: ground to pin 6, the adapter's RX to pin 8 (GPIO 14, TXD),
   its TX to pin 10 (GPIO 15, RXD); 115200 baud, 8N1. Leave
   `enable_uart=1` in `config.txt`. The firmware's SPCR names whichever
   UART is on those pins - the PL011 with the `dtoverlay=miniuart-bt`
   the firmware's `config.txt` comes with, otherwise the mini UART - and
   the kernel drives either.
5. **What to look for** in the log:
   - the loader's network lines (step 2), then `[ramdisk] xz image:
     compressed 4.7 MiB -> 64.0 MiB in ... ms`, `[ramdisk] ramdisk0: 65536
     KiB image at physical ...`, `[fs] ramdisk0p1: ext4 "FPOSROOT"`
     and `[init] System volume: /ramdisk0p1`;
   - `[acpi] N platform devices`, and `devices` in the debug shell: the
     `BRCME88C`, `BCM2849`, `PNP0D10` and `BCM6E4E` devices with their
     memory, GSIs, "not coherent" and `dma ... at bus C0000000` (if the
     tables have `_DMA`);
   - `[mailbox] VideoCore mailbox, ...firmware revision ...` and the
     `[board] Raspberry Pi 4 Model B rev 1.x, ... MiB` lines (`board` in
     the shell gives clocks and temperature again);
   - `[sdhci] diskN: SDHC card "...", ... on \_SB_....SDC3 (ACPI
     BRCME88C) ..., ADMA2, 4-bit high speed at 50 MHz, interrupts,
     non-coherent DMA`, then the card's partitions and `[fs] ... fat32
     ... mounted` (the ESP itself; `ls` and `cat` in the shell);
   - `[xhci] Controller \_SB_....XHC0 (ACPI PNP0D10), N ports,
     interrupts, non-coherent DMA` and `[usb] Port N: device ...` for a
     USB keyboard (typing in the shell then works on the HDMI screen);
   - `[genet] ...` and `[net] eth0: Broadcom GENET v5, address
     DC:A6:32:..., ... interrupts by line`, then a link line when a
     cable is in.
   - Problems to report: a missing line above, `the card did not come
     up` (with the step), a panic, or nothing after `kernel starting`.
6. **Without a serial adapter: the log over the network.** The log
   also appears on the HDMI screen (the framebuffer console), but it
   scrolls away, and a panic later on is lost. The kernel can send every
   line to your PC instead (see "Diagnostics over the network"):
   - connect the Pi's Ethernet port to the network your PC is on;
   - find your PC's IPv4 address (`ip -4 addr` on Linux, `ipconfig` on
     Windows), say 192.168.1.20, let UDP port 5140 in through its
     firewall (`sudo ufw allow 5140/udp`, or `sudo firewall-cmd
     --add-port=5140/udp`), and run the listener from this repository:
     `scripts/netlog.py --output pi.log` (Python 3, nothing else);
   - add `netlog=192.168.1.20` to `FreePascalOS/options.txt` on the SD
     card, on the one line with the other options, for example
     `kshell netlog=192.168.1.20 netshell=2323`.

   The Pi needs an address of its own first: from the network service
   by DHCP once user mode is up, otherwise from the kernel's own DHCP
   client 30 seconds after networking started (`netdhcp=SECONDS`), or a
   fixed one, `netaddr=192.168.1.50/24,192.168.1.1`. Then netlog.py shows
   the whole log from the first line (it was kept in memory until then)
   and every line after it, each with the Pi's address, its number and
   the uptime; `REBOOT` when the numbers start again, `GAP` where lines
   were lost. A panic is sent too. If nothing arrives: look on the
   screen for the `[netlog]` and `[netaddr]` lines and `[net] eth0: ...
   link up`; try `netlog=broadcast` (no address of your PC needed, but
   the Pi still needs one of its own); check the firewall.

   With `netshell=2323` the kernel debug shell answers on TCP port 2323:
   `nc 192.168.1.50 2323` (the Pi's address is in the `configured` or
   `kernel DHCP lease` line of the log). It has **no authentication**:
   anyone on the network can read files and reset the board, so only on
   a network you trust. It serves one connection at a time; one quiet
   for ten minutes is closed, a peer that vanished is found by
   keep-alives (after a minute, then every 10 s, six times), and one
   that stops reading is dropped after a minute.
7. **Getting back without touching the board.** The PM watchdog is armed
   at start-up (15 seconds, the most it can count; `[watchdog] BCM2835
   PM watchdog ... armed`) and petted by a kernel timer, so a kernel that
   hangs resets the board. After a panic the message is shown and sent,
   and the watchdog, no longer petted, resets the board about 15 seconds
   later; `panicreset=SECONDS` resets after that many seconds instead
   (through PSCI), `panicreset=0` keeps the panic on the screen, and
   `watchdog=0` does not arm the watchdog at all. `reboot` (the debug
   shell, or user mode) resets through PSCI SYSTEM_RESET; `poweroff`
   halts the board until its power is cycled, so prefer `reboot` from
   afar. A board that panics at every boot restarts again and again
   (netlog.py says `REBOOT` each time); changing the options then needs
   the SD card, or a network boot.
8. **Iterating, and getting out of trouble.** A rebuild on the PC is
   picked up at the next reset: `reboot` in the debug shell (`netshell=`)
   or user mode, the watchdog after a hang or a panic, or the power. The
   system runs from the RAM disk, so whatever it writes (logs, settings,
   passwords) is gone at the next boot, and a broken system image cannot
   damage the card. Without the server (or the network) the loader says
   `no network for the network boot, using the boot volume` and boots
   the card's own kernel, which then has no system volume and stops
   after its self tests (`kshell` for the debug shell); with the server
   but no system image (`netboot-serve.py --no-system-image`) the kernel
   looks for one on its disks. Kernel options are changed in the
   server's options file without touching the card; the card's
   `options.txt` (any PC, FAT32) is needed only to change the server's
   address. To update the loader itself, copy a new `BOOTAA64.EFI` to
   the card, or flash a new image. Things to watch on the first boots:
   the firmware's network stack needs its random number generator (on
   the Pi it has one); the loader switches the firmware's IPv4 setting
   for the Ethernet port to DHCP and the firmware keeps that; with no
   address after 30 seconds (cable, DHCP server) the loader falls back
   to the card.

### Trying it on a Raspberry Pi 5

The Pi 5 boots differently from the Pi 4, so the Pi 4 section above
(UEFI firmware, the loader, ACPI) stays for Pi 4 owners only. There is
no UEFI port to use here. The Pi 5's own EEPROM bootloader loads the
native kernel `fpos.img` (Linux arm64 Image format) and the system image
as its RAM disk, and starts it with the firmware's device tree
(`bcm2712-rpi-5-b.dtb`, edited by the firmware: memory, the command
line, the RAM disk's place, the framebuffer). There is no ACPI. The
bootloader in the EEPROM includes the GPU firmware, so the card needs no
`start*.elf`, `fixup*.dat`, `bootcode.bin` or armstub.

The plan has three steps: (1) an SD card that boots on its own, to see
the HDMI log; (2) once, an EEPROM configuration that tries the network
(TFTP from your PC) before the card; (3) after that, a rebuild and a
reset is all an iteration takes, and the card is only the fallback.

**Downloads** (into `~/Downloads/pi5/`; the scripts name what is
missing; nothing of this goes into the repository):

- `~/Downloads/pi5/boot/`: `bcm2712-rpi-5-b.dtb` and
  `bcm2712d0-rpi-5-b.dtb` from
  https://github.com/raspberrypi/firmware/tree/master/boot (raw:
  `https://github.com/raspberrypi/firmware/raw/master/boot/<name>`).
  Both go on the card, for the C1 and D0 steppings (8 GB boards come
  with either); the firmware chooses.
- `~/Downloads/pi5/boot/overlays/vc4-kms-v3d-pi5.dtbo` from
  https://github.com/raspberrypi/firmware/raw/master/boot/overlays/vc4-kms-v3d-pi5.dtbo,
  for the HDMI framebuffer (see below). Whatever is in `overlays/` goes on
  the card.
- `~/Downloads/pi5/eeprom/`: the newest `pieeprom-YYYY-MM-DD.bin` and
  `recovery.bin` from
  https://github.com/raspberrypi/rpi-eeprom/tree/master/firmware-2712/default
  (the stable channel; `latest/` is newer and less tested). Needed for
  step 2 only.

`PI5_FIRMWARE=dir` and `PI5_EEPROM=dir` name other directories.

**The HDMI framebuffer.** HDMI is the only screen, so the kernel needs
the framebuffer the firmware sets up. The firmware describes it with a
`simple-framebuffer` node (`reg`, `width`, `height`, `stride`, `format`)
that it adds to the device tree it passes on. Linux on a Pi 5 reports
one at `3f800000` (`simple-framebuffer 3f800000.framebuffer`). It adds
that node when the KMS overlay `vc4-kms-v3d-pi5` is loaded: the overlay
disables the old `bcm2708-fb` node (`/soc@107c000000/fb`) and enables
the `vc4` display nodes. The firmware then leaves a simple framebuffer
for the kernel to show its console on until a KMS driver takes over.
FreePascalOS has no vc4 driver, so that framebuffer stays. Without the
overlay the `bcm2708-fb` node stays enabled and the firmware may add no
`simple-framebuffer` node at all (Linux would then ask the firmware for a
framebuffer through the mailbox). `config.txt` therefore loads the
overlay when it was downloaded, and the script warns when it is missing.
The other settings:

- `hdmi_force_hotplug=1`: use HDMI even if the hotplug signal is not
  seen;
- `disable_overscan=1`: no black border;
- `disable_fw_kms_setup=1`: no `video=` options appended to the command
  line (the Pi 5's default anyway);
- `framebuffer_depth=32` and `framebuffer_ignore_alpha=1`: 32-bit pixels.
  The firmware's default is 16 (`r5g6b5`, as in the Linux log above).
  These are legacy options that the KMS firmware may ignore, so the
  kernel takes whatever `format` the node names (`r5g6b5`, `x8r8g8b8`,
  `a8r8g8b8`);
- `max_framebuffers` is left alone: one display, on the HDMI port next to
  the USB-C power socket (HDMI0).

The rest of `config.txt`: `arm_64bit=1`, `kernel=fpos.img`, `initramfs
system.img followkernel` (the RAM disk right after the kernel, its place
in `/chosen` as `linux,initrd-start`/`-end`; `system.img` is the
xz-compressed system image, which the firmware passes on as it is and
the kernel unpacks, see "A compressed RAM disk"), `os_check=0` (otherwise
the Pi 5 firmware checks for a device tree compatible with the kernel
before booting, meant for Raspberry Pi OS kernels), and
`enable_rp1_uart=1`. That last one sets up RP1's UART0 at 115200 on GPIO
14/15 (header pins 8 and 10) and leaves RP1, the south bridge with the
Ethernet, USB and UARTs, as the bootloader set it up instead of
resetting its PCIe link. This helps a serial adapter later, and early
RP1 drivers.

`cmdline.txt` holds the kernel options in the format of `options.txt`:
`netlog=SERVER` and whatever `PI5_OPTIONS="..."` adds (for example
`PI5_OPTIONS="kshell netshell=2323"`). The firmware merges in options of
its own (`reboot=w coherent_pool=1M ...` from the device tree's
`bootargs`), which the kernel ignores.

1. **The SD card (plain SD boot, no EEPROM change).**
   ```
   make pi5-sd-image                     # SERVER=<PC address> if the guess is wrong
   lsblk                                 # find the card: /dev/sdX or /dev/mmcblkN
   xzcat build/arm64/pi5-sd.img.xz | sudo dd of=/dev/sdX bs=4M conv=fsync status=progress
   ```
   It builds `build/arm64/native/fpos.img`, the native kernel (`make
   ARCH=arm64 native`, see "Native boot (device tree)"), and the system
   image, compressed (`system-disk.img.xz`, copied as `system.img`). The
   image
   (`scripts/make-pi5-sd-image.py`, Python and mtools, no root) is
   257 MiB: an MBR with one bootable FAT32 partition (type 0Ch, 256 MiB)
   holding `config.txt`, `cmdline.txt`, the two device trees,
   `overlays/`, `fpos.img` and `system.img`. A Pi 5 with its factory
   EEPROM settings (`BOOT_ORDER=0xf461`: SD, NVMe, USB) boots it as it
   is. The bootloader's own screen (its version, the board, `boot: mode
   SD ...`) shows on HDMI first, then the kernel's log. Raspberry Pi
   Imager works too ("Use custom"). Since the partition is FAT32,
   `cmdline.txt` can be edited on any PC.
2. **The EEPROM, once: network first.**
   ```
   make pi5-eeprom-image                 # SERVER=<PC address>
   xzcat build/arm64/pi5-eeprom.img.xz | sudo dd of=/dev/sdX bs=4M conv=fsync status=progress
   ```
   This is a bootloader recovery card (`scripts/make-pi5-eeprom-image.py`):
   `recovery.bin`, `pieeprom.bin` (the downloaded release with its
   configuration replaced) and `pieeprom.sig` (its SHA-256, `ts:` and
   `target-soc: 2712`). The configuration lives inside the EEPROM image
   as a file, `bootconf.txt` (see `scripts/pi5_eeprom_image.py` for the
   format), which the script replaces without the `rpi-eeprom-config`
   tool or Raspberry Pi OS:
   ```
   [all]
   BOOT_UART=1
   BOOT_ORDER=0xf12            network, then SD, then start again
   TFTP_IP=<SERVER>            the TFTP server, whatever DHCP says
   DHCP_TIMEOUT=15000          15 s without an address: on to the card
   TFTP_FILE_TIMEOUT=60000     the longest one file may take (the
                               compressed system image, 4.9 MB, takes
                               about 21 s at the bootloader's 230 KB/s)
   NET_INSTALL_AT_POWER_ON=0   no network install screen at power on
   ```
   (`make-pi5-eeprom-image.py --client-ip A.B.C.D --subnet MASK` sets a
   fixed address instead of DHCP, `--gateway` too if the PC is on
   another network; `--sd-first` makes it `0xf21`.) Put the card in the
   Pi 5 and power it on. The boot ROM runs `recovery.bin`, which writes
   the EEPROM. When the green LED blinks rapidly without end and an
   HDMI screen turns green, it is done (red, or another blink pattern,
   is a failure). Power off, then flash the card again with
   `pi5-sd-image` as the fallback for when the PC does not answer. To
   undo, the factory settings come back with Raspberry Pi Imager's "Misc
   utility images > Bootloader > SD Card Boot". The Pi 5's address comes
   from the network's DHCP server as usual: a home router needs no
   change, because `TFTP_IP` names the server.
3. **The server, on your PC.**
   ```
   sudo sysctl net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start=69   # once per PC boot
   make pi5-netboot-serve
   ```
   This writes `build/arm64/pi5-boot/` (the card's files; `fpos.img`
   and `system.img` as links into the build, `system.img` to the
   compressed `system-disk.img.xz`; `SYSTEM_IMAGE_COMPRESSION=none` links
   the plain image, which takes too long over TFTP) and serves it with
   `scripts/netboot-serve.py --pi5`: TFTP on UDP port 69 (the Pi's
   bootloader has no other port) and HTTP on 8000, for checking with
   curl. It prints the files, their sizes, `cmdline.txt` and the PC's
   address. Port 69 is below 1024, so it needs one of: the `sysctl` above
   (lets anyone bind ports from 69 up, until the next reboot); running
   the server with `sudo`; or `sudo setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep` on
   the Python binary (`readlink -f $(which python3)`, which then lets
   every Python program do it). Let UDP 69 and 5140 in through the
   firewall (`sudo ufw allow 69/udp`, or `sudo firewall-cmd
   --add-service=tftp`). The bootloader first asks for
   `<serial>/config.txt` (`TFTP_PREFIX=0`, the default) and keeps the
   prefix for every file if that is found. The server answers files with
   or without such a directory, so no per-board directory is needed. Each
   request is logged (`TFTP 192.168.1.50 2c3a1b0f/fpos.img: 3.1 MiB in
   0.4 s`).
4. **The log.** On the HDMI screen: the bootloader's diagnostics (`boot:
   mode NETWORK 2 order f12 ...`), then the kernel's console. Over the
   network: `scripts/netlog.py --output pi5.log` on the PC (UDP 5140),
   with `netlog=SERVER` in `cmdline.txt`, as on the Pi 4 (step 6 of the
   Pi 4 section). The kernel drives the Pi 5's Ethernet (behind pcie2
   and RP1; see "What the Pi 5 drivers log" below for the lines to look
   for on the screen until netlog works); the debug shell answers on
   `netshell=2323` once there is an address.
5. **Iterating.** Leave `make pi5-netboot-serve` running. After a change,
   rebuild the native kernel and/or `make ARCH=arm64 system-disk`, then
   reset the Pi (power, or `reboot`, or the watchdog). The files are read
   at each request, so the next boot takes the new build. Kernel options
   change in `build/arm64/pi5-boot/cmdline.txt` (rewritten by the next
   `make pi5-netboot-serve`; make it stick with `PI5_OPTIONS=`). Without
   the server, the bootloader gives up on the network after the DHCP or
   TFTP timeout and boots the card. With no card either, it shows its
   diagnostics screen and tries again.

### What the Pi 5 drivers log

Without a serial adapter the HDMI console is the only witness until
Ethernet works, so every driver on the way says what it found and, when
something fails, `FAILED at` the step with the registers that tell why.
The lines appear in this order; a photo of the screen after the
`[pci]` lines and another after `[net]` cover them. All of these drivers
are written from Linux's and **untested on the board**.

1. **The PCIe root complex** (`Drivers.BrcmPcie`, pcie2 where RP1 is;
   pcie1, the external connector, only if `dtparam=pciex1` enabled it):
   ```
   [pcie] pcie@1000120000: rev 0x304, status 0xb0: the firmware left the link up
   [pcie] pcie@1000120000: link kept from firmware, gen 2 x4, segment 2
   [pcie] pcie@1000120000: 01:00.0 1de4:0001 rev 02 class 0200
   [pcie] pcie@1000120000: 01:00.0 BAR1 4 MiB bus 0x0 = 0x1f00000000
   [pcie] pcie@1000120000: 01:00.0 BAR2 64 KiB bus 0x400000 = 0x1f00400000
   [pcie] pcie@1000120000: 01:00.0 BAR0 16 KiB bus 0x410000 = 0x1f00410000
   [mip] msi-controller@1000130000: 64 vectors on SPIs 128-191, doorbell 0xfffffff000 (bus), registers 0x1000130000
   [pci] 01:00.0 1de4:0001 network controller
   ```
   The watchdog comes first now (`[watchdog] BCM2712 PM watchdog at
   ...` and `... armed for 15 s ...`, item 6): it is armed before any
   bus is brought up, and while the root complexes are probed the
   kernel timer stops petting it (only the probe pets it, between
   steps), so a bring-up that stalls the bus resets the board within
   15 s instead of freezing it. SErrors are unmasked during the probe:
   an asynchronous abort shows the panic screen (`SError (asynchronous
   abort)` with ESR) instead of staying pending.

   The status word: bit 4 PHY link up, bit 5 data link up, bit 7 root
   complex mode (B0h = all three). With `pciex4_reset=0` in config.txt
   (the config.txt that make-pi5-sd-image.py writes has it) the firmware
   leaves the link to RP1 up and it is kept, as above. With the kernel
   option `pcireset`, or a link found down, it starts from cold and says
   `link down, starting it` (or `the firmware left the bridge in reset:
   starting it from cold` if the bridge's reset line is asserted, in
   which case not a register of the root complex is read before the
   reset sequence), then `link up, gen 2 x4`. A `(was 0x...)` after a
   BAR means the firmware had put it elsewhere.

   The cold sequence (`Drivers.BrcmPcie.Setup`, after Linux's
   pcie-brcmstb.c for the 7712 generation) drives the resets through
   the tree's reset controllers (`Drivers.BrcmResets`): the "bridge"
   line of `brcm,brcmstb-reset` (pcie2: line 44 of
   reset-controller@1504318), "swinit" if named, and the
   `brcm,bcm7216-pcie-sata-rescal` calibration. While the bridge line is
   asserted nothing of the root complex is touched: on this generation
   its registers do not answer then and an access stalls the processor
   (that is what froze the first cold boot, which wrote PERST# in
   PCIE_CTRL during the bridge reset). PERST# is PCIE_CTRL's PERSTB bit
   (bit 2, 0 = held). The pcie nodes name no clock, PERST# GPIO or
   supply; if a tree did, a line says it is left as the firmware set it.

   A failure is two lines and then the boot goes on without the host
   (no RP1: no USB, Ethernet or RP1 peripherals):
   ```
   [pcie] pcie@1000120000: FAILED at step 6 (link): no link 200 ms after PERST# was released
   [pcie] pcie@1000120000:   status 0x1e080 (PHY link 0, data link 0, RC mode 1), ctrl 0x4, debug 0x00200000, misc 0x00303480, rev 0x500; bridge reset line 44 deasserted
   [pcie] pcie@1000120000: left down: no devices behind it (for pcie2: no RP1, so no USB, Ethernet or RP1 peripherals)
   ```
   `ctrl` is PCIE_CTRL (bit 2 PERST# released), `debug` HARD_DEBUG (bit
   27 SerDes still in IDDQ), `misc` MISC_CTRL. When the bridge is in
   reset the second line says `registers not read (the bridge is in
   reset)` instead. The steps:
   - `step 1 (resources)`: a reset line the node names cannot be driven
     (a preceding `reset line "bridge": ...` line says why);
   - `step 2 (bridge out of reset, SerDes calibration)`: the rescal
     calibration did not finish within 1 ms (`rescal status 0x...`);
   - `step 3 (bridge reset)`: the bridge line does not deassert, or the
     root complex reads 0 or all ones after its reset;
   - `step 4 (windows)`: the tree's `dma-ranges` are missing, or the
     controller is strapped as an endpoint (status bit 7 clear);
   - `step 5 (SerDes and bus tuning)`: the SerDes MDIO bus did not take
     its 54 MHz clock settings within 200 us;
   - `step 6 (link)`: RP1 did not train within 200 ms;
   - `the link is up but nothing answers at 01:00.0, read 0xffffffff`.
2. **RP1** (`Drivers.Rp1`, `Drivers.Rp1Interrupts`):
   ```
   [rp1] RP1 at 2:01:00.0 rev 02
   [rp1] BAR1 4 MiB at 0x1f00000000 (bus 0x0), BAR2 64 KiB at 0x1f00400000
   [rp1] chip id 0x20001927, platform 0x2 (RP1 C0)
   [rp1] MSI-X on: 61 vectors, table in BAR0 at 0x1f00410000
   [rp1] 30 peripherals; window 0xc040000000 = bus 0x0
   ```
   `not found on the PCI buses` means pcie2 failed above; `BAR1 too
   small` that RP1's own firmware is not running; `SYSINFO reads all
   ones` that BAR1 does not reach RP1 (window or BAR wrong); `NOT where
   BAR1 is: offsets used` that the tree's `rp1` ranges and the BARs
   disagree (the BARs win). Each peripheral interrupt connected later
   adds `[rp1] interrupt 6 (/axi/pcie@1000120000/rp1/ethernet@100000):
   MSI-X data 0x0 to 0xfffffff000, level, cfg 0x9` and the routing's
   `[interrupts] GSI 160 on vector 0x3., processor N` (MIP vector N is
   SPI 128 + N, INTID 160 + N); `cfg` is RP1's MSIX_CFG (bit 0 enabled,
   bit 3 level).
3. **Ethernet** (`Drivers.CadenceGem`):
   ```
   [gem] ethernet@100000: id 0x0007...., dcfg1 0x........, dcfg6 0x........, 4 queues, non-coherent DMA
   [gem] ethernet@100000: PHY 0x600d84a2 at 1 (BCM54213PE), rgmii-id, address 2C:CF:67:..:..:..
   [net] eth0: Cadence GEM (RP1), address 2C:CF:67:..:..:.., link down, interrupts by RP1 MSI-X
   [net] eth0 (Cadence GEM (RP1)): link up, 1000 Mbit/s full duplex
   [netaddr] eth0: kernel DHCP lease 192.168.1.50/24 via 192.168.1.1 from 192.168.1.1
   ```
   (the DHCP line 30 seconds after networking started, `netdhcp=`).
   Failures: `identification: not a GEM (all ones: RP1 unreachable)`,
   `design: no 64-bit DMA`, `address: no usable Ethernet address`, `PHY
   search: no PHY answers on MDIO (held in reset by RP1 GPIO 32?)`, the
   PHY steps `reset write`, `reset wait`, `autonegotiation start` with
   the PHY's control and status words (high and low 16 bits). If the
   link is up and nothing arrives for 10 s, one line `link up 10 s,
   nothing received: rx 0 tx N fcs F nobuf B ovr O rsr .. tsr .. ncr ..
   cfg .. imr .. bus errors E`: `rx` 0 with `fcs` counting means the
   RGMII delays are wrong; `nobuf` counting means the receive ring is
   not being given back; `bus errors` means the GEM's DMA cannot reach
   RAM (inbound windows); `tx` 0 means transmission never started.
   `gemdebug` logs that line every 10 s. With no card at all the kernel
   DHCP says once: `[netaddr] no network card: no kernel DHCP (netlog,
   netshell) until one appears`.
4. **USB** (`Drivers.Dwc3`, then `Drivers.Xhci`), twice:
   ```
   [dwc3] usb@200000: GSNPSID 0x5533....., design mode 2 (0 device, 1 host, 2 dual), GCTL 0x........
   [xhci] Controller /axi/pcie@1000120000/rp1/usb@200000 (DT snps,dwc3), 2 ports, interrupts, non-coherent DMA
   ```
   Failures: `FAILED at identification (GSNPSID; all ones: RP1
   unreachable)`, `core soft reset (DCTL still resetting after
   100 ms)`; then the xHCI driver's own lines.
5. **The SD card** (`Drivers.Sdhci.Bcm2712`, then `Drivers.Sdhci`):
   ```
   [sdhci] /soc@107c000000/mmc@fff000: BCM2712 cfg: pin select 0x. -> SD, ctrl 0x........ -> card forced present; tree clock 200 MHz
   [sdhci] /axi/mmc@1100000: an SDIO device (Wi-Fi) below it, not an SD slot: left alone
   [sdhci] diskN: SDHC card "...", ... (DT brcm,bcm2712-sdhci) ..., ADMA2, 4-bit high speed at 50 MHz, ...
   ```
   The card runs at 3.3 V high speed; UHS modes are not used.
6. **The watchdog**: `[watchdog] BCM2712 PM watchdog at 107D200000
   (brcm,bcm2712-pm), up to 15 s; reset status ...`, armed by default
   as on the Pi 4 (`watchdog=0` leaves it off); `reboot` resets through
   PSCI.
7. **The VideoCore mailbox** (`brcm,bcm2835-mbox`), before the storage
   drivers:
   ```
   [mailbox] VideoCore mailbox, message at bus address 0000.000, firmware revision ........
   [board] Raspberry Pi 5 rev 1.0, ...
   ```
   The message's bus address is its physical address (below 1 GiB). `the
   firmware does not answer: mailbox not used` means the firmware wants
   another address; HDMI audio then stops at its step 2.
8. **HDMI audio** (`Drivers.Bcm2712Dma`, `Drivers.HdmiAudio`; see "HDMI
   audio (Raspberry Pi 5)"), after the mailbox, for a display on HDMI0:
   ```
   [dma] dma@10000: BCM2712 DMA at 0x1000010000, channels 0,1,2,3,4,5 free (40-bit: none), enable 0x........, not coherent
   [dma] dma@10600: BCM2712 DMA at 0x1000010000, channels 6,7,8,9,10 free (40-bit: 6,7,8,9,10), enable 0x........, not coherent
   [hdmi-audio] hdmi0: clocks: HDMI state machine ... Hz, pixel BVB ... Hz, firmware pixel clock ... Hz (from the firmware); audio 108000000 Hz (from the tree)
   [hdmi-audio] hdmi0: display connected, 1920x1080 (2200x1125 total) at 60.000 Hz (measured), 24-bit colour, pixel clock 148.5 MHz (148500... Hz from the timing and frame rate), audio on
   [hdmi-audio] hdmi0: N 6144 CTS 148500 for 48000 Hz (the HDMI table's, TMDS clock 148500000 Hz)
   [hdmi-audio] hdmi0: MAI sample clock 2250/1 of 108000000 Hz, C1 thresholds, audio InfoFrame sent; MAI_CTL 0x... MAI_THR 0x101C1C?? ...
   [dma] dma@10600 channel 6: cyclic, 48 periods of 8192 bytes from 0x... to 0x107C72001C, DREQ 10, CS 0x00FA0301
   [hdmi-audio] hdmi0: DMA moving: 4800 frames in 100 ms = 48000 Hz (48000 expected), MAI_CTL 0x........
   [audio] /dev/audio: HDMI (hdmi0), 2 channels, 48000 Hz, volume by the mixer
   [hdmi-audio] hdmi1: clocks: ...
   [hdmi-audio] hdmi1: no display connected (HOTPLUG 0x...): no audio on this port
   ```
   (hdmi1 may instead say `held in reset (DVP SW_INIT 0x...)`.) Then
   each sound adds `[hdmi-audio] hdmi0: playing from slot N, DMA in slot
   M, MAI_CTL 0x...` and, half a second after it ends, `stopped after N
   periods in all, MAI_CTL 0x...`. A failure is one line, `[hdmi-audio]
   hdmi0: FAILED at step N (name): ...` with the registers that tell
   why, and the port registers no output:
   - `step 1 (resources)`: a register block missing from `reg-names`;
     `no "dmas" in the tree` is the overlay's `noaudio` (not a failure);
   - `step 2 (clocks)`: no mailbox, or the state machine clock reads 0
     (`hdmiaudio=force` goes on regardless), or no rate for "audio";
   - `step 5 (link)`: the firmware drives the display as DVI;
   - `step 6 (mode)`: the timing registers hold no mode; `(ASSUMED: the
     frame counter did not move)` in the mode line is not a failure but
     means 60 Hz was taken;
   - `step 7 (N and CTS)`, `step 9 (MAI)`: no values for the clocks;
   - `step 8 (DMA)`: no channel, memory or bus address (`[dma] hdmi0:
     FAILED at channel request: ...`);
   - `step 10 (DMA moving)`: the DMA did not move at the sample rate;
     the line has the channel's CS, CB, DEBUG, TI, SRC, DEST, LEN and the
     controller's enable register, then the MAI's and the core's
     registers. CS bit 0 clear: the channel stopped (bit 10 error, then
     DEBUG bits 0-3 say which); CS bit 3 (DREQ) never set with SRC at the
     first block: the MAI asks for nothing (MAI_CTL bit 3 enable, bits
     1-2 FIFO errors).
   `InfoFrame NOT sending` in the MAI line means packet 4 never started
   (the packet RAM's status); audio may still play.

   **Testing it.** Boot with a TV or monitor with speakers on HDMI0
   (the port next to the USB-C socket), then over SSH:
   ```
   mixer -l                  # /dev/audio is listed as HDMI
   tone 440 2                # two seconds of 440 Hz
   tone -r 44100 1000 1      # a 44.1 kHz stream (the mixer converts it)
   tone -o /tmp/a.wav 660 2 && play /tmp/a.wav && soundinfo /tmp/a.wav
   mixer 30; tone 440 1      # quieter (the mixer scales the samples)
   ```
   and send the `[dma]`, `[mailbox]` and `[hdmi-audio]` lines and the
   `[audio] /dev/audio` line from netlog (`grep -E
   'dma|mailbox|hdmi-audio|audio\]' pi5.log`), with what was heard
   (nothing, clicks, the tone, the tone at the wrong pitch).

The kernel debug shell's `devices` lists RP1's peripherals with their
memory (`mem 1f00100000+4000`) and RP1 interrupts (`line 6 level`), and
the driver that took each.

Why TFTP and not HTTP: the Pi 5 bootloader's HTTP boot (`BOOT_ORDER`
mode 7, `HTTP_HOST`, `HTTP_PATH`) fetches `boot.img`, a FAT image of the
boot files, and `boot.sig`. Every HTTP download must be signed: with a
custom `HTTP_HOST` that means an RSA-2048 key of our own written into
the EEPROM (`rpi-eeprom-config -p`), and the key is lost again with the
next official EEPROM update. TFTP needs no signature.

## Heap checking

Freed memory that keeps its old contents hides bugs: an object used after
it was freed goes on working until its memory is reused, often far from the
cause, and a test that repeats the same steps in another program may pass
by luck. Heap checking (in the spirit of the Windows debug heap, glibc's
`MALLOC_PERTURB_`, Linux's `slub_debug` and `init_on_free`, macOS's
`MallocScribble` and OpenBSD's junking and delayed reuse) makes such bugs
show where they happen, in the kernel heap and in every program's heap.
`make test` boots every test machine with it.

**Switching it on.** The kernel option `heapchecks` (or `heapchecks=all`)
turns on everything, `heapchecks=fill` only the fill patterns, guards and
double free detection (no quarantine), `heapchecks=off` nothing. The kernel
heap reads it before its first allocation. User programs take the
environment variable `HEAP_CHECKS` (same values; `1` also means all) and,
when it is not set, the kernel option - the environment does not reach
every program (login starts sessions with a fresh environment), the option
does. So one option checks the kernel and every program, and
`HEAP_CHECKS=off program` (or `HEAP_CHECKS=all program` on a system booted
without the option) changes it for one program. The level is decided before
anything is allocated (right after `InitHeap` in System's initialization,
reading the environment in place and the options into a stack buffer), so
every block of a program carries the checking header, and no block from
before the checks can be taken for a bad one.

**The page heap** (`HEAP_CHECKS=pages`, user programs only, from the
environment only: `rtl/fpc/syspageheap.inc`) puts every block on pages
of its own: a reservation (`CallReserveMemory`) of the pages for a
16-byte header and the block, committed read-write, and one more page
left reserved after them. The block ends where its last page does (after
rounding to the heap's 16-byte alignment; those few bytes hold `$FD` and
are checked when the block is freed), so a read or write past the end
touches the reserved page and faults at once, at the instruction that
did it and the byte it touched: `EAccessViolation` with the program's
own back trace, not a report much later. A freed block's pages are
decommitted at once, so a use after free faults the same way, and its
reservation waits among the 1024 most recently freed before it is
released, so its addresses are not reused soon. A double free or a stray
pointer finds no committed header (`CallQueryMemory`) and is reported
like the checking heap's mistakes. `ReAllocMem` always moves. Every
block costs two pages of address space, a page of memory and a few
system calls: it is for finding a bug. `heaptest --pages` and
`--overrun-page` check it (coretest).

**Patterns** (the same in the kernel and in user mode; each repeated over
eight bytes is a non-canonical address, so a pointer read from such memory
faults when it is followed):

| Byte  | Where | Catches |
|-------|-------|---------|
| `$A5` | new blocks (`GetMem`, `New`, the part `ReAllocMem` adds, `AllocateKernelMemory`) | reads of memory that was never set |
| `$DF` | freed blocks | use after free: a method call through a freed object reads the method table `$DFDFDFDFDFDFDFDF` and faults at once |
| `$FD` | the guard after the requested bytes | writes past the end, found when the block is freed |

`AllocMem`, `AllocateZeroedMemory` and `AllocateZeroedKernelMemory` still
return zeroed memory, `ReAllocMem` keeps the contents, and objects still
start with zeroed fields (`InitInstance`).

**Quarantine.** Freed blocks wait in a first in, first out queue before
their memory can be reused, so a stale pointer keeps finding `$DF` for a
while, and a write through it is found when the block leaves the queue: its
fill is checked, and a changed byte stops the program (or the system) with
the block, its size, the offset of the first changed byte, what it holds,
and where the block was freed. Freeing a block that is in the quarantine is
a double free. Sizes: the kernel keeps up to 1024 small blocks or 512 KiB
(`Memory.KernelHeapChecks`), a program up to 1024 blocks or 512 KiB
(`rtl/fpc/sysheapquarantine.inc`); blocks over 64 KiB in user mode are
filled and freed at once rather than pushing out everything else.

**User mode** (`rtl/fpc/sysheapcheck.inc` and the include files named in
`system.pp`): a memory manager in front of Free Pascal's heap. Every block
gets a 16-byte header (a state - allocated, quarantined, given back - and
the size asked for) and at least 8 guard bytes. `FreeMem`, `ReAllocMem` and
`MemSize` check the header: a freed block or a pointer that is not a heap
block is reported (with where it was freed before, if it is still in the
quarantine). `MemSize` returns the size asked for. `ReAllocMem` grows a
block in place while it fits and otherwise moves it (keeping room to grow,
so growing step by step stays cheap) - so a pointer kept into the old block
finds the free fill too. The quarantine has its own lock (the word lock of
`systhrd.inc`) and is never held while the heap's lock is taken; blocks
leaving it are checked and freed outside it. A failed check writes a report
to standard error and, when that is not the console, to the console (which
is the kernel log on the serial line), and ends the process at once with
exit status 204 (Free Pascal's "invalid pointer operation"); exit
procedures and finalizers do not run on a damaged heap:

```
heap check in /bin/heaptest (process 3070): memory was written after it was freed
  block:     $0000100000002050, 136 bytes
  offset:    10 holds $00 instead of $DF
  freed at: $00007F00001B425A $0000000000402A92 $0000000000402B79 ...
  found at: $00007F00001C0C73 ...
```

The code addresses come from the frame chain, which user code keeps for
this (`-OoNOSTACKFRAME` in `userland.mk`; it also gives the backtrace after
a runtime error). Program addresses can be looked up with
`addr2line -f -e build/amd64/user/bin/PROGRAM`; library addresses
(`$00007F...`) are relative to the library's load address (libraries are
placed one after another from `$00007F0000000000` in load order, libsystem
first).

A use after free usually needs no report: the program faults at once. The
processor raises a general protection fault, not a page fault, for a
non-canonical address, so the kernel looks at the faulting instruction
(`Kernel.Arch.PrivilegedInstructions`): only a privileged instruction is
reported as one (runtime error 218); anything else is an access violation
(runtime error 216, `EAccessViolation`), like any other bad pointer.

**Kernel** (`Memory.HeapChecks` for the setting, patterns and reports,
`Memory.KernelHeapChecks` for the checks of the kernel heap,
`Memory.HeapQuarantine` for the queue):

- Small blocks (up to 2 KiB) get the full treatment. The header's
  `RequestedBytes` marks where the guard starts. A free block always holds
  `$DF`: pages carved into blocks are filled, freed blocks are filled, and a
  block is checked again when it is handed out, so even a write long after
  the block left the quarantine is found at the next allocation. The
  header's magic tells allocated, quarantined and free blocks apart; freeing
  a quarantined or free block is a double free.
- Large blocks (their own mapped pages) are filled with `$A5` when
  allocated. Their pages are unmapped when they are freed, so a stale
  pointer faults; with the quarantine their address range waits too (up to
  256 ranges, 4 GiB of the 1 TiB dynamic region), so nothing is mapped there
  again soon. They have no guard.
- Reports are panics (`PanicHeapCorruption`) naming the problem, the block,
  its size, the offset and byte found, and the code that freed the block
  (`FreeKernelMemory` keeps a frame to find its return address; look it up
  with `addr2line -f -e build/amd64/kernel.elf`).
- The heap may be used at dispatch level, so the quarantine is a fixed
  table under a spin lock of its own (no memory of its own, no sleeping);
  the heap lock and the quarantine lock are never held together.
- Physical pages (`Memory.PhysicalPages`, `Memory.PageQuarantine`; with
  the quarantine level): a page whose last holder frees it - a page
  table, a DMA buffer, a user page, a kernel stack - is filled with `$F7`
  and held back in a ring of the last 256 freed pages (1 MiB) with the use
  `PageUsageQuarantined`, so freeing it again is a double free. When it
  leaves the ring, just before it can be handed out again, its fill is
  checked: a changed byte stops the system with the page and the offset
  (`physical page written after it was freed`) - a device still writing
  into a buffer its driver gave back, a stale translation. Held back
  pages count as free memory, and when the free list runs dry the oldest
  one is let go early, so the checks never make memory run out.
- Not covered: device mappings. DMA buffers come from the page allocator,
  so filling heap blocks never changes memory a device is using; a device
  that writes into a freed heap block is caught as a write after free.

**Tests.** `heaptest` checks the promises (fills, zeroed memory,
`ReAllocMem`, `MemSize`, threads allocating at once) and makes each mistake
on purpose in a child process: coretest checks that a use after free ends
with runtime error 216 and that a write after free, a double free and a
write past the end end with status 204 and the right report. With the
quarantine on, the kernel self test `Kernel.HeapCheckTest` damages blocks
on purpose and checks that the functions the heap uses before it panics
find the damage at the right offset (then repairs it). The test scripts
fail when the log shows a heap check report from any other program, and
`Kernel.SelfTest`'s heap test empties the quarantine before it counts
pages.

In user programs a quarantined block remembers which thread allocated
it (the header's `Owner`, from the thread's threadvar block address),
and a thread about to end releases its own blocks from the quarantine
before the heap gives up its chunks: otherwise one small block waiting
there keeps a whole heap chunk of an ended thread, and a region, for
every thread a program ever ran (2000 threads left about 470 regions
behind before; now 2).

**Not done:** a page heap (each block on its own pages, end-aligned against
an unmapped guard page, freed pages unmapped). The region tree would hold
a region per block, but first-fit reuse would not keep freed addresses
unused; it needs a reserve / commit / decommit system call first (see
TODO.md).

## Back traces and crash reports

**Kernel back traces.** A panic ends with the chain of calls that led
to it, on the screen, the serial port and the network log (the trace is
ordinary kernel log, so `FlushNetworkLogAtPanic` sends it with the rest):

```
Back trace:
  #0 0xFFFFFFFF800779FB Kernel.PanicTest.PanicTestInnermost+0x3B
  #1 0xFFFFFFFF80077A19 Kernel.PanicTest.PanicTestMiddle+0x9
  #2 0xFFFFFFFF80077A39 Kernel.PanicTest.PanicTestOutermost+0x9
  ...
```

The kernel is compiled with `-OoNOSTACKFRAME` (and its RTL too), so
every routine keeps a frame and the frame pointer chain is complete: on
both processors a frame is the caller's frame pointer with the return
address above it (x86-64: CALL then PUSH RBP; AArch64: STP X29, X30).
`Debug.StackTrace` walks it, trusting nothing: each frame must lie in
the stack being walked (the thread's kernel stack, or up to 32 KiB
above the first frame when there is no thread yet or the frame is
elsewhere - but only as far as the pages there are mapped, so the walk
cannot fault on a guard page while panicking), above the frame before it, with a return address in the
kernel's code; it stops after 32 frames, and at a frame whose saved
frame pointer is 0 (a thread's first routine, which nobody called). A
return address is named by the call before it (address - 1). Where the
trace starts: for a processor exception at the interrupted instruction
and frame (`SetPanicTraceStart` from both architectures' exception
handlers), otherwise at the caller of `BeginKernelPanic`. Each
processor notes its own start (two may fault at once, and only the
first to panic reports), so the trace is always the panicking
processor's - so a failed
`KernelAssert` shows `Kernel.Panic.KernelAssert` and then the code that
asserted.

**The symbol table** comes from the build. The kernel is linked twice:
first with an empty table, then `scripts/make-kernel-symbols.py` reads
that image's code symbols with nm and writes the table as an assembly
file, and the second link puts it at the end of `.rodata`
(`KernelSymbolTable`, about 140 KiB for 4700 routines). The code comes
before the read-only data, so it cannot move between the links, and the
script checks that it did not. The table holds the routines' start
addresses (offsets from the image start, sorted) with their unit's and
their own names, each unit name once; Free Pascal's decorated upper
case names (`KERNEL.PANIC_$$_KERNELASSERT$BOOLEAN$PCHAR`) are written as
in the sources (`Kernel.Panic`, `KernelAssert`), the spelling taken from
the declarations in the kernel's source folders; nested routines are
`Outer.Inner`. `Debug.KernelSymbols` finds an address's routine by a
binary search, without locks or memory, so it works in a panic. The
native AArch64 image keeps the table (it is loaded data, not debug
information). Because compiler options are not part of what Free
Pascal checks to decide whether a unit is up to date, the Makefile
keeps the kernel's options in `build/ARCH/kernel/flags.stamp` and
compiles every unit again when they change.

The same traces are used elsewhere: the hang watch writes each thread's
kernel stack (see "Diagnosing hangs"), and the debug shell's `trace`
command any thread's. For a thread that is not running the walk starts
from the state its last switch saved (`ArchSwitchFramePointers`: the
saved RBP and return address on x86-64, X29 and X30 on AArch64); one
running on another processor is only named, its stack changing under
the walk.

**Testing it:** the kernel option `testpanic` (or `testpanic=fault`)
makes phase 1 fault on purpose three calls deep, `testpanic=assert`
fail an assertion there (`Kernel.PanicTest`); with `netlog` it first
waits for the network log to reach its listener.
`scripts/test-panic-trace.sh ARCH ESP` (`make panic-trace-test`, part
of `make test`; `make ARCH=arm64 panic-trace-test`) boots both and
checks that the trace names the chain in order, in the serial log and
in what `scripts/netlog.py` received.

**User crash reports.** A program's addresses mean something only
together with the module they lie in and where it was loaded, which
will differ between runs once modules load at random addresses. The
kernel keeps each module's load bias and the end of its pages
(`TLoadedModule.Base`, `Limit`) and hands the list to the process with
`CallGetProcessModules` (136, `TAbiModuleInformation`:
Base, Limit, Name). The runtime (`rtl/fpc/syscrash.inc`) replaces Free
Pascal's `BackTraceStrFunc`, so every back trace address - of an
unhandled exception, a runtime error, a heap check report - names its
module and offset, and a process that ends with an error after writing a
back trace lists its modules on the error output as its last words:

```
An unhandled exception occurred at $0000000000407AB6:
EAccessViolation: Access violation
  $0000000000407AB6  coretest+$7AB6
  $00007F0000204E5D  libsystem.so+$1BCE5D

Modules:
  $0000000000400000-$000000000041C000 coretest
  $00007F0000048000-$00007F0000357000 libsystem.so
```

The kernel's own report of a program it ends (no dispatcher, the
dispatcher failed) does the same in the kernel log
(`Processes.LoadedModules`), with the chain of calls that led to the
fault between the first line and the modules (`Processes.UserBackTrace`):

```
[process] coretest (44): page fault at 0x0000000000407AB6 (coretest+0x7AB6) accessing 0x0000000000000000, terminated
[process]   #0 0x0000000000407AB6 coretest+0x7AB6 CORETEST.CRASHONPURPOSE+0x6
[process]   #1 0x0000000000407B9B coretest+0x7B9B main+0xEB
[process]   #2 0x00007F00002F31A6 libsystem.so+0x1AF1A6 SYSTEM.SYSENTRY+0x26
[process]   #3 0x0000000000408C4E coretest+0x8C4E SI_PRC.ENTERPROGRAM+0x9F
[process]   #4 0x0000000000408BAB coretest+0x8BAB SI_PRC.PROGRAMENTRY+0xC
[process]   module coretest at 0x0000000000400000-0x000000000041C000
```

**User back traces.** The kernel walks the program's stack itself, in
the ending thread (passive level, its address space), trusting
nothing: user memory is read only through the copy routines, so a bad
pointer ends the trace rather than faulting; each caller's stack
pointer must lie above its callee's; the walk stops after 32 frames,
at address 0, or at a return address in no module and no executable
region (what lies above the outermost frame, `_start`'s). A frame is unwound by DWARF call frame information
where there is some for its address (`Processes.CallFrameEntries`
finds and decodes the entries, `Processes.CallFrameRules` runs their
programs: the advances, offset, register, same value and undefined
rules, remember and restore state, the CFA definitions; a rule given
as a DWARF expression makes that register unknown, a CFA given by one
ends the walk):

- C code (gcc) has its loaded `.eh_frame`, found through the binary
  search table of the `.eh_frame_hdr` its `PT_GNU_EH_FRAME` names
  (augmentations z, R, P, L, S; pointers absolute, pc- or
  data-relative, of any size);
- Free Pascal writes `.debug_frame` only, which is not loaded: it is
  read from the module's file (the file of the mapped file behind the
  module's image regions, `Processes.ModuleFiles`, which stays open
  even if its name is gone), up to 8 MiB, once per report. Free
  Pascal's internal assembler writes an FDE's CIE pointer there as 8
  bytes instead of 4; an FDE's layout is the one that puts its first
  address inside the module's code. AArch64 Free Pascal code has no
  call frame information at all.

Everything else steps by the frame pointer (the saved one and the
return address at it: every routine of the system's Pascal code keeps
a frame, `-OoNOSTACKFRAME`), which must lie at or above the stack
pointer and be aligned. Call frame information matters where frames
are not complete: C code built without frame pointers, and a fault at
a routine's first instruction or in its epilogue, where the frame
pointer still is the caller's. A return address is looked up by the
call before it (address - 1). The routines are named from the module
file's `.symtab` (one pass over it in chunks for all the trace's
addresses in that module: the function symbol with the highest value
at or below the address that covers it, a sized one before an unsized
one at the same value - main before PASCALMAIN), else from the
dynamic symbols the loader kept (a stripped library's exports), and
written as `scripts/symbolize.py` does (`Processes.SymbolNames`).
Libraries a C program's own dynamic linker maps are not in the
kernel's module list: their frames show the bare address, stepped by
the frame pointer. A program run without read permission (mode 0711)
gets no trace at all ("no back trace: the program may not be read"):
its stack, image and files stay unread (`ProcessImageIsReadable`).
`tools/CallFrameInfoTest` (`make
call-frame-info-test`, part of `make test`) runs the unwinder on the
host over `.eh_frame`, `.eh_frame_hdr` and `.debug_frame` fixtures
`make-cfi-fixtures.py` writes (x86-64 and AArch64, both `.debug_frame`
layouts, hand-made stacks) and checks the names;
`scripts/test-symbolize.py` checks that the kernel's report of
`coretest --crash-without-dispatcher` names CrashOnPurpose, the main
program and the runtime's SysEntry in that order.

`scripts/symbolize.py --report REPORT build/ARCH/user` reads either form
(or a whole serial log, report by report; the kernel's back trace lines
too), takes the bases from the
report, finds each module's file by name under the given folders and
names the routines (addr2line, the names demangled to `UNIT.ROUTINE`);
`symbolize.py PROGRAM LIBRARY_DIRECTORY ADDRESS...` still lays the
modules out at the fixed addresses for an old report.
`scripts/test-symbolize.py`, run by `test-qemu.sh`, symbolizes the
kernel's report of `coretest --crash-without-dispatcher` from the test
run's serial log, and again with every module moved elsewhere in both
report forms; a coretest line checks the runtime's report format.

## Diagnosing hangs

With the kernel option `hangdump=SECONDS`, a system thread
(`Processes.HangWatch`) notes when processes start and end. If neither
happens for that long while user processes exist, it writes every user
thread to the kernel log - process, state, whether it waits on a list or
with a timeout, alertable, suspended, priority, last processor, run time,
where in the program it last entered the kernel (from the register frame
at the top of its kernel stack), the system call it is in and its kernel
stack trace (where in the kernel it waits; see "Back traces and crash
reports") - and what each processor runs, with the routine it was
interrupted in. The tests set `hangdump=20`, so a hung
test run leaves its explanation in the log.

Without the option the same thread still watches endings: a process
that was told to end (killed, crashed, or asked by a request it did
not take) and is still there 10 seconds later is written to the log
once, the same way, under `[ending]` - ending takes no longer than
reaching the next safe point, so such a process is stuck where the
kernel cannot reach it, and the report says where.

## Diagnostics over the network

For a board without a serial cable (the Raspberry Pi: see "Trying it on a
Raspberry Pi 4"), the kernel sends its log over the network, serves its
debug shell over TCP, and keeps a hardware watchdog that resets the board
when the kernel hangs or panics. Kernel options:

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `netlog=HOST[:PORT]`, `netlog=broadcast[:PORT]` | every kernel log line as a UDP datagram to HOST (an IPv4 address) or 255.255.255.255, port 5140 by default |
| `netshell=PORT` | the kernel debug shell on TCP PORT; no authentication, off by default |
| `netaddr=A.B.C.D/PREFIX[,GATEWAY]` | a fixed address (and default route) for the first Ethernet interface |
| `netdhcp=SECONDS` | the kernel's own DHCP client, if no interface has an address that long after networking started; default 30 with netlog or netshell (and no netaddr), 0 off |
| `watchdog=SECONDS` | arm the hardware watchdog (0: never); default on the Pi: 15 s |
| `panicreset=SECONDS` | reset that long after a panic (0: never, and stop the watchdog); default: when the watchdog runs out |

**The log in memory** (`Debug.LogRing`). Everything `Debug.Output` writes
is also gathered into lines, each with a sequence number (from 1 each
boot) and the uptime when it ended; lines longer than 112 characters are
cut (the rest marked as continued). The first 1024 lines of the boot are
kept for good, the later ones go round a ring of 3072 slots (512 KiB in
all, in the kernel's BSS, so it works from the first line, before the
heap). Slots are found from the number, so a reader keeps only the
number it wants next and sees a gap when the ring overtook it. Capturing
only copies into a slot under a spin lock at high level: safe in
interrupt handlers and inside any lock.

**Sending it** (`Network.LogStreaming`). A system thread (`NetworkLog`)
opens a kernel UDP socket and, every 100 ms, checks under the network
lock that the host has a route through an interface with an address
(for broadcast: any interface with one), notes the route a panic would
take (adapter, Ethernet addresses - the next hop's from the ARP cache -
IP addresses and ports), and sends what it has not sent yet: the whole
memory log the first time ("[netlog] sending the kernel log to ... from
line N"), then new lines. While the next hop's Ethernet address is being
asked for (up to 3 s), it sends one line per round, since the ARP entry
holds only a few datagrams; then bursts of 16 with a millisecond between
them. A send that fails (no route now) is tried again later. Writers
never wait on it, so nothing changes for code that logs.

A datagram is one line: `SEQUENCE UPTIME TEXT`, `SEQUENCE+` for a
continued line, the uptime in seconds with six decimals:

    42 3.141592 [network] eth0: configured 192.168.1.50/24

**After a panic** the thread cannot run (interrupts are off, the other
processors stopped). `Kernel.Panic` calls, after the message: the reset
policy's announcement ("The machine resets in 15 seconds"), the flush
routine (`FlushNetworkLogAtPanic`), the panic hook (leaving QEMU under
test), then the reset. The flush sends the unsent lines - at most the
last 200 - through `Network.PanicTransmit`: it builds Ethernet, IPv4 and
UDP headers itself (no UDP checksum) on the route noted beforehand and
calls the driver's `Transmit` at dispatch level with interrupts still
off, waiting up to 50 ms for room per frame (the virtio-net, e1000 and
GENET drivers reclaim finished frames inside `Transmit`). Best effort: if
a stopped processor held the driver's transmit lock, the flush never
returns, and the watchdog resets the board. A panic before any interface
had an address sends nothing.

**An address without user mode** (`Network.FallbackAddress`). The network
service normally configures eth0 by DHCP, but when user mode does not
come up nobody would. With `netaddr` the first Ethernet interface gets
the fixed address as soon as it exists. Otherwise, with netlog or
netshell on and no interface addressed after `netdhcp` seconds, the
kernel runs a minimal DHCP exchange (DISCOVER, OFFER, REQUEST, ACK,
broadcast replies; address, mask, router; a random transaction
identifier; an offered address that cannot be a host's, or a router off
the subnet, is not taken) on the first Ethernet interface with a link, brings it up, sets the address and default route
(`[netaddr] eth0: kernel DHCP lease ...`), and tries again every minute
until some interface has an address. The lease is not renewed: it is a
diagnostic address, and the network service, when it starts, sets its
own lease (setting an address drops the routes through the interface).
If UDP port 68 is taken, the network service's own client is running and
the kernel leaves it to it. The test runs use `netdhcp=0`, since
networktest checks the service's DHCP from an unconfigured interface.

**The listener** (`scripts/netlog.py [--port 5140] [--bind ADDRESS]
[--output FILE]`) prints `SOURCE SEQUENCE UPTIME TEXT` for each datagram
and notes (lines starting with `#`) for the first line from a source, a
reboot (numbers starting again) and a gap; `--output` adds the same lines
to a file.

**The debug shell over TCP** (`Kernel.NetworkShell`). With `netshell=PORT`
a system thread listens on PORT and serves one connection at a time
(`nc BOARD PORT`, or telnet: its option bytes are skipped). Each line is
run by `Kernel.DebugShell` (`RunDebugShellCommand`); while it runs,
everything written to the log is copied (`SetDebugOutputCopy`) into a 64
KiB buffer that is sent afterwards, LF as CR LF - so other log lines
written meanwhile come along. `exit` closes the connection; `poweroff`
and `reboot` do what they say. It has no authentication and no
encryption: only for a trusted local network.

**Hardware watchdogs** (`Io.Watchdog`). A driver registers its watchdog
with routines to arm it for a number of seconds, pet it, stop it and
reset the machine at once; the first one registered is used. At start-up
(`StartWatchdogPolicy`, right after the drivers that find watchdogs) it
is armed if `watchdog=` says so, or by default if the driver asks for it,
and a kernel timer pets it every third of its timeout from a deferred
call - a kernel stuck with interrupts off or at a high level stops
petting it. The panic policy: with `panicreset=N` the panic path waits N
seconds (petting the watchdog, so N may exceed what it can count), then
resets through the HAL (`HalResetMachine`: PSCI SYSTEM_RESET on AArch64,
the keyboard controller and port CF9h on x86-64) and then through the
watchdog; without it an armed watchdog simply runs out (the HAL is tried
two seconds after it should have); `panicreset=0` stops the watchdog so
the message stays. `Io.AcpiSleep.ResetMachine` (reboot) also falls back
to the watchdog. Drivers:

- `Drivers.Bcm2835Watchdog`: the PM block of the BCM2837 and BCM2711 at
  peripheral base + 100000h (FE100000h on the Pi 4): PM_WDOG (24h) holds
  the count in 1/65536 s (20 bits, so at most 15 s), PM_RSTC (1Ch) the
  reset kind (full reset) or 102h to stop, every write with the password
  5Ah in the top byte. The community firmware's ACPI tables describe no
  watchdog, so it is found from the VideoCore mailbox's address (ACPI
  BCM2849, peripheral base + B880h) on a board whose revision word names
  a BCM2837 or BCM2711. Armed by default, for 15 s.
- `Drivers.I6300EsbWatchdog`: the Intel 6300ESB's (PCI 8086:25AB), which
  QEMU emulates (`-device i6300esb`): two stages at about 1 kHz, each
  given half the timeout, written after an unlock sequence; the reset
  output on, no interrupt. Not armed by default.

**Tests.** `scripts/test-qemu.sh` boots with `netlog=10.0.2.2:PORT
netdhcp=0` (QEMU's user networking hands 10.0.2.2 to the host's
loopback) and runs `scripts/netlog.py` on that port: the run fails unless
the first lines arrived (the replay), the `[netlog]` line and lines
written after it, with no reboot seen. It also gives the machine an
`i6300esb`: the kernel self test `Kernel.WatchdogSelfTest` arms it for 4
seconds and sleeps 9 while the timer pets it (a reset would end QEMU,
which runs with `-no-reboot`), and checks the pets were counted. It runs
only under `test-exit` or with the option `watchdogtest` (on a Pi too),
so ordinary boots do not wait for it.

## The kernel debug shell

With the kernel option `kshell`, `Kernel.DebugShell` runs on the console
once the system is up, before the first program: `help`, `echo`, `ls`,
`cat`, `volumes`, `disks`, `ps`, `trace [THREAD]` (the kernel stack
trace of the thread with that id, or of every thread, each named with
its state and process), `mem`, `cache`, `netcards`, `interrupts`,
`devices` (the ACPI platform devices: ids, resources, DMA, driver),
`board` (the Raspberry Pi's model, revision, serial, firmware, clocks
and temperature, from the VideoCore mailbox), `uptime`, `watchdog` (the
hardware watchdog: which, armed, its timeout, how often it was petted),
and `exit` to go on with the boot. With `netshell=PORT` the same commands
are served over TCP (see "Diagnostics over the network"). It reads lines through the console like a program
(with line editing) and writes through the kernel debug output, so it
works on the serial port and the screen. The input test starts with a
few of its commands.

## Coding conventions

- Descriptive names for everything; no abbreviations or clever one-liners.
- One responsibility per unit; small files.
- Interfaces are documented at the top of each unit.
- Loops over unsigned counts use `while` (or `for I := 1 to Count`), never
  `for I := 0 to Count - 1`, which wraps around when `Count` is zero.
- A routine that takes the address of a record parameter declares it
  `constref` or `var`, never `const`, which may pass a copy.
- Assembly is Intel syntax (`{$asmmode intel}`) and limited to small,
  commented routines in architecture specific units.
